en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Commentary on the Basket of Conduct (*Cariyāpiṭaka-aṭṭhakathā*) within the Minor Collection (*Khuddakanikāya*).
I pay homage to that Leader of the World,
the Great Sage, whose conduct is for the welfare of the entire world and whose majesty is inconceivable.
I pay homage to him at the commencement of this work.
I pay homage to that supreme Dhamma, honored by the Fully Enlightened One, by which those endowed with true knowledge and conduct are led out from the world.
To him who is perfected in virtues such as moral discipline and stands firm in the paths and their fruits—
I pay homage to that Noble Saṅgha, the unsurpassed field of merit.
By the power of whatever merit has been generated through this homage to the Triple Gem,
may I be free from obstacles everywhere.
In this auspicious aeon, the perfections beginning with generosity—
which were accumulated through such great hardships and have reached the highest pinnacle—
reveal the majestic power of those practices for the sake of perfect enlightenment.
While dwelling in the Nigrodha Monastery among the Sakyans, the Great Sage—
the Lord of the World, the General of the Dhamma, and the banner of all disciples—
taught what is known as the Cariyāpiṭaka.
That which the great seers, the compilers of the Teacher’s Dhamma, recited in the Khuddakanikāya as an exposition of the perfection of causes—
because it is joined with the method for analyzing the requisites for enlightenment;
Although it is difficult to provide a commentary on the meaning,
I have done so because, together with this commentary, the Teacher’s dispensation endures;
thus the exposition of the ancient master-lions remains established.
Therefore, having relied upon that [text] and having immersed myself completely in it,
I have followed the method of the ancient commentaries based on the Jātakas—
a path of recitation that is well-purified and unconfused.
I shall provide a commentary on the meaning of the Cariyāpiṭaka,
which elucidates the perfections (pāramī) through the distinctions between the definitive and interpretable meanings,
and which offers a precise determination of the meaning for the residents of the Mahāvihāra.
"Thus, for the sake of the long endurance of the True Dhamma, listen well, O virtuous ones, as I analyze its meaning for one who so desires.
In that regard, in what sense is it the *Cariyāpiṭaka*? Because it reveals the power of the Teacher’s conduct throughout his past births.
It is called "Pariyatti" (the teaching) because this word *piṭaka* has the sense of "teaching," as in such passages as "not by the acquisition of the Piṭakas.

Alternatively, it is called the "Cariyāpiṭaka" (Basket of Conduct) because that teaching serves as a vessel for the manifestation of the power of the deeds performed by that very Teacher in his previous births; for the word *piṭaka* is also explained in the sense of a "vessel."
It is as in such passages as: “Then a man might come along, taking a spade and a basket.
Furthermore, this *Cariyāpiṭaka* is included within the *Suttanta Piṭaka* among the three *Piṭakas*: the *Vinaya Piṭaka*, the *Suttanta Piṭaka*, and the *Abhidhamma Piṭaka*.
Within the five *Nikāyas*—the *Dīgha Nikāya*, the *Majjhima Nikāya*, the *Saṃyutta Nikāya*, the *Aṅguttara Nikāya*, and the *Khuddaka Nikāya*—it belongs to the *Khuddaka Nikāya*.

Among the Nikāyas, it is included in the Khuddakanikāya. Among the nine branches of the teaching (sāsanaṅga)—Sutta, Geyya, Veyyākaraṇa, Gāthā, Udāna, Itivuttaka, Jātaka, Abbhutadhamma, and Vedalla—it is comprised within the Gāthā branch.
“I received eighty-two [verses] from the Buddha, and two thousand from the Bhikkhus.”
“Eighty-four thousand sections of Dhamma that have been proclaimed by me.

Thus, regarding the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dhamma acknowledged by the Dhamma-treasurer (the Buddha), this is a compendium of certain aggregates of Dhamma. By way of chapters (*vagga*), it comprises a compendium of three chapters:
the Akitti-vagga, the Hatthināga-vagga, and the Yudhañjaya-vagga. By way of conduct (*cariyā*)...
There are ten in the Akitti chapter, ten in the Hatthināga chapter, and fifteen in the Yudhañjaya chapter, making a total of thirty-five deeds.
Among the three chapters, the Akitti chapter is the first; among the deeds, the Akitti deed is the first.
Regarding that as well: “In a hundred thousand aeons and four incalculable aeons...”
"Whatever conduct was practiced during this interval, all that ripens the Bodhi"—this verse is the beginning.
From here onwards, there follows a gradual commentary on the meaning.
The introductory discourse on the commencement of the book is finished.
As for this commentary on the meaning (*atthasaṃvaṇṇanā*), since it is spoken after showing these three origins— the distant origin, the not-distant origin,
and the proximate origin— it is well understood by those who hear it, starting from its full accomplishment (*samudāgama*).
Therefore, this classification of those causes should be understood.

From the moment the Great Bodhisatta, having made his resolution at the feet of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara, was reborn in the Tuṣita heaven, the course of narration that ensued is called the "distant cause" (dūrenidāna). From the Tuṣita heaven onwards...
The attainment of omniscient knowledge at the seat of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), and the course of discourse proceeding up to that point, is called the "remote cause" (*dūrenidāna*).
However, the course of discourse proceeding from the great seat of enlightenment down to the present subject matter is called the "proximate cause" (*santikenidāna*).
Among these three causes, since the remote and proximate causes are common to all [Buddhas], they [are not specifically detailed].
These matters should be understood in detail according to the method already explained in the *Jātakaṭṭhakathā*.
However, there is a distinction regarding the proximate cause (*santikenidāna*); therefore, this is a concise account of all three causes from the beginning.
At the feet of the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara, the Protector of the World, while existing as a Bodhisatta, made a resolution (*abhinīhāra*) in accordance with his own aspiration.
Having fulfilled the thirty perfections and brought the equipment for omniscient knowledge to its ultimate peak, he was reborn in the Tusita heaven,
awaiting the time of his manifestation as a Buddha. Remaining there for the duration of his lifespan,
he passed away from that state and took rebirth in the royal family of the Sakyans, growing with boundless excellence and great majesty and splendor.
Having gradually reached youth and at the age of twenty-nine, he made the Great Renunciation;
after exerting himself in the Great Struggle for six years, on the full moon day of Vesākha, while sitting at the foot of the Bodhi tree before the sun had even set, he shattered the host of Māra.
In the first watch of the night, he recollected his previous births, and in the middle watch, he [attained] the divine eye.
Having purified himself and exhausted one thousand five hundred defilements during the final watch of the night, he awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.
Then, having spent seven weeks right there, on the full moon day of Āsāḷha, he went to Bārāṇasī and, at the Deer Park in Isipatana,
set in motion the Wheel of Dhamma while administering the nectar of the Dhamma to eighteen koṭis of Brahmās, headed by Aññā Koṇḍañña.
Having set [the wheel of Dhamma] in motion, and having established Yasa and others among those to be trained in Arhatship, he dispatched all sixty of them as Arhats for the benefit of the world.
Then, while proceeding toward Uruvelā, he established the thirty members of the Bhaddavaggiya group in the fruits of stream-entry and the other stages within the Kappāsika grove.
Having reached Uruvelā and displayed one thousand four hundred miracles, he [established] Uruvelakassapa and the others...
Having guided the three brothers who were matted-hair ascetics, along with their retinue of a thousand, and being surrounded by them,
he sat in the Laṭṭhivana grove on the outskirts of the city of Rājagaha; there, having established twelve hundred thousand brahmins and householders, headed by Bimbisāra, in the Teaching,
he dwelt in the Veḷuvana monastery built by the King of Magadha.
While the Blessed One was thus dwelling in the Bamboo Grove, after Sāriputta and Moggallāna had been established in the position of chief disciples and an assembly of followers had gathered,
King Mahāsuddhodana heard: "My son, it is said, having practiced austerities for six years and attained supreme perfect enlightenment,
has set in motion the sublime Wheel of Dhamma and is staying near Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove."
Having heard that [the Buddha] was dwelling there, he dispatched ten ministers in succession, each accompanied by a retinue of ten thousand men, with the instruction:

"Bring my son here and show him to me. When they had gone to Rājagaha and established themselves in Arahatship through the Teacher’s teaching of the Dhamma, and when the Elder Kāḷudāyin had informed the King of his intention, the Blessed One, surrounded by twenty thousand who had destroyed the taints, departed from Rājagaha.
Having departed, he reached Kapilavatthu, sixty *yojanas* away, in two months.
The Śākya kings, thinking, “We shall see our most excellent kinsman,” assembled and had the Nigrodha Monastery prepared as a suitable dwelling for the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of monks;
then, with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings in their hands, they went out to meet the Teacher and [brought him] to the Nigrodha Monastery.
They led him inside. There, the Blessed One sat upon the excellent Buddha-seat that had been prepared, surrounded by twenty thousand *khīṇāsavas*.
The Sākiyas, stubborn in their pride, did not prostrate themselves before the Teacher.

The Blessed One, observing their disposition and intending to break their pride and make them fit vessels for the teaching of the Dhamma, attained the fourth jhāna as a basis for direct knowledge (*abhiññā*).
Rising up and soaring into the sky, as if scattering the dust from his feet upon their heads, he performed the Twin Miracle, similar to the miracle performed at the foot of the Kaṇḍamba tree.
When the King beheld that marvel, he prostrated himself, thinking, "This is the foremost person in the world.
But once the King had paid homage, they were unable to remain standing; all the Sākiyas likewise prostrated themselves.
At that time, it is said, while performing the Twin Miracle, the Blessed One also performed the miracle of revealing the world:
while this was taking place, people in the human world— just as they stood or sat—
saw all the devas from the realm of the Four Great Kings up to the Akaniṭṭha heaven, sporting in their respective abodes there by means of their divine power.
Experiencing great divine success while shining, experiencing the peaceful bliss of meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), and discussing the Dhamma with one another,
they see [all this] with their own fleshly eyes through the power of the Buddha. Likewise, they see [beings] down below in the earth,
in the eight great hells, the sixteen secondary hells (*ussada-niraya*), and the hell between the worlds (*lokantara-niraya*)— in each of those places.

They see beings experiencing great suffering. In the ten-thousandfold world system, the gods, approaching the Tathāgata with the great majesty of their divine power, having conceived a sense of wonder and amazement, wait upon him with palms joined in reverence;
reciting verses connected with the qualities of the Buddha, they praise him, clap their hands, laugh, and experience joy and gladness.
They proclaim it. It is with reference to this that it was said:

"The earth-dwelling deities, the Mahārājikas, the Tāvatiṃsas, the Yāma gods, the Tusita gods, the Nimmānarati gods, those who are Paranimmitavasavatti, and the Brahmakāyika gods—all rejoicing, raised a vast cry."
For at that time, the One of Ten Powers, incited by great compassion with the thought,

"I shall demonstrate my own incomparable Buddha-power," fashioned a walking-path in the sky where ten thousand world-systems converged; standing upon that walking-path made of all kinds of jewels and twelve yojanas wide,
he displayed that wonder— unshared by any other— which became a single gathering point for the eyes of gods, humans, and birds, as previously described.

Having displayed a miracle that illuminated the power of the Buddhas’ concentration and knowledge, he again walked back and forth on that same walkway, teaching the Dhamma with the peerless grace of a Buddha and inconceivable majesty, in accordance with the inclinations of those to be trained. Thus it is said:
“Neither gods nor humans know this: what kind of person is this supreme among men, the Buddha?”
“What is the power of psychic potency like? What is the power of wisdom like? What is the power of a Buddha like, for the benefit of the world?
“Neither gods nor humans know these things: that this Buddha is such a supreme among men;
that his power of psychic potency is such, his power of wisdom is such, and the power of a Buddha for the benefit of the world is such.”
“Come now, I shall display the unsurpassed power of a Buddha;
I will construct a walkway in the sky adorned with jewels.
Having thus displayed this miracle demonstrating his own Buddha-power while the Tathāgata was teaching the Dhamma, the Venerable...
The Dhamma-Senāpati Sāriputta, standing on Vulture Peak Mountain at Rājagaha, saw with his divine eye;

and through that manifestation of the Buddha’s power, a sense of wonder and amazement arose in him. Thinking, "Well now, I shall make the Buddha’s power even more manifest to the world," he formed this reflection and addressed those who were his own followers:
Having reported that matter to the five hundred bhikkhus, he returned through the air by means of his psychic power in that very moment.

Accompanied by his retinue, he approached the Blessed One, paid homage with the five-fold prostration, and raising his joined palms—resplendent with ten fingers pressed together—to his head, he inquired of the Tathāgata regarding his great resolve and the fulfillment of the perfections. The Blessed One [replied] to him...

Having made himself a body-witness (kāyasakkhi), he taught the *Buddhavaṃsa* while manifesting his own Buddha-power to the people assembled there as well as to the ten thousand world-systems of devas and brahmās. Therefore it is said:
"Sāriputta, of great wisdom, skilled in concentration and jhāna..."
Having reached perfection in wisdom, he asks the Leader of the World:
“Of what kind was your resolve, O Great Hero, supreme among men?
At what time, O Wise One, was the supreme enlightenment aspired to by you?”
“What is giving and virtue, and what is renunciation? What are wisdom and energy?
What are patience, truthfulness, and resolve? And what are loving-kindness and equanimity?
O Wise One, Leader of the World, what are these ten perfections like in you?”
“How is the perfection of rebirth fulfilled? How is the ultimate perfection fulfilled?
Being thus questioned, he whose voice was as sweet as the karavīka bird answered, quenching the hearts [of beings] and gladdening the world with its devas.
When the Blessed One had thus taught the lineage of the Buddhas, the Venerable Dhammasenāpati exclaimed: "Oh, the perfection of causes of the Buddhas!

Oh, the excellence of their realization! Oh, the success of their great resolve! Indeed, difficult was that which was performed by the Blessed One while fulfilling the perfections for so long; it is truly worthy of such an accumulation of the requisites for enlightenment."
“This is the fruit, namely: omniscience, mastery over the powers, such great majesty, and such great power.

Thus he directed his knowledge toward the qualities of the Buddha as its object. He [perceived] the Blessed One’s virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, the knowledge and vision of liberation, moral shame, moral dread, faith, energy, mindfulness, clear comprehension, and the purification of virtue—qualities not shared by others.
Purification of view; serenity and insight; the three roots of the wholesome; the three types of good conduct; the three right thoughts;
the three blameless perceptions; the three elements; the four foundations of mindfulness; the four right efforts; the four bases of psychic power;
the four noble paths; the four noble fruits; the four analytical knowledges; and the knowledge that delimits the four modes of birth.
The four noble lineages, the four grounds of self-confidence, the five factors of striving, right concentration with its five factors,
the five faculties, the five powers, the five elements of escape, the five kinds of knowledge regarding the bases of liberation,
the five qualities that ripen liberation, the six qualities conducive to amity, the six subjects of recollection, and the six respects.
The six elements of escape, the six constant abidings, the six unsurpassed states, the six perceptions partaking of penetration,
the six direct knowledges, the six unique knowledges, the seven factors of non-decline, the seven noble treasures, the seven factors of enlightenment, the seven qualities of a true person,
the seven grounds for praise, the seven perceptions, and the teaching on the seven persons worthy of offerings.

The teaching on the seven powers of one whose taints are exhausted; the teaching on the eight causes for the acquisition of wisdom; the eight rightnesses; the eight transcendences of worldly conditions;
the eight bases for exertion; the teaching on the eight inopportune moments; the eight thoughts of a great person; the teaching on the eight bases of mastery;
the eight liberations; the nine states rooted in wise attention; the nine factors of striving for purification; the nine...
The nine abodes of beings, the nine teachings on the removal of malice, the nine kinds of wisdom, the nine teachings on diversity,
the nine successive dwellings, the ten qualities that provide protection, the ten bases of totality, the ten courses of wholesome action,
the ten rightnesses, the ten noble abodes, the ten qualities of one beyond training, the ten jewels, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, and the eleven benefits of loving-kindness.
The twelve modes of the Wheel of Dhamma, the thirteen qualities of ascetic practice (*dhutaṅga*), the fourteen knowledges of a Buddha, the fifteen states that ripen liberation,
the sixteenfold mindfulness of breathing, the sixteen successive states, the eighteen qualities of a Buddha,
the nineteen knowledges of review, the forty-four bases of knowledge, and the fifty knowledges of rise and fall.
The fifty-one wholesome states (*kusaladhamma*), the seventy-seven bases of knowledge (*ñāṇavatthu*), the great diamond-like knowledge that traverses twenty-four million meditative attainments,

the knowledges of the infinite methods of the *Paṭṭhāna*— its analysis, review, and teaching— and likewise the knowledges that discern the inclinations and other traits of infinite beings throughout infinite world-systems: such are the inconceivable powers of the Buddha’s qualities.
Following and recollecting them according to the sequence of the Dhamma, he saw neither their end nor their measure.
For even when the Elder himself, reflecting upon his own virtues, could not see their end or measure, how could he see the measure of the Blessed One’s virtues?
Indeed, whoever possesses great wisdom and clear knowledge perceives the Buddha’s virtues as vast.
He has faith; thus the Elder, seeing neither the measure nor the limit of the Blessed One’s qualities, thought:
"Even for one like me, established in the knowledge of the perfection of a disciple, it is not possible to delimit the Buddha's qualities by means of knowledge, let alone for others.
Oh, how inconceivable, of immeasurable variety, and of great power are the qualities of the Omniscient One! Yet these..."
He reached the conclusion: "They are entirely within the range of the knowledge of a single Buddha alone, and not that of others.
Furthermore, even by the Perfectly Enlightened Ones themselves, it would be impossible to describe them in detail. For this has been said:
"Even a Buddha, were he to speak the praise of another Buddha for an entire eon, without speaking of anything else..."
“An eon might pass away in the course of its vast duration, yet the praise of the Tathāgata would never be exhausted.
Thus, supported by the greatness of the Buddhas’ qualities, he felt a powerful surge of joy and gladness and further reflected:
“How truly majestic are the perfections (*pāramitā*), those qualities that serve as the cause for such Buddha-qualities and constitute the very making of a Buddha! Which ones?”
"Have the perfections been brought to fulfillment throughout my births? Or how have they reached maturity?
Come, by asking about this matter, starting from the very beginning, I shall make the majesty of the Buddha even more manifest to this world with its devas.
Having reflected thus, he asked the Blessed One this question: "In which [births]..."
“Venerable sir, in which births were these qualities that produce a Buddha brought to maturity, and how did they reach such maturity?
Then the Blessed One, seated upon that jewel-walkway with his legs folded in the triple-jointed cross-legged posture, shining like the rising sun upon Mount Yugandhara, said:
“Sāriputta, my qualities that produce a Buddha, from their initial undertaking...”
"From that time on, through continuous and careful practice and by the support of energy, they remained ripening from existence to existence and birth to birth throughout all aeons;
however, in this auspicious aeon, in these births, they have become fully ripened.
Thus, in order to demonstrate this, he spoke the *Cariyāpiṭaka* and the *Buddhāpadāniya* with the words beginning "In a hundred thousand aeons... and so forth.

He spoke the second discourse on the Dhamma. Others, however, say: "While walking on the Jewel Walkway, being honored by gods, Brahmas, and others, the Blessed One—the god beyond gods—descended into the Nigrodha Monastery.

Seated upon the excellent Buddha-seat prepared for him and surrounded by twenty thousand arahants whose taints were exhausted, the Blessed One, when questioned by the Venerable Sāriputta in the manner already described, taught the Cariyāpiṭaka."
Thus they say. Having thus briefly shown the distant and proximate origins (*nidāna*), it should be understood that the proximate origin of the *Cariyāpiṭaka* has been explained in detail.
As for the distant origin, however, it will be made clear in the exposition of the incalculable eons (*asaṅkhyeyya*). 1.

Now follows the commentary on the meaning of the text of the *Cariyāpiṭaka*, which proceeds according to the method beginning with the words: "In a hundred thousand aeons... (*kappe ca satasahasse*) and so forth.
It exists. In this context, the word *kappa*—whether with or without prefixes—is seen in reference to:

thought (*vitakka*), classification (*vidhāna*), resemblance (*paṭibhāga*), designation (*paññatti*), time (*kāla*), lifespan (*paramāyu*), the terminology of ascetics (*samaṇavohāra*), all-encompassing state (*samantabhāva*), conviction (*abhisaddahana*), cutting (*chedana*), application (*viniyoga*), discipline (*vinaya*), action (*kiriyā*), a boundary (*lesa*), an intermediate eon (*antarakappa*), craving (*taṇhā*), views (*diṭṭhi*), incalculable eons (*asaṅkhyeyyakappa*), great eons (*mahākappa*), and so forth.

For instance, it occurs in reference to "thought" (*vitakka*) in such passages as "the thought of renunciation (*nekkhamma-saṅkappa*), the thought of non-malice (*abyāpāda-saṅkappa*)," and so on. [In the passage] "regarding robes... [it refers to]...
In such passages as "he would fall into a conceptualization," it refers to a method; the meaning is that he would fall into an excessive method.
In such passages as "Indeed, sir, while consulting with a disciple who is like the Teacher, we did not know," it refers to a resemblance.
For here the meaning is "one who resembles the Teacher. In such passages as "Here, venerable sir, there is a kappa," it refers to a designation. [And] "by which, indeed, for the whole kappa..."

In such passages as “I dwell,” it refers to time. In such passages as “If he so desires, Ānanda, the Tathāgata might remain for an eon or for the remainder of an eon,” it refers to the maximum lifespan; for here, “eon” (kappa) is intended in the sense of a lifespan.

In such passages as “Monks, I allow you to consume fruit according to the five monastic conventions” (samaṇakappa), it refers to monastic usage. [And] “the entire Jeta Grove” (kevalakappaṃ jetavanaṃ)...
In such passages as “having illumined,” it means pervasiveness. In such passages as “faith, believing, conviction, serene confidence,” it means to believe;

the sense is that they have faith. In such passages as “adorned, with hair and beard trimmed,” it means cutting. In such passages as “even so what is given here benefits the departed,” it means application.
In such passages as “what is made allowable by what is not made allowable becomes interwoven,” it means... [the text continues].
In the context of formal disciplinary acts (*vinayakiriyā*): [as in] “There is the opportunity (*kappa*) to lie down; come now, let me lie down,” and so forth, it refers to a brief moment.

In [passages such as] “One who causes a schism in the Saṅgha is bound for a state of loss, destined for hell, remaining there for an eon (*kappa*)... he shall boil in hell for an eon,” it refers to an intermediate eon (*antarakappa*).
[And in the verse: “They do not construct [fancies], they do not hold [them] foremost; even the teachings are not accepted by them.”
"A brahmin is not to be led by virtue alone; one who has reached the further shore does not return, such a one.
In such passages, this refers to craving and views. For it is said in the *Niddesa*: "Eons (*kappa*): in brief, there are two eons—the eon of craving and the eon of views.
And in passages such as "through many eons of contraction (*saṃvaṭṭa-kappa*) and many eons of expansion (*vivaṭṭa-kappa*)," it refers to incalculable eons (*asaṅkhyeyya-kappa*).
“In these four, monks, are the incalculable aeons of an eon,” and so forth—these refer to *mahākappas* (great aeons). Here too, it should be understood as referring specifically to *mahākappas*.
Regarding the derivation of the term: it is called a *kappa* because it is reckoned (*kappīyati*).
It is reckoned by way of years as being "this many years," or "this many hundreds of years," or "this many thousands of years," or "this many hundreds of thousands of years."
The meaning is that because it is impossible to count, its measure can only be conceived and estimated through similes such as the heap of mustard seeds.
For this has been said:
"How long, venerable sir, is an aeon (kappa)? Long, bhikkhu, is an aeon; it is not easy to calculate."
“‘So many years,’ or ‘so many hundreds of years,’ or ‘so many thousands of years,’ or ‘so many hundreds of thousands of years.
But, Bhante, is it possible to provide a simile? “It is possible, bhikkhus,” the Blessed One said.
“Suppose, bhikkhu, there were a cube one yojana in length, one yojana in width, and one yojana in height.”

"A great heap of mustard seeds. If, at the end of every hundred years and every thousand years, one were to remove a single mustard seed from it, that great heap of mustard seeds, monk, would more quickly reach exhaustion and depletion by this method than an eon. So long, monk, is an eon."
This great eon (*mahākappa*) comprises four incalculable eons (*asaṅkhyeyyakappa*) by way of the periods of dissolution and so forth.

And this has been said: “Monks, there are these four incalculables of an eon. Which four? The period of dissolution (*saṃvaṭṭa*), the period of the persistence of dissolution (*saṃvaṭṭaṭṭhāyī*), the period of evolution (*vivaṭṭa*), and the period of the persistence of evolution (*vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyī*).

In that regard, there are three types of dissolution: dissolution by fire (*tejosaṃvaṭṭa*), dissolution by water (*āposaṃvaṭṭa*), and dissolution by wind (*vāyosaṃvaṭṭa*). There are three boundaries of dissolution (*saṃvaṭṭasīmā*).
—the Ābhassara, Subhakiṇha, and Vehapphala [heavens]. For when the eon dissolves by means of fire, everything below the Ābhassara realm is consumed by flames.
When it dissolves by means of water, everything below the Subhakiṇha realm is dissolved by water.

When it dissolves by means of wind, everything below the Vehapphala realm is scattered away by the wind. As for its extent, however, it is a hundred thousand times ten million world-systems (*cakkavāḷa*).

It perishes—that which is called the field of the Buddhas' authority. Among those three types of dissolution, from the great cloud that destroys the aeon until the cessation of the flames, or the water, or the wind, respectively, this is one incalculable period known as *saṃvaṭṭa* (dissolution).
From the cessation of the flames and so forth that destroy the aeon until [the destruction] fills a hundred thousand million world-systems...
The great cloud of prosperity arises; this is the second incalculable eon called the period of dissolution and stabilization (*saṃvaṭṭaṭṭhāyī*).
From the great cloud of prosperity until the manifestation of the moon and sun, this is the third incalculable eon called the period of evolution (*vivaṭṭo*).
From the manifestation of the moon and sun until the great cloud that destroys the world-system once again, this is the fourth incalculable eon.

The period of the world’s expansion and its duration (vivaṭṭaṭṭhāyī) is called the "expansion-and-duration. Within these sixty-four intermediate aeons (antarakappa), the expansion-and-duration is comprised.

The periods of expansion and so forth should be understood as having the same temporal limits as that. Some say it is comprised of twenty intermediate aeons. Thus, these four incalculables (asaṅkhyeyya) constitute one great aeon (mahākappa). Therefore it was said: "This great aeon comprises four incalculable aeons by way of the contraction [of the world] and so forth."

And the plural form of the instrumental case is employed here by way of absolute connection (*accantasamyoga*). In the term *satasahasse*, this masculine designation is due to its connection with the word *kappa*;
here too, the plural is used precisely by way of absolute connection. For these two words are in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*).
The same principle applies here as well in the phrase "four incalculables" (*caturo asaṅkhyeyye*); however, in the question "of what [period] are they incalculable? it refers to something else.
Because the *kappa* (aeon) is mentioned and because it is mentioned within the treatise (*pakaraṇa*), this meaning is indeed understood: "of the *kappas*.
For it is not logical to include anything that has not been mentioned by omitting what was stated. The word *ca* (and) has the sense of conjunction; its meaning here is:
"four *asaṅkhyeyyas* and a hundred thousand *mahākappas* of *mahākappas*. Regarding the term *asaṅkhiya*: [the following applies] here...
They cannot be calculated, thus they are "incalculable" (*asaṅkhiyā*); the meaning is that they have transcended counting.

Some say, "The 'incalculable' (*asaṅkhyeyya*) is a specific numerical category. For they claim that, having omitted fifty-nine positions starting from one and ending with the "great power of ten thousand" (*mahābalakkha*), ten "great powers of ten thousand" are called "incalculable," which is the sixtieth position. That is not correct, because it is a position following a number.

A "name" (*nāma*) is a specific type of calculation; since it lacks the state of being incalculable (*asaṅkhyeyya*), it is contradictory to say that one numerical position is both "incalculable" and [a name].
But surely, even if it is incalculable by virtue of its being beyond number, its fourfold division would not be logical?
It is not illogical, because the state of being incalculable is intended in respect to four positions. In this regard, first: [The text continues with the explanation of the four stages.]
The Analysis Beginning from [the Past]:
It is said that in a past eon, four Perfectly Enlightened Ones—Taṇhaṅkara, Medhaṅkara, Saraṇaṅkara, and Dīpaṅkara—appeared in the world in succession.
Among them, during the time of the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara, there was a city named Amaravatī.

There lived a brahmin named Sumedha, well-born on both sides, from his mother’s side and his father’s side, of pure descent as far back as the seventh generation, unblemished and irreproachable by birth;
he was handsome, pleasing to behold, gracious, and endowed with the highest excellence of complexion. Without performing any other work, he...
He mastered the very craft of a brahmin. While he was still in his childhood, his parents passed away.
Then the treasurer-minister brought forth the register of wealth, opened the inner chamber filled with gold, silver, gems, pearls, and so forth, and said:
"This much, prince, is your mother’s inheritance; this much is your father’s inheritance; and this much is your grandfather’s and great-grandfather’s."
Having enumerated the wealth down to the seventh generation of his family, he said, "Take possession of this wealth.
The wise Sumedha thought: "My parents and others, having accumulated such vast wealth, have departed for the next world without taking even a single kahāpaṇa with them;
it is fitting that I take some and make provision for my journey."
Having thus informed the king, he had a drum beaten throughout the city, gave alms to the great multitude,

and went to the Himalayan region. There, having gone forth into the ascetic life of a forest-dweller, he attained within seven days alone the eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) and the five higher knowledges (*abhiññā*),
and dwelt in the states of those attainments.

At that time, the Ten-Powered One Dīpaṅkara, having attained supreme perfect enlightenment and set in motion the excellent Wheel of Dhamma, was traveling by stages on a journey surrounded by four hundred thousand who had destroyed the taints.
Upon reaching the city named Rammavatī, he stayed in the great monastery called Sudassana, not far from that city. The inhabitants of the city of Rammavatī [heard]: "The Teacher..."
Having heard that he was staying at the Sudassana Mahāvihāra after arriving in our city, they approached the Teacher with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings in their hands.
After paying homage, worshipping him with perfumes, garlands, and the like, and sitting to one side, they listened to his teaching of the Dhamma.
Having invited him for the following day’s meal, they rose from their seats and departed. On the next day, they prepared a great almsgiving.
Having adorned the city, they cleansed the path for the arrival of the One Possessing the Ten Powers, joyful and elated.
At that time, the ascetic Sumedha, traveling through the air, saw those people who were joyful and elated and asked, "Ho there!
For whom are you clearing this road? They replied, "For the road of the arrival of the Fully Enlightened One."
When it was said, "Cleanse it," he—having heard the word "Buddha" and having experienced joy and gladness because of the service he had rendered to past Buddhas—immediately descended from the sky.
Saying, "Give me a place as well; I too shall cleanse it," he entered the space shown by them, thinking:
"Although I am indeed capable of making this place adorned with the seven treasures through my supernormal power (iddhi), today..."
Thinking, "However, it is fitting for me to perform bodily service;
I shall acquire merit that is worthy of the body," he cleared away grass, rubbish, and the like, brought earth, and leveled it as he cleaned the site.
Even before the cleaning of that place was finished, the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara [appeared] with the six great powers, the six supernormal knowledges, and the destruction of the taints.
Surrounded by four hundred thousand followers, he set out on that path. Thinking,
"Let neither the Perfectly Enlightened One nor his disciples tread upon the mud," the wise Sumedha spread out his own bark garment, his piece of hide, and his mass of matted hair,
and lying down face downwards with his head toward where the Blessed One was, he thought thus:
“If I so desire, having become a disciple of this Blessed One, I could destroy the defilements this very day.
But what is the use of my crossing over the great flood of *saṃsāra* all alone?

What if I too were to become such a Perfectly Enlightened One and ferry across the world with its devas from the great ocean of *saṃsāra*? Thus, by means of the Great Resolve endowed with eight factors...

He made a mental aspiration. Then the Blessed One arrived, stood at his head, and having understood the movement of his mind and the fact that his aspiration would be fulfilled, prophesied all this regarding the Blessed One’s future:

"After four incalculable eons plus one hundred thousand kappas from now, he will become a perfectly enlightened Buddha named Gotama. Having thus explained this entire matter, the Blessed One departed.

Then, beginning with the Blessed One Koṇḍañña and continuing in succession until the end of the time of Kassapa the Great Seer, other Perfectly Enlightened Ones also prophesied of the Great Being, saying, "He will become a Buddha.
Thus, while our Bodhisattva was fulfilling the perfections, twenty-four Perfectly Enlightened Ones appeared. However, in the eon in which the Great Seer Dīpaṅkara appeared—
When [the Buddha] appeared, there were three other Buddhas as well during that same eon. Since there was no prophecy concerning the Bodhisatta in their presence, they are not included here.
However, in the ancient commentary (*porāṇa-aṭṭhakathā*), this was stated in order to show all the Buddhas starting from that eon:
“Taṇhaṅkara, Medhaṅkara, and also Saraṇaṅkara;
the Sambuddha Dīpaṅkara, and Koṇḍañña, supreme among bipeds.
Maṅgala, Sumana, Revata, Sobhita, and the Muni.”
Anomadassi, Paduma, Nārada, Padumuttara;
Sumedha, Sujāta, Piyadassi of great renown;
Atthadassi, Dhammadassi, Siddhattha, the Leader of the World.
“Tiṣya, Puṣya, and the Sambuddha Vipassī, Śikhin, and Vessabhū;
Kakusandha, Koṇāgamana, and Kassapa the Leader—
these were the Sambuddhas, free from passion and composed in mind.”
"Like the sun arisen, dispelling the great darkness;
like masses of fire that have blazed forth, they have attained parinibbāna together with their disciples.
In this context, between the time of the Ten-Powered One Dīpaṅkara and the Ten-Powered One Koṇḍañña, there is one incalculable aeon (*asaṅkhyeya-kappa*).
The world was empty of Buddhas during the interval between the Blessed One Koṇḍañña and the Blessed One Maṅgala;
likewise during the interval between the Blessed One Sobhita and the Blessed One Anomadassi;
and likewise during the interval between the Blessed One Nārada and the Blessed One Padumuttara. For this is said in the *Buddhavamsa*:
“Between the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara and the Teacher Koṇḍañña,
there were aeons beyond counting.
After Koṇḍañña, the Leader named Maṅgala appeared.”
The eons between them were also incalculable by number.
After Sobhita, there was the one of great renown, Anomadassi;
the eons between them were also incalculable by number.
“Between the Blessed One Nārada and the Teacher Padumuttara,
the eons [that passed] were incalculable by way of number.
Thus, although they are called "incalculable" (asaṅkhyeyya) because they transcend calculation, it is because the great eons (mahākappa) exceed all counting in four specific instances.
It should be understood that when it is said, “and four incalculable [aeons],” this does not refer to a specific numerical distinction.
For between the Dasabala Padumuttara and the Dasabala Sumedha there were thirty thousand aeons;
and between the Dasabala Sujāta and the Dasabala Piyadassī there were sixty-eight thousand eight hundred and eighty-two aeons.
Between the Ten-Powered One Dhammadassi and the Ten-Powered One Siddhattha there were twenty *kappas*;
between the Ten-Powered One Siddhattha and the Ten-Powered One Tissa there was one *kappa*; between the Blessed One Vipassi and the Blessed One Sikhin there were sixty *kappas*;
and between the Blessed One Vessabhu and the Blessed One Kakusandha [there were forty *kappas*].

"Thirty aeons": this refers to the hundred thousand great aeons (*mahākappa*) beginning from the aeon in which the Ten-Powered One Padumuttara appeared, including the aeons in which various other Buddhas appeared, as well as this present Bhaddakappa.
It is with reference to these that it is said, "and a hundred thousand aeons. However, if this matter were to be explained in detail, all...
Thinking that it ought to be expounded by bringing forth the *Buddhavaṃsa-pāḷi*, we did not elaborate [here], out of regard for the minds of the general public who fear excessive prolixity.
Those who desire [the details] should take them from the *Buddhavaṃsa*.

Furthermore, whatever method of exposition might be mentioned here, that may be found in the *Aṭṭhasālinī* (Commentary on the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*), the commentary on the *Dhammasaṅgaṇī*, and the *Jātakaṭṭhakathā*.
And this should be understood in the manner already stated.
Regarding the phrase "in this interval" (*etthantare*):
here, the word *antara* [is used] as in the verse: "On riverbanks, in dwellings, in assembly halls, and on carriage roads..."
In such passages as, “People gather and deliberate; what is the difference between me and them?,” it occurs in the sense of a cause.
In such passages as, “Venerable sir, a certain woman saw me through a flash of lightning while she was washing a vessel,” it refers to a moment;
the meaning is “at the moment of the flash of lightning. In such passages as, “He within whom there are no angers...,” [it occurs in the sense of the interior].
In the word *citte*: in the sense of an interval, as in “between Gayā and Bodhi,” and so forth;
in the sense of the middle, as in “one should not interrupt with side-talk while the preceptor is speaking,” and so forth. Here too, it should be understood in the sense of the middle;
therefore, the meaning is “in this interval, in the middle. This is what is meant: in whichever great aeon our Blessed One [appeared]...
Having become the wise Sumedha, at the feet of the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara he made this vow:
“Human birth, the perfection of gender, The cause,
the sight of the Teacher, Renunciation, the perfection of virtues, Service, and zeal.”
Having spoken thus, he made the Great Resolve (mahābhinīhāra) endowed with these eight factors;
he investigated and undertook the thirty perfections (pāramīs), and began to fulfill all the qualities that produce a Buddha.

It was in this mental state that, having completely fulfilled the perfections during the Auspicious Aeon (bhaddakappa), he awakened to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment (anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ). Of these—
It refers to a specific period within the interval between two great aeons (*mahākappa*), according to the aforementioned delimitation.

But how is this to be understood? For the statement, “A hundred thousand aeons and four incalculables,” is a demonstration of the number of great aeons both by way of their delimited and undelimited extent.
Now, this number [is established] without grasping the beginning or the end of that which is to be numbered.

It is understood that the phrase "in between" (*etthantare*) is shown here in its actual meaning as referring to both the point where the requisites for enlightenment (*bodhisambhāra*) begin and the point where they are completed, taken together as the two limits. Furthermore,

this limit should be understood in the sense of inclusion (*abhividhi*), not in the sense of exclusion (*mariyādā*), because the beginning and the conclusion are included within it by way of a single part.

But is it not the case that, because they have not been fully encompassed without remainder, neither the sense of "pervasive inclusion" (*abhividhi*) nor the sense of "exhaustion" (*pariyādāna*) is possible here? No;

this is not so, because even with respect to a single part of them, the designation for the whole is applied. For whatever eon constitutes a single part of those [aeons], that too is considered exhausted in its entirety.

And regarding the statement, "Whatever conduct there is, all that ripens enlightenment," here "conduct" (*carita*) means "course of action" (*cariyā*), which comprises the thirty perfections (*pāramitā*).

The practice of giving, virtue, and so forth, is included within these because it is subsumed under the conduct for the benefit of oneself, the conduct for the benefit of the world, and the conduct for the benefit of Buddhahood.
Likewise, there are these eight types of conduct, namely: the conduct of posture among those endowed with aspiration regarding the four postures;
the conduct of the sense bases among those who guard the doors of the faculties regarding the internal sense bases; and the conduct of heedfulness among those dwelling in diligence...
The practice of mindfulness in the four foundations of mindfulness; the practice of concentration in the four jhānas for those devoted to higher mind-culture;
the practice of knowledge in the four noble truths for those endowed with wisdom; the practice of the path in the four noble paths for those practicing rightly;
the practice of attainment in the four fruits of recluseship for those who have reached the fruits; [and the practice] of the three Buddhas.

“Worldly conduct for the benefit of all beings. In this context, worldly conduct for the benefit [of others] is partial for two types of bodhisattvas, for paccekabuddhas, and for the disciples of a Buddha;
however, it is complete for mahābodhisattvas and for the perfectly enlightened Buddhas (sammāsambuddhas).
For this has been stated in detail in the Niddesa: “Conduct means eight kinds of conduct: conduct of posture, conduct of the sense bases,” and so forth. “While resolving...”
He courses with faith; he courses with energy while exerting himself; he courses with mindfulness while establishing it;
he courses with concentration while remaining undistracted; he courses with wisdom while understanding; he courses with consciousness while cognizing.
Thus, for one practicing in this way, wholesome states come to their full extent—this is "coursing in the sphere of arrival. Thus, practicing in this way, one attains distinction.

Regarding the statement, "He practices the specific practice," it should be understood that the inclusion of all those other eight practices mentioned is contained within the perfections (pāramitā) themselves.
Therefore, it was said: "'Practice' (carita) means 'practicing' (cariyā); it is the undertaking of giving, virtue, and so forth, comprised within the thirty perfections.

However, since only the causal practice (hetucariyā) is intended here, it should be understood that the practice of the path (maggacariyā) and the practice of attainment (patticariyā) are not included herein.
Therefore it was said: "All that ripens the Bodhi.

In this context, the word *sabba* (all) is seen in four senses: all-in-all (*sabbasabba*), the all of the sense-bases (*āyatana-sabba*), the all of the aggregates (*sakkāya-sabba*), and the partial all (*padesa-sabba*). For instance:
"All phenomena (*sabbe dhammā*) in every aspect [are known] at the door of wisdom of the Buddha, the Blessed One..."
In such passages as "coming within range," it refers to the all-in-all. In the passage, "Bhikkhus, I will teach you the all; listen to that. And what, bhikkhus, is the all? It is the eye and forms...
the mind and mental objects," it refers to the all in terms of the sense bases (*āyatana*).
In such passages as "one perceives the all from the all," it refers to the all in terms of personal existence (*sakkāya*). "Sāriputta, everything spoken well by all of you... [is so stated].

In such passages as "by way of method" (*pariyāyena*), it refers to a partial totality (*padesasabbasmiṃ*). Here too, it should be understood as referring to a partial totality, because what is intended is the conduct that constitutes the requisites for enlightenment (*bodhisambhāra*).

"Enlightenment" (*bodhi*) may refer to the tree, the Noble Path (*ariyamagga*), Nibbāna, or omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*). [As in: "He was first fully enlightened at the foot of the Bodhi tree."
And in the passage, "Between Gayā and Bodhi," the tree is called *bodhi* because one awakens (*bujjhati*) there.
In the passage, "Knowledge regarding the four paths is called *bodhi*," the noble path is called *bodhi* because by means of it one awakens to the Four Noble Truths.
In the passage, "Having attained *bodhi*, the deathless, the unconditioned," one awakens [to it].

In this context, *nibbāna* is "enlightenment" (*bodhi*) as the sign. In the passage, “The one of excellent and vast intelligence attains enlightenment,” *bodhi* refers to the knowledge of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*), because by means of it one awakens to all phenomena in all their aspects. Here too, it is the knowledge of omniscience that is intended.

Alternatively, it should be understood that both the path of Arahantship and the knowledge of omniscience are meant here by the term "enlightenment," in reference to the Great Enlightenment (*mahābodhi*).

Because it is intended by the Blessed One. For omniscient knowledge (sabbaññutaññāṇa) has the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (āsavakkhayañāṇa) as its proximate cause, and the knowledge of the destruction of the taints has omniscient knowledge as its proximate cause;
thus, they are called the "Great Enlightenment" (mahābodhi). Herein, this is the summary of the meaning:
whatever conduct consisting of the practice of giving, virtue, and so forth was mine within the time-period already described, all that without exception [is for] the Great Enlightenment.
"Digestive, accomplishing, and productive. By this, he shows the uninterrupted cultivation of the requisites for enlightenment (*bodhisambhāra*).
Alternatively, "all" refers to whatever conduct was practiced within the aforementioned temporal limits;
all of that, in its entirety and without exception, constitutes the requisites for enlightenment. By this, he shows the cultivation of every single requisite.
For in the requisites for enlightenment, cultivation consists of: cultivation of all requisites, uninterrupted cultivation, long-term cultivation, and thorough cultivation.
Among these, long-term cultivation is expressed by the words, "In a hundred thousand aeons and four incalculable [aeons].
And as for the absolute conjunction (*accantasamyoga*) here, it implies uninterrupted cultivation through the inclusion of the word "all" in the first alternative meaning.
In the second interpretation, by the phrase "all conduct," the cultivation of all the requisites is stated;
and by the phrase "ripening of enlightenment," careful cultivation is expressed, because it demonstrates the state of being that ripens such conduct into perfect enlightenment.
For it is only in this way—and not otherwise—that it deserves to be called "the ripening of enlightenment. But how is this so?
Is the state of being uninterrupted in the conduct of awakening (bodhicaryā) to be understood [in this way]?

If it were not tenable on account of the continuity of the mind itself, then one could not say that after the Great Resolve (mahābhinīhāra) of the Great Bodhisattvas, no other thought arises than the thought of accumulating the requisites for awakening (bodhisambhāra).
Or, perhaps, it might be said with reference to the occurrence of thoughts consisting of action (kiriyāmayacitta)?
Even this is not tenable; for not all of their volitional minds proceed solely by way of accumulating the requisites for enlightenment.
By this very fact, it should be understood that uninterruptedness of application is also rejected.
Rather, uninterrupted cultivation is to be understood as uninterruptedness of birth. For in whichever birth a Great Bodhisattva makes the Great Resolve...

From that point until his final existence, there is no birth to be found in which he would not have accumulated the requisites for enlightenment in their entirety, at least to the extent of the perfection of giving.
For this is the natural law (*dhammatā*) of Bodhisattvas who are fixed in their destiny. And as long as they do not attain mastery over karma and the other factors, even a partial [perfection]—

They apply themselves to the requisites for enlightenment. But when they have attained mastery over karma and the other factors in every respect, from that point onward, the gathering of the requisites for enlightenment becomes entirely complete and their practice is constant.
However, thoroughness in performance occurs at all times; thus, in whatever way the Bodhisattvas act in various situations according to their intention—

"It succeeds" means it is accomplished. Thus, by this verse, it should be understood that four kinds of cultivation are revealed: the cultivation of all the requisites for enlightenment, long-term cultivation, uninterrupted cultivation, and thorough cultivation.
In this regard, since the conduct of a Bodhisatta, the requisites for enlightenment, the practice for enlightenment, the supreme vehicle, and the perfections (pāramīs) are identical in meaning;

There is only one difference, which is in the phrasing; and since this is a general statement for what will later be explained in detail as the "conduct" consisting of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramī*) and so forth, the perfections (*pāramīs*) must be described here in order to generate proficiency regarding all the requisites for enlightenment.
We shall describe them in every aspect later, in the miscellaneous discussion (*pakiṇṇakakathā*).

2. Thus the Blessed One, having shown without distinction that his own conduct while on the stage of a bodhisatta— from its commencement until its conclusion— was solely for the ripening of great enlightenment, now,
in order to show how it was preeminently a ripener of enlightenment through its attainment of the highest excellence, [he describes] several of his previous deeds performed in this Bhaddakappa.
Explaining by way of analysis, he says, "In past aeons," and so forth.
Therein, "in past aeons" (*atītakappe*) means in all those great aeons (*mahākappa*)—defined as previously stated—that have passed since before this, or even further back;
that is to say, in the four incalculable aeons (*asaṅkhyeyya*) plus a hundred thousand aeons. "Conduct" (*carita*) means what has been practiced (*ciṇṇa*).
The practice of giving and so forth. "Setting aside" means having released, having not grasped; the sense is "having left behind. Regarding "existence and non-existence" (*bhavābhava*):
it refers to both existence and non-existence. For in the phrase "discourse on such existence and non-existence," increase and decrease are called "existence and non-existence.

In the phrase "and having transcended such existence and non-existence," existence and non-existence refer to success and failure, increase and decrease, permanence and annihilation, and merit and demerit.

These are intended. However, in the passage: “Or, bhikkhus, craving arises in a bhikkhu because of ‘being this’ and ‘being that’ (itibhavābhavahetu),” it is superior and more superior medicines such as ghee and butter that are intended by the terms “being this” and “being that.

They say that among states of success (sampattibhava), the more superior and most superior states are also intended by the terms “being this” and “being that”; therefore, here too, it is that [which is intended].
The meaning should be understood in this way: "in both small and great existences" is what is meant.
"In this aeon" means in this auspicious aeon (*bhaddakappa*). "I shall speak" means I shall tell. "Listen" is an exhortation for the General of the Dhamma to listen.
"From me" means in my presence; the sense is "from my speech."
The Nidānakathā is concluded.
1. The Chapter on Akitti. 1.
The Exposition of the Conduct of Akitti.
3. Thus, having inspired enthusiasm in the Venerable Sāriputta Thera and the assembly of devas and humans for hearing of his own former conduct,
the Blessed One now spoke the words beginning with "When I was in the great forest," making that past life— which had been concealed by the interval of existence—
directly manifest as clearly as an *āmalaka* fruit on the palm of one's hand.

In this context, *yadā* means "at which time. *Brāhma-raññe* means in a great forest (*mahā-araññe*), in a wilderness (*araññāniye*), or in a vast wood; such is the meaning. *Suññe* means secluded from people.
*Vipina-kānane* means in a wood that has become a thicket (*vipinabhūte kānane*); by these two terms, he illustrates the dense nature of that forest.
All of this was said with reference to Kāradīpa. *Ajjhogāhetvā* means having entered into.

"I dwell" means that by severing bodily suffering through the dwelling in postures produced by the specific bliss arising from the divine, brahma, noble, and imperturbable dwellings, I maintain my physical existence.
"The ascetic named Akitti" means that when I was an ascetic of such a name, I dwelt in that forest. At that time, the Teacher [described] his own state as the ascetic Akitti.
He speaks concerning the General of the Dhamma. Herein, this is the sequential narrative:

It is said that in the past, during this very Bhaddakappa, while a king named Brahmadatta was reigning in Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was reborn into a family of a wealthy brahmin mahāsāla possessing eighty koṭis of wealth; his name was Akitti.
They performed [the rites]. While he was traveling on foot, his sister was also born; they gave her the name Yasavatī.
When he reached the age of sixteen, he went to Takkaśilā, mastered all the arts, and returned. Then his parents passed away.
After performing their funeral rites and the passage of a few days, he [performed] the Ratnāvalokana.
While having it carried out by his appointed officials, he heard that "this much was from my maternal grandfather, this much from my paternal grandfather, and this much from my great-grandfather.
With a heart moved by spiritual urgency, he thought, "Only this wealth is seen here, but no one who gathered this wealth remains;
everyone has departed, leaving this wealth behind. I, however, shall take it with me. Having thus requested leave from the king, he [had] the drum...
He caused it to be proclaimed: "Let those who have need of wealth come to the house of the wise Akitti.
Having offered a great almsgiving for seven days, and seeing that his wealth was not being exhausted, he thought, "What is the use of this play with wealth? Those who need it shall take it.
He opened the gate of his residence and had the inner chambers, filled with gold, bullion, and other treasures, thrown open.
Thinking, "Let them take what has been given," he left his home while his circle of kinsmen lamented;
taking his sister with him, he departed from Bārāṇasī, crossed a river, and after traveling two or three *yojanas*, he went forth into homelessness.
Having built a leaf-hut on a delightful stretch of ground, he lived there. The gate through which he then departed is known as Akitti’s Gate.
The place where he was born became known as Jātana. The ford by which he entered the river became known as Akittitittha.
When people living in villages, market towns, and royal capitals heard of his renunciation, their hearts were drawn toward him by his virtues, and they followed him into the homeless life.
He came to have a vast retinue, and great gain and honor arose for him; it was as if a Buddha had appeared in the world. Then the Great Being—
Thinking, "This gain and honor are great, and the retinue is vast; yet even a mere physical seclusion cannot be found here.
It is fitting that I dwell alone," he—out of an extreme state of fewness of desires and a natural inclination toward solitude—departed by himself without informing anyone.
Traveling by stages, he eventually reached the Damila kingdom and arrived near the city of Kāveripaṭṭana.
While dwelling in the park, he attained the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and the supernormal powers (*abhiññā*). There, too, great gain and honor arose for him.
Loathing that, he abandoned it and traveled through the air, landing on Kāradīpa—at that time known as Ahidīpa.
There, relying upon a large *kāra* tree, he constructed a leaf-hut and made his dwelling. Out of fewness of desires...

But not going anywhere else, he spent his time in meditative attainments (*jhāna-samāpatti*), eating the fruits of that tree when they were in season, and when there were no fruits, eating its leaves after sprinkling them with water.
By the power of his virtue, the stone throne of Sakka, known as Paṇḍukambala, began to feel hot. Sakka [thought], "Who indeed..."
Thinking, "He wishes to displace me from this position," and perceiving that he was wise, [Sakka] reflected:
"For what purpose does this ascetic practice such difficult austerity? Does he aspire to the status of Sakka, or perhaps something else?
I shall test him. For his conduct of body, speech, and mind is perfectly pure; he is indifferent to life, [even regarding] these water-soaked leaves."
"He eats; if he aspires to the position of Sakka, he will give me his own cooked *kāra* fruits, but if not, he will not.

Thinking thus, Sakka approached him in the guise of a brahmin. The Bodhisatta, having boiled the *kāra* fruits, sat at the door of his leaf-hut thinking, "I shall eat them when they have become cool. Then, in front of him, Sakka appeared in the form of a brahmin.
He stood there desiring alms-food. Seeing him, the Great Being was filled with joy, thinking, "It is indeed a gain for me; it is truly well-gained by me;
after such a long time, a petitioner has finally been seen by me.
Resolving, "Today I shall fulfill my heart's desire and give a gift," he took his vessel of cooked rice and went forth, reflecting upon the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*).
Without leaving any for himself, he placed it into the monk’s alms-bowl. Sakka took it and, having gone a short distance, vanished.
The Great Being, having given it to him, did not seek further, but spent his time in that very joy and happiness.
On the second day, however, after cooking some *kāra* leaves, he thought: "Yesterday I obtained a worthy recipient; what shall happen today?"
He sat at the door of the leaf-hut. Sakka also arrived in the same manner. The Great Being gave to him as before and let him pass.
On the third day, having given in the same way, he thought: "Oh, what a gain for me! Truly, I am producing much merit.
If I could obtain a worthy recipient of offerings, I would give alms just like this for a month or even two months. Thus he reflected during all three days.
During those days, he established his mind according to his specific purpose, thinking: "By this gift, I do not aspire for gain, honor, or fame;
nor for the prosperity of a wheel-turning monarch, nor the prosperity of Sakka, nor the prosperity of Brahmā; nor for the enlightenment of a disciple, nor for the enlightenment of a paccekabuddha;
rather, may this gift of mine be a condition for the knowledge of omniscience. Therefore it was said:
“Then the Conqueror of the Three Worlds, scorched by the heat of my asceticism,
approached me for alms while assuming the guise of a brahmin.
He brought from the forest leaves that were neither fried in oil nor seasoned with salt.”
Seeing him standing at my door, I poured [the food] from my cooking pot.
Having given him the leaf-plate and turned the vessel upside down,
I abandoned my search once more and entered the leaf-hut.
“A second time and a third time he approached my presence;
unshaken and undaunted, I gave him [the gift] in this very manner.
Because of that, there is no discoloration in my body.”
With joy and happiness, I pass that day in delight.
“If for a month or even two months I were to obtain a worthy recipient of offerings,
unshaken and without hesitation, I would give the supreme gift.”
“While giving that gift, I did not seek fame or gain;
desiring omniscience, I performed those deeds.
In this context, “then” means when I, having become an ascetic named Akitti, was dwelling in the Karā forest on that island.
Then [he thought]: "It burns me. It burns by means of the power of the perfection of virtue (*sīlapāramitā*).
For virtue is called "austerity" (*tapo*) because it burns away the defilement of misconduct; or else, it is by means of the power of the perfections of renunciation and energy.
For these too are called "austerity" because they burn away the defilement of craving and laziness; and these have reached their highest excellence in the Bodhisatta at this time.

“Attabhāve” means: because he had reached the highest excellence even in the restraint of patience, it is indeed appropriate to say, “by the power of the perfection of patience (khantipāramitā). For it is said: “Patience is the supreme austerity. “Santatto” means:

heated by the state of warmth produced upon the stone seat of the pale blanket (paṇḍukambala-silāsana) through the power of the aforementioned qualities, which is established by the very nature of things (dhammatā). “Tidivābhibhū” means: the lord of the world of the gods.

The meaning is that he is able. Although the leaf-offering was taken near the leaf-hut, it is said to have been "brought from the forest" because the leaf-hut was situated in the middle of the wilderness.
And as for the phrase "without oil and without salt," although the gift itself may not be of superior quality, through the excellence of the donor's intention, the nature of the gift [is perfected].
This was said in order to demonstrate his state of great radiance. "At my door" means at the door of my leaf-hut.
"They poured [the food] from their cart" shows that he gave away everything he had without leaving anything behind for himself.

"Having abandoned further seeking" means that, reflecting that "seeking food twice in a single day is not conducive to spiritual refinement," and feeling as if satiated by the joy of giving, he did not engage in the search for food again on that day.
"Unshaken" means unshaken by stinginess because it has been thoroughly suppressed; it means not allowing even the slightest wavering from the inclination toward giving.
"Unattached" means not clinging in the least, even for an instant, due to greed.
"And a third time as well"—by the word "also" (pi), he includes "and a second time as well. "In this very way I gave": just as on the first occasion, so too on the second and on the third, I gave.
The verse beginning with "Na me tappaccayā" clarifies the very meaning already stated. Therein, "tappaccayā" means: by reason of that gift (*dānapaccayā*).
Regarding the discoloration that ought to have occurred in my body due to the lack of food for three days—such discoloration in my body does not exist even because of the gift itself. Why?
Because of the joy and happiness arising from the object of giving; indeed, [the color] is due to the object of giving alone.
"And with joy. "I spend that day" means I spend that entire three-day period;
and not only three days, but even for a time of two or three months, he says "if even for a month" and so forth to show that he is able to give in this very way.
"Unshrunken" (anolīna) means one whose mind is not shrunken; the meaning is that his mind does not contract when giving.
"Of him" refers to Sakka, who had arrived in the form of a brahmin. "Fame" (*yasa*) means reputation or the excellence of his retinue.
"And gain" (*lābhañca*) means that he did not long for the gains to be obtained among gods and humans by way of being a universal monarch (*cakkavatti*) or similar status.

Rather, longing for and desiring omniscience (*sabbaññutā*) and perfect enlightenment (*sammāsambodhi*), [he reflected on] those gifts consisting of giving that had arisen many times during those three days.
"Meritorious deeds" refers to meritorious actions such as bodily good conduct that serve as the accompaniments to giving; [the Buddha] said, "I performed these meritorious deeds.
Thus, in this context, the Blessed One revealed to the Great Elder only his own extremely difficult practice of merit within that particular existence.
However, in the teaching of the Jātaka, on the fourth day, having approached Sakka, [he spoke of] the Bodhisatta's...
By means of the boon, the discernment of his underlying intention (*ajjhāsaya*) was shown; by way of the invitation to choose a boon, the Bodhisatta’s acceptance of the boon was indicated;
and by way of the discourse on the Dhamma, the suitability of the gift and the worthiness of the recipient were revealed, as well as Sakka’s desire that he might not return again. For it is said:
“Having seen Akitti in perfect composure, Sakka, the Lord of Beings, spoke:”
“What are you longing for, Great Brahmā, that you meditate alone in the heat?
“Rebirth is suffering, Sakka, as is the breaking up of the body;
death in delusion is suffering—therefore, Vāsava, I pay homage.”
“Since you have spoken so well, with words that are fitting and well-said,
I grant you a boon, Kassapa, whatever you desire in your heart.
If you would grant me a boon, Sakka, Lord of all beings,”
"That greed by which men, having obtained children, wives, wealth, grain, and beloved things, are not satisfied—that greed does not dwell within me. Regarding this well-spoken word of yours...
[you] desire it in your mind."
“If you would grant me a boon, O Sakka, Lord of all beings:
let the fault that causes fields, lands, gold, cattle, horses, slaves,
and servants to be lost through birth not reside in me.”
“Since you have spoken so well... [and so forth] ...you may choose a boon.
“If you would grant me a boon, O Sakka, Lord of all beings:
May I neither see nor hear a fool, nor dwell together with a fool.”
One should neither engage in nor take pleasure in idle chatter with a fool.
"What has this fool done to you? Tell me the reason, Kassapa;
for what reason, Kassapa, do you not desire the sight of a fool?"
“The foolish man leads himself astray and yokes himself to what is burdensome;
his wrong course becomes his highest good, and he grows agitated when spoken to rightly.
He does not understand discipline; it is better not to see him.”
“Since you have spoken so well... [and so forth] ...you may choose a boon.
“If you would grant me a boon, O Sakka, Lord of all beings:
May I see the wise, hear the wise, and dwell together with the wise.”
“Engage in conversation with the wise one; you will find that pleasing.
“What indeed have I done for you, O Wise One? Tell me the reason, Kassapa.
For what reason, Kassapa, do you long for the sight of the Wise One?”
“The wise man does not lead one astray, nor does he yoke one to what is burdensome;
good guidance is better, for one who speaks rightly does not become angry.
He understands discipline; it is good to have association with such a person.”
“Since you have spoken so well... [as before] ...you may choose a boon.
“If you would grant me a boon, O Sakka, Lord of all beings, then at the end of this night, as the sun rises, [grant it].”
“May divine foods appear, and may those who are virtuous come as supplicants.
‘May my wealth not be exhausted while I give, and having given, may I have no regret;
may I gladden my heart by giving’—this, Sakka, is the boon I choose.”
“Since you have spoken so well... [as before] ...you may choose a boon.
“If you would grant me a boon, O Sakka, Lord of all beings, I choose this boon from you, Sakka: that you shall not come to visit me again.”
“Indeed, by means of many vows and practices, men and women long for a sight of you;
what fear could there be for me in being seen?
You are such a one, with the appearance of a god, perfected in all desires.”
"Having seen this, I might neglect my asceticism; this is the danger in your sight.

Then Sakka said, "Very well, venerable sir, from now on I shall not come near you," and having paid homage to him, he departed. The Great Being remained right there for the rest of his life, and at the end of his lifespan, he was reborn in the Brahma-world.
At that time, the Elder Anuruddha was Sakka, and the Protector of the World was the wise Akitti.
Because he went forth in a manner resembling the Great Renunciation, there is the perfection of renunciation (*nekkhamma-pāramī*).

Because of his state of perfectly purified virtue and conduct, there is the perfection of virtue (*sīla-pāramī*). Because sensual thoughts and the like were thoroughly suppressed, there is the perfection of energy (*vīriya-pāramī*).

Because he reached the highest excellence of the restraint of patience, there is the perfection of patience (*khanti-pāramī*). Because his practice was in accordance with his promise, there is the perfection of truthfulness (*sacca-pāramī*). In all respects...

The perfection of resolve (*adhiṭṭhāna-pāramī*) consists in the firm determination of unwavering commitment. The perfection of loving-kindness (*mettā-pāramī*) consists in the disposition toward the welfare of all beings.
The perfection of equanimity (*upekkhā-pāramī*) consists in attaining a state of neutrality regarding the various manifestations produced by the conditioned formations of beings.

Preceding these [three] is the perfection of wisdom (*paññā-pāramī*), which arises simultaneously with them, having understood the phenomena that are beneficial and those that are not, and having abandoned the non-beneficial phenomena while inducing engagement in those that are beneficial.

Furthermore, wisdom that consists in skillful means (*upāyakosalla*) and which accomplishes an extremely austere way of life is also called the perfection of wisdom (*paññāpāramī*); thus, these ten perfections are obtained.
However, because of the exceedingly exalted nature of one whose inclination is toward giving, the teaching proceeded by way of the door of generosity (*dāna*).

Therefore, there is great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) equal in all respects, both accumulations of merit and knowledge (*puññañāṇasambhāra*), and the three types of good conduct of a bodhisattva (*bodhisattvasucarita*), beginning with bodily good conduct.
The four foundations, beginning with the foundation of truth; the four stages of Buddhahood, beginning with exertion;
the five qualities that ripen great enlightenment, beginning with faith; the six inclinations of Bodhisattvas, beginning with the inclination toward non-greed;

the seven qualities of formal commitment, beginning with "Having crossed over, I shall help others cross"; and [the teaching]: "This Dhamma is for one of few desires; this Dhamma is not for one who is not."
The eight thoughts of a great man beginning with "of one with great desire," the nine states rooted in wise attention,
the ten inclinations of a great man beginning with "inclination toward giving," and the ten bases for meritorious action beginning with "giving and virtue"— all such qualities of a Mahābodhisatta,
which consist of the requisites for enlightenment and are divided into many hundreds and thousands of types, must all be explained here as appropriate by way of selection.
Moreover, here there was his departure from home like a great renunciation, having abandoned a vast mass of wealth and a large circle of kinsmen;
and after departing and going forth, though he was highly esteemed by the multitude,
there was his lack of attachment to families and social groups due to his state of supreme fewness-of-wishes, his utter loathing for gain, honor, and fame, and his delight in seclusion.

It is the relinquishment that is indifferent to body and life; it is the sustaining of a body free from agitation while one remains without food for even three days, being fully satisfied by the joy of giving;
and it is the sublime state of conduct that, when a supplicant appears, gives away food in the same manner for as long as two or three months, resolving:
"I shall sustain my body solely by the joy and happiness derived from giving," thereby perfecting the practice of non-attachment in relinquishment.

The Great Being’s qualities and powers should be understood as his inclination toward generosity, his supreme mode of life characterized by extreme effacement—which serves as the cause for no longer seeking food after having given a gift—and so forth. Therefore, this is said:
“Thus these [qualities] of the Great Seer are wonderful and marvelous;”
The Greatly Compassionate and steadfast ones, the sole kinsmen of the entire world;
possessing inconceivable power, always having the true Dharma as their sphere of activity—
these are the Bodhisattvas, the Mahāsattvas, whose lives are pure and characterized by austerity.
“Even the great ocean, with its garland of waves tossed up by mighty winds, might overstep its shore;
but Bodhisattvas do not overstep the nature of Dhamma.
Though they have been born and raised in the world, they are not those whose being has been fully developed [by worldly things].”
They glide through the worldly conditions, like a lotus through water.
"For those who have affection for themselves, as that [self-affection] diminishes more and more,
so too does their compassionate affection for sentient beings increase more and more."
“As the mind comes under one’s control and does not follow the sway of the mind,
so too, karma comes under one’s control and does not follow the sway of karma.
They are not overcome by faults, nor do they fail to eradicate them.”
“The wise ones, those thoroughbred men, wander in search of enlightenment.
Even a mere clarity of mind toward them can liberate one from suffering,
let alone performing services for them in accordance with the Dhamma.”
The commentary on the *Akitti-cariyā* within the *Cariyāpiṭaka-saṃvaṇṇanā*, known as the *Paramatthadīpanī*, is completed. 2.
Commentary on the *Saṅkha-brāhmaṇa-cariyā*.

11–12. "Furthermore, another" (*punāparaṃ*) means once again; the intention is: "Not only this account of Akitti’s conduct, but furthermore, I shall speak of another, namely the conduct of Saṅkha as well—listen!
This same method applies to the subsequent sections as well. "Named Saṅkha" (*saṅkhasavhayo*) means one whose name is Saṅkha.
"Desiring to cross the great ocean" (*mahāsamuddaṃ taritukāmo*) means wishing to go to Suvaṇṇabhūmi.
Desiring to cross the great ocean by means of a ship, I am approaching the port; that is, I am going toward the port of Tāmaliptī.
Because he has attained private enlightenment (paccekabodhi) through his own self-existent knowledge (sayambhuñāṇa), he is "Self-Existent" (Sayambhu).
Because he has not been defeated by any [of the Māras], such as the Māra of the defilements (kilesamāra), he is "Unconquered" (Aparājita); having crushed the heads of the three Māras—
The meaning is "standing. "On that ground which had become hard" means on a ground that was rough and harsh because it was heated by the summer's heat and covered with gravel and sand.
"Him" refers to that Paccekabuddha. "This matter" refers to what will now be stated, beginning with "this is the field," and so forth.
"Reflecting on the goal": the Teacher says that at that time, having become the Brahmin Saṅkha, he reflected. Herein, this is the sequential narrative:
