In the past, this Bārāṇasī was called Moḷinī. While Brahmadatta was reigning in the city of Moḷinī, the Bodhisatta, having been born as a Brahmin named Saṅkha, was wealthy and possessed of great riches; [he lived] at the four city gates and in the center of the city.

At the gate of his residence, having constructed six alms-halls at six locations, he established a great distribution of gifts for the poor, the destitute, and others, dispensing six hundred thousand coins every day.
One day he thought: "When the wealth in my house is exhausted, I will not be able to give alms;
therefore, while the wealth is still unexhausted, I shall go by ship to Suvaṇṇabhūmi and [acquire] wealth."
“I shall bring it back. Having filled his ship with merchandise and addressed his wife and children,
saying, “While I am away, you must continue the practice of giving without interruption,” he set out toward the port city,
surrounded by his slaves and laborers, mounted on a carriage and with a parasol being held over him.

At that moment, on Mount Gandhamādana, a certain Paccekabuddha who had entered the attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) for seven days emerged from that state and surveyed the world. Seeing him going to fetch the treasure, he thought:
"This Great Being is going to fetch the treasure; will there be some obstacle for him in the great ocean?"
Having adverted [his mind] thus, and knowing that "it will happen," he thought: "When this man sees me, he will give me both a parasol and sandals;
by the result of that gift of sandals, he will find a firm footing when his ship is wrecked at sea. I shall do him a favor.
Having traveled through the air, he descended not far from him at the time of midday, amidst the fierce wind and heat.
As he was trampling the hot sand, which was like a bed of glowing coals, he approached him.
Upon seeing him, he was filled with joy and satisfaction, thinking, "A field of merit has come to me; today it is fitting for me to sow seed here.
Therefore it is said: "Having seen him on the opposite path, I reflected upon this matter," and so forth.

In this context, the passage beginning with "this is the field" (*khetta*) is an illustration of the manner in which [the object] was contemplated. "Field" (*khetta*): it is called a field because it protects (*tāyati*) the seed that has been sown by making it yield great fruit;
it is the ground for the growth of grain, both paddy and non-paddy. Here, however, it is "like a field," thus a "field";
namely, the Pratyekabuddha, who is the foremost among those worthy of offerings. For this very reason, he said: "for a person desiring merit."
14. *Mahāgamanti* means "a source of abundant fruit"; the sense is that it bestows the excellence of crops. *Bījaṃ na ropetīti* means "he does not sow seed.
*Khettavaruttamanti* means "the most excellent among fields. For noble disciples (*ariyasāvaka*), who are endowed with virtues such as moral discipline (*sīla*), are especially excellent fields;
even more than them, the Paccekabuddha, being the foremost of all, is the most excellent field. *Kāranti* means "honorable treatment" (*sakkāra*). If...

The connection is with the words "I do not perform. This is what is meant: having obtained such an unsurpassed field of merit as this, if I were not to perform worship and honor toward it, I would not truly be one who desires merit. 16–17.
The summary meaning of these two verses beginning with "Just as a minister" is as follows: just as anyone...
An official appointed by the king to the office of accounting— a minister bearing the royal seal or a general— who,
within the inner palace or among the external forces and so forth, does not act according to the king’s instructions, nor provides them with wealth and grain,
and neglects his various duties and obligations, falls from his position; he is deprived of the prosperity obtained through his office of accounting.
Just as that [person] falls away, even so I too— delighting in meritorious deeds, desiring merit consisting of the fruits obtainable from merit,
and seeing the vastness [of the result] by making the gift’s fruit abundant— having obtained this sublime object worthy of offerings,
if I do not give that gift, I shall fall away from merit and from the future fruits of merit.
"Therefore, I must certainly perform a meritorious deed here.
Having reflected thus, the Great Man descended from his sandals even from afar, approached with haste,
and having paid homage, said, "Venerable Sir, please come to the foot of this tree for my sake," and [he led him] to that foot of the tree.
As he was approaching, he spread sand there, prepared his upper robe as a seat,
and when the Paccekabuddha had sat down, he paid homage to him. He washed the Buddha’s feet with scented, strained water, anointed them with fragrant oil,
wiped his own sandals, anointed them with fragrant oil, and fastened them onto the Buddha’s feet, saying, “Venerable Sir,…”
“Mount these sandals and go, holding this parasol over your head,” he said, and gave him the parasol and sandals.

Out of gratitude for his kindness, and in order to increase [the king’s] faith, the Elder took them and, while the king was still looking on, rose into the air and went to Gandhamādana. Thus it is said:
“Having thought thus, I took off my sandals, and after bowing at his feet, I gave him the sunshade and the sandals.
Having seen this, the Bodhisatta, with a heart exceedingly full of faith, went to the port and boarded the ship. Then, for him—
As they were crossing the great ocean, on the seventh day the ship sprung a leak. They were unable to bailing out the water.
The great multitude, terrified by the fear of death, paid homage to their respective deities and raised a great cry of lamentation.
The Bodhisatta, taking one attendant with him, smeared his entire body with oil and [mixed] sugar-dust with ghee.
Having eaten as much as he desired and having caused him to eat as well, he climbed with him to the top of a bone in the middle of the pit; then,
determining the direction by thinking, "In this direction lies our city," and liberating himself from the danger posed by fish and turtles through a resolve of truth (*saccādhiṭṭhāna*),
he traveled with him for a distance of about a bull's length and fell into the ocean.
He began to cross over, but the great multitude perished right there. Seven days passed while he was still crossing.
Even during that time, having rinsed his mouth with salt water, he remained strictly observant of the Uposatha.
At that time, however, for the sake of protecting such distinguished persons, the jeweled girdle had been stationed by the four World-Protectors.

The goddess Nāma, having become negligent for seven days due to her own sovereign power, saw him on the seventh day and was moved by a heart of agitation, thinking, "If he were to die here, he would be exceedingly contemptible.
She quickly arrived with a golden bowl filled with divine food and said, "Brāhmaṇa, eat this divine food. He looked up at her.
Having refused, saying, "I am not eating, for I have observed the Uposatha," he asked her:
"O lady of great majesty, you who look upon me with such ease and say to me, 'Eat your meal';
I ask you, are you a goddess or are you a human woman?"
She replied to him:
“O Saṅkha, I am a queen of great majesty who has come here into the midst of the ocean’s waters;
compassionate and not of a corrupt mind, I have come here for your very sake.”
“Here, food and drink, bedding and seats, and various kinds of vehicles in abundance—I shall provide all of this for you, whatever your heart desires.
Having heard these verses, the Great Being thought: “This daughter of the gods, on the surface of the ocean, [is offering] this and that to me...”
Thinking, "She says, 'I give'; whatever she gives to me is also due to my own merit.
But does this daughter of the gods know that merit, or does she not? I shall ask her," he spoke this verse while questioning her:
"Whatever has been offered or sacrificed for me, you are the mistress of it all, O fair-limbed one."
“O lady with beautiful hips and lovely thighs, with a slender waist—of what karma is this the result for me?
In this context, *yiṭṭha* means that which has been sacrificed by way of giving; *huta* means that which has been given by way of offerings and hospitality.
“You are the mistress of all our meritorious deeds”—you are the sovereign over all our wholesome actions [thinking], “This is the result of this, and this...”
They were capable of answering, "Of this. "Sussonī" means one with beautiful hips. "Subbhūrū" means endowed with beautiful eyebrows and thighs.
"Vilaggamajjhā" means having a slender, well-proportioned waist. "Kissa me" means:
"Of which deed among those performed by me is this the result, that today I obtain a foothold in the great ocean where there is no footing?"
Hearing this, the goddess thought, "This brahmin seems to ask because he believes that he does not know the wholesome kamma he himself performed;
I shall explain it to him. She then spoke, identifying the cause as the merit from giving the parasol and sandals to the Paccekabuddha on the day she boarded the ship.
“O Brahmin, on a hot road, you provided a single monk—whose feet were blistered, who was thirsty and exhausted—with a conch-shell water-vessel and sandals.
This gift of yours today shall be a cow that milks all desires. Thus he spoke this verse.
In that context, "one bhikkhunī" refers to a certain paccekabuddha. "With feet bruised" means with feet struck by hot sand;
the meaning is that her feet were afflicted. "Thirsty" means parched with thirst. "She provided" means she supplied or furnished.
"Kāmaduhā" means the one who grants all desires.

Hearing this, the Great Being, with a heart full of joy, thought: "Even in such a supportless great ocean, the gift of the sunshade and sandals given by me has become a granter of all my desires; oh, it is well-given! He then said:
"Let that ship, equipped with planks, leak-proof, and driven by the *eraka* wind, proceed;
for there is no ground here for any other vehicle. May she bring me, wearing my hair-knot, to my destination this very day."
He spoke this verse.

In that context, "furnished with planks" means equipped with many planks due to the great size of the ship. "Not leaking" means because there was no entry of water. "Yoked to the *eraka*-grass wind" means driven by the wind that carries it along as it is properly seized.
Having heard his words, the daughter of the gods, delighted and joyful, [constructed a ship] eight *usabhas* in length and four *usabhas* in width.

Having fashioned a ship twenty fathoms deep made of the seven precious gems, and having constructed masts, rudders, and fittings made of sapphire, silver, gold, and other materials, he filled it with the seven jewels, embraced the brahmin, and helped him board the ship; however, he did not even look at his attendant.
The brahmin, because of the merit he had performed himself, gave the gift to the Buddha, who then expressed his appreciation.

Then the goddess, having embraced him and placed him upon the ship, brought that ship to the city of Moḷinī, deposited wealth in the house of the brahmin, and returned to her own dwelling place. Regarding this, the Blessed One said:
“Delighted there, joyful and glad, she fashioned a beautifully adorned ship;”
"Taking the conch shell, he brought it with the man to the city, which was most delightful.

Indeed, due to the excellence of the Great Man's intention and because the Paccekabuddha had emerged from cessation (*nirodha*), among the seven types of volition (*cetanā*), this initial volition became one to be experienced in this very life (*diṭṭhadhammavedanīya*) and produced an exceedingly magnificent fruit. This too was [the result] of that gift.
It should be understood as having a limited fruit. For that gift, being a constituent of the equipment for enlightenment (bodhisambhāra), has an immeasurable fruit. Therefore it was said:
“For that very reason, though I was delicate and nurtured in luxury, yet fulfilling my duty of giving, I gave to him in this manner.”
In this context, "from him" means from that Paccekabuddha. "A hundredfold" means by a hundredfold [increase]. At that time, I was Saṅkha, a man of delicate refinement;

therefore, I was nurtured in comfort and brought up in luxury. Nevertheless, even while being thus, as I fulfilled the perfection of giving—thinking, "May my perfection of giving be fulfilled in this way"—I disregarded the suffering of my own body for the sake of that Paccekabuddha.
The Teacher proclaimed the greatness of his own inclination toward generosity by saying, "I gave him a sunshade and a throne.

Even while dwelling in a house of immeasurable wealth for as long as he lived, the Bodhisatta gave gifts in even greater measure, guarded his moral precepts, and at the end of his life, together with his retinue, filled the city of the gods.
At that time, Uppalavaṇṇā was the daughter of the gods, Ānanda Thera was the man, and the Lord of the World was the brahmin Saṅkha.
For him, the perfection of virtue (*sīlapāramī*) consists in his perfectly purified constant virtue, Uposatha virtue, and so forth;
the perfection of renunciation (*nekkhammapāramī*) consists in wholesome states (*kusaladhamma*), because it has emerged from the opposites of giving, virtue, and the rest;

and the perfection of energy (*vīriyapāramī*) consists in the exertion for the sake of accomplishing giving and the other perfections, as well as the effort in crossing the great ocean. For that same purpose, there is the perfection of patience (*khantipāramī*) by way of endurance.

The perfection of patience; the perfection of truth through practice in accordance with one’s promise; the perfection of determination by way of an unwavering resolve and undertaking in all circumstances;
the perfection of loving-kindness through the inclination toward the welfare of all beings;

the perfection of equanimity through the attainment of a state of neutrality toward the various manifestations produced by the formations of beings; and having understood the phenomena that are conducive or non-conducive to all the perfections.

Wisdom that consists in skillful means—which precedes the practice of promoting beneficial qualities while abandoning unbeneficial qualities, and which is co-nascent with them—is called the perfection of wisdom (*paññāpāramī*);
thus these perfections are also found here.
However, because the inclination toward giving is exceedingly exalted, the teaching proceeds by way of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramī*). And because in this context:

The ten perfections (pāramiyo) are obtained; therefore, the qualities of a Bodhisatta mentioned below, such as great compassion (mahākaruṇā) and so forth, should also be extracted here as appropriate.

Likewise, disregarding one's own wealth and happiness, out of great compassion and with the thought, "I shall fulfill the perfection of giving," there is the crossing of the ocean for the sake of gathering the requisites for giving; and even when one has fallen into that ocean—

The resolve on the Uposatha, and the refusal to take food even when approached by a celestial maiden out of fear that his virtue might be impaired—such qualities of the Great Being are to be understood.
Now, regarding the remaining deeds that will be described, the determination of his virtues should be understood in this very same manner;
we shall mention only the specific distinctions in each respective case. Therefore, it is said:
“Thus these things of the Great Seer are wonderful and marvelous... [as before]...
even before, they acted in accordance with the Dhamma, following the way of the Dhamma.
The commentary on the conduct of the Brahmin Saṅkha is finished.

3. Explanation of the Conduct of the King of Kuru (Kururājacariyāvaṇṇanā) In the third [chapter], "in Indapatta, the most excellent city"—that is, in the preeminent city named Indapatta, the supreme capital of the kingdom of Kuru.

"A king" (rājā): he is called a king because he delights the assembly with righteousness, impartiality, and the four bases of sympathy (saṅgahavatthu). "He has arrived at the ten wholesome [courses of action]" (kusale dasahupāgato).
The meaning is that he was endowed with the ten wholesome [qualities], or associated with the ten bases of meritorious action beginning with giving, or with the ten courses of wholesome kamma.
"From the territory of the kingdom of Kaliṅga": this means from the territory known as the kingdom of Kaliṅga.
"Eight brahmins approached me," they said, having been dispatched by the King of Kaliṅga; those eight brahmins drew near to me. Having drawn near, they made a request of me for a state elephant.

They entreated me, who had become an elephant, a great nāga. "Fortunate" means one who has attained prosperity and excellence worthy of being esteemed as wealth, and who is endowed with auspicious marks.
"Consented to as an omen" means that because of that very perfection of marks, he was recognized by people as an omen that causes the increase of welfare.
22. "Without rain" means devoid of rainfall. "Famine" means food is difficult to obtain. "Great drought" means a vast [period of] lack of rain.
The meaning is that the affliction of hunger prevails. "Dadāhi" means "give. "Nīla" means blue-colored.
"Añjanasavhaya" means that which is to be called by the name "añjana"; the meaning is "named añjana. This is what is said:
our kingdom of Kaliṅga has had no rain; therefore, a great famine has now arisen there, and a vast fear of drought has come upon it.
"Give me this auspicious elephant named Añjana, who resembles Mount Añjana, for the sake of pacifying [the calamity].
For when he is led there, the rain-god will send down rain, and by that, all fear will be pacified. Herein is the sequential account:
In the past, in the city of Indapatta in the kingdom of Kuru, the Bodhisatta took rebirth in the womb of the chief queen of the King of Kuru.
Having been taken [in], he gradually reached maturity; having gone to Takkasilā and mastered the various fields of craft and branches of knowledge taught through disciplined application, he returned.
His father appointed him as viceroy, and later, upon his father’s passing, he attained the kingship.
Ruling righteously without violating the ten duties of a king, he was known by the name Dhanañjaya. He, in the four...
Having established six halls for giving— at the city gates, in the center of the city, and at the doors of his residence—
he bestowed gifts throughout the entire land of Jambudīpa, making it free from the plow, while expending six hundred thousand pieces of wealth daily.
His inclination toward giving and his delight in generosity spread across the whole of Jambudīpa.
At that time, three fears arose in the kingdom of Kaliṅga: the fear of famine, the fear of drought, and the fear of disease.
All the inhabitants of the kingdom went to Dantapura and raised a clamor at the gate of the royal palace, crying out, "O King, make the rain fall!
When the king heard this, he asked his ministers, "For what reason are these people shouting?"
The ministers reported that matter to the king. The king asked, "What did the kings of old do when the rain did not fall?
They replied, "They gave gifts, saying, 'May the rain fall! Having undertaken the Uposatha and observed the precepts, they would enter the inner chamber and lie upon a bed of grass for seven days.
Upon hearing this, the king acted accordingly. But the rain did not fall; thus it was with the king.
"I have performed the duty that was to be done by me, yet the rain does not fall; what shall we do?
"Sire, when the auspicious elephant of Dhanañjaya, the King of the Kurus, is brought to the city of Indapatta, the rain will fall.
"That king is powerful, well-equipped with a great army, and difficult to overcome; how shall we bring his elephant? "Great King, together with him..."

There is no need for war; that king, being inclined toward generosity and delighting in giving, would—if requested—cut off even his own decorated arm, pluck out his very eyes which were endowed with clarity, and surrender his entire kingdom.
There is nothing to be said regarding the elephant: he will certainly give it when asked. But who is capable of making such a request?
"O Brahmins, Great King! Thus addressed, the king summoned eight Brahmins, honored them with hospitality and respect, and provided them with travel expenses, dispatching them to request the elephant.
They traveled with great haste, staying only one night at each place along the way.
After spending several days at the city gates, eating in the alms-halls and refreshing their bodies, they set out on the path by which the king’s almsgiving procession would arrive.
Waiting for the appointed time, they stood at the eastern gate.
The Bodhisatta, too, having bathed and anointed himself early in the morning and being adorned with all his ornaments, mounted the back of a magnificent, decorated state elephant;
accompanied by great royal splendor, he went to the hall of giving, descended from the elephant, and personally bestowed gifts upon seven or eight people.
Having given [the gift] and said, "Give it in this very manner," he mounted his elephant and went to the southern gate.
Because the protection at the eastern gate was so strong, the brahmins found no opportunity there;
they went to the southern gate and, standing on an elevated spot not far from the gate, watched for the king as he approached. When the king arrived, they—
Raising their hands, they made him victorious. King Vajiraṅkusa turned back the elephant and, approaching those brahmins, asked them, "What do you desire?
The brahmins replied, "The kingdom of Kaliṅga is afflicted by the fear of famine, the fear of drought, and the fear of disease.
That affliction [must be removed] by this auspicious elephant of yours."
“When brought here, it will be mixed with collyrium. Therefore, give us this elephant named Añjana. To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
“From the territory of the kingdom of Kaliṅga... [the elephant] named Añjana. The meaning of that has already been explained.
Then the Bodhisatta thought: “It is not fitting for me that there should be a frustration of the desires of those who ask of me, nor for myself...”

Thinking, "There might be a difference in the formal undertaking [of the gift]," he descended from the back of the elephant and said, "If there is any part that is not adorned, I shall adorn it and give it.

Looking all around and seeing no unadorned spot, he took the elephant by its trunk, placed it in the hands of the brahmins, poured water scented with flowers and perfumes from a jeweled pitcher, and gave it away. Thus it is said:
“When a petitioner has approached me, refusal is not fitting for me.
Let not my commitment fail; I shall give away this magnificent elephant.
Taking the elephant by its trunk, [I shall pour from] the jeweled jars.”
"Having poured water into my hand, I gave it to the brahmins," he said.
Therein, "when the supplicants had arrived" means when the beggars had come. "Suitable" means appropriate and fitting.
"May my undertaking not be broken" means that for the sake of omniscience, everything desired by every supplicant [should be] blameless.
"My vow was: 'Giving, I shall fulfill the perfection of generosity; may that resolve of mine not be broken. Therefore, I will give;
I will give this great, auspicious elephant. Thus he gave.
When that elephant had been given away, the ministers said this to the Bodhisatta: "Why, Great King, [did you give] the auspicious elephant?"
“Give it! Surely another elephant should be given; indeed, such a state elephant, a bringer of prosperity, should not be given by a king who desires sovereignty and victory.
The Great Being replied, “Whatever the supplicants ask of me, that alone must be given by me.
Even if they were to ask for my kingdom, I would give them even the kingdom; for what use have I for a kingdom?”
"Even more dear than life itself is omniscient knowledge; therefore, he gave that elephant," so it was said.
By this, it is stated: "When that elephant was given," and so forth. In that context, *tassa* means "to him by him" or "when that elephant was given.
26. *Maṅgalasampannaṃ* means endowed with auspicious qualities. *Saṅgāmavijayuttamaṃ* means supreme in victory in battle.
"Supreme" means either supreme in victory in battle or a supreme, excellent steed (*nāga*). "What will your kingdom do?
means: once that steed has departed, what will your kingdom do? It shows that it will not perform the duties of a kingdom;
indeed, the kingdom itself has vanished.
"27. Let alone the elephant, who is but a mere animal; let me give even my entire kingdom to supplicants.
As for the phrase 'I would give even my own body,' what need is there to say more regarding the kingdom?
I would give even my own body to supplicants, for every possession of mine, both internal and external, was acquired by me solely for the benefit of the world."

It was surrendered. He shows that he gave away the elephant, thinking: "Since omniscience is dear to me, and since omniscience cannot be attained without fulfilling all the perfections—beginning with the perfection of giving—it is for this reason that I have given the elephant.
Even when that elephant had been brought there, it still did not rain in the kingdom of Kaliṅga. King Kaliṅga [thought], "Even now..."
"It is raining; what indeed is the cause? Having asked this, and having understood—"The King of Kuru observes the heavy rules (garudhamma);
therefore, in his kingdom, it rains every half-month and every ten days.
This is the power of the king's virtue, not that of this animal"—they said, "We too shall observe the heavy rules; go to Dhanañjaya Koravya and tell him:"
"Have them written on golden plates and bring them here," he sent to his ministers. The "heavy rules" (garudhamma) are said to be the five precepts;
the Bodhisatta observes these having made them perfectly pure, just as the Bodhisatta does.
Likewise, his mother was the chief queen, his younger brother was the viceroy, the chaplain was a brahmin, the official who took charge of the kingdom was a minister, and the charioteer—
The treasurer, the granary-measurer, the gatekeeper, and the city-beautifying courtesan. Therefore it was said:
“The king, the mother, the chief queen, the viceroy, the court chaplain;
The land-surveyor, the charioteer, the treasurer, the granary-measurer, and likewise the gatekeeper;”
“Your courtesan has established herself in the eleven weighty rules.
Those ministers approached the Bodhisatta, paid homage to him, and reported that matter to him.
The Great Being said, “I have scruples regarding these weighty rules; however, my mother protects her well-guarded daughter-in-law, so receive them from her.”
Having spoken thus, they requested of him, “Great King, remorse arises for one who desires to train and lives in austerity; please grant this to us.

He had it written upon golden plates: “No living being is to be killed, nothing not given is to be taken, sexual misconduct is not to be practiced, falsehood is not to be spoken, and intoxicants are not to be drunk. Even though this was so, [he said] regarding his mother:
"Take it from me," she said.
The messengers, having paid homage to the king, went into her presence and said, "Queen, it is said that you observe the heavy rules (garudhamma);
grant them to us. The Bodhisatta’s mother likewise [informed them] of the existence of her own remorse.
Having spoken thus, when requested by them, she gave [the precepts]. Likewise did Mahesī and the others.
They had all the heavy rules (garudhammas) inscribed upon golden plates in the presence of everyone, went to Dantapura, gave them to the King of Kaliṅga, and reported that matter to him.
That king, conducting himself according to those teachings, fulfilled the five precepts. Thereupon, rain fell throughout the entire kingdom of Kaliṅga.
It rained. The three fears were pacified; the kingdom became secure and possessed of abundant food.
The Bodhisatta, having performed meritorious deeds such as giving throughout his life, filled the city of heaven together with his retinue.
At that time, the courtesans and others became Uppalavaṇṇā and the rest. For this has been said:
“Uppalavaṇṇā was the courtesan, Puṇṇa the gatekeeper at that time;
Kaccāna the rope-handler, and Kolita the measurer of grain.
Sāriputta was the merchant then, and Anuruddha the charioteer.”
The Elder Kassapa the Brahmin, and the wise Uparājānanda;
Mahesī Rāhulamātā, Queen Māyā the mother,
and the Bodhisatta as the King of Kuru— thus you should remember this Jātaka.
Here too, the remaining qualities, such as the perfection of renunciation (*nekkhamma-pāramī*) and so forth, are to be determined in the same manner already described.
The commentary on the conduct of the King of Kuru is finished.
4. Commentary on the Conduct of Mahāsudassana.
28. "In the fourth [chapter], 'in the city of Kusāvatī' means in the city named Kusāvatī, the site where Kusinārā is now situated.

'Lord of the earth' means a kṣatriya; by name he was called Mahāsudassana. 'Wheel-turning monarch' (cakravartin) means one who sets the wheel-treasure in motion, or who turns by means of the four wheels of prosperity, and causes others to turn by them for the benefit of others."

He is also called a *cakkavattī* because he possesses the turning (*vatta*) of the wheels of the modes of conduct (*iriyāpatha*). Alternatively, he is a *cakkavattī* because he possesses the turning of the wheel known as his command—which cannot be overcome or transgressed by others—being endowed with the four wonderful qualities and the four bases of sympathy (*saṅgahavatthu*).
[He is accompanied] by the jewel of the counselor (*pariṇāyakaratana*) at the forefront, with the jewel of the elephant (*hatthiratana*) and others as the principal [jewels].
He is "possessed of great strength" because he is endowed with a body of great power produced by the majesty of his merit (*puññānubhāva*) and with physical strength.
The connection is with the word "when" (*yadā*). Herein, this is the sequential narrative:
It is said that in the past, in his third existence following the Sudassana existence, the Great Man was reborn into a householders' family.
During the dispensation of a living Buddha, a man entered the forest on his own business and,
seeing an elder dwelling in the wilderness seated at the foot of a tree, thought, "It is fitting that I build a leaf-hut here for this noble one.
Abandoning his own work, he cut timber and constructed a leaf-hut suitable for habitation.
Having secured the door and prepared a bed of wood, he sat to one side, wondering, "Will he make use of it, or will he not?
The Elder, having come from within the village, entered the leaf hut and sat down upon the wooden bed.
The Great Being approached him and asked, "Is the leaf hut comfortable, venerable sir? "It is comfortable, my dear friend."
"Suitable for one who has gone forth. "Will you stay here, venerable sir? "Yes, lay follower.
Knowing from his very manner of acceptance that he would stay, and having made him promise, "You must come regularly to my house," he had the meal-offering always prepared in his own home.
He spread out a mat of straw in the leaf-hut.
He prepared beds and stools, set up a backrest, and placed footstools; he dug a lotus pond, constructed a walking path, and scattered sand over it;
for the sake of warding off dangers, he surrounded the leaf-hut with a fence of thorns, as he did for the lotus pond and the walking path;
and along the inner boundary of the enclosure, he planted rows of palm trees. In this manner...

Having completed the dwelling, he gave the Elder all the requisites for a recluse, beginning with the three robes. For at that time, the Bodhisatta had not yet given to the Elder any of the articles used by those who have gone forth, such as the three robes, alms-food, a bowl,
a water-pot, a water-strainer, a needle-case, vessels for personal use, a sunshade, sandals, a water-jar, a needle, a small stick, a reed-pin, a nail-cutter, or oil for lamps.
He had no other name. Guarding the five precepts and observing the Uposatha, he attended upon the Elder for as long as he lived.
While dwelling right there, the Elder attained Arahantship and passed away into Parinibbāna.
The Bodhisatta, too, having performed meritorious deeds for the duration of his lifespan, was reborn in the world of the devas; when he passed away from there, he returned to the human world.
Having been reborn in the royal capital of Kusāvatī, he became a wheel-turning monarch named Mahāsudassana.

The extent of his sovereign power has indeed come down in the Sutta in this manner: "In the past, Ānanda, there was a consecrated kshatriya king named Mahāsudassana," and so forth. It is said that he had eighty-four thousand cities.
The eighty-four thousand palaces headed by the Palace of Dhamma, the eighty-four thousand gabled chambers headed by the Mahābyūha gabled chamber, and the eighty-four thousand couches and elephants—

all these were produced as the natural result of that single leaf-hut built for the Elder. The eighty-four thousand palaces headed by Kusāvatī the royal capital, the eighty-four thousand gabled chambers headed by the Mahābyūha gabled chamber,
the eighty-four thousand couches, and the eighty-four thousand elephants— [all these were produced as the natural result of that single leaf-hut built for the Elder].
There were a thousand horses and a thousand chariots for that bed and chair which was given; eighty-four thousand jewels for that lamp which was given;

eighty-four thousand lotus ponds for each single pond; and eighty-four thousand women, eighty-four thousand sons, and eighty-four thousand householders for one who is worthy of using bowls, basins, and other such articles.
These were produced as the natural result of his gift of requisites for those who have gone forth, his gift of eighty-four thousand cows with their five products of milk,
his gift of eighty-four thousand sets of lower and upper garments, and his gift of eighty-four thousand pots of cooked rice as food.
Thus, he was a supreme king endowed with the seven treasures and the four supernormal powers.
Having offered sacrifice and having conquered the entire circle of the earth bounded by the ocean through righteousness, he dwelt there.
Having caused alms-halls to be built in many hundreds of places, he established a great distribution of gifts. Three times a day, he had the drum beaten in the city, saying:
"Whoever desires anything, let him come to the alms-halls and take it. Therefore it was said: "There, I..."
“Three times a day, I had it proclaimed here and there,” and so forth.
Regarding that, “there and there” means in that city. There is also a reading, “Then I said,” which means “then I, at the time of Mahāsudassana.
“There and there” means in each respective place, both inside and outside of each respective wall.
"Meaning": Who desires what? Any being whatsoever among the brahmins and others desires anything whatsoever among the objects of giving such as food and so forth.
"Longs for" is a synonym for that same word. The phrase "To whom shall wealth be given?

is stated in order to show that the proclamation of giving was carried out on many occasions through various methods; by this, he shows the essential nature of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).
For the perfection of giving (dānapāramī) of Bodhisattvas is indeed free from any discrimination regarding the recipient of the gift.
Now, in order to show the praise of the various persons appropriate for each specific object of giving through the proclamation of giving, it is said: “Who is hungry? and so forth.

In this context, “hungry” means one who suffers from hunger; “thirsty” means one who suffers from thirst. “Who desires a garland? Who [desires] ointment?”—thus [it is asked]. “Who desires? is understood.
The word should be brought forward and connected [to the previous]. "Naked" (*nagga*) means lacking clothing; the intended meaning is that he has need of a garment.

"He will clothe himself" (*paridahissati*) means he will wear it as an undergarment. 31. "Who takes an umbrella on the road?"—who, being a traveler, takes an umbrella on the path for the sake of protection against rain, wind, and heat;
the meaning is that he has need of an umbrella. "Soft and beautiful sandals"—"beautiful" (*subhā*) because of their visual appeal.
The sandals are soft because of their pleasant touch, for the purpose of protecting one’s own feet and eyes.

"Who takes them? means "Who has need of them?"—this is the intended meaning. Regarding the phrase "both evening and morning," the word "and" (ca) implies that "at midday" should also be supplied, for it was stated: "I have them sounded three times a day."
32. "Not in ten places" means that this gift was not prepared in ten places; such is the construction.
Nor was it prepared in a hundred places, but rather it was prepared in many hundreds of places.
"Wealth for beggars" means wealth prepared and set aside specifically for beggars. For in a city twelve *yojanas* in length and seven *yojanas* in breadth...
Within the seven inner enclosures were seven rows of palm trees;
by each of those palm rows, eighty-four thousand lotus ponds were established, and on the banks of each individual lotus pond, a great almsgiving was instituted. For this was said by the Blessed One:
"Ānanda, King Mahāsudassana instituted such a kind of almsgiving on the banks of those lotus ponds."
"Food for one who needs food, drink for one who needs drink, clothing for one who needs clothing, a vehicle for one who needs a vehicle,
a bed for one who needs a bed, a woman for one who needs a woman, silver for one who needs silver, and gold for one who needs gold."
33. Herein, this is the manner in which the giving was carried out: the Great Man had ornaments fashioned suitable for both women and men;
he established there a group of women solely for the purpose of entertainment, while setting aside everything else for the purpose of relinquishment.
Then he had a drum beaten, [proclaiming]: "King Mahāsudassana gives a gift; enjoy it as you please."
He caused [the lotus pond] to be made available. Great crowds of people went to the bank of the lotus pond, bathed, put on their clothes and other garments, and enjoyed great prosperity.
Those who possessed such things left them behind as they departed; those who had none took them with them.
Some, having sat upon elephant-vehicles and the like, wandered about as they pleased, and having slept upon excellent couches, experienced that prosperity.

Having experienced prosperity even with women, having adorned themselves with the seven kinds of precious ornaments and enjoyed that prosperity, those who had need of anything took what they required and departed; those who had no need left it behind and went on.
Yet that gift was given day after day, rising up again and again. At that time, for the inhabitants of Jambudīpa...
There was no other work for him; wandering about enjoying his prosperity, he partook of the offerings.
There was no limit to the duration of that giving. Whether by night or by day, whenever those in need arrived, it was given then and there.
In this way, throughout his life, the Great Man made the whole of Jambudīpa free from plowing and bestowed great alms.
He set it in motion. Therefore it was said: “Whether by day or by night, if a beggar comes,” and so forth.
Therein, by the phrase “whether by day or by night, if he comes,” he shows that his giving occurs at the appropriate time.
For indeed, the very moment when supplicants approach out of hope for gain is called the time for the Bodhisattvas’ giving. “Vanibbaka” means a beggar.

"Having obtained whatever wealth he desires": by this, it is shown that he gives according to his own inclination. For whichever supplicant desires whichever object of merit (*deyyadhamma*), the Bodhisatta gives that very thing to him.
He did not consider whether it was expensive or rare, nor did he think of any personal hardship. "He goes with his hands full": by this, he demonstrates giving as much as is desired.
Indeed, whatever the supplicants desired, the Great Being gave it all without exception, owing to his sublime aspiration and his great supernormal power.
By the phrase "for as long as life lasts," he shows that there is no limit to the duration of this giving, starting from the moment of its formal undertaking.
For great beings do not set a time limit until their fulfillment is complete;
because they lack any shrinking back in the accumulation of the requisites for enlightenment, there is no interruption even by death due to falling into despondency midway.
Since they continue to practice in that very same way even thereafter, it is said to be "for as long as life lasts" with reference to the conduct of Mahāsudassana.

"Nor do I give wealth that should not be given" means: "This wealth is not to be given by me because it is unpleasant"—giving such a great gift, I cause wealth to be brought out from my house. "Nor is there no store with me" means:
there is indeed a store of wealth, a collection of wealth near me; nor am I one who lacks all possessions, like a monk living in austerity.
This is the meaning. This was stated in order to show the underlying intention (*ajjhāsaya*) by which this great gift was bestowed.
35. Now, in order to clarify that through a simile, he said: "Just as a man who is ill," and so forth.
Herein, the explanation of the meaning together with the application of the simile is as follows: Just as a man who is ill, overcome by disease, desiring to liberate himself from that illness...
Just as one who satisfies and propitiates a physician with wealth such as gold and bullion, and proceeds according to the prescribed method,
is thereby liberated from disease;
even so, in this very same way, I too [liberate] the entire world, which has become afflicted, from the disease of the defilements and from the disease of all the suffering of saṃsāra.
And desiring to liberate [beings] from that, knowing and understanding that this relinquishing of all one's possessions is the means (*upāya*) for the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*),
he— by way of the objects to be given and the recipients without exception, and by way of a great gift without remainder—
acts to fulfill the aspirations of sentient beings and [realizes]: "My own perfection of giving is not yet complete."
Therefore, thinking, "I give this gift to those who beg and entreat me to fulfill their deficient minds and set them on the path," I give such a great gift;
and yet, being detached from that act of giving and its fruit,
without expectation or longing for anything whatsoever, I give solely for the sake of attaining full enlightenment and realizing omniscience.
Thus, while bestowing the great gift, the Great Being ascended the Dhamma Palace produced by the power of his own merit;
having turned back thoughts of sensual desire and the like right at the door of the Mahābyūha gabled chamber,
he sat upon a golden royal couch there, developed the jhānas and higher knowledges (abhiññā), and then, emerging from that, entered the golden gabled chamber.
There, seated upon a couch made of silver, he cultivated the four divine abidings (*brahmavihāra*) and spent eighty-four thousand years in meditative attainments (*jhānasamāpatti*).
At the time of his death, to the eighty-four thousand women of the harem headed by Queen Subhaddā, as well as to the ministers, assembly members, and others who had approached to see him—
“Impermanent indeed are conditioned phenomena, subject to arising and passing away;
having arisen, they cease—their subsiding is bliss.
Having exhorted him with this verse, at the end of his life, he reached the Brahma-world as his final destination.
At that time, Queen Subhaddā was the mother of Rāhula; the Jewel of the General was Rāhula; the rest of the assembly was the Buddha’s assembly;

and Mahāsudassana was the Protector of the World. Here too, the ten perfections (pāramīs) are indeed found in their own form; however, because of the excellence of his inclination toward giving, only the perfection of giving (dānapāramī) is mentioned in the Pāli text.
The remaining qualities are exactly as described in the previous method. Likewise, in that [kingdom] which was magnificent and resplendent with the seven jewels...
Even while established in the sovereignty over the four continents, not adorning himself with such sensual pleasures,
but having suppressed sensual thoughts and the like from afar, and while engaged in such great acts of giving, he spent eighty-four thousand years in meditative attainments; yet,
even after delivering a discourse on the Dhamma connected with impermanence and other such themes, he showed no complacency regarding insight.
"Unattached in all things"—such qualities and powers are to be extracted [from the text].
The commentary on the *Mahāsudassana-cariyā* is finished.
5. Commentary on the *Mahāgovinda-cariyā*.
In the fifth [verse], "the family priest of the seven kings" refers to the chaplain who instructed all the affairs of the seven kings, beginning with Sattabhū.
"Honored by men and gods" means he was honored by those very kings, as well as by all the kṣatriyas in Jambudvīpa, through the four requisites and through respectful salutation.
"The brahmin Mahāgovinda" is so called because of his great majesty and his consecration as Govinda.
And because of his consecration, the brahmin came to be known as "Mahāgovinda.
Indeed, from the time of his consecration onward, this became the Bodhisatta’s conventional title; however, by name, he was called Jotipāla.
It is said that on the day of his birth, all weapons blazed with light. At dawn, the king also saw his own auspicious weapon flaming.
Terrified, he questioned his own chaplain who had come to pay respects to the Bodhisatta’s father.
[The chaplain replied: “Do not fear, Great King! My son has been born; by his power, not only in Rājagaha but throughout the entire city did weapons burst into flame.
There is no danger for you because of him; however, in all of Jambudīpa, in terms of wisdom—”
“There will be no one equal to him; this is a premonitory sign of that,” the chaplain reassured him.
With a joyful heart, the king gave a thousand [pieces of gold], saying, “Let this be the prince’s sustenance for milk,” and added, “When he reaches maturity, you must give it to me.
Later, when he had grown up, Alamatthadassa became the advisor on all affairs for seven kings.
Having gone forth, he protected beings from misfortunes pertaining to both the present life and the future life, and established them in what is beneficial.
Thus, because of his brilliance and his capacity for protection, they gave him the name "Jotipāla. Therefore it is said: "By name, Jotipāla by name.
Therein, the Bodhisatta was born as the son of the brahmin Govinda, who was the family priest to King Disampati.
Upon the passing of his own father and that king, his son Reṇu— along with his seven companions,
Sattabhū, Brahmadatta, Vessabhū, Bharata, and the two Dhataraṭṭhas— established these seven kings so that they would not quarrel with one another.
Having thus established them in their kingdoms, while instructing them in their welfare and the Dhamma, he [reigned] over all the kings upon the surface of Jambudīpa.
He became honored, revered, esteemed, worshipped, and respected by other brahmins, as well as by gods, nāgas, and householders, attaining the position of supreme dignity.
Because of his skill in matters of welfare and the Dhamma, the designation "Mahāgovinda" (Great Steward) arose for him.
As it is said: "Oh, what a steward indeed is this brahmin! Oh, what a great steward indeed is this brahmin! Therefore it was said:
“Furthermore, when I was the chaplain to seven kings,
the brahmin Mahāgovinda, honored by men and gods. Then,
by the power of the Bodhisatta’s merit, the kings, their vassals, the kshatriyas, brahmins, and householders were stirred to action.
And as he was being brought higher and higher by the people of the towns and the countryside,
an immeasurable and sublime gain and honor arose, overwhelming him like a great flood from all sides— such as befits one who has accumulated a vast store of merit over countless births,
who is of noble birth, whose virtue and conduct are pure, who is gentle, and whose every craft is perfectly refined among all beings.
His heart was moistened by the expansion of a great compassion that was like that for his own son. He thought: "At present, I possess great gain and honor;
what if I were to satisfy all beings with this and thereby fulfill the perfection of generosity?
He then had six halls of giving constructed—at the four gates of the city and at the door of his own residence.
Every day he established a great almsgiving by the relinquishment of immeasurable wealth.
Whatever gift was brought as an offering, and whatever was prepared for his own use, he sent it all to the halls of distribution.
Even as he made such great sacrifices day after day, there was no satiety or contentment in his mind; how much less [could there be any lack thereof]?

However, there was a contraction [of the city]. Both within and outside the city, the great multitude of people— who had come to the site of the giving with the hope of obtaining alms, who were taking the objects to be given,
and who were proclaiming the special virtues of the Great Being— formed a single surging flood,
like the great ocean tossed about by the impact of the great winds at the end of an eon.
There was a single clamor, a single roar. Therefore it was said:
“Then, whatever offerings I had from the seven kingdoms, With those I gave a great gift, unshakeable like the ocean.”
In this context, "Tadāhanti" means: when I was the brahmin Mahāgovinda, the chaplain to the seven kings, then I [was so].

"In the kingdoms of the seven kings" means in the realms of the seven kings beginning with Reṇu. "Unshakable" (akkhobhaṃ) means unshakeable by anyone because it could not be resisted by internal or external adversaries.
There is also a reading, "Accubbhaṃ. [This refers to] one whose intention for giving is exceedingly full.
The meaning is that it is exceedingly full due to the loftiness and abundance of the gift to be given.
"Like the ocean" means similar to the ocean; just as the water in the ocean cannot be exhausted even if the entire world were to carry it away, so too is the gift to be given in that almsgiving.
39. In the concluding verse, *varaṃ dhanaṃ* means the best wealth or the desired wealth. The rest is exactly as previously stated.
Thus, like the great cloud at the beginning of an eon (*paṭhamakappika-mahāmegha*), the Great Being, raining down a vast torrent of giving without distinction, remained engaged in acts of charity;
yet, even while occupied with giving, he remained diligent in instructing the remaining seven kings in matters of welfare and righteousness (*attha-dhamma*).
He taught the knowledge and skills to seven great brahmin householders and had seven hundred bath-graduated brahmins recite the mantras.
At a later time, an excellent report concerning him spread abroad:
"The brahmin Mahāgovinda truly sees Brahmā; the brahmin Mahāgovinda truly converses with, speaks to, and consults with Brahmā."
He thought: "At present, this false report concerning me has spread abroad:
'The Great Steward Brahmin sees Brahmā; he converses with, speaks with, and consults Brahmā.
What if I were now to make this true? He [summoned] those seven kings and the seven wealthy brahmins...

Having made a mental aspiration, thinking, “May I see Brahmā after taking leave of my hundred wives who have bathed and my sons and wife,” he devoted himself for the four months of the rainy season to the cultivation of the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra*).
Knowing the reflection in his mind with his own mind, Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra appeared before him. Upon seeing him, the Great Man asked:
“Endowed with beauty, renown, and glory—who indeed are you, O worthy one?
Not knowing you, we ask: how may we come to know you?
Then Brahmā, making himself known to him—
“‘They indeed know me as the youth Sanantana in the Brahma-world;
all the gods know me— know me thus, O Govinda,’ having said this by him— ”
“‘A seat, water for the feet, and food with honey and vegetables—O Brahmā, we ask you regarding these honors; may you accept our offering.
Although Brahmā had no need for the hospitality thus presented, he accepted it in order to gladden his mind and to inspire confidence in him.”
Accepting it, he said: "We accept your offer, Govinda, whatever you say. Having spoken thus, for the sake of granting him leave to speak, he added:
"For the benefit and welfare in this present life, and for happiness in the life to come—being granted leave, ask whatever you desire."
He granted him the opportunity.
Then the Great Man, concerning only the welfare of the future life, said:
"I ask Brahmā Sanaṅkumāra, being one who doubts about things that should be known by others."
"Abiding where and training in what does a mortal attain the deathless Brahma-world?"—
thus he asked.
To him, Brahmā replied:
“O Brahmā, among human beings, having abandoned possessiveness, become solitary, and be intent on compassion;
free from the stench of raw flesh and abstaining from sexual intercourse— one who stands here and trains here,
that mortal attains the deathless world of Brahmā.”
He spoke of the path leading to the Brahma-world.

Regarding the phrase "they certainly know me as a youth": they indeed know me one-pointedly as a "youth. "In the Brahma-world" means in the supreme world. "Sanantana" means ancient, belonging to the past. "Thus, Govinda, know me": O Govinda, remember me thus. "The seat":
this seat has been prepared for the venerable Brahmā to sit upon. "This water" is for his use.
Water for washing the feet is for the purpose of quenching thirst. This is the foot-paste; this is the oil for anointing the feet, intended to dispel fatigue.
By "sweet vegetables," he means vegetables that are unseasoned with buttermilk, unsalted, and unfried, having been merely steamed with water.
For at that time, the Bodhisatta’s four-month period of holy living was characterized by the highest degree of ascetic austerity.
"Let us make all these things an offering for him and ask: 'May your lordship deign to assign a value to this; may your lordship accept this as its value.

This is what was said. Thus, although the Great Man knew that Brahmā would not consume them, he spoke thus while standing at the head of his duty, demonstrating his own habitual practice of honoring guests. Brahmā also understood his intention.
Knowing this, he said, "We accept your price, O Govinda, which you have spoken.
In that context, the meaning is: "May we be as if seated on those seats of yours; may our feet be as if washed with water for the feet;
may we be as if having drunk the drinking water; may our feet be as if anointed with foot-ointment; and may even the water-cress be as if consumed by us."

"Having become free from doubt regarding what is to be known by others": being possessed of doubt, I became free from doubt concerning those questions to be known by others—those things made manifest by another because they were personally conditioned by him.
"Having abandoned possessiveness": having cast off the craving for requisites that functions as "this is mine, this is my own.
"Among men": among beings. "The Brahma": he addresses the Bodhisatta. "Become solitary": one who rises and proceeds alone is "become solitary" (*ekodibhūta*).
"Become one" (*ekībhūto*) indicates physical seclusion by means of being alone. Alternatively, "one-pointed" (*ekodi*) refers to concentration (*samādhi*), as it arises as one;
one who has become that is "become one-pointed" (*ekodibhūto*), meaning he is concentrated through access and absorption concentration.

Showing this state of one-pointedness by way of the divine abode of compassion, he said, "devoted to compassion" (*karuṇedhimutto*). This means he is devoted to the jhāna of compassion, having produced that jhāna.
The meaning is as follows: "Free from the stench of raw flesh" (*nirāmagandha*) means devoid of the foul odor known as the defilements (*kilesa*).
"Established herein" (*etthaṭṭhita*) means established in these qualities, having accomplished these qualities. And "training herein" (*ettha ca sikkhamāna*) means training in these qualities;
the sense is that one is developing this meditation on the divine abodes (*brahmavihāra-bhāvanā*). This is the summary here; the detailed exposition, however, is found in the canonical text itself.
Then the Great Man, having heard the words of that Brahmā and loathing the stench of raw flesh, said, "I shall go forth this very day.
The Brahmā also said, "Excellent, Great Man! Go forth. If this is so, my coming into your presence will indeed be a welcome arrival;
for you, dear one, are the foremost person in all Jambudīpa and stand in the prime of your youth."
"Thus, to renounce such great prosperity and sovereignty is truly most extraordinary—like a scent-elephant breaking its iron bonds and departing for the forest;
this is indeed the lineage of the Buddhas. Having thus strengthened the Great Bodhisatta’s resolve, he returned to the Brahma-world.
The Great Being, however, thought: "It is not fitting for me to depart from here and go forth into homelessness."
"I am the one who administers the affairs of the royal families; therefore, if they too go forth after I have informed them, that would be excellent.
But if not, I shall hand over the position of domestic chaplain and then go forth. Having thought this, he informed King Reṇu first.
Although he was invited by the king with even greater abundance of sensual pleasures, [he remained firm] because of his own sense of spiritual urgency and his absolute desire to go forth.
Having made this announcement, when he said, "If that is so, I too shall go forth," they accepted his proposal, saying, "Very well.
Following this same method, he took leave of the six kṣatriyas beginning with Sattabhū, seven wealthy brahmins, seven hundred ascetics purified by bathing, and his own wives;
then, remaining for only seven days to protect their hearts, he departed.
Having gone forth in a manner resembling the Great Renunciation, he ordained.
All those seven kings, beginning with the first, followed him into the homeless life. That assembly became vast.
Surrounded by an assembly extending for many yojanas, the Great Man wandered through villages, market towns, districts, and royal capitals, teaching the Dhamma.
He traveled about, establishing the great multitude in merit. In every place he visited, there was a clamor like that for a Buddha.
Hearing that "the wise Govinda is coming," people would already have pavilions constructed and decorated them beforehand;
they would go out to meet him, lead him into the pavilion, and honor him with various kinds of choice food. Thus, his gain and honor were great.
It arose like a great flood, overwhelming everything. The Great Man established the great multitude in merit:

in the perfection of virtue, in the restraint of the sense faculties, in moderation in eating, in the practice of wakefulness, in the cultivation of the kasiṇas, in the jhānas, the direct knowledges, the eight attainments, and the divine abodes.
It was like the time of a Buddha’s appearance.
The Bodhisatta, fulfilling the perfections for as long as his lifespan lasted, spent his time in the bliss of meditative attainments;

at the end of his life, he was reborn in the Brahma-world. His holy life flourished, prospered, spread, became widely known, and grew vast, being well-proclaimed among gods and humans for a very long period of time. Of that...
Those who understood the teaching in its entirety, upon the dissolution of the body after death, were reborn in a happy destination, the Brahma-world.
Those who did not understand it, some were reborn in the company of the Paranimmitavasavatti devas;
some among the Nimmānarati... [and so on] ...the Tusita, the Yāma, the Tāvatiṃsa, and the Cātumahārājika devas.
They were reborn into the company of the gods. Those who were the very lowest filled the host of gandhabbas.
Thus, the great mass of people for the most part went to the Brahma-world and to the heavenly realms. Consequently, the worlds of the gods and Brahmas became full.
The four states of misery became as if empty.
Here too, the extraction of the requisites for enlightenment (bodhisambhāra) is to be understood as in the Akittijātaka:
at that time, the seven kings were the great elders (mahātheras), the rest of the assembly was the Buddha’s assembly, and Mahāgovinda was the Lord of the World (lokanātha).
Just as Reṇu and the other seven kings were established in their respective kingdoms without mutual conflict, so too in the great sevenfold [sacrifice]...
In his kingdom, he was diligent in instructing them in their welfare and the Dhamma;
for four months, he lived the supreme life of purity (*brahmacariya*) in order to truly fulfill the reputation that had spread that "he even engages in conversation with Brahmā.
Because of this, Brahmā entered into him, and while abiding by Brahmā’s instruction, he received the honor and offerings presented by seven kings and the entire world.
Having cast it away like a lump of spittle, there is the undertaking of the going-forth (pabbajjā) as a sign of the future going-forth of an immeasurable assembly of khattiyas, brahmins, and others;
and there is the long-term continuity of one’s own dispensation, just like that of the Buddhas’ dispensation—
such qualities and powers are to be made manifest.
The commentary on the life of Mahāgovinda is finished.
6. Commentary on the Life of King Nimi: 40.
In the sixth [chapter], "In Mithilā, the supreme city," refers to the preeminent city of the Videhas named Mithilā. [There lived] one named Nimi.
He was named "Nimi" because he appeared as if he were turning the wheel [of sovereignty], like one who sets the rim in motion;
he was a "Great King" (mahārāja) because he was endowed with great royal majesty as well as the distinguished qualities of generosity, virtue, and so forth.
He was "wise and seeking the wholesome" (paṇḍito kusalatthiko), meaning he desired merit for both himself and others.
In the past, it is said, in the kingdom of Videha at the city of Mithilā, our Bodhisatta was a king named Maghadeva.

Having spent eighty-four thousand years in princely play, eighty-four thousand years exercising the vice-regency, and while ruling the kingdom for eighty-four thousand years, he [instructed his son]: "When you see grey hairs upon my head,..."
Having said to his barber, "Then you should inform me," at a later time, when the barber saw grey hairs and informed him, he had them pulled out with golden tweezers and placed them in his hand.
Gazing at the grey hair, overcome with a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*), he thought, "The messenger of the gods has appeared for me;
it is now fitting for me to go forth. He then gave away the excellent village that yielded a hundred thousand [pieces of gold] per day.
Having given [the gift] to the barber and summoned the eldest prince, he said to him:
“These hairs of my head, grown upon my noble body, have now reached maturity;
they have appeared as messengers from the gods; it is time for me to go forth.”
Having spoken thus and having ruled the kingdom well, although he still had eighty-four thousand years of life remaining,
nevertheless, regarding himself as if standing in the presence of Death, his heart was filled with spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) and he took delight in going forth. Therefore it is said:
“Seeing grey hair upon his head, Maghadeva, the lord of Disā, was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency; the wise one resolved upon the going-forth.
He [the king] said to his son: “You should conduct yourself in this very manner, just as I have practiced; do not become the last man.”

Having thus exhorted him, he departed from the city, went forth into the monk’s renunciation, and spent eighty-four thousand years in the attainment of meditative absorptions (*jhāna-samāpatti*); at the end of his life, he was destined for the Brahma-world.
His son also ruled the kingdom righteously for many thousands of years, and by that same means, having gone forth, was likewise destined for the Brahma-world.

So it was with his son, and so it was with his son’s son; in this manner, eighty-four thousand kshatriyas, less two, went forth into homelessness as soon as they saw grey hair upon their heads. Then the Bodhisatta, while remaining in the Brahma-world, reflected:
"Is the wholesome deed performed by me in the human world still bearing fruit, or does it not? As he looked into the matter, he saw that for such a long duration...
“[The lineage] has proceeded, but now it will no longer proceed.

Thinking, “I shall not allow my own lineage to be cut off,” he took rebirth in the womb of the chief queen of the king born in his own family, being reborn as if joining the rim of the wheel of his own dynasty.
Therefore it is said: “He arose as if joining the rim.”
"He was given the name Nimī.
For on the day of his naming, fortune-tellers were brought by his father. Having examined his marks, they said, "Great King, this prince will uphold your lineage;
he is even more majestic and possessed of greater merit than his own father and grandfather."
They explained it thus. Having heard this, the king gave him the name "Nimi" according to the meaning as described;
from his childhood, he was devotedly engaged in virtuous conduct and the observance of the Uposatha.

Then, his father, seeing the grey hair upon him just as before, gave a choice village to the barber, instructed his son in the kingdom, and having departed from the city, went forth into homelessness.
Having attained the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*), he became destined for the Brahma-world.

King Nimi, however, because of his inclination toward generosity, had five halls of giving constructed—at the four city gates and in the center of the city—and established a great distribution of alms.
He provided one hundred thousand [pieces of gold] for each hall of giving, and thus daily...

He renounced five hundred thousand [pieces of gold], observed the five precepts, undertook the observance of the Uposatha on the fortnightly days, and exhorted the great multitude toward meritorious deeds such as giving.
He pointed out the path to heaven, intimidated them with the fear of hell, and restrained them from evil.
Standing by his advice, the great multitude performed meritorious deeds such as giving, and from there...
Having passed away from that world, he was reborn in the deva realm; the deva realm became filled, while hell became as if empty.
Then, proclaiming the sublime nature of his own inclination toward giving and how he had fulfilled the perfection of generosity in an especially distinguished manner, the Teacher said:
“Then, having constructed a four-sided hall with four entrances...”
"In that place I bestowed gifts upon animals, birds, humans, and others"—thus he spoke at the beginning.
Therein, "at that" means during the time of King Nimi. "Having caused to be built" means having had it constructed. "Four-halled" means a hall connected on four sides.
"Four-faced" means provided with four doors on the four sides. For [this was] a hall for giving.

Because the gift to be given was so vast and the number of supplicants was so great, it was not possible to establish a limit for the practice of giving or to bring the distribution of gifts to an end through a single door alone;
therefore, he had four great gates constructed at the four directions of the hall. There, from the gate to the corners, the gifts were piled up.
It remains so. Beginning from dawn until the time for his natural rest, he distributes gifts.
During the other period as well, many hundreds of lamps are kept burning. Whenever those in need arrive, at those very times gifts are given.
And that gift is not given only to the poor, the destitute, the mendicants, and the beggars; rather, it is given even to the wealthy and the very rich.

By way of providing what was necessary, because he relinquished gifts even more exalted and refined than those of the Mahāsudassana sacrifice, all the human inhabitants of the entire Jambudīpa both accepted and consumed them.
Indeed, having made the whole of Jambudīpa free from ploughs, the Great Man then distributed that great gift. And just as it was for humans, so too was it for the beasts and birds.
Beginning with those animals, he established almsgiving outside the hall for the distribution of gifts, providing for them in a suitable manner on one side.
Thus it is said: "There I bestowed gifts upon deer, birds, humans, and others.
And not only for animals, but he also caused alms to be given daily to the *petas*. Just as he did at one hall for the distribution of gifts, so too...
In this manner, almsgiving was carried out in all five halls of distribution. However, in the Pāḷi it is stated as if there were only one:
“Then, having had it built, a four-hall [structure] with four entrances. This refers specifically to the hall of distribution located in the center of the city.
Now, indicating the items to be given there by way of illustration, he said: “Clothing and bedding, food, drink, and nourishment.”
Therein, "clothing" refers to various kinds of lower and upper garments, such as fine linen and so forth.

"Lying down" refers to many kinds of things upon which one may lie, such as beds, couches, woolen rugs, and embroidered coverlets; it should be understood that seating is also included here by the very mention of "lying down.
"Food and drink" refers to various excellent flavors according to the preference of each respective being.
"Food and drink, and various kinds of remaining food preparations.
"Having made it uninterrupted" means having made it continuous day and night from the time of its commencement until the end of his life. 43–4.
Now, regarding that gift, [the text explains] how it proceeded by way of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramī*) directed toward supreme enlightenment (*sammāsambodhi*).
In order to demonstrate by way of a simile how his own intention proceeded at that time, he said, "Just as a servant," and so forth.

Its meaning is as follows: just as a servant-man, having approached his master from time to time in the manner of service, for the sake of the wealth he might obtain, is pleased in every way—by body, speech, and mind—through all actions of body, speech, and mind, such that he is satisfied; [so too was the Bodhisatta].
Just as one seeks and searches for that which is to be propitiated, so too I, while existing as a bodhisatta, desiring to serve the unsurpassed state of Buddhahood—
which is the sovereignty over the world including the devas— sought to propitiate it; and for the sake of propitiating it,
throughout all existences, in every birth I took, I [strived] by means of giving, through the fulfillment of the perfection of giving, toward all beings.

Having satisfied [myself], I shall seek and search for in every way through various means that omniscient knowledge (sabbaññutaññāṇa) which is named "born of enlightenment" (bodhija) because it arises from the noble path-knowledge known as enlightenment;
I desire and aspire to that supreme enlightenment, the perfect awakening (sammāsambodhi),
by doing whatever is necessary, even at the cost of sacrificing my life.

Thus, in this instance, the teaching was presented specifically by way of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramī*) in order to demonstrate the sublime nature of one whose inclination is toward generosity.
However, in the Jātaka teachings, the fulfillment of the perfections of virtue (*sīlapāramī*) and the others is likewise clearly manifested;

for, as previously stated, having adorned himself with the virtues of virtue and so forth, and having established the great multitude therein, the deity reborn [as a result] abided by his instruction.
Assembled in the Sudhammā assembly hall of the gods, they praised and extolled the virtues of the Great Being, saying:

“Aho! It is by depending on our King Nimi that we have attained this prosperity; indeed, such wonderful beings arise in the world who, even when no Buddha has appeared, accomplish the work of a Buddha for the great multitude. Thus it is said:
“It is indeed a marvel in the world that those with clear vision arise;
when King Nimi appeared, he was wise and sought after what is skillful,” and so forth.
Having heard that, all the gods, beginning with Sakka, lord of the devas, desired to see the Bodhisatta.

Then one day, when the Great Being had observed the Uposatha and was seated cross-legged in the upper chamber of the palace during the last watch of the night, this reflection arose in his mind: "Is giving better, or is the holy life?"
Thus, he was unable to sever his own doubt. At that moment, the abode of Sakka manifested a state of heat.
Sakka, reflecting on the cause of this, saw that the Bodhisatta was thinking in such a manner;
thinking, "I shall cut through his thought," he arrived and stood before him. When asked by the Bodhisatta, "Who are you?", he declared his status as the King of the Devas.
Having announced this, when he was asked, "What were you thinking, Great King?", he related the matter.
Then Sakka, demonstrating that the holy life alone is supreme, said:
"By a lowly holy life, one is reborn among Khattiyas;..."
“By the middling [practice] one attains the state of a deva, and by the supreme, one is purified.
‘For these bodies are not easily obtained by anyone through mere begging;
those who are born in such bodies are homeless ascetics.’”
He said:
"In that regard, among various sectarian systems, the mere abstention from sexual intercourse is called 'low holy life' (brahmacariya); by means of it, one is reborn in a kṣatriya family.
The mere access concentration (upacāra) of jhāna is called 'middling'; by means of it, one is reborn among the devas. The production of the eight attainments..."
However, that which is called "supreme" leads to rebirth in the Brahma-world. For outsiders describe that very state as "Nirvana.

Therefore, it is said: "one is purified. But in the Dispensation (Sāsana), for a bhikkhu of perfectly pure virtue who aspires to one of the divine hosts, the volition of the holy life (brahmacariyacetanā) is called "inferior" because of its inferiority; by means of that, [he is reborn] in the world of the gods as he has aspired.
It is reborn. For one of pure virtue, the attainment of the eight meditative absorptions (*aṭṭhasamāpatti*) is called "middling," by which one is reborn in the Brahma-world.
Furthermore, for one of pure virtue, the attainment of Arahantship after having developed insight (*vipassanā*) is called "supreme," by which one is purified.
Thus Sakka said: "Great King, compared to giving, the life of holy conduct (*brahmacariyavāsa*) is a hundredfold, a thousandfold..."
"...is of great fruit by a hundred thousandfold. "Kāyā" means the hosts of Brahmās. "By way of supplication" (*yācayogena*) means joined with a request.
There is also a reading in the text as "by way of sacrifice" (*yājayogena*), which means joined with sacrificing or joined with giving. "Tapassino" means those who depend on austerity.
With this verse as well, he illuminates the great power of living the holy life (*brahmacariya*). And having spoken thus: "Even though..."
“Great King, of all things, the holy life (*brahmacariya*) alone is of great fruit; yet both of these are duties to be performed by a Great Man.
Being diligent in both, give gifts and guard your virtue. Having spoken thus and exhorted him, he returned to his own place.
Then the host of devas asked him, “Great King, where have you gone? Sakka replied, “To Mithilā, to resolve the doubt of King Nimi.”
Having explained that matter with the words, "Let him cut it," he praised the virtues of the Bodhisatta in detail.
Hearing this, the gods said, "Great King, we wish to see King Nimi; please summon him.
Sakka, accepting their request by saying, "Very well," addressed Mātali: "Go to King Nimi at the Vejayanta Palace..."

“Having placed him [on the chariot], bring him back. Having agreed, saying “Very well,” he went by chariot, placed the Great Being upon it, and at his request, pointing out the respective abodes of those who have committed evil deeds and those who have performed meritorious deeds, he gradually led him to the world of the devas.
When the devas heard that King Nimi had arrived, they came forth with divine perfumes, incense, and flowers in their hands as far as...
The gatekeepers of Cittakūṭa came forth to meet the Great Being, honoring him with celestial perfumes and other offerings, and led him to the Sudhamma assembly hall of the gods.
The King descended from his chariot and entered the assembly hall;
sitting on the same seat as Sakka, he was invited by him to enjoy celestial sensual pleasures. The King replied, "Enough, Great King! To me, these things are like borrowed goods."

Having thus rejected [the offer] with the words "by means of sensual pleasures," and having taught the Dhamma in many ways, he remained for exactly seven days by human reckoning and said, "I shall go to the world of men; there I will perform meritorious deeds such as giving.
Sakka commanded Mātali, "Take King Nimi to Mithilā. He placed him upon the Vejayanta chariot and, by way of the eastern direction—
He arrived at Mithilā. When the great multitude saw the divine chariot, they went out to meet the king.

Mātali, having helped the Great Being descend from the lion-window, took his leave and returned to his own place. The great multitude also surrounded the king and asked, "O Lord, what is the Devaloka like?
The king described the splendor of the Devaloka and said, "You too [should practice] giving and the other virtues..."
"Perform meritorious deeds; in this way you will be reborn in that world of the devas," he taught the Dhamma.

Later on, having seen grey hair in the manner previously described, he handed over the kingdom to his son, abandoned sensual pleasures, went forth into homelessness, and by developing the four divine abodes (brahmavihāra), became one destined for the Brahma-world.
At that time, Sakka was Anuruddha; Mātali was Ānanda; the eighty-four thousand kings were the Buddha’s retinue; and King Nimi was the Lord of the World.
Here too, his accumulations for enlightenment (bodhisambhāra) should be extracted according to the method explained below.

Likewise, out of great compassion, having renounced the excellence of the Brahma-world, [he descended] into the human world with the thought: "I shall continue the virtuous conduct previously practiced by myself."
His rebirth, his sublime inclination toward generosity, his practice of giving and other virtues in accordance with that inclination,
his establishment of the great multitude therein, the widespread fame of his fame reaching as far as gods and humans, the extreme wonderment of Sakka, King of the Gods, upon approaching him,
and even when invited by Sakka to enjoy celestial prosperity, his refusal to adorn himself for that sake in order to further increase his accumulation of merit— [all these are described].
