Furthermore, such qualities as returning once more to dwell among human beings and remaining entirely unattached to gains and prosperity—these powers of his virtues are to be extracted [from the text].
The commentary on the conduct of King Nimi is concluded.
7. Commentary on the Conduct of Prince Canda.

45. "The son of Ekarāja" means the legitimate son of the Kasi king named Ekarāja. "In the city of Pupphavatī" means in the city called Pupphavatī. "Named Canda" means one who is addressed by the word *canda*; the meaning is that his name was Canda.
It is said that in the past this Bārāṇasī was named Pupphavatī.
There, a son of King Vasavatti named Ekarāja reigned. The Bodhisatta took rebirth in the womb of his chief queen, named Gotamī.
He took her. They gave him the name Candakumāra. When he was able to walk on his own feet, another son was born;
they gave him the name Sūriyakumāra. When he too was able to walk on his own feet, a daughter was born;
they gave her the name Selā. They also had two half-brothers, Bhaddasena and Sūra. Thus the Bodhisatta...
Gradually reaching maturity, he attained mastery in the arts and the fields of knowledge.
The king brought him a suitable royal daughter named Canda and gave him the rank of viceroy. A son was born to the Bodhisatta, and they named him Vāsula.
Now, that king had a chaplain named Khaṇḍahāla, whom the king—
He appointed him to the office of judge. Having become a receiver of bribes, he would take bribes and turn those who were not owners into owners, and those who were owners into non-owners.
Then one day, a man who had lost his case at law, having departed from the court while protesting, saw the Bodhisatta as he was going to attend upon the king; he fell at his feet.
“Master, Khaṇḍahāla is devouring the case through corruption; I was bribed by him and made to lose,” he cried out with a plaintive voice.
The Bodhisatta comforted him, saying, “Do not fear,” and having brought the case before the court, he restored the rightful owner to his own property.
The great multitude gave a loud shout of approval.

When the king heard that the Bodhisatta had indeed adjudicated the lawsuit well, he summoned him and said, "Dear son, from now on, you yourself shall adjudicate cases in the court of justice," and thus he entrusted the judicial authority to the Bodhisatta.
Khaṇḍahāla’s income was cut off; from then on, harboring resentment toward the Bodhisatta, he wandered about seeking an opportunity [to harm him].
However, that king was credulously trusting. One day, having seen the world of the gods in a dream and desiring to go there, he said, "Purohita, explain to me the path leading to the Brahma-world.
He replied, "Perform a sacrifice with every fourfold gift, giving exceedingly generous gifts.
When asked by the king, "What is an exceedingly generous gift? he said, "One's own beloved son, one's beloved wife..."

He made them understand: "Beloved daughters of a merchant of great wealth, these four—auspicious elephants, horses, and so forth—having been given away in groups of four as two-footed and four-footed beings for the sake of sacrifice, the offering with their blood from the throat is called 'the supreme gift'.
Thus, he who said, "I shall explain the path to heaven," explained the path to hell.
The king, too, perceiving him to be a wise man and thinking, "The method he has described is the path to heaven," desiring to practice it, had a great sacrificial enclosure constructed.
There, beginning with the four princes headed by the Bodhisatta, he gave the command:
"Lead all bipeds and quadrupeds mentioned by Khaṇḍahāla to the place prepared for the sacrifice. And all—
The materials for the sacrifice were prepared. Hearing this, the great multitude raised a loud clamor.
The king, filled with remorse, yet supported by Khaṇḍahāla, issued that same command once again.
The Bodhisatta thought, "Khaṇḍahāla, having failed to obtain a position in the court of justice, has harbored malice toward me; he intends my very death."

Knowing that he had brought ruin and disaster upon the great multitude by his desire, the king strove by various means to dissuade him from that wrongful grasp, yet he was unsuccessful. The great multitude wailed and showed great compassion.
Even as the people were still lamenting, he completed all the rites at the sacrificial enclosure. [He prepared] the prince...
Having led him forward and bent him down by the neck, they made him sit. Khaṇḍahāla, having presented a golden platter and taking up a sword, stood there thinking, "I shall cut off his neck.
Seeing this, the queen of the prince named Candā thought, "I have no other refuge;
by the power of my own truth, I shall bring safety to my husband," and she raised her hands in reverent salutation.
Taking it up, she walked among the assembly, saying: "This which Khaṇḍahāla calls the path to heaven is nothing but an evil deed.
By this word of truth, may there be safety for my husband!
Whatever deities dwell here in this world, to all of them I have gone for refuge."
"Protect me, who am without a protector, so that I may have a husband.

Thus she made a declaration of truth (*saccakiriyā*). Sakka, the king of the gods, hearing the sound of her lamentation and learning of the situation, took up a glowing iron hammer, arrived there, and after terrifying the king, caused all [the others] to be released. At that time, Sakka himself...
Displaying a divine form, blazing and aflame, he brandished his thunderbolt and cried out:
"Ho there, evil king, ill-omened one! When have you ever seen anyone go to a happy destination through the taking of life?
Release Prince Canda and all these people from their bonds; if you do not release them, right here—both for you and for this wicked brahmin—"
"I shall split open his head! he cried, and stood poised in the air. Seeing that marvel, the king and the brahmin quickly released everyone from their bonds.
Then the great multitude raised a tumultuous clamor and suddenly overwhelmed the sacrificial enclosure;
hurling clods of earth one after another at Khaṇḍahāla, they brought him to his death right there, and then began to kill the king as well.
The Bodhisatta, having already embraced his father and stood there, did not allow him to be killed.
The great multitude said, "We shall grant this evil king his life for now, but we will not give him the royal parasol, nor will we allow him to dwell in the city;
having made him a caṇḍāla, we shall cause him to live outside the city. Thus, they stripped him of his royal robes, made him put on saffron-colored garments, and with a piece of turmeric cloth...
Having wrapped his head [in a turban] and made him a Caṇḍāla, they sent him away to a village of Caṇḍālas.
But all those who sacrificed that animal slaughter-sacrifice, who caused it to be sacrificed, and who rejoiced in it, all had hell as their destination. Therefore the Blessed One said:
"All find their footing in hell, Just as those who have committed evil."
"For having committed an evil deed, it is not possible to go from here to a happy destination.
Then the entire royal assembly, as well as the citizens and the people of the provinces, gathered together and consecrated the Bodhisatta in the kingship.
Ruling the kingdom with righteousness, he [remedied] that calamity and ruin which had arisen for himself and his great multitude of people without any cause.

Having recollected this, filled with a sense of spiritual urgency and inspired with even greater zeal for performing meritorious deeds, he bestowed great alms, guarded his moral precepts, and undertook the observance of the Uposatha. Thus it is said:
“Then, released from the sacrifice, I departed from the sacrificial enclosure;”
"Having generated a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega), he set forth a great gift," and so forth.
In that context, "released from sacrifice" means released from the sacrificial rites performed by Khaṇḍahāla, according to the method described, from which he was to be put to death.
"Departed from the sacrificial enclosure" means [departed] together with the great multitude who had become enthusiastic for the purpose of performing the consecration (abhiseka). From there...

"Departed from the sacrificial ground. "Having generated a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega)" means: having thus produced an intense sense of urgency, thinking, "Life in this world is beset by many obstacles.
"I bestowed a great gift" means: having had six alms-halls constructed, I gave a great gift like the gift of Vessantara through the relinquishment of vast wealth.
By this [it is meant] starting from the time of my consecration...
This shows that the great gift had been set in motion. 47.
“Without giving to those worthy of offerings” means without relinquishing the object of charity to persons who are deserving of offerings.
“Even for six or five nights” shows that at times he would not even partake of his own drinking, eating, or food for six or five nights.
At that time, it is said, the Bodhisatta, having made the whole of Jambudīpa free from ploughing, caused a great rain of alms to fall like a massive cloud.
Although in the halls of giving, food, drink, and other excellent, refined,
and most exquisite things were given day after day to supplicants according to their desires, nevertheless, his own prepared food— even royal-worthy delicacies— [was also given].
He does not eat without having given to beggars; it is with reference to this that it was said, “I do not drink,” and so forth.
Now, showing the reason for giving to beggars in such a manner, he first brings forward a simile beginning with, “Just as a merchant named...”.
Its meaning is as follows: just as a merchant, having gone to a place of trade with a small amount of capital...

Having sold much merchandise and accumulated a vast store of goods, knowing the proper place and time—where his profit and gain would be great—he carries, brings, and sells that merchandise to that place or at that time. 49.
*Sakabhuttāpi*: “Even from what he himself has eaten”; there is also a reading, *sakaparibhuttāpi* (“even from what he himself has consumed”).
"Pareti" means in another person who is a recipient. "Satabhāgo" means that in the future there will be a hundredfold part, or even many hundreds of parts.

This is what is meant: just as merchandise bought by a merchant, if instead of being sold right then and there, is sold in a suitable place and at a suitable time, yields great profit and abundant fruit—even so with one's own property.
"What has been given by one who does not enjoy it themselves, but bestowed upon another person who is a recipient, will be of great fruit, becoming a hundredfold or more;
therefore, even if one does not enjoy it oneself, it must certainly be given to another. For this was said by the Blessed One:
"Having given a gift to an animal, a hundredfold merit is to be expected. [But] to an ordinary person of immoral conduct..."
“Having given a gift, [the merit is] a thousandfold”—this is the detailed explanation. Furthermore, it is said:

“If, monks, beings were to know the ripening of the fruit of giving and sharing as I know it, they would not eat without having given, nor would the stain of stinginess remain taking hold of their minds.
Even that which is their very last morsel, their very last mouthful, from that too...”
"...they should not eat without having shared [the food]," and so forth.

50. "Having understood this purpose" means having known this purpose and reason, namely, that giving is of great fruit and that it serves as a condition for perfect enlightenment (*sammāsambodhi*). "I do not turn back from giving" refers to the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).

"I do not turn back even slightly; I only advance. For what purpose? 'In order to attain full enlightenment'—that is, for the sake of attaining, for the purpose of reaching, full enlightenment, which is omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).
At that time, while the Bodhisatta was being given a suitable travel allowance by the great multitude as his father entered the village of the Caṇḍālas..."

He caused robes for the lower body and upper garments to be given [to him]. He, too, being unable to enter the city, would approach the Bodhisatta whenever he had gone out for pleasure-trips in the garden and other such excursions;
yet, perceiving him as his son, he did not bow down, nor did he perform the gesture of joining his palms, but merely said, "Long live my lord!
On the days when he saw him, the Bodhisatta would show him exceptional honor. Thus, in accordance with the Dhamma...
Having exercised his sovereignty, at the end of his lifespan, he and his retinue filled the world of the gods.
At that time, Khaṇḍahāla was Devadatta; Queen Gotamī was Mahāmāyā; Princess Candā was Rāhula’s mother;
Vāsula was Rāhula; Selā was Uppalavaṇṇā; Sūra was Mahākassapa; Bhaddasena was Mahāmoggallāna; and Suriyakumāra was...
Sāriputta was the King Canda, the Lord of the World.
Here too, his remaining perfections should be deduced as appropriate according to the method already explained.
At that time, although he knew Khaṇḍahāla’s harsh and cruel nature, he remained equanimous and rendered a judgment on the legal case in accordance with the Dhamma and justice.
The absence of mental agitation toward Khaṇḍahāla even after learning of his sacrificial preparations,
despite his desire to kill him; and the steadfastness in obeying the command of his father— who, though capable of becoming his enemy by taking his own retinue,
wished to have him executed as a human sacrifice for a bull, thinking, "It is not fitting for one like me to oppose my elders"— [all this was due to] Kosiya’s...
When his father, the royal priest, took up a sword and prepared to cut off his head, he maintained equanimity by pervading himself, his son, and all beings with loving-kindness (*mettā*);
and when the great multitude prepared to kill his father, he gave them the gift of life by embracing him;
and even while giving great gifts day after day like the *Vessantara-dāna*, he did so through the power of generosity (*dāna*).

The quality of never being satisfied, the nourishing of his father—who had been made to dwell among the Caṇḍālas—by giving him what was due to him, and the establishing of the great multitude in meritorious deeds: such powers of virtue are to be extracted [from this account].
The commentary on the conduct of Prince Candaka is finished.
8. The Account of the Conduct of King Sivi 51.
"In the city named Ariṭṭha" means in the city called Ariṭṭhapura. "A kshatriya named Sivi" means there was a king of such a name because of his lineage; he was known as Sivi.
It is said that in the past, while King Sivi was ruling in the city of Ariṭṭhapura in the kingdom of Sivi, the Great Being was his son.
Having offered the sacrifice, he was reborn. They gave him the name Prince Sivi. When he reached maturity, he went to Takkasilā;
having returned with his craft mastered, he demonstrated his skill to his father and received the position of viceroy. Later, upon the passing of his father, he became king.
Abandoning the path of ruin and without violating the ten duties of a king, he ruled the kingdom while stationed at the four gates of the city.

Having caused six alms-halls to be constructed at the gate of his residence in the center of the city, he established a great distribution of gifts by giving away six hundred thousand [pieces of gold] daily.
On the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth days of the lunar fortnight, he would personally go to the alms-hall and oversee the distribution of the offerings.
Once, on the full-moon day, sitting at dawn upon his royal throne with a white parasol raised high, he reflected upon the gift he had given.
While reflecting, and seeing nothing that was not already his own among external objects, he thought:

"An external gift does not satisfy my mind as much as an internal gift. Oh, would that some supplicant, at the time I go to my hall of giving, should not ask for an external object but should ask only for what is internal!
For if someone were to ask for flesh or blood from my body, or even my head..."
"Whether it be my heart-flesh, my eyes, half my body, or even my entire self, if he should ask for me as a slave, I am able to give whatever his heart desires," he thought.
However, in the Pāli text, it is mentioned specifically by way of the eyes. Therefore it was said:
“Seated in the excellent palace, I then thought thus:
‘Whatever human gift there may be, nothing remains that I have not given away;
even if someone were to ask me for my eye, I would give it without hesitation.’”
In this context, "human gift" refers to gifts such as food and drink that are to be given by ordinary people.
When such a sublime inclination toward giving arose in the Great Being, the stone throne of Sakka known as Paṇḍukambala displayed signs of heat.
As he reflected on the cause of this, he perceived the Bodhisattva’s intention and thought: "Today, King Sivi has reached the point where those who have come as supplicants [seek] his eyes..."
When Sakka said to his assembly of deities, "I shall think, 'Whatever they ask for, I will give it to them,
even plucking out my own eyes,' I will first investigate whether he will indeed be able to give that or not," he bathed the Bodhisatta with sixteen jars of scented water,
adorned him with all ornaments, and placed him upon the back of a decorated state elephant.

Acting like a blind Brahmin aged by decrepitude as he was proceeding to the head of the almsgiving procession, he stood on a certain elevated spot within the King’s line of sight, stretching out both hands and wishing the King victory.
When the Bodhisatta, having directed the elephant toward him, asked, "Brahmin, what do you desire?", [the Brahmin replied]: "By virtue of your inclination toward generosity..."
"The entire inhabited world is filled without interval by the sound of my fame; yet I am blind. Therefore, I beg of you.
Thus, by way of formal courtesy, he requested one eye. For this reason it was said:
"Knowing my intention, Sakka, the lord of the gods..."
Seated amidst the assembly of devas, he spoke these words:
“Sitting in his magnificent palace, the highly powerful King Sivi was reflecting upon various kinds of gifts; he saw nothing that could not be given.”
“Is this true or is it false? Come, let me investigate that.
Wait a moment, while I ascertain his intention. [He spoke thus:
“Trembling, with grey hair, his body wrinkled and afflicted by old age;”
Having become blind in appearance, he approached the king.
Then, raising his left and right arms and placing his palms together in reverence upon his head, he spoke these words:
“I entreat you, O Great King, righteous increaser of the realm;
your fame for delighting in giving has risen high among gods and men.
Both my eyes, the guides of my sight, are blind and impaired.”
"Give me one eye; you may subsist with the other.

Therein, "reflecting upon various gifts" means reflecting upon the various gifts he himself has given, or attending to the gift, or reflecting upon the various external objects of charity (deyyadhamma) given by himself. "He does not see anything that cannot be given" means...
The intention is that he did not see even his internal physical basis as something unyielding or impossible to give, like an external object;

rather, he thought, "I will even pluck out my eyes and give them. Regarding the phrase "Is this true or false?"—does it mean that this perception, which views even the internal basis as something not to be given, yet perceives it as being fit for giving, is indeed true, or is it untrue?

The meaning is as follows: "Having then exerted" means having then exerted both the left and the right arms—that is, having raised both arms. "Raṭṭhavaḍḍhana" means one who causes the kingdom to prosper.
"You too shall maintain yourself with one" means that you, seeing the level and uneven ground with one eye, must maintain your own person.
"I too shall sustain myself with one portion obtained from you," he said, thereby demonstrating his intent.
Hearing this, the Great Being was delighted in heart and thought: "Just now, while sitting in my palace, I came here having thought such a thing;
and this man, as if knowing my very mind, asks for my eye. Oh, what a gain for me! Today my heart's desire is fulfilled."
“I shall reach the summit; indeed, I will give a gift never given before! Thus he became filled with zeal.
To clarify this matter, the Teacher said:
“Having heard her words, joyful and with a heart moved by awe,”
With palms joined and filled with joy, I spoke these words:
"Having reflected upon this, I have now come here from my palace;
you, having understood my mind, have come to ask for my eye."
“‘Aha! My mind has attained its goal; my intention is fulfilled.
Today I shall give to a supplicant that supreme gift which was never given before.
In this context, “of him” refers to Sakka, who had assumed the form of a brahmin. “Haṭṭho” means joyful. “Saṃviggamānaso” means with a heart moved by spiritual urgency.
"Knowing my mind as it were, this brahmin has asked for my eye; for so long I have been negligent, never having thought of this"—thus he was moved with agitation.
"Vedajāto" means one who has experienced joy and gladness. "Abraviṃ" means I spoke.
"Mānasaṃ" means that which exists in the mind (*manasi bhavaṃ*); it refers to the inclination toward giving—the inclination toward giving that had arisen [in him] thinking, "I shall give my eye."
This is the meaning. *Saṅkappa* means intention or desire. *Paripūrito* means fulfilled.
Then the Bodhisatta thought: "This brahmin, as if he knew the movement of my heart, asks me for my eye, though it is so difficult to give;
could it be that he has been instructed by some deity? I shall question him first."
Having reflected thus, he questioned that brahmin. Regarding this, the Blessed One said in the Jātaka teaching:
“By whom were you instructed, O mendicant, that you have come here to beg for the range of my eyes?
You beg for the most difficult thing to give—a supreme limb, which they call the eye, so hard for a man to part with?”
Having heard this, Sakka, wearing the form of a brahmin, said:
"He whom they call Sujampati among the gods, and Maghava in the world of men—
I have come here instructed by him, a beggar to ask for the paths of vision."
“O forest-dweller, grant me the unsurpassed forest, as I have entreated you for the paths of vision.
Grant me the unsurpassed path of vision, which they call the eye that is so difficult for a man to give up.
Thus spoke the Great Being.
“For whatever purpose you have come, and for whatever goal you have aspired, may those intentions of yours be fulfilled; receive your eyes, O Brahmin.
To you who asks for one, I shall give both.”
"Go, O one with vision, while the people look on;
whatever you desire, may that be fulfilled for you.
Therein, "beggars" (vanibbaka) is how he addresses him. "Within the range of sight" (cakkhupathāni) refers to the eyes themselves, because they constitute the path of seeing.
“Nāmaṃ” means that which people in the world call “difficult to give. “Vanibbato” means of one who begs; “vana” means begging.
“Te te” means those intentions of yours for that blind man. “Sa cakkhumā” means you, having become possessed of eyes through my eyes.
“Tada te samijjhatu” means may that which you desire from me be fulfilled for you.
Having spoken thus much, the king thought, "This brahmin says he has come here instructed by Sakka;
surely his eyesight will be restored through this means.

Realizing this, and considering that it would be improper for him to pluck out his own eyes and give them right here, he took the brahmin, went to the inner palace, sat upon the royal throne, and [addressed] Sīvaka.
He summoned a physician. Then, a great clamor arose throughout the entire city: "It seems our king wishes to pluck out his own eyes and give them to a brahmin.

Thereupon, the king’s kinsmen, the commander-in-chief and others, the royal favorites, ministers, courtiers, citizens, and the women of the harem—all gathered together and tried to dissuade him by various means. The king also exhorted them; thus it was said:
“O King, do not take away our sight; do not drive us all away.
Grant us wealth, O Great King—many pearls and beryl gems.
Give us yoked chariots, O King, and well-adorned thoroughbreds.”
“O Nāga, O Great King, give me the golden-helmeted horses.
Give them, O Bull among Charioteers, so that all the Śivis, with their yokes,
chariots, and banners, may surround you on every side.”
Then King Tissa spoke these three verses:
“He who, having said ‘I will give,’ sets his mind on not giving,
fastens the snare that has fallen upon the ground around his own neck.”
“He who, having said ‘I shall give,’ sets his mind on not giving,
becomes more evil than the evil person, having fallen under the power of Yama.
For one should give what is asked for, and one should not give what is not asked for.”
“Svāhā! I shall give him that very thing which the brahmin asks of me.
In this context, “mā no, deva” (O King, do not [give us])—the word *no* is merely a particle.
“O King, do not give away our eyes; do not abandon us all. For if the eyes are given away, you will not be able to rule the kingdom; thus, by you, we...
They spoke thus with the intention, "We shall become those who have renounced [all].
"They would surround" means they would attend upon [him]. "'Give it thus' means: 'Give him wealth alone;
do not give his eyes. For he shows that if the eyes were given, the Śivis would not attend upon him for long, as they did when his sight was unimpaired."
"He fastens on" means he causes it to enter back in. "He becomes more evil than the evil" means he becomes more base than the base.
"Having reached the abode of Yama's executioners" means he has reached the Ussada hell, which is the place where Yama’s commands are carried out.
For whatever thing a petitioner asks for, the donor should give that very thing and not what was unasked; and this brahmin—
"He asks for my eye, not for wealth such as pearls and the like; I shall give it," he said.
Then they asked him, "O Deva, what have you prayed for regarding your lifespan and other things that you give your eyes?
The Great Being replied, "I do not give them desiring prosperity either in this present life or in the future; rather, it is the constant practice of the Bodhisattvas."
“This is an ancient path, namely, the fulfillment of the perfection of giving,” he said. Therefore it was stated:
“Is it for long life, or beauty, or happiness, or strength? Desiring what, O Lord of Men, do you give?
For how could a king, unsurpassed as Śivi, give his eyes for the sake of the next world?”
“I do not give this out of fame, nor do I desire sons, nor wealth, nor a kingdom;
rather, because the ancient Dhamma of the virtuous has been practiced, my mind delights in giving alone.

Regarding that, [the question was]: “O Great King, how could a wise man such as yourself, having abandoned visible sovereignty equal to the attainment of Sakka, give away his eyes for the sake of the next world?”
"I do not drive [others], nor indeed do I [drive myself]. Not for the sake of fame, nor for the sake of divine or human sovereignty;

rather, it is because the Dhamma of the hundred Bodhisattvas—the Dhamma that makes one a Buddha, practiced, observed, habitual, and ancient—is for this very reason that my mind is thus devoted to giving alone."
Having spoken thus, the king instructed his ministers and commanded the physician Sivaka: “Come, Sivaka! Quickly pluck out both my eyes and place them in the hands of this brahmin.
Thus it was said: “Come, Sivaka, arise! Do not delay, do not hesitate!
Pluck out both eyes and give them to this beggar.”
“Then, thus urged by me, Sivaka, acting on my word, pulled it out and gave it to the beggar, just like the kernel of a palmyra fruit. In this context, “Arise!
means: “Exert yourself with the energy of effort; perform the duty of an assistant in this gift of my eye by me.”
He shows this. "Do not delay" means do not tarry. For this most rare, long-cherished, and supreme opportunity for giving has been obtained by me;
the intention is that it should not be missed. "Do not tremble" means: do not let your body shake due to mental terror, thinking, "I am gouging out the eyes of our king. Both eyes...

"Both eyes. "To the mendicant" means "to me, the beggar. "Having extracted them, he gave them" means that the physician, having gouged out both eyes from the king's eye-sockets, placed them in the king's hand.
And when giving them, he did not extract them with a knife. For he thought: "It would be improper for one such as I, a well-trained physician..."
Thinking, "The king’s eye has been pierced by a blade," he ground medicinal herbs, infused a blue lotus with the medicinal powder, and had the king smell it at his right eye;
the eye turned and painful sensations arose. Having infused it again, he had him smell it once more;
the eye was released from its socket, and even stronger sensations arose. On the third occasion—
Having crushed it extremely hard, he presented it [to the king]. By the power of the medicinal herb, the eye rolled around, emerged from the socket, and remained hanging by a strand of sinew.
Intense pain arose, blood flowed, and even the lower garment was soaked with blood.
The attendants and ministers fell at the feet of the king and said, "Sire, do not give away your eyes."
“O King, do not give us your eyes! they wailed with great lamentation.
The king, enduring the pain, said, “Dear sons, do not make such a fuss.
He replied, “Very well, Your Majesty,” and holding his eye with his left hand, he took a lancet in his right hand, cut the tendon of the eye, and extracted the eye.

He placed [it] in the hand of the Great Being. He, looking from his left eye to his right eye and experiencing a painful sensation overcome by the joy of renunciation, called out to the brahmin, saying, "Come, brahmin!
To me, the universal eye itself is dearer than this eye by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, and a hundred-thousandfold."
"Let this gift of my eye be a condition for my merit," he said, and gave his eye to the brahmin.
The brahmin plucked it out and placed it in his own eye; through its power, it appeared like a blossoming blue lotus.
When the Great Being saw that eye with his own left eye, he thought, "Oh, what a noble gift I have given! and with tears welling from within...
His body having been continuously suffused with rapture (*pīti*), he gave yet another gift.
Sakka, having done the same, departed from the royal palace and, while the great multitude was looking on, left the city and went straight to the world of the gods.
Before long, the king’s eyes, which had not yet reached the state of being sunken, became like a ball of wool, covered by a protruding mass of flesh.
Once it was filled, they grew like the flesh of a work of art; his sensation was severed. Then the Great Being, having stayed in the palace for a few days, thought:
"What is the use of sovereignty for one who is blind? Having handed over the kingdom to his ministers and gone to the park, he resolved, "I shall go forth and practice the duty of a recluse.
He informed the ministers of this matter, saying: "The provider of water for washing my face and such..."
"Let one man remain by my side, and even at the places where the funeral rites for my body are performed, bind a rope for me," he said.
Having spoken thus, he went in a palanquin and sat upon the royal throne on the bank of the lotus pond. The ministers also paid their respects and departed.
The Bodhisatta, too, reflected upon his act of giving. At that moment, the seat of Sakka showed signs of becoming warm.
Seeing him, Sakka thought, "I shall restore the Great King's eye to its former state by granting him a boon," and approaching the Bodhisatta, he made the sound of his footsteps.
When the Mahāsatta asked, "Who is this? he replied:
"I am Sakka, the lord of the gods; I have come into your presence."
“Choose a boon, O King, whatever you desire in your mind,” he said.
To him [the king] replied:
“I have abundant wealth, Sakka, and my army and treasury are small.”
“Now that I am blind, death alone is pleasing to me.
When this was said, Sakka spoke to him: “King Sivi, do you desire death because you wish to die, or because of your blindness?
“Because of my blindness, O Lord,” he replied. “Great King, giving is not for the sake of the future life alone;”
“It is given; it also serves as a condition for welfare in this very life. Therefore, perform an act of truth (saccakiriya) relying solely upon the merit of your own giving;
by its power alone, your eye shall be restored. When this was said, he replied, “In that case, I have indeed given a great gift,” and performed an act of truth:
“Those mendicants of various clans who come to beg from me—
even he among them who begs from me there is dear to my heart.
By this utterance of truth, may my eye be restored!”— so he spoke.
He said:
"In that regard, those who come to ask me—when they have arrived, even one who asks me while uttering the words 'Give such-and-such' is dear to my mind.
By this [statement], if all my supplicants are indeed dear to me..."
"Truly, this which has been spoken by me is the truth; by this word of truth, let one eye arise for me.
Immediately after his speech, the first eye appeared. Then, for the sake of the second arising:
"That brahmin who came to beg of me, saying 'Give me an eye'—"
I gave my eyes to that brahmin who was seeking alms.
“Even more rapture entered me, and no small measure of joy;
by this utterance of truth, may a second [birth] arise for me.”—
He said:
"Therein, *yaṃ manti* means 'to me. *So* refers to that brahmin who was begging for eyes. *Āgāti* means 'he came. *Vanibbato* means 'of one who is begging.
*Maṃ āvisī* means that even after giving his eyes to the brahmin, such a feeling [of pain] arose even in the state of blindness."
Disregarding [the cost], as I reflected, "Oh, a gift so well given by me!", an even more excessive rapture (pīti) entered me.
An immeasurable joy (somanassa) arose; it was not slight.
By this—if at that time an immeasurable rapture and joy arose in me, and this which I have spoken is indeed the truth—by this word of truth, for a second time...
"May my eye arise!
At that very moment, a second eye arose for him. However, those eyes were neither ordinary nor divine.
For it was impossible to restore to its natural state the eye given by Sakka the Brahmin; [it remained] impaired.
Furthermore, it is not that the so-called divine eye (dibbacakkhu) does not arise;

rather, according to the method already stated, because he produced—by means of the pervasion of joy based on his own unerring joy of giving at the beginning, middle, and end—the "eyes of the perfection of truth" (saccapāramitācakkhu), they are so described. Therefore it was said:
“For me, while giving, while bestowing, and being one who has given a gift;”
“There is no change in the mind, solely for the sake of enlightenment.
In this context, “of one giving” means of one who has his eyes plucked out by a physician; “giving” means placing those plucked-out eyes in the hand of the Sakka-brāhmaṇa;
“of one who has given the gift” means of one who has bestowed the gift of his eyes. Of the mind...
“Otherwise” means that his inclination toward giving has changed. “For the sake of enlightenment alone” means that it is for the very cause of omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*). 66.

Because omniscient knowledge is so exceedingly difficult to attain, he says the concluding verse, “I have no one to be given away,” demonstrating that this was not done out of a lack of affection for his eyes nor even for his own person. Therein, “self” (*attā*)...
“*Na me na dessiyo*”: the first *na*-kāra is merely a particle. The meaning is: “My self should not be angry;
it should not be disliked. There is also the reading: *“Attānaṃ me na dessiyaṃ”*. Its meaning is: “I should not dislike my own self;
I should not be angry; I ought not to be angry; that [self] should not be made angry by me. There is also the reading: *“Attāpi me na dessiyo”*.
They recite: "I gave, I did not withhold. There is also a reading: "I gave here.

At that time, through the power of Sakka, as soon as the Bodhisatta’s eyes had appeared by virtue of his act of truth, the entire assembly of kings gathered together. Then Sakka, standing in the air in the midst of the great multitude, said:
"The verses spoken according to the Dhamma, O increaser of the kingdom of the Sivis!"
"These divine eyes of yours appear clearly.
May you enjoy vision extending a hundred yojanas in every direction, penetrating through walls, through rocks, and over mountains."
Having offered this praise with these verses, he departed for the world of the gods.

The Bodhisatta, surrounded by a great multitude and entering the city with great honor, sat upon a royal couch beneath a raised white parasol in a magnificent pavilion well-adorned at the gate of the royal palace.
There, he received the citizens who had come to see him, their hearts filled with joy, exultation, and delight at having regained their sight.
While teaching the Dhamma to the people and the royal assembly, he said:
“Who here, when asked, would not give away their wealth—even that which is most excellent and dearly beloved?
Therefore, all you Śivis gathered here, behold today my divine eyes!”
“Penetrating through walls and through rocks, having crossed over the mountain,
I enjoy a vision extending for a hundred leagues all around.
And there is nothing beyond this measure for mortals here in this life.”
“Having given away human vision, I have obtained superhuman vision.
‘Seeing this too, O Śivis, give gifts and enjoy [them];
having given and enjoyed according to your power, being blameless, go to the heavenly realm.’”
He spoke these verses. Regarding them: "Spoken according to the Dhamma" means, O Great King, that these verses of yours were spoken in accordance with the Dhamma, by their very nature.
"Divine" means endowed with divine power. "Are seen" means they appear. "Through walls" means through another's wall. "Through rocks" means through another's rock.
"Having completely transcended" means having passed beyond. "A hundred yojanas in all ten directions."
May they experience and accomplish the sight of forms.
Who indeed is there? Who is it here? Even those who are distinguished, though they be supreme, [do not excel]. There is nothing better than the measure of generosity;
there is no other thing called "excellent" apart from the extent of one's giving. "In this life" means in this world of living beings. They also read it as "idha jīvataṃ."
"In this world, among those who are living" is the meaning. "Non-human": divine vision has been obtained by me;
for this reason it should be understood that "there is nothing superior to generosity. "Having seen even this": having seen even this divine vision obtained by me.
Thus, by these four verses, not only at that very moment, but also every half-month on the Uposatha day—
Having assembled the great multitude, he taught the Dhamma. Having heard it, the great multitude performed meritorious deeds such as giving and became destined for the world of the devas.
At that time, the physician was the Venerable Ānanda, Sakka was the Venerable Anuruddha, the rest of the assembly was the Buddha’s retinue, and King Sivi was the Lord of the World.
In this case as well, the perfections (pāramīs) should be determined according to the method already explained and as appropriate.
Likewise, for one who daily bestows immeasurable great gifts such that there is no external object of giving previously ungiven, yet remains unsatisfied by that, [he reflects]:
"How indeed might I give a gift of internal objects? When indeed..."
Should anyone come to me and ask for an internal object to be given, if indeed some supplicant were to mention the name of my heart-flesh,

I would draw it out with a golden needle and give it to him— drawing out my heart while it drips with drops of blood, like one pulling up a lotus with its stalk from clear water. If [someone were to mention] the name of the flesh of my body...
If he should mention "palm-sugar," I will tear away the flesh of my body, like peeling off a layer of palm-sugar with a scraper, and give it to him.
If he should mention "blood," I will pierce myself with a sword or fall before a machine, fill a vessel brought to me, and give the blood.
But if someone should say, "Work does not proceed in my house; I need a servant there..."
If someone were to say, "Do it," he would think: "Having cast off my royal attire and made myself known to him, I shall perform the work of a slave.
Or, if anyone were to demand his eyes, he would think: "I shall pluck out my eyes and give them to him, like one extracting the kernel from a palmyra fruit.
Such are the unique qualities belonging exclusively to Great Bodhisattvas who have attained mastery not shared by others.

The arising of a loftier reflection; and having obtained the petitioner for his eye, despite being dissuaded by his ministers, assembly members, and others, he disregarded their words and experienced supreme joy through his conduct in accordance with that reflection;
and based on the truthfulness of that joyful state of mind, he performed an act of truth (*saccakiriyā*) in the presence of Sakka; by means of that—

Furthermore, the restoration of his own eyes to their natural state and the possession of divine power by them— such as these should be understood as the qualities and majestic powers of the Mahāsatta.
The commentary on the conduct of King Sivi is concluded.
9. Commentary on the Vessantara Deeds 67.
Regarding the ninth [verse], "She who was my mother," the Teacher speaks here referring to himself as the one who had become Vessantara.
For this reason he says: "The noble lady named Phussatī. At that time, his mother was indeed named Phussatī.
She was a Kṣatriya woman. "In past births" means in the birth immediately preceding that one;
for this plural form is used in the sense of a singular. The connection is: "She was the beloved chief queen of Sakka.
Alternatively, she who was my mother in this final existence was named Phussatī in past births; there, in that past birth, she was a Kṣatriya.
"In that [existence] immediately preceding this one, I was born in her womb as Vessantara, and I was the beloved chief queen of Sakka.
Herein, this is the sequential narrative:
Ninety-one aeons ago, a Teacher named Vipassī appeared in the world. In his time, there was the city of Bandhumatī.
While [the Buddha] was dwelling at the Khema Deer Park, King Bandhumā gave a precious piece of choice sandalwood sent by another king to his eldest daughter.
She had it ground into a fine powder, filled a casket with it, and went to the monastery;
there she worshipped the Teacher’s gold-colored body and placed the remaining powder in the fragrant chamber (*gandhakuṭi*).
Having scattered [the powder], she made an aspiration, saying, "Venerable Sir, may I become the mother of a Buddha such as yourself in the future.
Passing away from there, as a result of that offering of sandalwood powder, her body— as if sprinkled with red sandalwood—
migrated through the realms of gods and humans, until she became the chief queen of Sakka, the king of the gods, in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven.

Having offered [the sacrifice], she was reborn. Then, when the signs of the end of her life had appeared and Sakka, King of the Devas, knew that her lifespan was exhausted, he spoke out of compassion for her, saying: "Bhadde, Phussati, I shall grant you ten boons;
take them. Thus it is said:
“Having perceived her exhaustion of life, the Lord of Devas said this:
‘I grant you ten boons; choose a boon, O blessed lady, whatever you desire.

In that context, *varā* means “choose a boon,” “take a boon. “O blessed lady, whatever you desire” (*bhadde, yadicchasi*) means: “O blessed lady Phussati, whatever you wish for, whatever is dear to you—that, choose as a boon, receive it!”—thus he speaks in ten sections.
69. Furthermore, she spoke this again; not knowing her own nature as subject to death, she said, "What fault have I committed?

and so forth. For, having become negligent and unaware of the exhaustion of her own lifespan, she thought that he who was saying, "Take a boon," must be desiring her rebirth somewhere, and thus she spoke.
In this context, *aparādhatthī* means "there is a fault" (*aparādho atthi*).
"Is it so?"—why indeed am I, who was once dear to you, now become one to whom you should be angry and who is no longer beloved?
"You have driven me from this delightful place"—you have expelled me from this beautiful spot.
"Like the wind from a tree"—just as a powerful gale uproots a tree, why do you wish to drive me away from this heavenly world? Thus he asks him the reason.
70. *Tassidaṃ* means "this belongs to her. *Na ceva te kataṃ pāpaṃ* means that no evil has been committed by you at all, such that there might be an offense on your part.
*Na ca me tvaṃsi appiyā* means that you are not unloved by me; the intention is that you are not someone who, being hateful, would be called unloved by me.

71. Now, showing the intention with which he wished to grant boons, he said, "Your life span is only this much; your time of passing away will come," and then, making him choose the boons, he said: "Accept these ten most excellent boons given by me.
In that context, *varuttame* means the most excellent, the foremost among boons. 72.

*Dinnavarā* means having been granted boons by virtue of the promise, "I shall give you boons. *Tuṭṭhahaṭṭhā* means [they were] thrilled and delighted by the satisfaction of obtaining what they desired.
She was "satisfied" (tuṭṭhā) by seeing that he had reached the pinnacle [of his power], and "delighted" (haṭṭhā) through the influence of joy.
She was "gladdened" (pamoditā) by intense gladness. "Making me her innermost [wish]" means making me the foremost among those boons.

Having learned of her own state of having reached the end of her lifespan, and having been granted an opportunity by Sakka for the purpose of granting boons, she chose ten boons for the entire surface of Jambudīpa.
Looking about and seeing King Sivi’s residence as worthy of herself,
she chose these ten boons there: the status of his chief queen, her own dark-blue eyes, dark-blue eyebrows, the acquisition of a son endowed with distinguished virtues named Phussatī,
an unprotuberant belly, the ability to reach her knees, hairlessness, delicate skin, and the power to release those condemned to death.
Thus, having taken those ten boons, she passed away from there and was reborn in the womb of the chief queen of King Madda.
As she was being born, she was born with a body as if sprinkled with sandalwood powder; therefore, on the day of her naming ceremony, they gave her the name Phussatī.
Having grown up with a great retinue, at the age of sixteen, she possessed the most excellent beauty.
So it happened. Then King Sīva of Jetuttara brought her back for his son, Prince Sañjaya;
he raised the white parasol over her, made her the senior among sixteen thousand women, and installed her in the position of chief queen.
Thus it is said:
“Then, having passed away from there, Phussatī was reborn among the kṣatriyas;
in the city of Jetuttara, she met with Sañjaya.
She became dear and pleasing to King Sañjaya. Then Sakka, reflecting, [considered] “among the boons granted by me to Phussatī...”
Seeing that "the nine boons have been fulfilled," he thought, "The boon for a son has not been fulfilled; I shall cause even that to be fulfilled.

Then, seeing that the Bodhisatta’s lifespan in the Tāvatiṃsa deva-world was exhausted, he went into his presence and said, "Venerable sir, it is fitting for you to take rebirth in the womb of the chief queen of King Sivisañjaya in the human world."
Having obtained the promise of himself and sixty thousand other sons of the gods who were subject to death, he returned to his own abode.
The Great Being, too, passed away from that state and was reborn there. The remaining sons of the gods were likewise reborn in the houses of the sixty thousand ministers.
When the Great Being had entered her womb, Queen Phussatī [stationed herself] at the four city gates.

Having had six alms-halls constructed at the gate of her residence in the center of the city, she became pregnant with a longing to give alms by distributing six hundred thousand [pieces of gold] every day.
When the king heard of her longing, he summoned the brahmin soothsayers and questioned them.
They replied, "Great King, a sublime being who delights in giving has been conceived in the queen’s womb; she will find no satiety through giving."

Having heard, “He will not attain it,” he set his mind at ease and established the aforementioned kind of giving. He satisfied ascetics, brahmins, the aged, the sick, the poor, the destitute, forest-dwellers, and beggars.
From the moment of the Bodhisatta’s conception, there was no limit to the king’s income.
By the power of his merit, kings throughout the whole of Jambudīpa sent him tribute. Thus it is said:
“When I had descended into the womb of my dear mother Phussatī,
my mother became devoted to giving because of my splendor.
To the poor, the afflicted, the aged, beggars, and travelers— ”
"To the ascetics and brahmins who have exhausted [their defilements], he gives a gift to those who possess nothing.

In this context, "by my power" means by the majesty of my inclination toward giving (*dānajjhāsaya*). "Exhausted" refers to those whose wealth and so forth are completely depleted and who have reached a state of destitution.

"Possessing nothing" refers to those who have no property. In all these cases, the locative case is used for the object (*visaya*), for the poor and others are the objects for the practice of the virtue of giving.
The Queen, carrying her pregnancy with great care, when the ten months were complete, desired to see the city and informed the King.
The King had the city decorated like the city of the gods, placed the Queen upon a magnificent chariot, and caused her to circumambulate the city.
At the moment she reached the middle of the street of the Vessas, the winds born of karma...
They moved along. The ministers informed the king. He had a lying-in chamber constructed for her right there on Vessavaṇa Street and provided it with guards.
There she gave birth to a son. Thus he said:
“Having carried him for ten months, while performing a circumambulation of the city;”
“Phussatī gave birth to me in the midst of the street of the Vessas.
(77) ‘I have no name derived from my mother’s side, nor any originating from my father’s side.
Since I was born here in the street of the Vessas, therefore I became known as Vessantara.’”
Therein, "making the city circumambulate to the right" refers to when King Sañjaya, taking the queen with him, was performing a circumambulation of the city. "Of the Vessas" means of the merchants.
"Not called after the mother" means not named after the maternal line, such as the maternal grandfather and so forth. "Born from the father": *pettika* means "of the father";
*sambhava* means "that which arises from this"; that which has its origin (*sambhava*) in what is paternal (*pettika*) is "born from the father" (*pettikasambhava*).
This indicates that the name was not given on account of his relationship to his mother and father. "Born here" (*jāto ettha*) means "born in this place.

There is also a reading, "I am born" (*jātomhi*). Therefore, regarding the phrase "he became Vessantara": because he was born at that time in the street of the Vessas (*vessa-vīthiyaṃ*), he was named Vessantara;
the meaning is that they gave him the name Vessantara.
As the Mahāsatta was emerging from his mother’s womb, he did so free from impurity, opening his eyes as he came forth.
Immediately upon being born, he extended his hand toward his mother and said, “Mother, I wish to give a gift; is there anything?
Then his mother, saying, “Dear son, give a gift according to your desire,” placed a purse containing a thousand pieces near his hand. Thus spoke the Bodhisatta.
Indeed, in the *Ummagga Jātaka*, in this present birth, and as his final existence—thus in these three places—he spoke [of himself] as soon as he was born.
The King appointed sixty-four nurses for the Great Being, whose milk was sweet and free from such defects as being too thick;
he also provided nurses for the sixty thousand boys born together with him. Together with those sixty thousand boys...
He grew up together with a vast retinue. The king had a prince’s ornament worth a hundred thousand coins made and gave it to him.
When he was four or five years old, he took it off and gave it to his nurses; thereafter, he would not accept it even when they offered it back to him.
Hearing this, the king said, "What my son has given away is truly well-given," and had another ornament made for him.
He also gave that away. Even as a young child, he gave ornaments to his nurses nine times.
But when he was eight years old, sitting on his couch, he thought: "I am giving gifts to outsiders; that does not satisfy me.
I desire to give internal gifts. For if someone were to ask for my heart, I would give it."
Having extracted my heart, I would give it. If he should ask for my eyes, having gouged them out, I would give them.
If he should ask for the flesh or even the blood from my entire body, having cut the flesh from my whole body and pierced [my veins] with a sword to draw the blood, I would give it.
Or if someone should say, "Be my slave," I would offer myself to him.

"May he give it. As he was thus reflecting upon its essential nature and its own inherent quality, this great earth—two hundred thousand and forty thousand yojanas in thickness, bounded by water—trembled. Mount Sineru, the king of mountains, inclined and stood facing the city of Jetuttara.
Therefore it is said:
“When I was a young boy, eight years from my birth,
while sitting in the palace, I thought of giving a gift.
‘I would give away my heart, my eye, my flesh, and even my blood.’”
Having made the proclamation, "I would give my body if anyone should ask of me," while I was contemplating its true nature— unshakable and unestablished—
the earth, with Sineru and its forest garlands as its crest-ornament, trembled there.
In that context, "having announced" means having announced one's status as a slave, saying: "From this day forward, I am his slave.

"If anyone should entreat me" means if someone should make a request of me. "While considering my true nature" means while considering my own true nature—which is unerring, as it actually is, insatiable, and according to one's own intention; the meaning is "while considering me," or "in me."

"Unshaken" means devoid of trembling. "Unstuck" means devoid of contraction. The meaning is: free from that greed and so forth by which the minds of those who are not Bodhisattvas might experience trembling—consisting of fear—and contraction—consisting of shrinking—at the time of giving their eyes and other organs.

"Unshakable" means immovable. "The forest-garland of Sineru" refers to the forests of the wish-fulfilling trees, such as the Nandana, Phārusaka, Missaka, and Cittalatā groves, which have arisen upon Mount Sineru.
Sineru-vana. Alternatively, Sineru and the delightful groves in Jambudīpa and other regions constitute Sineru-vana;
she who has that grove as her crest-ornament is Sineruvanavaṭaṃsikā.
And while such a trembling of the earth was occurring, a sweet and deep rain-cloud thundered and sent down a brief shower.
Lightning bolts flashed forth, the great ocean surged upward, Sakka, king of the gods, clapped his hands, and Mahābrahmā gave his approval;
from the human world up to the Brahma realm, there was a single tumultuous roar. At the age of sixteen, the Great Being attained mastery in all arts.
His father, desiring to give him the kingdom, consulted with his mother.
Having brought from his own royal family the princess named Maddī, the daughter of his maternal uncle, and having appointed her as the chief consort over sixteen thousand women,
he consecrated the Great Being in the kingship. From the time the Great Being was established in the kingdom,
he bestowed six hundred thousand [pieces of gold] daily, maintaining a great distribution of alms, and every half-month...
He approached to observe the distribution of alms. Later on, Queen Maddi gave birth to a son.
They received him with a golden net, and therefore they gave him the name Jāli Kumāra.
At the time when he was walking about on foot, she gave birth to a daughter. They received her with a black antelope skin, and therefore they gave her the name Kaṇhājinā.
They did so. Therefore it was said:
“On the fifteenth day of each half-month, on the full-moon Uposatha day, having mounted the elephant Nāga, he came to give a gift.”
In this context, *anvaddhamāse* means "every half-month"; the sense is "at each half-month. *Puṇṇamāse* means "on the full-moon day";
the connection is that they approached to give a gift on the fifteenth day, which is endowed with the completion of the month and the fullness of the moon.
Herein, the construction is as follows: having mounted the support (the elephant), they went to the hall of giving every half-month to give a gift.

I approached him; and as I was approaching, when I came on the fifteenth day of the full moon during the Uposatha to give a gift, the brahmins from the province of the Kaliṅga kingdom arrived there, saying, "We have come for the elephant named Paccaya," that auspicious elephant.
For on the very day the Bodhisattva was born, a female elephant capable of traveling through the sky...
Having brought a young elephant entirely white in color, which was considered highly auspicious, and having placed it in the position of the state elephant, he departed.
Because it had been obtained by making the Great Being the condition (*paccaya*), they gave it the name "Paccaya.
Having mounted that state elephant named Paccaya, she approached to give alms. Thus it is said:
“Brahmins from the region of the Kaliṅga kingdom approached me;
they begged me for a noble elephant, one esteemed as an auspicious omen.
‘The country is without rain, there is famine, and great hunger prevails.’”
“You give me the noble elephant, all-white, the best of tuskers.
In this regard, the verse beginning with “From the territory of the Kaliṅga kingdom” has already appeared below in the account of the King of Kuru;
therefore, their meaning and the method of the narrative should be understood according to the manner explained there. However, here [the point] is because the auspicious elephant was white.
“It is all-white, the best of elephants,” it was said. Seated upon the noble back of the elephant, the Bodhisatta declared:
“I give and do not waver when Brahmins ask of me;
I do not withhold what is at hand; my mind delights in giving.”
Proclaiming his own delight in giving, he said:
“When a supplicant has approached me, a refusal is not fitting for me;
let not my commitment be broken—I shall give away the elephant in its full majesty.”
Having made this promise, he descended from the back of the elephant and walked around it to inspect the unadorned parts;
finding no such part, he took a golden pitcher filled with scented water mixed with flowers and said, "Sirs, come this way.
Placing the elephant's trunk—which resembled a well-adorned silver wreath—into their hands, he caused them to pour out the water.
He gave away an adorned elephant. Therefore it was said:
"Having seized the elephant by its trunk, with jeweled water-pots, he poured water into their hands and gave the tusker to the brahmins."
In this context, "existent" (*santa*) refers to the gift that is currently available. "I do not conceal" (*nappaṭigūhāmi*) means I do not hide it.
For one who thinks of what belongs to oneself, "let it be mine alone," or who refuses when asked, conceals it in effect even if it stands directly before the supplicants.
However, the Great Being, beginning with his own head, [gave] the gift of internal things.
As if desiring to give, how could he reject what is external? Therefore he said, "Being present, I do not conceal it.
For this very reason he said, "My mind delights in giving. The rest has already been explained in meaning below.
Furthermore, the ornaments on the four feet of that elephant were worth four hundred thousand [pieces of gold]; on both...
For the girths, there were two hundred thousand ornaments; for the belly, a woolen rug worth one hundred thousand;
for the back, three nets—namely, a net of pearls, a net of jewels, and a net of gold—each worth three hundred thousand;
for both ears, two hundred thousand ornaments; for the back, a spread woolen rug worth one hundred thousand; and for the frontal globes, one hundred thousand.
There were three hundred thousand for the three crest-ornaments, one hundred thousand for the ear-ornaments,
two hundred thousand for the ornaments of the two tusks, one hundred thousand for the svastika ornament on the trunk,
one hundred thousand for the tail-ornament, one hundred thousand for the ladder for mounting, and one hundred thousand for the feeding-bowl— excluding these...
This priceless treasure amounts to twenty-four hundred thousand [pieces of gold]. Furthermore, there are these six priceless items:

the gem on the handle of the sunshade, the crest-jewel, the gem in the pearl necklace, the gem on the goad, the gem in the pearl necklace used for wrapping the elephant’s neck, and the gem on the elephant’s frontal globe;
and the elephant itself is also priceless—thus, together with the elephant...
He gave all seven priceless items to the brahmins. Likewise, he gave five hundred elephant-attendants, together with the elephant-herders and elephant-guards.
Along with this gift, earthquakes and other such phenomena occurred, just as described in the manner previously stated. Therefore it was said:
“Furthermore, when he gave away that supreme elephant,
all-white in every limb, even then the earth, with Sineru’s forest as its crest-ornament, trembled.
Thus it is also said in the Jātaka:
“At that time there was a terror, at that time there was a thrill of the hair;
when the noble elephant was given away, the earth trembled all over. (88) Regarding the gift of that elephant:
together with the six priceless [treasures], it included an array of ornaments worth two million four hundred thousand [pieces of gold].
By the sacrifice of that auspicious elephant. "The Sivis" refers both to Prince Sivi and the inhabitants of the kingdom of Sivi;

furthermore, "the Sivis" is merely a designation for the teaching. For therein—ministers, assembly members, brahmins, householders, town-dwellers, country-folk, citizens, and all the inhabitants of the kingdom—[honored] King Sañjaya, Queen Phussatī, and Queen Maddī.
Setting aside all [others]. "Enraged" means they were angry with the Bodhisatta because of his treatment of the deities. "Assembled" means they had gathered together.
It is said that those brahmins, having obtained an elephant, mounted it, entered through the great gate, and proceeded through the middle of the city.
And when the great multitude asked, "O brahmins, from where has our king's elephant been mounted? they replied, "By the Great King Vessantara."
"No elephant has been given; who are you? they asked, as they went along poking him with their hands and other gestures.

Then, beginning with the ministers, the great multitude gathered at the palace gate and said, "A king should indeed give wealth, grain, fields, land, or male and female slaves and attendants to the brahmins; how can it be that this Great King Vessantara—"
“He will give us a state elephant worthy of a king; we shall not now allow him to ruin the kingdom in this way.
Having thus complained and reported the matter to the great king Sañjaya, they departed without complying with his entreaties. However, they merely said:
“Do not punish him with staff or sword, for he is not deserving of bondage.”
“Exile him from the kingdom; let him dwell on the Vaṅka mountain,” they said.
Therefore it was said:
“They exiled him from his own kingdom; let him go to the Vaṅka mountain.”
Therein, "they caused him to go forth" means they made efforts for him to dwell outside the kingdom.
The king, thinking, "This opposition is great; come now, let my son dwell outside the kingdom for a few days," said:
"If this is the desire of the Sivi people, we shall not reject their desire."
“Let him dwell this night and enjoy sensual pleasures.
Then, at the end of the night, with the rising of the sun,
let the Śivis, having become united, banish him from the kingdom.”
Having spoken thus, he dispatched a messenger to his son, saying, "Report this matter to my son. He did so.
Upon hearing it, the Great Being thought:
"With whom am I angry? I see no misdeed of mine; why are the young birds enraged with me?"
“O Kāṭṭha, explain that to me: for what reason do they banish me?
Thus he asked the cause. When Kāṭṭha replied, “Because of your gift of elephants,” he was filled with joy and said:
“I would give my heart and my eyes; what need have I for external wealth?
“Whether it be gold or fine gold, pearls, beryl, or gems—
seeing a supplicant arrive, I would give even my right arm as a gift;
I would not waver, for my mind delights in giving.”
"Let all the Sivis wish to either ordain me or kill me;
I shall not desist from giving. Let them cut me into seven pieces as they please," he said.
Then, [he added], "Let the citizens grant me the opportunity to give alms for one day; having given alms tomorrow, on the third day..."
Having said, "I shall go," he dispatched Kattāra to them, saying: "Tomorrow I shall give a great almsgiving called the 'Seven Hundreds.
Prepare seven hundred elephants, seven hundred horses, seven hundred chariots, seven hundred women, seven hundred male slaves, seven hundred female slaves, and seven hundred cows;
and provide all kinds of food, drink, and other things worthy of being given."
Having thus commanded the minister in charge of all affairs, "See that she is attended to," he went alone to Queen Maddī’s residence.
He exhorted her toward generosity, saying, "Dear Maddī, when you are laying down a treasure for your future journey, you should give it to those who are virtuous.
Having explained the reason for his own departure, he said, "I shall go to the forest to dwell there; you remain right here."
"Do not be distressed; dwell here," he said. She replied, "Great King, I shall not live even for a single day apart from you.
On the second day, she offered a great almsgiving consisting of seven hundred items. While she was still giving that gift of seven hundred items, evening fell.
Having gone by means of a decorated chariot to the residence of her parents, she said, "I shall depart tomorrow."
Having taken leave of them while they were weeping with tearful faces against their will, and having paid homage and circumambulated them clockwise, he departed from there.
Having stayed in his own residence that day, on the following day he descended from the palace, thinking, "I shall go.
Although Queen Maddī was being urged to turn back by her mother-in-law and father-in-law through various pleas, she disregarded their words.
Having paid homage and performed a circumambulation, and having taken leave of the remaining women, she took her two children and went ahead of Vessantara, standing upon the chariot.
The Great Being, having ascended the chariot and stood there, took leave of the great multitude, saying: "Be heedful in giving and the other perfections..."
Having given him this exhortation, "Perform meritorious deeds," he departed from the city. The Bodhisattva’s mother, thinking, "My son is a master of giving;
let him give," sent out carts filled with the seven precious gems along with her own ornaments on both sides.
He, too, gave away the ornaments and goods upon his own person to the beggars who had arrived—eighteen [cartloads].
Having given the price for the horse, he gave away everything else. As soon as he had departed from the city, he wished to turn back and look upon it.
Then, through the power of his merit, the great earth split and turned at a spot the size of a chariot, causing the chariot to face back toward the city.
He looked toward the dwelling place of his parents; because of that compassion, the earth shook.
Thus it was. Therefore it is said: “As they were being driven out,” and so forth. 89–90.
Therein, “nicchubhamānānaṃ” means as those Śivis were casting them out; the sense is that they were expelling them. Or, it refers to those who were departing.
“To offer a great gift” means to give the Great Gift of the Seven Hundreds. “They will entreat” [means they will request].
"I entreated. "Having caused it to be heard" means having had it proclaimed. "Kaṇṇabherim" refers to a pair of great kettledrums. "Dadāmahaṃ" means "I give. 91.
"Then there" (athettha) means then, while this gift was being given, at this offering.

"Tumulo" means a state of tumultuous uproar. "Bheravo" means terrifying, bringing about fear. For, with the exception of the Great Being, it produces fear in others; such is its manner of generating fear.
In order to show this, he said, “By means of this gift,” and so forth.
By reason of the gift of this Great King Vessantara, the Śivis expelled him from the kingdom and sent him into exile; nevertheless, he continues to give such a gift as this.

(Verses 92–94) Now, in order to demonstrate that gift, he spoke the verse beginning with “The elephant. In that context, *gavaṃ* means a cow; *catuvāhiṃ* means one that carries a load on four [sides].
"Carriers" (*vāhino*) means those who carry [the burden] well by giving a chariot; the meaning is that they gave four noble thoroughbred horses and a chariot to the brahmins.

For as the Great Being was thus departing from the city, he turned back his sixty thousand ministers born with him and the rest of the people who were following behind with tearful faces, and driving the chariot forward, he said to Maddī:
“Bhadde, if beggars should come from behind, you must look out for them. She sat watching.
Then, four brahmins arrived, unable to catch up with the great gift of seven hundred [cows] and the gifts she had made at the time of departure;
they asked, “Where is Vessantara? and were told, “He has gone away in his chariot after giving the gift.”
“Let us ask for the horses,” they said, and followed after him. Seeing them approaching, Maddī announced, “O King, there are beggars.
The Great Being stopped the chariot. They came forward and asked for the horses. The Great Being gave them the horses. Having taken them, they departed.
But once the horses were given away, the front of the chariot remained suspended in mid-air. Then four sons of the gods, having approached in the guise of red deer, [spoke].
Having taken up the yoke of the chariot, they departed. The Great Being, knowing their state as sons of gods, said:
"Come now, Maddī, look! They appear like forms created by thought;
bearing me on the right, they draw the chariot in the guise of deer."
Maddī said:
"In that regard, 'like a wondrous form' means like a marvelous form. 'The draft-animals' means they carry me as well-trained horses would.
Then, while he was going in this manner, another brahmin approached and asked for the chariot. The Great Being [gave] his wife and children..."
Having alighted, he gave him the chariot. But once the chariot was given away, the sons of the gods vanished.
From that time forth, they were all on foot. Then the Great Being said, "Maddī, you take Kaṇhājina;
I shall take Jāli-kumāra," and taking both children upon his hips, they conversed with one another in affectionate dialogue as they traveled along the path.

As they were asking people for the way to Vaṅkapabbata, and while the trees bent down of their own accord so that they could give fruit to the children, they reached Cetaraṭṭha on that very day because the path had been shortened by benevolent deities.
Therefore it is said: “Having given a chariot drawn by four horses,” and so forth.

"Standing there at the crossroads" (*cātummahāpathe*) means that he stood at what is called a "four-way junction" (*catukka*), because it was a place where one could pass through by piercing the path of the brahmin who had come along his own way of travel and the path by which he himself had come.
"Having given the chariot to that brahmin. "Alone" (*ekākiyo*) means being solitary due to the absence of companions such as ministers or servants; for this very reason, he said:
“Without a second”: he spoke this to Queen Maddi;
he addressed Queen Maddi with these words. 96–99. “Like a lotus, like a white water-lily”: like a *paduma* and like a *puṇḍarīka*. “He took a black antelope skin”:
he took a black antelope skin. “Of noble birth”: one endowed with a distinguished lineage. “Uneven and even ground”: uneven and level portions of the earth.
*Enti* means they come. Regarding *anumagge paṭippatheti*, one should understand that there is an elision of the word *vā*, as in "on the path along [the road] or on the opposite path.

*Karuṇaṃ* is a neuter abstract noun; the meaning is "the state of being compassionate" (*karuṇāyitattaṃ*). "They inform them of their suffering" means: "These people, so delicate, are traveling on foot;
Vaṅkapabbata is still far from here"—thus, out of compassion for us at that time, [they spoke].
They experience suffering for themselves; likewise, the meaning is that they make known the suffering that has arisen within themselves.
100–1. *Pavane* means in the great forest. *Phaline* means possessing fruit. *Ubbiddhā* means risen upwards, lofty.
*Upagacchanti dārake* means that just as fruits come within the reach of children’s hands, so too do the trees themselves [bring them] by their own branches.
Having bowed down, they approach the children.
(102) "Acchariya" means worthy of a *accharā* (a celestial nymph); it is appropriate to clap one's hands (*accharaṃ paharituṃ*). "Abbhuta" means that which has become what was never before.
Because it is capable of making the hairs of the body bristle, it is called "lomahaṃsana. "Sāhukāra" means a cry of "well done" (*sādhukāraṃ*); this very [term is used].
Or this is another reading. She is called *sabbaṅgasobhanā* because she shines with all her limbs and members by virtue of being the Woman-Treasure (*itthiratana*).
103–4. “Accheraṃ vata” means “O, how wonderful! “By the majesty of Vessantara” means by the power of Vessantara’s merit.
“The *yakkhas* shortened the road” means that the deities, impelled by the splendor of the Great Being’s merit, caused that path to diminish.
They committed [the act], yet they did only a small amount; however, because it was done as if out of compassion for the children, it is said, "out of pity for the children.
For from the city of Jetuttara, there is a mountain named Suvaṇṇagiritāla five *yojanas* away;
from there, a river named Kontimārā five *yojanas* away; and from there, a mountain named Mārañjanāgiri five *yojanas* away.
From there, the village named Daṇḍabrāhmaṇagāma was five yojanas away; from there, Mātulanagara was ten yojanas away;
thus, that kingdom was thirty yojanas from the city of Jetuttara. Urged by the splendor of the Bodhisatta’s merit, deities cleared the road.
They traversed all of that in a single day. Therefore it is said:
“On the very day he departed, he arrived at Cetaraṭṭha.
Thus, having reached the city of his maternal uncle in Cetaraṭṭha during the evening, the Great Being sat in a hall near the gate of that city.
Then Queen Maddī wiped the dust from his feet, massaged them, and said, “Of Vessantara...”
Thinking, “I shall make him know that I have arrived,” he emerged from the sal grove and stood at the gate of the grove within his line of sight.
The women entering and exiting the city saw him and surrounded him.
When the great multitude saw Vessantara, his sons, and likewise [his wife] thus arrived, they informed the kings. Sixty thousand kings...
Weeping and lamenting, they approached him; having dispelled the fatigue of the journey, they asked the reason for his coming.
The Great Being related everything, beginning with the gift of the elephant. Having heard this, they invited him to rule their kingdoms.
The Great Man said, "Let my acceptance of your kingdoms be as it is; however, the king has banished me from the realm."
"Therefore, I shall go to Vaṅka Mountain itself," he said; and although they entreated him in various ways to stay there, he did not accept their invitation.
Having received their protection, he stayed that night in the hall itself.
On the following day at dawn, after eating a meal of various choice flavors, he set out surrounded by them and traveled the fifteen-league road.
Having stood at the forest gate and turned them back, he proceeded for fifteen yojanas ahead of them along the path exactly as they had instructed.
Therefore it is said:
"Sixty thousand kings were then dwelling in Mātula;..."
All of them, with palms joined in reverence, approached weeping.
Having exchanged greetings there with the Cetans and the sons of the Cetans,
they departed from that place and went to Mount Vaṅka.
"Having conversed here and there" means having engaged in friendly greetings and conversation upon meeting with those kings there.
"By the sons of the Ceta king" means by the princes of Ceta.
"When they had departed from there" means when those kings had turned back from that location at the forest gate. "We went to Vaṅka Mountain" means that we four people went toward Vaṅka Mountain.
Then the Great Being, proceeding by the path pointed out by them, reached Mount Gandhamādana; having stayed there that day,
he then went toward the northern direction along the foot of Mount Vepulla,
sat on the bank of the Ketumatī River, ate the honey and meat given by the forest-dweller, gave him the golden needle, and bathed.
Having drunk and his thirst being allayed, he crossed the river and sat for a short while at the foot of a banyan tree standing on a mountain ridge.
Rising and proceeding, keeping Nālika Mountain to his left, he went to the Mucalinda Lake;
reaching the northeastern corner of the lake’s shore, he entered the dense forest by a single-path track.
Having passed beyond that, he reached the Caturassa lotus pond ahead of the mountain fastnesses and river sources.
At that moment, Sakka, reflecting, thought: "The Great Being has entered the Himālaya; it is necessary to find a dwelling place for him.
Having thus reflected, he dispatched Vissakamma: "Go to a delightful spot on the slopes of Mount Vaṅka."
“Construct a hermitage. He then constructed there two leaf-huts, two walking-paths, and two places for staying by night and by day;
in those various locations he displayed trees laden with diverse flowers, flowering shrubs, and groves of plantain trees.
Having prepared all the requisites for those who have gone forth, he said, “Whoever desires to go forth, let them take them.”
Having written the letters and having caused the non-human beings, the terrifying sounds, and the wild animals and birds to retreat, he returned to his own place.
Seeing a footpath, the Great Being thought, "This must be the dwelling place of those who have gone forth.
He left Maddī and his two sons right there, entered the hermitage grounds, and upon examining the letters, realized, "I have been sent by Sakka."
