Having opened the door of the leaf-hut, he entered; then, setting aside his sword and bow, removing his garment, and assuming the guise of an ascetic, he took up a walking staff and went out. With a tranquility equal to that of a Paccekabuddha, he approached the children.
Queen Maddi, too, seeing the Great Being, fell at his feet and wept, and remained there together with him.
Having entered the hermitage and gone to his own leaf-hut, he assumed the guise of an ascetic. Afterwards, they also made their sons into young ascetics.
The Bodhisatta requested a boon from Maddī: “From now on we are called ‘those who have gone forth’;
and a woman is indeed a stain upon the holy life (brahmacariya). Do not come into my presence again at an improper time. She replied, “Very well.”
Having accepted [the proposal], she also requested a boon from the Great Being: "Your Majesty, you two take our children and remain right here;
I shall fetch fruits and roots. From then on, she brought fruits and roots from the forest and tended to the three people.
Thus, the four kṣatriyas dwelt within the womb of Vaṅka Mountain for about seven months. By that...
It is said: “Having summoned Vissakamma, the lord of gods, who possesses great supernormal power,” and so forth.
Therein, “having summoned” means having caused him to be called. “Possessing great supernormal power” means endowed with great divine psychic power (*iddhi*).
“Having made the hermitage well-constructed” means having fashioned the hermitage site so that it was well-made, delightful, and suitable for Vessantara to dwell in.
*Paṇṇasālaṃ*: "Sumāpayā" means construct well. There is an ellipsis for the verb "āṇāpesi" (he ordered). "Sumāpayi" means he constructed properly.
111. "Asuñño": Just as that hermitage was not empty, so by making it not empty for him, I am "not empty.
Or, reading it as "asuñne," I dwell protecting the children in the hermitage which is not empty because of my own dwelling there.
I dwell there. By the power of the Bodhisatta’s loving-kindness (*mettā*), all the animals within three *yojanas* around also attained loving-kindness.
While they were thus dwelling there, a brahmin named Jūjaka, a resident of the kingdom of Kaliṅga, [set out] for Amittatāpanā...
When his wife said, "I am not able to do for you constantly the threshing of grain, fetching water, cooking rice-gruel and meals, and so forth;
bring me a male or female slave as an attendant," he replied, "Lady, where shall I find a poor man like me a male or female slave? To which she said, "This King Vessantara lives on Mount Vaṅka."
When she said, "Ask for his sons to be my attendants and bring them here," he—
unable to disregard her words because his mind was bound to her by the power of defilement— had provisions prepared and eventually reached the city of Jetuttara,
where he asked, "Where is the Great King Vessantara?"
The great multitude, saying, "Because of excessive giving to these beggars, our king has been banished from the kingdom;
having thus destroyed our king, he is coming back here again," pursued the brahmin, shouting abuse with clods of earth, sticks, and other weapons in their hands.
Possessed by a deity, he emerged from there and ascended the path leading to the village of Vaṅkapabbata.

In due course, having reached the forest gate and entered deep into the great forest, he became lost and was wandering about when he encountered a servant boy appointed by those kings for the purpose of guarding the Bodhisatta.
When asked by him, "Where are you going, O Brahmin? and he replied, "To the presence of the Great King Vessantara," [the boy said], "Certainly..."
Thinking, "This brahmin is going there to ask for his son or his daughter," and being threatened by him with the words,
"Do not go there, O brahmin! If you do go, I shall cut off your head right here and make it food for my dogs," he,
terrified by the fear of death, thought, "I am a messenger sent by his father."
"I have come because I thought, 'I shall bring him back,'" he said, speaking a falsehood. Hearing this, the son of the Cetan tribe was delighted and joyful;
he paid honor and respect to the brahmin and pointed out the path to Vaṅkapabbata village.
As he proceeded further from there, he encountered an ascetic named Accuta on the way, asked him for the path, and when that man also pointed out the way, [he continued on].
Following the path indicated by that sign, he proceeded in due course until he reached the vicinity of the Bodhisatta’s hermitage.
At a time when Queen Maddi had gone out to gather fruits, he approached the Bodhisatta and requested the two children. Thus it is said:
“A traveler came to me while I was dwelling in the forest.”
“Both Jāli and Kanhājina, my two little sons, I beg of you.
When the brahmin had thus asked for the children, the Great Being, filled with joy at the thought, “At long last a petitioner has come to me;
today I shall fulfill the perfection of giving without remainder,” extended his hand and [offered] the purse containing a thousand pieces.
As if setting them down, gladdening the brahmin’s heart and making the entire interior of that mountain resound, he said:
“I give these two sons of mine to you; however, Queen Maddī will go to the forest in the morning for the sake of fruits and return in the evening.
When she has returned, show her these two sons, and you [should provide] roots and fruits.”
“Having eaten and stayed for one night, you shall depart at dawn once your fatigue has vanished,” he said.
The brahmin thought, “Granted, he gives away his children out of a noble disposition; however, the mother, being greedy for her calf, might come and create an obstacle to the gift.
What if I were to press him and take the children now, this very day? Having reflected thus, he—
“If my sons have been given to you, what is the point now in sending them after showing them to their mother? Take the children and let us depart this very day,” he said.
“If you, O Brahmin, do not wish to see the princess, their mother, then take these children and go to the city of Jetuttara;
there, King Sañjaya will receive the children with great…”
"He will give you wealth; with that, you will take male and female slaves and live in comfort.
Otherwise, these delicate royal princes—what service will they perform for you?
he said. The brahmin replied, "Even this I cannot do; I am afraid of the king's punishment. I shall take them to my own village."

He said: "Having heard this conversation between them, the children thought, 'Our father indeed wishes to give us to the brahmin,' and they departed, went to the lotus pond, and hid themselves among the lotus stalks.
Not seeing them, the brahmin said, 'You said, "I give the children," yet you have caused them to depart; this is not your virtuous conduct. Then the Great Being—"
Rising up suddenly and searching for the children, he saw them hidden within a lotus thicket and said: "Come here, dear ones!
Do not create an obstacle to my perfection of generosity; bring my aspiration for giving to its ultimate fulfillment.
This brahmin will take you and go into the presence of your grandfather, King Sañjaya."
“Dear Jāli, if you wish to be free, you may become free by giving a thousand *nikkhas* to the brahmin;

and if you give a hundred male slaves, a hundred female slaves, a hundred elephants, a hundred horses, a hundred bulls, and a hundred *nikkhas*—that is, a total of seven hundred—to Kaṇhājinā, you will become free.
Having thus caused the princes to value their freedom, having comforted them, and having taken them with him, he went to the hermitage.
Having gone there and taken water with his water-pot, making it a condition for the attainment of omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*), he poured the water into the hand of the brahmin.
Becoming filled with exceeding joy and gladness, he caused the earth to resound and gave the gift of his beloved son.
Here too, as previously described, earthquakes and other such phenomena occurred. Thus it was said:
“Seeing a beggar approach, joy arose within me;
taking both my sons, I then gave them to the brahmin.
When I was giving away my own sons to that aged brahmin,”
“Even then the earth shook, with Sineru as its forest-ornament.

Then the brahmin, wishing for the children to go, bound their hands with a creeper and dragged them. Where they were bound, the skin was torn and blood flowed. Striking them with the creeper-staff, he dragged them along. They looked at their father and said:
“Mother and father have departed, and you, dear father, will give us [to others].”
"Father, do not give us away until our mother has also come;
then let this brahmin sell us or kill us as he pleases.
Having said this, [he added]: "Furthermore, such a one is of terrible appearance and cruel in his deeds—"
“Are you a human or a *yakkha*, a consumer of flesh and blood?
Having come from the village to the forest, you ask for that wealth, my dear.
While being led away by a *pisāca*, why indeed do you look on, my dear?”
Wailing such cries, they lamented. Therein, "wealth" refers to the wealth of children.
Even as the children were thus lamenting, Jūjaka beat them, seized them, and departed.
Due to the Great Being’s piteous lamentation for his children and that brahmin’s heartlessness, a powerful grief arose within him, and remorse followed.
And this thought arose in him: he immediately recalled the lineage of the Bodhisattvas:
"All Bodhisattvas indeed become Buddhas after having made the five great renunciations; I too am among them.
And the gift of one's children is one of those great renunciations; therefore, it is not fitting for you to feel regret after giving the Vessantara gift."
Having reproached himself and bolstered his spirit with the thought, "From the moment they were given away,
they are nothing to me," he made a firm resolve and sat upon a stone slab at the door of the leaf-hut like a golden statue.
Then Queen Maddi, returning from the forest after gathering various fruits, thought, "May there be no obstacle to the Great Being's gift."
When the path had been blocked by deities wearing the forms of wild beasts, and those beings had departed, he reached the hermitage after a long time.
Thinking, "Today I have seen a bad dream and ill omens have arisen; what indeed will happen?
he entered the hermitage. Not seeing his two little sons, he went to the Bodhisatta and said, "O Lord..."
“I do not see my two little sons; where have they gone? she said. He remained silent.
Searching for her two sons, she ran here and there, seeking them everywhere; not seeing them, she went back again and asked.
The Bodhisatta, thinking, “I shall cause her to abandon her grief for her children by means of a harsh discourse,” said:
“Surely you are Maddī of the noble form, the illustrious daughter of a king;
you went out for alms in the morning, so why have you returned now at evening?
Having said this, when she had explained the reason for her long delay, he said nothing further regarding the children. She, out of grief for her sons—
Searching again, they wandered through the forests with the speed of the wind. The area they covered while wandering for a single night was fifteen yojanas in extent.

Then, at the break of dawn, having gone into the presence of the Great Being and standing there, they were overcome by intense grief at not seeing the children; like a severed plantain tree, they collapsed at his feet.
Falling unconscious upon the ground like a tree, he thought, "She is dead," and though trembling and overcome by intense grief,
he established mindfulness, thinking, "I shall first find out whether she lives or not. Although he had never before engaged in physical contact with her,
since there was no one else, he lifted her head, placed it on his thighs, and sprinkled her with water.
He wiped his chest, his face, and his heart. Maddī, having waited a short while, regained her senses and established a sense of shame and modesty;
she asked, "My lord, where have your children gone?
He replied, "Queen, I gave them away as slaves to a certain brahmin who came to ask for me. When she asked, "Why? he said:

When she said, "Your Majesty, you did not tell me while I was wandering about, lamenting all night after giving my children to the brahmin," he replied, "If it had been told to you at the very beginning, your mental suffering would have been great; but now, because of the physical pain, it will be diminished. Having said this—
“Look at me, Maddī; do not [grieve] for your sons, do not lament so bitterly.
We shall regain our sons while still living, and we shall remain free from disease.
Having thus comforted her, he spoke again:
“O Maddī, when a seeker has come, a good person should give a gift of children, cattle, grain, and whatever other wealth there is in the house;
rejoice with me, O Maddī, over this supreme gift of my children.”
Having spoken thus, she had him give thanks for her gift of her two sons.
She too said:
“I give thanks to you, O King, for this supreme gift of your two sons.”
"Having given, gladden your heart; you shall become one who gives even more.
Having said this, he offered his thanks.
While they were thus exchanging friendly greetings with one another, Sakka thought: "The Great Being, yesterday..."
Having made the earth resound for Jujjaka, he gave the children to him.
Now, if some base man were to approach her, beg for Maddī-devī, and take her away, the King would be left without recourse;
therefore, let me approach her in the guise of a brahmin, beg for Maddī, cause her to grasp the peak of the Perfections, and make her something that cannot be surrendered to anyone.
“Having given it back to him, I shall return. At the time of sunrise, he went into his presence in the guise of a brahmin.
Seeing him, the Great Being, filled with joy and gladness, thinking, “A guest has come to us,” exchanged sweet greetings with him and asked, “Brahmin, for what purpose have you come here? Then—
Sakka requested Maddidevī from him. Therefore it was said:
"Once again Sakka, having descended and assumed the likeness of a brahmin, requested from me the virtuous Maddidevī, who was devoted to her husband."

In this context, "once again" means immediately after the day the two children were given away; that is the sense of "right after that. "Having descended" means having come down from the world of the gods. "Resembling a brahmin" means having a complexion identical to that of a brahmin.
Then the Great Being, thinking, "Yesterday I gave both my children to the brahmin, and I too am all alone in the forest;
how can I give Maddī, who is virtuous and devoted to her husband?"—without saying anything, he placed the priceless jewel into the outstretched hand [of the brahmin].

As if setting it aside, without attachment or clinging, with a mind free from dejection, he was joyful and elated, thinking, "Today the perfection of generosity shall reach its culmination for me," and as if shouting to the mountain:
"I give, I do not waver; whatever you ask of me, O Brahmin!"
“I do not conceal my virtue; my mind delights in giving.
Having said this, he quickly fetched water with his water-pot, poured the water into the brahmin’s hand, and gave his wife to him. Thus it is said:
“Having taken Maddī by the hand, and having filled the hollow of his hands with water;”
"With a mind of serene resolve, I gave Maddi to him.
In this context, *udakañjali* means water in the hollowed palms; the word "water" (*udaka*) is used in the accusative case with the sense of the instrumental.
Thus, the meaning is: having filled the hollowed palms—the hands extended as a hollowed vessel—of that brahmin with water. *Pasannamanasaṅkappo* means: with a mind characterized by serene resolve.
With a heart and intention purified by the faith and confidence that arose— thinking, "Surely, by means of this sacrifice, having brought the perfection of giving (dānapāramī) to its ultimate peak,
I shall attain perfect enlightenment (sammāsambodhi)"— at that very moment all the miracles described above appeared. Thinking,
"Now perfect enlightenment is not far for him," the hosts of devas and brahmas were filled with exceeding joy and gladness.
Thus it was said:
"While Maddī was being given away, the gods in the sky were filled with joy;
even then the earth trembled, with Sineru and its forest-garlands as its crest-ornament."
Moreover, as she was being given away, Queen Maddī showed no tears, no frowning face, nor even the slightest frown; rather, she thought to herself: "Let the King do whatever he wishes. She said:
"I am a maiden who has become his wife; my husband is my master.
To whomever he wishes to give me, let him give me; he may sell me or even kill me."
He said:
"O Brahmin, even for a Great Being like me, omniscient knowledge is indeed dearer than [this earth] by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, and a hundred-thousandfold;
this gift of mine is a condition for the penetration of omniscient knowledge."
Having said, "Let it be so," he gave her. Therefore it was said:
"Even while giving away Jāli, my daughter Kaṇhājinā, and Queen Maddi, my devoted wife, I did not worry, solely for the sake of enlightenment."
"Neither both my sons were to be given by me, nor was Queen Maddī to be given;
omniscience is dear to me, therefore I gave what was dear.
In this context, "while giving, I did not think" means that while relinquishing, I did not think due to distress; the meaning is that I relinquished having become resolute.
Here it is asked: Why did this Great Being renounce his own wife and children—who were of noble birth and of the Kṣatriya caste—to become the slaves of another?
For surely, making even those who are free into slaves is not a virtuous practice for anyone.

It is said: Because it is in accordance with the Dhamma (*anudhammabhāvato*). For this is the quality of being followed by the Dhamma in the qualities that produce Buddhahood; namely, [the renunciation] of everything.
It is the relinquishing without remainder of whatever object has been grasped as "mine" or "belonging to oneself.

Indeed, for Bodhisattvas who have set out with the intent to fulfill the perfection of giving—which is free from the conceptualization of a recipient of the gift—it is not fitting not to relinquish to a petitioner anything that has been grasped as "mine";
for this is also the ancient, natural law (anudhamma) for all of them. For all...
This is the customary practice, the family lineage, and the ancestral tradition of the Bodhisattvas, namely: the relinquishing of everything.
And therein, specifically, is the relinquishing of even more beloved objects;

for no Bodhisattvas have failed to relinquish the wealth of sovereignty and kingship inherited through their lineage, nor the relinquishing of their own heads, eyes, and other limbs, nor the relinquishing of their own dear lives.

There have indeed been those who were formerly called Buddhas without having relinquished these five great sacrifices: the sacrifice of their beloved son, the founder of the family lineage; and the sacrifice of their beloved wife, who acted agreeably.

For instance, when the Blessed One was a Bodhisatta seeking enlightenment, in his third existence prior to his final birth, while he was wandering in search of awakening, [he gave away his son and wife].
While he was living on a certain mountain with his wife and children, a yakkha named Kharadāṭhika,
having heard of the Great Being’s inclination toward generosity, approached him in the guise of a brahmin and asked for the two children.
The Great Being, with a heart overflowing with joy, said, "I give the two children to the brahmin," and [gave them away] as far as the ocean-bound earth.

Trembling, he gave both children. Standing at the edge of the walkway leaning against a support-beam, the yakkha devoured the two children like a bundle of mulāla stalks, even as the Great Being looked on.
As the Great Man gazed upon the yakkha’s mouth, from which streams of blood were gushing out like flames of fire, he thought: "Alas, this yakkha has deceived me!"

Because of his well-developed skill in means (*upāyakosalla*), which does not allow space for the arising of unwholesome states of consciousness, and because past phenomena lack the nature of re-linking (*appaṭisandhi*) and because he has thoroughly mastered the conditioned factors (*saṅkhārā*) by way of their impermanence and so forth, [he reflects]:

"Indeed, my perfection of giving (*dānapāramī*) is fulfilled; indeed, my... [greatness is fulfilled] by this mass of conditioned factors (*saṅkhārakalāpa*), which is thus short-lived, fragile, and devoid of essence.
Having accomplished his purpose, the thought "this has been attained" arose as pure joy.
Knowing his own mental state at that moment—which was not shared by others—he made this aspiration:
"By the result of this, may rays of light issue forth from my body in this very manner in the future when I have become a Buddha. Based on that aspiration of his, when he had become a Buddha—
The radiance of his body remained constantly pervading the ten-thousandfold world system.
In this way, other Bodhisattvas as well, having renounced their own children and wives whom they held dearer than themselves, penetrated the knowledge of omniscience.
Furthermore, it is just as if some man were to take a village or a district from someone by means of a contract (*keṇiyā*).
While performing service for the king, he might have held wealth that had become rotten through the negligence of his own pupils.
The king, having had him seized, would cause him to be cast into prison. He would think to himself:
"While performing service for this king, I was holding such an amount of wealth; because of that, I have been cast into prison by the king. If I..."
"I might remain right here and suffer myself, and my wife, children, workers, and servants might lose their livelihood and fall into great misfortune and ruin.
What if I were to inform the king, leave one of my sons or my younger brother here, and then depart?
In this way, once freed from these bonds, I shall before long [rejoin] my friends."
"Having gathered the wealth as it was seen and given it to the king, I shall also release him from bondage;
then, being heedful, I will restore my own prosperity through the power of exertion. He would do exactly so.
This should be understood in the same way.
Herein, this is the correlation of the simile: action is like the king; saṃsāra is like the prison;
the great person standing in the prison of saṃsāra by virtue of his action is like the man placed in the prison by the king;
and the making of one’s own son or brother subject to another within that prison for the man standing there is like [the making of oneself subject to another].

And just as the liberation from suffering [of others] is like a Great Being giving his own children and so forth to others and, through the attainment of omniscient knowledge, liberating all beings from the suffering of the round of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*);
and just as that one whose suffering has vanished establishes them, together with himself, in the prosperity intended for them;
so too is the Great Being, who has removed the suffering of the round of existence by means of the path of Arhatship, [established in] the state of Buddhahood.
The abandonment of wife and children by Great Beings is itself an irreproachable nature, consisting in their possession of the perfection of the ten powers and all-knowing wisdom,
and the possession of the perfection of the threefold clear knowledge and so forth by those who carry out their word. By this same method,
it should be understood that any objection regarding their abandonment of limbs or life has likewise been cleared away.
When the Great Being had thus spoken to Queen Maddi, Sakka, filled with a sense of wonder and amazement, said:
“All obstacles, both divine and human, have been conquered by you;
the earth resounds with your fame, and your renown has reached the triple heaven.”
“To those who give what is hard to give, who perform what is difficult to do—the wicked do not follow their example;
the Dhamma of the virtuous is hard to emulate.
Therefore, the destination after death is different for the virtuous and the wicked.”
“The wicked go to hell, while the virtuous have heaven as their ultimate destination.
In this manner, he offered praise by way of rejoicing in the Great Being’s generosity.
In that context, *paccūhā* means enemies; *dibbā* means those who obstruct divine glory; and *mānusā* means those who obstruct human glory.
And what are those? It shows that all those states of stinginess were conquered by the Great Being when he gave away his children and wife.

"Hard to give" means that other disciples and solitary-bodhisattvas do not imitate the deed of those like you who perform that very difficult task of giving what is hard to give—such as children, wife, and so forth—let alone those who are wicked and stingy. Therefore...
The Dhamma of the virtuous, the practice of the Great Bodhisattvas, is difficult to follow; it is hard for others to emulate.
Thus Sakka, having offered praise by way of expressing his appreciation for the Great Man, presented Maddī to him, saying:
“I give to you, sir, my wife Maddī, who is beautiful in every limb.”
“Channa is indeed yours by marriage, and Maddī is your wife.
Having said this, he returned her to Maddī and, standing in the sky blazing with a divine body like the rising sun, identified himself:
“I am Sakka, the lord of the gods; I have come into your presence.”
“Choose a boon, O Chief of Kings; I shall grant you eight boons,” he said, and invited him to choose.
The Great Being also chose: “May my father establish me once again in the kingdom;
may he release from execution one who has reached the point of death; may I be a refuge for all beings; may I not go to another’s wife; [and] of women...”
“May I not fall under the power [of death]; may my son be long-lived; may there be abundant gifts of food, drink, and other requisites;

and may I give them with a devoted heart so that they are never exhausted. Having thus performed great acts of giving, may I go to the world of the gods, and returning from there, may I attain omniscience.
Thus he requested these eight boons. Sakka said, “Before long, your father—”
"King Sañjaya will come here himself, seize him, and establish him in the kingdom;
all your other desires will reach their fulfillment. Do not worry; be vigilant," he advised, and then departed for his own place.
The Bodhisatta and Queen Maddi lived together in joy in the hermitage provided by Sakka.

As the prince Jūjaka was being taken away, the deities provided him with protection. Day after day, a certain goddess would come during the night and attend to the prince, assuming her own divine beauty.

Possessed by the deity, he resolved, "I shall go to the kingdom of Kaliṅga," and in half a month, he reached the city of Jetuttara itself. While the king was sitting in the court of justice, a brahmin...
Seeing them walking through the royal courtyard with the children, and recognizing them, the king summoned them along with the brahmin.
Having heard the account of what had occurred, he gave the wealth according to the instructions previously stated by the Bodhisatta;
having purchased the princes, he bathed them, fed them, adorned them with all manner of ornaments, and placed the boy upon his own lap and the girl upon the lap of Queen Phussati.
They heard news of the Bodhisatta and the princess.
Upon hearing this, the king, his heart filled with agitation at the thought, "Alas,
a heinous crime has been committed by me," immediately mustered an army numbering twelve akkhobhaniya units and set out toward Vaṅka Mountain together with Queen Phussatī and the two children.
Traveling by stages, he eventually met with his son and daughter-in-law. Upon seeing his beloved children, Vessantara was unable to restrain his grief;
he lost consciousness and fell right there. Maddī, his parents, his siblings, and the sixty thousand ministers did likewise.
Among those witnessing that piteous sight, not a single person was able to maintain their composure.
The entire hermitage became like a grove of *sāla* trees crushed by the wind from Mount Yugandhara.
To dispel their state of unconsciousness, Sakka, the king of the gods, caused a rain of lotuses to fall;
those who wished to be wet were indeed wetted, yet the water, having fallen upon the lotuses, turned back and flowed away. All of them regained consciousness. Even then...
Marvelous phenomena such as the quaking of the earth, of the kinds described below, appeared. Therefore it was said:
"Furthermore, in the great forest, at the meeting of mother and father, they lamented piteously, conversing of pleasure and pain."
“Out of great shame and fear of wrongdoing, he approached both of them;
even then the earth shook, with Sineru and its forest-garlands as its ornament.
In this context, “lamenting piteously” means while all the people who had gathered, beginning with his mother and father, were lamenting piteously.
"Conversing pleasantly" means engaging in talk and conversation by way of friendly greetings after inquiring about one's happiness and suffering.
"With reverence born of shame and fear of wrongdoing toward both" means that, instead of becoming mentally agitated— thinking, "Having accepted these words of the Sivis, they have banished me,
though I am innocent and established in the Dhamma"— he maintained a mind uplifted by reverence for the Dhamma toward both of these parents.
Indeed, it was through moral shame and dread of blame that he approached me in such a manner. By the power of my Dhamma, even then the earth trembled.
Then King Sañjaya, having asked the Bodhisatta for forgiveness and handed over the kingdom, had him immediately have his hair and beard trimmed and so forth;
having bathed him, he adorned him with all kinds of ornaments until he shone like a king of the gods, and together with Queen Maddī—
Having been consecrated in the kingdom, from that very moment he surrounded his son with a fourfold army numbering twelve akṣauhiṇīs;

then, having had the sixty-yojana road from Vaṅka Mountain to the city of Jetuttara adorned, he entered the city in comfort within two months. The great multitude experienced sublime joy and gladness.

He experienced [these things]. The throwing of garments and other such acts took place. They caused the Nandi-bherī drum to be sounded throughout the city. Even down to the cats, there was a release from bondage for all those held in captivity.
On the very day he entered the city, at dawn, he thought: "Tomorrow, when night has turned to light, beggars will come upon hearing that I have arrived."
"What shall I give them? At that moment, Sakka’s seat showed signs of heat.

Reflecting on this, he understood the reason and immediately caused a rain of the seven treasures to fall, filling the eastern and western grounds of the royal palace to the depth of a man's waist like a thick cloud.
It rained knee-deep throughout the entire city. Thus it is said:
“Furthermore, having departed from the great forest with my kinsmen,
I entered the delightful city, Jetuttara, the most excellent of cities.
Seven treasures rained down, and a great cloud poured forth rain.”
Even then the earth, with Mount Sineru as its forest-diadem, shook:
“This earth is insentient, it knows neither pleasure nor pain;
yet even she has trembled seven times by the power of my giving.”
When the rain of the seven treasures had fallen in this manner, on the following day the Great Being,
having caused it to be given with the thought, "Let that wealth which fell upon the houses of whichever families be theirs alone," and having had the remainder brought back,
he had it poured together with the [previously existing] wealth into his own storehouses upon his own house-site, and then set forth a great almsgiving. "This earth is insentient."
This great earth consists of the primary elements (mahābhūta) and is devoid of volition (cetanā), whereas the deity is endowed with volition.

"Without perceiving pleasure or pain" means that, precisely because it lacks volition, it does not know pleasure or pain. Even when in conjunction with the conditions for pleasure and pain, it does not experience them.
"By the power of my gift"—even though it is such as this, that great earth [is stable] by virtue of the influence of my merit from giving. Seven times...
"Shook" means that on these occasions—when he was eight years old and resolved to give even his heart-flesh and other parts to supplicants;
at the giving of the auspicious elephant; at the time of his renunciation; at the great almsgiving he performed; at the giving away of his son; at the giving away of his wife;
at the gathering of kinsmen on Vaṅka Mountain; on the day he entered the city; and during the rain of jewels—he shook seven times.

Thus, having performed great acts of giving throughout his entire lifespan—acts which served as the cause for the manifestation of sevenfold wonders such as the shaking of the great earth within that very same single existence—the Great Being was reborn in the Tusita heaven at the end of his life. Therefore, the Blessed One said:
“Then King Vessantara, the kshatriya, having given his gift...”
"With the breakup of the body, that wise man was reborn in heaven.
At that time, Jūjaka was Devadatta; Ciñcamāṇavikā was Amittatāpanā; Cetaputta was Channa;
the ascetic Accuta was Sāriputta; Sakka was Anuruddha; Maddī was Rāhulamātā; Jālikumāra was Rāhula; and Kaṇhājinā was Uppalavaṇṇā.
His parents were of royal lineage; the rest of the assembly was the assembly of Buddhas; and Vessantara was the King, the Protector of the World.
Here too, the remaining perfections should be extracted as appropriate according to the method explained below.
Likewise, when the Great Being had entered his mother’s womb, she possessed a craving for the desire to give alms, spending six hundred thousand [pieces of gold] every day. Just so...
The inexhaustibility of his wealth even as it was being given away; the utterance of the words, "I shall give a gift; do I have anything? upon stretching out his hand at the very moment of birth;
the desire not to take back his own ornaments when they had fallen into the hands of his nurses at the age of four or five years;
and [the offering] of a portion of his own body, such as the flesh of his heart, at the age of eight years.

The power of the qualities of the Great Man (mahāpurisa) here must be made manifest as that which, beginning with the desire to give, has seven times been the cause for the appearance of many wonders such as the shaking of the great earth. Therefore, this is said:
“Thus these [qualities] of the Great Seer are wonderful and marvelous... [and so forth].”
"Even the mere clarity of mind toward them could liberate one from suffering;
how much more so their actual practice in accordance with the Dhamma!
The commentary on the Vessantara-jātaka is finished.
10. The Description of the Deeds of the Hare Sage (Sasapaṇḍitacariyāvaṇṇanā) 125–6.

Regarding the tenth [birth], when I was a hare, Sāriputta—meaning, when I was the Hare Sage while wandering in search of enlightenment—for Bodhisattvas, even though they have attained mastery over their karma, act in such ways for the sake of favoring animals of that kind.
They are reborn in the animal realm. "A forest-dweller" means one who roams in the great forest.

"One whose food consists of grass, leaves, vegetables, and fruits" means one for whom grass, dabbha-grass, leaves from trees and shrubs, any kind of vegetable, and fruits fallen from trees constitute food.
"Free from harming others" means devoid of causing pain to others. "A young dog and a young otter" means a puppy and an otter cub. "I, at that time... [means...]

"When I am a rabbit, then I advise these three companions—the monkey and the others—regarding action (*kiriya*), both wholesome and unwholesome, that is, regarding both skillful (*kusala*) and unskillful (*akusala*) deeds. 'Evil' (*pāpa*) is a way of showing the manner of instruction.
In this context, 'you should avoid evils' means: you should avoid these evils, namely, killing living beings... up to ... wrong view."
"Adhere to what is wholesome" means: generosity, virtue... [and so on]... right action of view—this is the wholesome.
"Adhere" means: settle your own body, speech, and mind by way of being directed toward this wholesomeness;
the meaning is: practice this wholesome conduct.

Thus, although the Great Being was reborn in the animal realm, because he was endowed with wisdom, he became a virtuous friend and taught the Dhamma by way of exhortation to those three people whenever they approached him from time to time.
Having accepted his advice, they would enter their own dwelling places and live there. As time passed in this manner, the Bodhisatta—
Looking up at the sky and seeing the full moon, he exhorted them, saying, "Perform the Uposatha rites. Therefore he said:
"On the day of the Uposatha, having seen the full moon, I then informed them there: 'Today is the Uposatha day.'"
“Prepare gifts, for there is one worthy of offerings to receive them;
having given gifts to one worthy of offerings, observe the Uposatha.
In this context, “having seen the moon, it has not yet been fulfilled” refers to the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight, because [the moon] is slightly incomplete.
Having seen that the moon was not full, when the night had turned to dawn at the time of sunrise on the fifteenth day of the Uposatha,
they explained the method of practice for that Uposatha day to their companions—
the monkey and the others— by saying, "Prepare gifts," and so forth; this is how the passage should be connected.
In this context, "gifts" refers to the objects to be given. "Prepare them" means to arrange them according to your capacity and strength.
"To be given" means to bestow. "Observe the fast" means to perform the Uposatha rite; guard the Uposatha precepts.
A gift given by one established in virtue yields great fruit; therefore, when a petitioner arrives, you should give from the food you yourselves would have eaten.
"Let you eat," he said, thus indicating.
They, saying "Very well," accepted the Bodhisatta’s instruction with their heads and resolved upon the factors of the Uposatha.
Among them, at dawn, the otter went to the riverbank thinking, "I shall seek food. Then a fisherman [caught] seven...
Having pulled up a rohita fish, strung it on a vine, and hidden it in the sand on the riverbank, he went downstream in the river to catch more fish.
A crocodile, smelling the scent of the fish, stirred up the sand, saw the fish, and dragged them out.
Crying out three times, "Is there perhaps an owner of these?", and seeing no owner, [he bit] the vine—
Having fastened it and placed it in his own dwelling-thicket, he lay down reflecting upon his own virtue, thinking, "I shall eat this at the proper time.
The jackal, too, while searching for food, saw two meat skewers, one iguana, and a pot of curd in the hut of a field-guard;
having called out three times, "Is there perhaps an owner of these? he [continued].
Without seeing her husband, she placed the rope used for lifting the curd-pot around her neck, bit a meat-spike and a lizard with her mouth, and set them in her own dwelling-thicket.
Thinking, "I shall eat them at the proper time," she lay down reflecting upon her own virtue.
The monkey, too, entered the forest grove, brought back a cluster of mangoes, and [placed them] in his own dwelling-thicket.
Setting aside [the food], he lay down reflecting on his own virtue, thinking, "I shall eat only at the proper time.
In all three of them, the thought arose: "Oh, would that a supplicant might come here! Therefore it is said:
"Having said 'So be it' to me, according to their capacity and according to their strength..."
"Having prepared gifts, they will search for those worthy of offerings.
But the Bodhisatta, thinking, "I shall go out at this very hour and eat dabbha grass," sat right there in his own dwelling-grove and reflected:
"It is not possible for the supplicants who have come to me to eat grass; even sesame, rice, and other such things..."
"I have nothing; if a supplicant should come to me, I shall sustain myself on grass and give my own body-flesh.
Therefore the Blessed One said:
"Sitting down, I reflected upon a gift worthy of a sacrificial offering."
“If I were to find one worthy of offerings here, what gift would I have?
I have no sesame, mung beans, black gram, rice, or ghee;
I subsist on grass, and it is not possible for me to give grass.”
“If anyone who is worthy of offerings should come to me for alms, I would give my very self; he shall not depart empty-handed.
In this context, “a gift suitable for an offering” means a gift that is appropriate by virtue of its being an offering to one who is worthy of offerings (*dakkhiṇeyya*).
I thought about the gift that ought to be given: "If I were to obtain [something] today—if I were to obtain some object worthy of offerings (dakkhiṇeyya) today—what would my gift be?
What will I have to give? [I thought: "It is not possible to give grass.
If I have no sesame, mung beans, or the like to give to one worthy of offerings, then as for that which constitutes my own food, [how can I give it?]
"It is not possible to give grass to one worthy of offerings. 'I would give my own self'—what need have I for such thoughts regarding material gifts?
Is this not my own body, blameless, easily obtained because it is not dependent on others, and fit to be used by others?
If anyone worthy of offerings should come into my presence, then this very self of mine—"
"I shall give it to him. This being the case, he who has come into my presence will not depart empty-handed or with his hands unfulfilled.
As the Great Being was thus reflecting upon the true nature of things as they are, by the power of that reflection, Sakka’s Pandukambala stone seat appeared hot to the touch.
Surveying the situation, he perceived this cause and [thought]: "Together with the king..."
Thinking, "I shall investigate," he first went to the place where the crab lived and stood there in the guise of a brahmin.
When the crab asked him, "For what purpose, brahmin, do you stand here?
he replied, "If I might receive some food, I would observe the Uposatha and practice the duties of a recluse. The crab said, "Very well, I will give you food. Thus it was said:
“Seven red fish have been pulled from the water onto dry land;
this, O Brahmin, is what I have. Eat this and dwell in the forest.
The Brahmin replied, “Let that be for now; we shall see about it later,” and he did exactly as the jackal and the monkey had suggested.
Having gone into their presence, he was invited by them as well with whatever gifts they had available, but he said, "Let that wait for now;
we shall see later. Therefore it is said:
"The field-guard's cloth and his meal for the night have not yet been brought; ... [the rest of the verse follows] ..."
“Two iguanas with meat on their backs, and one bowl of curd—this, O Brahmin, is what I have; eat this and dwell in the forest.
“Mangoes ripe, water cool, and delightful cool shade.”
“Brahmin, this I have; having eaten this, dwell in the forest.
In this context, *dussa* means “of him. *Rattibhattaṃ apābhataṃ* means removed from the evening meal. *Maṃsasūlā ca dve godhā* means two spits of meat and one iguana, roasted on coals.

*Dadhivārakaṃ* means a vessel of curd. Then the brahmin went into the presence of the wise hare. When he was asked by the hare, “For what purpose have you come? he spoke exactly as before. Therefore it is said: “Having understood my intention,” and so forth.

Therein, "having understood my intention" means having known the reflection previously described. "In the form of a brahmin" means by means of a physical existence possessing the appearance of a brahmin.
"The dwelling place" refers to the thicket where he resides. 135–7. "Contented" means satisfied equally with every portion. "For the sake of food" means for the purpose of nourishment.
"Never given before" means never given before by anyone who was not a Bodhisatta. "The supreme gift" means the most excellent gift. "Today I shall give to you..."
Having said, "I will," you, being endowed with the virtue of moral conduct (*sīlaguṇa*), thought, "It is improper for you to harm another.
Thus, having dissuaded him from taking life, he now said, "Come, light the fire," and so forth, in order to make himself fit for his consumption and give himself up.

In that context, "I will cook myself" means: "I myself, having fallen into the pit of embers prepared by you, will cook myself. "You will eat what is cooked" means: "But you shall eat what has been thus cooked."
138–9. “He gathered various kinds of wood” means that Sakka, wearing the guise of a brahmin, acted as if he were collecting various logs.

He constructed a great funeral pyre; having made it, he described it as a “chamber of embers”—one that was smokeless, with its interior filled with glowing coals, blazing on all sides, and large enough at that very moment to submerge my body. Thus he prepared a great funeral pyre.
"He performed it, having suddenly manifested it through supernormal power (iddhi)—this is the intended meaning. Therefore he said:
"He kindled a fire there, so that it would quickly become great.
In that context, "he" means he kindled it in such a way that the mass of fire would quickly become vast. Having struck [the flint],...
When his body was covered with dust, thinking, "If there are insects in the pores of my hair, let them not die," he shook his dusty body three times.
Then they sat down to one side; because the wood had not yet caught fire, he sat down a short distance to one side, waiting for it to be lit.

140. "When a great heap of wood is burning and crackling"—this means when that pile of timber is ablaze on all sides and produces a "crackling" sound due to the crests of flames tossed up by the force of the wind;
then, leaping up and falling back into the midst of those crests of flame—at that time, [one thinks: "He is capable of burning my body."

Thinking, "This is a heap of embers," he leaps up and bounds over, and with a joyful heart like a royal swan in the midst of a cluster of lotuses within a mass of flames, he casts his entire body as an offering and falls into it. 141–2.
"Into whomsoever it enters": just as cool water, when entered by anyone during the heat of summer, [brings relief].
It calmed his distress and fever, and gave rise to satisfaction and joy.
"Just like a blazing fire"—in this way, when I had entered that mass of glowing coals, there was not even a trace of heat;
on the contrary, through the joy of giving, there was only the complete subsiding of all distress and fever. "At long last, indeed, my skin, hide, and so forth..."
Every part of my body has been offered as a gift; my cherished aspiration has reached its fulfillment.
Thus it was said:
“Skin, hide, flesh, sinew, bone, and the heart’s binding—”
“I gave the entire body, whole and complete, to the brahmin.
In this context, *hadayabandhana* means the muscle of the heart. For it is called *hadayabandhana* because it stands as if binding the physical seat of the heart (*hadayavatthu*).
Alternatively, *hadayabandhana* refers to both the heart and the binding; that is, the heart-muscle itself.
The meaning is: "as if bound, with his body bent low. "The entire body" (*kevalaṃ sakalaṃ kāyaṃ*) means the whole physical frame without exception.

Thus, being unable to produce even the warmth of a single pore in his own body within that fire, the Bodhisatta, as if having entered the interior of a mass of snow, spoke thus to Sakka who was wearing the form of a brahmin: "Brahmin, by you..."
“How can fire be so cold? What is this? “O wise one, I am not a brahmin;
I am Sakka, and I have come for the purpose of testing you, which is why I did this. “Sakka, let it be as it is for you;
even if the entire world were to test me with gifts, they could never cause in me even the slightest desire not to give—do you not see this? Thus the Bodhisatta uttered a lion’s roar.

Then Sakka, thinking, "O wise hare, may your virtues remain manifest for the duration of an entire aeon," pressed against the mountain, took its essence, and drew the image of the hare upon the lunar disk.
He then laid the Bodhisatta down right there in that forest thicket upon a seat of young *dabba* grass and returned to his own celestial realm. They too—
The four wise ones, being in harmony and full of mutual affection, fulfilled the perpetual precepts and the Uposatha precepts,
performed meritorious deeds as was appropriate, and departed according to their karma.
At that time, the otter was the Venerable Ānanda, the jackal was Mahāmoggallāna, the monkey was Sāriputta, and the wise hare was the Lord of the World.
In this case as well, his perfections such as virtue (sīla) and so forth should be determined according to their respective roles in the manner already explained above.
Likewise, even while reborn among animals, there is the realization of wholesome and other phenomena as they truly are;
seeing even the slightest fault in them as a source of fear, he thoroughly abstains from the unwholesome, and correctly [engages] in wholesome phenomena for himself.

Establishing others [in virtue] by showing them the danger—saying, "Such evil qualities, when grasped and clung to in this way, lead to such a destination and such a future state"—and thereby enjoining them to abstain from them;
and explaining, "This is called generosity, this is called virtue, this is called the observance of the Uposatha; for those established in these, there are the excellences of gods and humans."

By the passage beginning with "already in hand," the establishment [of others] by showing the benefits of meritorious deeds, his disregard for his own body and life, his assistance to other beings, and his sublime inclination toward giving—such qualities and powers of the Bodhisatta are to be manifested here.
Therefore, this is said: "Thus these wonders... [and so forth]... according to the Dhamma’s true nature."
The commentary on the conduct of the Wise Hare is finished.
Now, by means of the passage beginning with “Akitti the Brahmin,” the ten specific instances of conduct previously mentioned are summarized through inspired utterances (*udāna*).
In that context, the one who gave those excellent gifts—that is, the one who bestowed those supreme gifts—was none other than myself at that time; he was Akitti the Brahmin and the others.

"I myself was that one at that time; it was not another. Thus, although he had fulfilled the perfections of virtue and the rest as appropriate in those various existences, he presented the teaching specifically by way of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramī*), with reference to the exceedingly sublime nature of his own inclination toward giving at that time.
"These are the requisites for giving; these are the perfections of giving"—referring to these very things.
In the *Akittijātaka* and others, many varieties of renunciations were performed by me, including the relinquishing of external objects of charity,

as well as the relinquishing of my own limbs, children, and wife, which reached the highest pinnacle. Although these, being embraced by compassion and skillful means and directed solely toward omniscience (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*),
constitute the perfection of giving (*dānapāramī*) through the excellence of that generosity, nevertheless, my giving— which has become a perfection in the ultimate sense— [is as follows].
Because they are prepared through the process of cultivation by means of the requisites for giving, these are called "requisites of giving.
To show whose requisites these are, it is said: "Having given even his life to the supplicant, he fulfilled this perfection.

For here, with the exception of the conduct of the Wise Hare (*sasapaṇḍitacariyā*), in the remaining nine types of conduct, the perfection of giving (*dānapāramī*) and the perfection of giving as a means (*dāna-upapāramī*) are present as appropriate.
In the conduct of the Wise Hare, however, the perfection of the ultimate meaning of giving (dānaparamatthapāramī) is to be understood. Therefore it was said:
“Having seen one who had come for alms, I relinquished my own body;
there is no one equal to me in giving—this is my perfection of giving.”
For although there is no limit to the number of existences in which the Great Being fulfilled the perfection of giving— such as during the time of the Brahmin Akitti mentioned above,
and at other times such as during the great assemblies of people under Mahāsutasoma and others— nevertheless,
it must be demonstrated that it was specifically during the time of the Wise Hare that the perfection of giving reached its ultimate state of perfection.
From the *Paramatthadīpanī*, the commentary on the *Cariyāpiṭaka*,
specifically from the section on the tenfold conduct that particularly elucidates the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).
The commentary on the first chapter is finished.
2. The Chapter on the Elephant King (Hatthināgavagga). 1. Commentary on the Conduct of Supporting His Mother (Mātuposakacariyāvaṇṇanā).

1. In the first [sutta] of the second chapter, "elephant" (*kuñjara*) means a *hatthī*. "Supporter of his mother" (*mātuposaka*) refers to one who looks after a blind, aged mother. "On the earth" (*mahiyā*) means on the ground. "By virtue" (*guṇena*) means by the virtue of moral conduct (*sīlaguṇa*); at that time, there was no one equal to me.
For the Bodhisatta at that time was reborn in the region of the Himalayas in the womb of an elephant.
He was a great, all-white, handsome elephant endowed with the auspicious marks, surrounded by many hundreds of thousands of elephants. His mother, however, was blind.
Giving sweet fruits from his own tree to the elephants, he sent them to his mother.
However, the elephants did not give them to her, but ate them themselves. Observing this, he learned of the situation and thought, "I shall abandon the herd and support my mother alone.
Then, during the night while the other elephants were unaware, he took his mother and went to the foot of Mount Caṇḍoraṇa.
He supported his mother by relying on a mountain cave situated near a single lotus pond. 2–3.
"Seeing me in the forest, a forest-dweller... refers to a certain man wandering in that great forest who saw me and reported me to the King of Bārāṇasī.
For he, having lost his way and being unable to determine the direction, was lamenting with a loud cry. The Bodhisatta also...
Hearing his cry, [the man thought], "This person is helpless; it is not fitting that he should perish here while I am present.
He went to him and, seeing him fleeing out of fear, asked, "O man, there is no fear for you because of me; do not flee! Why are you wandering about lamenting?"
When he said, "Master, I am lost; today is my seventh day [here]," the other replied, "O man, do not fear;
I will place you on the path of men. Having seated him upon his back, he led him out from the forest and turned back.
That wicked man, thinking, "I shall go to the city and report this to the king," [saw] the sign of a tree and the sign of a mountain.
While doing so, he departed and went to Bārāṇasī. At that time, the king’s auspicious elephant had died.
That man approached the king and reported to him the fact of his having seen the Great Man. Therefore it was said:
“O Great King, an elephant worthy of you dwells in the forest,” and so forth.
In that context, "suitable for you" means it is appropriate and fitting to serve as your vehicle (*opavayha*).

"There is no need for its equipment" means that there is no need for the equipment to be dug around on all sides to prevent its movement when it is seized, nor for a tethering post (*ālāna*)—known as a *āḷaka*—to which it might be bound with a rope attached to its halter, while one hides oneself behind the ears of a female elephant (*kareṇu*) and throws the rope. Where...
Once entered, he is unable to go anywhere; nor is there any purpose or need for such deceptive speech.
"Simultaneously with being seized" means at the very moment of capture. "He will come" means he will arrive.
Having made this guide of the path his companion, the king went into the forest and said to the elephant trainer, "Bring back the noble elephant described by him."
He sent him along with his retinue. Having gone with him, he saw the Bodhisatta entering a lotus pond and taking up his food. Thus it is said:
“Having heard those words of his, the king too was delighted in mind;”
He dispatched an elephant trainer, a skilled teacher who was well-trained.
Having gone there, that elephant trainer saw [the boy] in the lotus pond,
pulling up lotus roots and stalks for the sake of sustaining his mother.

In this context, *cheācariyaṃ* means a skilled elephant trainer (*hatthācariya*) who is proficient in the methods for binding elephants and so forth. *Susikkhitaṃ* means well-trained through having reached the culmination of the science of training elephants.
"Having understood my virtuous qualities" (*viññāya me sīlaguṇaṃ*) means: "This noble elephant is not dull-witted, nor fierce, nor of mixed character"—having thus known my quality of virtue.
How so? "He observed my characteristics" (*lakkhaṇaṃ upadhārayī*); because of his mastery of the well-trained art of elephant-keeping, he perceived these traits.
He examined my marks all over. Having said, "Come, son," he took hold of me by the trunk.
Seeing the elephant trainer, the Bodhisatta thought: "This danger has arisen for me from this man;
however, I am possessed of great strength and am capable of destroying even a thousand elephants if I were to become angry."
"Thinking, 'I must destroy this army and its mounts of my own country; yet if I become angry, my virtue (sīla) will be broken;
therefore, even though I am struck by spears, I shall not become angry,' he resolved his mind and stood motionless with his head bowed.
Thus the Blessed One said: 'That natural strength which was inherent in my body at that time,' and so forth."

In this context, "natural" (*pākatika*) means established by its own inherent nature. "Accompanying the body" (*sarīrānugata*) refers to physical strength that follows the body itself, not to the wisdom characterized as skill in means;
this is the intended meaning. "Equal to the strength of a thousand elephants today" means equal to the combined strength of many thousands of elephants gathered together at the present time.
"Equal and identical to their bodily strength" means exactly the same as the physical power of those [elephants].
Having offered a comparison that is truly fitting, and not merely by way of a simple simile: for at that time, the Bodhisatta had been reborn in the Maṅgala elephant lineage.

"If I were to become angry with them"—if I were to feel anger toward those who had approached me for the purpose of seizing me, I would have been capable of destroying their lives. Not only theirs alone, but even as far as my own kingdom.
"From the moment they enter my kingdom, I would crush the entire sovereignty of those men who have come and reduce it to powder and dust.
Yet, because of my protection of virtue (*sīla-rakkhā*)—even though I am thus capable—I remain guarded by the protection and preservation of virtue established within myself, like one who is bound.
I do not allow any alteration in my mind; that is, I do not permit any change in that virtue."
I do not perform the act of beating or other such methods against those beings in my mind, nor do I even give rise to such a thought toward them.
Regarding the phrase "while they were throwing me into the stall," the word "ālāne" means while throwing me into the hitching post; there is an ellipsis of the word "even having seen.
Why? Because for the fulfillment of the perfection of virtue (sīlapāramitā), if I do not break my virtue in such circumstances, before long my perfection of virtue [will be fulfilled].
"‘He will fulfill’ means: ‘I shall not allow any alteration in his mind for the sake of fulfilling the perfection of virtue (sīlapāramī)’—this is the construction.

In the verse beginning with ‘If they should [strike] you,’ he likewise demonstrates the state of being firmly resolved upon virtue by making the protection of virtue steadfast. Therein, ‘they should strike’ means they should break it. ‘Out of fear for the breaking of my virtue’ means out of fear that my virtue might be impaired.
Having thought thus, while the Bodhisatta remained motionless, the elephant trainer descended into the lotus pond and [approached] him..."
Seeing his perfection of the marks, [the king] said, "Come, my son," and taking him by his trunk, which resembled a string of silver, he reached Benares on the seventh day.
While still on the way, he sent a message to the king. The king had the city decorated.
The elephant trainer led the Bodhisatta—whose body was anointed with perfumes and fully adorned—into the elephant stable.
Having led him away and had him enclosed with a variegated fence, they informed the king.
The king, taking various foods of exquisite flavor, went there and offered them to the Bodhisatta. He, thinking, "I will not take food without my mother," did not accept the alms.
Even when entreated, he would not accept it.
“She is surely that wretched woman, blind and without a guide;
she strikes a stump with her foot while seeking a mountain with fierce lions,” he said.
Having heard this, the king—
“Who is that blind woman without a guide, O Great Naga, who strikes a stump with her foot while you, a fierce lion, are lying on the mountain? Having thus asked, [the king replied]:
“She is my mother, O Great King, blind and without a guide.”
“He stirs up a stump with his foot and causes a mountain to fall with a fierce roar.
When this was said, [the king replied: “Today is the seventh day that he has not taken food, saying, ‘My mother did not obtain any alms.
Therefore, release this great nāga, who supports his mother! Thus it is said: “Release this Great Nāga, who sustains his mother.”
“Let the Naga meet with his mother and all his kinsmen,” he said, and then he caused him to be released:
“The Naga is freed from his bonds; the elephant is freed from his girth-strap.
Having rested for a moment, he went toward the mountain.”

In this context, *kapaṇikā* means "miserable ones. "She strikes a stump with her foot" means that, because of her blindness and the suffering of separation from her son, she wails and strikes the tree stumps here and there with her foot.
"She went toward Caṇḍoraṇa" means she was heading toward Mount Caṇḍoraṇa; the sense is that she was wandering about at the foot of that mountain. "She went to where the mountain was."
Thus the noble elephant, released from his bonds, rested for a short while and taught the Dhamma to the king by means of the verses on the ten royal duties.
Having given the exhortation, "Be heedful, Great King," he departed from the city while being honored with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings by the great multitude.
That very day, having met with his mother, he related the entire account of what had occurred. With a joyful heart, she—
“May that king live long, the increaser of the kingdom of Kāsi, who has released my son and is ever devoted to honoring his elders.
Thus he offered words of thanksgiving to the king. The king, having gained confidence in the Bodhisatta’s virtues, [established] a village not far from Naḷinī.
Having had [the city] built, he established a regular service for both the Bodhisatta and his mother.
Later, when the Bodhisatta’s mother passed away, he performed the funeral rites for her body and went to the Kuraṇḍaka Hermitage.
In that place, five hundred seers who had descended from the Himālaya were dwelling; the king gave that service to them.
Having had a stone statue made in the exact likeness of the Bodhisatta, they performed a great ceremony of honor.
The inhabitants of Jambudīpa gathered together every year and held what was known as the "Elephant Festival.
At that time, King Ānanda was the Bodhisatta, the female elephant Mahāmāyā, the forest-dweller Devadatta, and the world-protector Lokanātha was the elephant who supported his mother.

Here too, the perfection of giving and the other perfections should be extracted as appropriate. However, because the perfection of virtue (sīlapāramī) is preeminent, it alone has been introduced into this teaching.

Likewise, even though he was born in the animal realm, he established a mind of reverence toward his mother—befitting his state of being praised even by the Omniscient Buddha for having formerly been a Brahmā, a former deity, a teacher, and one worthy of offerings—and thought: "This is indeed my mother."
Reflecting thus: "She is of great benefit to her son;

therefore, attendance upon one's mother has been prescribed by the wise," that lord of many thousands of elephants, possessed of great majesty, being followed by them, disregarded the danger of living alone and, abandoning the herd, went forth as a solitary being, thinking: "I shall honor the field of merit."
Supporting my mother; out of compassion for a person who had lost his way, taking him in and leading him to a place frequented by humans;

enduring the offenses committed by him; and even though I was capable of it, not causing distress to the elephant trainers and others who came to bind me—lest there be even the slightest affliction for them or a breach, flaw, or defect in my own virtue.

Likewise, here [we see] the Great Man’s effortless approach to the capture, like that of Sudanta who had not acted [against him]; his seven-day fast, thinking "I shall not swallow anything without my mother";

his failure to give rise to the thought, "I have been imprisoned by this man," but rather his suffusion of the king with loving-kindness; and his teaching of the Dhamma to him through various methods—such things as these [are seen here].
The power of his qualities is to be made manifest. Therefore it was said: "Thus these are wonderful and marvelous for the Great Seer... [and so on]...
by way of the Dhamma that accords with the Dhamma.
The commentary on the Practice of Supporting His Mother is finished.
2. Commentary on the Bhūridatta Jātaka 11.
Regarding the second [name], *Bhūridatta*: this means "given by many" (*bhūri-samādatta*). For at that time, "Datta" was the name given to the Bodhisatta by his parents.
However, because he [dwelt] in the Nāga realm, in the realm of the Great King Virūpakkha, and in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven...

Furthermore, he correctly resolved questions as they arose. One day, having gone with the assembly of Nāgas to the city of the Thirty-three (Tidasapura) to meet the Great King Virūpakkha, while the Mahāsatta sat surrounded by Sakka among the gods, a question arose that no one was able to answer.
Then, permitted by Sakka, the Mahāsatta himself sat upon an excellent throne.
He preached [the Dhamma]. Then the King of the Devas, having honored him with celestial fragrant flowers, said:
"Datta, you are endowed with vast wisdom equal to the earth; from this time forth, you shall be named Bhūridatta.
For "bhūri" is a name for the earth; therefore, because he delights in the meaning that has become vast—equal to the earth—and because of his great wisdom reckoned as "bhūri," [he is so called].

Because he was endowed with these qualities, the Great Being became known as "Bhūridatta. Furthermore, because he was possessed of great Nāga-supernormal power (*iddhi*), he was called "Mahiddhika" (of Great Power).
In the past, in this very same kappa, the son of the King of Bārāṇasī was banished from the kingdom by his father.
While living in the forest, he entered into a union with a certain young female Nāga (*nāgamāṇavikā*). From their union, two children were born.
—A son and a daughter. They gave the son the name Sāgarabrahmadatta and the daughter the name Samuddajā.
Later, upon his father’s passing, he went to Bārāṇasī and ruled the kingdom.
Then, while a Nāga king named Dhataraṭṭha was ruling the Nāga realm from a Nāga palace five hundred yojanas in extent, [he was approached] by Cittacūḷa, who spoke untruths.
Having heard what was said by the tortoise Nāma Kacchapa— that "the King of Bārāṇasī desires to give his daughter to you,
and that royal princess named Samuddajā is beautiful, lovely to behold, and inspiring"— Dhataraṭṭha dispatched four young nāgas;
and when [the king] refused to give her, he terrified him with a nāga-horror and said, "I give her."
When this was said, [the King] sent a great gift and, with great Naga-supernormal power and a large retinue, led his daughter to the Naga-abode and established her in the position of chief queen.
Later, she gave birth to four sons by Dhatarattha: Sudassana, Datta, Subhoga, and Ariṭṭha.

He obtained them. Among them, Datta was the Bodhisatta; because Sakka, with a joyful heart, had given him the name "Bhūridatta" according to the manner previously described, he became known as Bhūridatta.
Then their father divided the kingdom into portions of one hundred leagues each and gave it to them.
He possessed great glory, and sixteen thousand Naga maidens attended upon him.
His father’s kingdom was likewise only one hundred yojanas. Three of his sons came every month to see their parents, but the Bodhisatta came every half-month.
One day, he went with the Great King Virūpakkha to attend upon Sakka at the Vejayanta Palace.

Having seen the Sudhammā assembly hall of the devas, the Pāricchattaka and Koviḷāra trees, the Paṇḍukambala stone seat, the retinue of celestial nymphs, and the utterly enchanting prosperity of Sakka, he thought, "Even such a thing as this is difficult to obtain while remaining in the state of a nāga;
how much more so, then, is perfect enlightenment? Thus, loathing his nāga existence, he resolved to go to the nāga realm and observe the Uposatha fast.
Having stayed there, he thought, "I shall exert myself even further in virtue; that will bring my enlightenment to maturity and will be the cause for my rebirth in this world of the gods.
Having reflected thus, he went to the Nāga abode and said to his parents, "Mother and Father, I wish to perform the Uposatha observance.
They replied, "Observe the Uposatha right here; there is great danger for Nāgas who go outside."
Having been told this, he did so once; but being harassed by the Naga maidens, on the second occasion, without informing his parents, he addressed his wife:
"My dear, having gone to the human world, there is a great banyan tree on the bank of the Yamunā;
not far from it, upon the summit of an anthill, I shall observe the Uposatha endowed with its four factors."
Having made a formal resolve and lain down, thinking, “I shall perform the Uposatha rite,” he departed from the Nāga realm and did so accordingly.
Therefore it was said: “By the great king Virūpakkha, I went to the world of the gods,” and so forth.

Therein, “by the great king Virūpakkha” means by the great king who is the lord of the Nāgas named Virūpakkha. “To the world of the gods” means to the Tāvatiṃsa heaven of the gods. “I went” (agañchahaṃ) means I went; I approached.
12. *Tattha* means in that world of the gods (*devaloka*). *Passiṃ tvāham* means "I saw. The word *tu* is merely a particle (*nipātamatta*).
*Ekantaṃ sukhasamappite* means endowed with absolute, ultimate happiness. For this was said by the Blessed One:
"Bhikkhus, there are heavens called the six spheres of contact (*phassāyatana*). To such an extent, bhikkhus, it is not easy..."
"And by means of narration, one may reach even the bliss of the heavenly realms. "For the sake of going to that heaven" means for the purpose of going there by way of rebirth in that very heaven.
"Virtue and observance" (*sīlabbata*) refers to the observance (*vata*) characterized as virtue (*sīla*).

Alternatively, "virtue and observance" refers both to the virtue of the Uposatha day and to the observance consisting in the undertaking of the renunciation of one's own bodily parts, such as saying, "Let those who need skin take my skin," and so forth.
13. *Sarīrakiccaṃ* means the maintenance of the body, such as washing the face and so forth.
*Bhutvā yāpanamattakaṃ* means having taken food merely sufficient for the sustenance of the body, in order to keep the sense faculties from becoming inactive. *Cattāro aṅge* means four factors.
*Adhiṭṭhāya* means having resolved. *Semī* means I lie down.
14. "Skin" (*chavi*) and so forth refers to the observation of those four factors. Among them, the relinquishing of the skin and hide constitutes one factor;
the remaining [factors] are each taken individually. It should be understood that by the mention of "flesh" (*maṃsa*) here, blood (*rudhira*) is also included.
"By this" means by these. "Let him take it" means: for whomever there is a need for these skins and so forth, this has been given by me to him.
"May he take everything," [he thought], and thus he offered an invitation that was indifferent even toward his own person.
In this manner, as the Great Being performed the Uposatha observance every half-month, a long period of time passed by.
As time was thus passing, one day a certain hunter-brāhmaṇa, together with Somadatta...
Having reached that place with his own son, Nāma, he saw the Great Being surrounded by nāga maidens at the time of sunrise and approached him.
At that very moment, the nāga maidens submerged into the earth and went back to the nāga realm.
The brahmin asked the Great Being: "Who are you, dear sir? Are you a deva?"
"Or are you a *yakṣa* or a *nāga*? The Bodhisatta, revealing himself as he truly was, thought:
"If this man were to go from here, my dwelling here would become known to the great multitude, and that would create an obstacle for my observance of the Uposatha.
What if I were to lead him from here to this *nāga* abode and provide him with great prosperity? In this way, he will remain right there."
"He will take delight [there], and by that my observance of the Uposatha will become long-lasting.
Then he said to her: "Brāhmaṇa, I shall grant you great glory; the Nāga realm is delightful;
come, let us go there. She replied: "My lord, I have a son; when he comes, I shall follow. He said: "Go, Brāhmaṇa, and bring your son."
The Brahmin went and informed his son of this matter and brought him back.
Taking both of them, the Great Being, by means of his own supernatural power, led them to the abode of the Nāgas. There, their divine forms became manifest.
Then, having bestowed upon them celestial splendor, the Great Being gave them four hundred Nāga maidens each. They [lived] in great...
They enjoyed prosperity.
The Bodhisatta, too, remained diligent and observed the Uposatha rites.
Every half-month, he would go to attend upon his parents, deliver a discourse on the Dhamma, and thereafter go to the presence of the brahmin to inquire after his health.

Having asked, "Tell me what you need," and having said, "Remain here without longing and enjoy yourself," he exchanged friendly greetings with Somadatta and departed for his own home. The brahmin lived there for a year, but due to his meager merit, he became homesick;
and though his son was unwilling, he took him and, having taken leave of the Bodhisatta, departed.

Because of his lack of merit, he did not accept the abundant wealth being offered by him, nor even the wish-fulfilling jewel (*maṇiratana*), but said, "Having gone to the human world, I shall go forth. The Great Being, having given instructions to the young Nāga, brought him along with his son to the human world.
Both of them removed their celestial ornaments and celestial garments and went to bathe.
They entered a certain lotus pond, but at that moment those [robes] vanished and they went back to the Nāga realm itself.
Then, only the first pieces of cloth and saffron-colored rags remained fastened to their bodies;
taking up bows and arrows, they went into the forest, killed deer, and maintained their livelihood according to their former custom.

At that time, a certain ascetic gave to a certain brahmin who was attending upon him the Alampāyana charm—which he had obtained from the king of the supaṇṇas—along with the appropriate medicinal herbs and the ritual for its application.
Thinking, "I have found a means of livelihood," the brahmin stayed for a few days; then, taking leave of the ascetic, as he was departing, he proceeded by stages.
Having reached the bank of the Yamunā, he proceeded along the Great Road reciting that mantra.

At that time, a young Nāga maiden who was an attendant in the Bodhisatta’s palace took that wish-fulfilling jewel and, placing it upon a heap of sand on the bank of the Yamunā, sported there by its radiance throughout the night;
then, at the rising of the dawn, she [returned] to that brahmin.

Hearing the sound of the mantra, and perceiving it to be that of a *supaṇṇa*, they were terrified with fear; not taking the jewel-treasure, they submerged into the earth and went to the abode of the *nāgas*.
The brahmin took that jewel-treasure and set out. At that moment, that hunter-brahmin was together with his son.
While going into the forest to hunt, he saw that jewel in the bird’s hand;

recognizing it as "this is Bhūridatta’s wish-fulfilling jewel," and desiring to take it, he conversed with him, and having discerned his skill in counsel, spoke thus: "If you give this jewel to me, then I..."
“I will show you a nāga of great power, whom you may capture and take with you as you travel through villages, market towns, and royal capitals,
and from whom you will obtain much wealth. When he said, “In that case, show him and let me catch him,” the nāga took the Bodhisatta to the place where he performed his observance,
lay down upon the top of an anthill with his coils folded, and standing nearby, the nāga extended his hand and presented him.
When the Great Being saw that hunter, he thought, "He might create an obstacle for my observance of the Uposatha.
He led him to the Naga-abode and established him in great prosperity, yet the man did not wish to stay. Departing from there, the Great Being desired to go of his own accord;
though the hunter offered him the jewel-treasure, he did not wish to accept it. Now, however, he is coming back having captured the snake-charmer.
"If I were to become angry with this betrayer of friends, my virtue would be broken.
Furthermore, I have already undertaken the Uposatha observance endowed with its four factors; let it remain exactly as it was undertaken.
Whether Alampāyana cuts me or not, I shall not be angry with him. Having thought thus, he closed his eyes.
Having made the perfection of resolve (adhiṭṭhāna-pāramī) his precursor, he thrust his head between the tusks and lay down, remaining perfectly motionless.
The Nesaḍa Brahmin said, "O Alampāyana, seize this nāga and give me the jewel.
Seeing the nāga, Alampāyana was delighted; disregarding the jewel as nothing at all, he said, "Seize him, Brahmin," and placed it in [the Brahmin's] hand.
He threw it. It slipped from his hand and, as soon as it fell upon the earth, it entered the ground and went straight to the abode of the nāgas.
Having lost both the jewel-treasure and his friendship with Bhūridatta, the Brahmin hunter departed, utterly destitute.

15. Āḷavaka, too, having smeared his own body with powerful medicinal herbs, having eaten a small amount, and having infused his saliva into his own body, approached the Bodhisatta while reciting a divine spell;
