seizing him by the tail and dragging him forward, he gripped him firmly by the head, opened his mouth, and ate the medicine.
He poured saliva into his mouth. Out of fear of breaking his virtue, the Great Being of pure birth did not get angry and did not open his eyes.

Then, by the power of medicinal charms, [the hunter] seized him by the tail, turned him upside down with his head below, shook him, made him discard the fodder he had taken, and laid him on the ground lengthwise; then, as if crushing a cushion, he pressed him with his hands.
He rubbed him all over; his bones felt as if they were being ground to powder.
Again, seizing him by the tail, he thrashed him as if beating a cloth. Even while experiencing such suffering, the Great Being did not become angry at all;
rather, he attended solely to his own virtue. Thus, [the hunter thought] that the Great Being was weak...
Having fashioned a basket from creepers and prepared it, he placed the Great Being inside. However, because his body was so large, it would not fit within it.

Then, forcing it in by striking him with his heel, he took the basket, went to a certain village, set it down in the middle of the village, and cried out, "Let those who wish to see the dance of the Naga come! All the inhabitants of the village [assembled].
They gathered together. At that moment, Alampāyana said, "Come forth, Great Naga! The Great Being thought:
"Today it is fitting for me to play so as to delight the assembly; thus Alampāyana, having received much wealth and being satisfied, will release me. Whatever he makes me do, I shall do."
Then, as he was emerging from the basket, the other said to him, "Become great! and he became great. "Become small;
become round, hoodless, one-hooded, two-hooded, up to a thousand-hooded; be tall, short, with a visible body, an invisible body, or with half a body visible;
be blue, yellow, red, white, or crimson; emit smoke; [emit] a crest of flames."
When he was told, "And release the water," he manifested various forms one after another and displayed a dance.
Seeing this, the people were struck with a sense of wonder and amazement and gave him much gold, bullion, clothing, ornaments, and so forth.
Thus, he received about a hundred thousand [pieces of money] in that village. Although he was catching the Great Being, he said, "A thousand..."

"Once I have obtained it, I shall release him," he said. But having obtained that wealth, he did not let go of it due to his greed for riches, thinking, "I have already obtained such great wealth even in this village; surely I shall obtain even more in the city.
Having established a household in that village, he had a casket made of jewels, placed the Great Being inside it, and—
Having mounted a comfortable carriage and accompanied by a great retinue, he took him to play in villages, market towns, and royal capitals, and eventually reached Bārāṇasī.
There he gave the Nāga king sweet parched rice and unhusked grain. However, because of his fear of not being released, the Nāga did not take the food.
Even though he would not eat, [the king] had him kept for about a month in various places, beginning at the four city gates.
He caused [the elephant] to play. Therefore it was said: “Betrayed by the ungrateful,” and so forth.
In that context, “betrayed” (*saṃsito*) means he was told of his location by saying, “This elephant is lying on top of an anthill near such-and-such a banyan tree.
“By the ungrateful” (*akataññunā*) means by one who betrays his friends and does not recognize the favor done for him by himself.
The intended meaning is that he was a *nesāda* (hunter) who had become a brahmin.
"Alampāyana" refers to a snake-charmer brahmin who received the name "Alampāyana" through the recitation of the *alampāyana* incantations. "He seized me" means he took hold of me.
"He made me play here and there" means that for the sake of his own livelihood, he made me perform as a spectacle in various villages, market towns, and royal capitals.
17. "Lighter than even a blade of grass" means that the sacrifice of one's own life presents itself to me as being lighter than even the sacrifice of a blade of grass.

"Like leaping over the earth" shows that the transgression of moral virtue presents itself to me as even more burdensome than turning over the great earth, which is two hundred and forty thousand yojanas in thickness.
18. "Throughout the continuous succession of my births—even through many hundreds of births and many hundreds of births—I have been constant because of the non-transgression of virtue.
'I would give up my life; I am able to give it up' means that I would not break even a single precept I have undertaken, nor would I let it perish.
'For the sake of the four continents' shows that this is for the purpose of the glory of universal sovereignty as a wheel-turning monarch."

19. Now, in order to show for what purpose she protected her virtue even at the cost of her own life, and how, through that protection of virtue, she did not allow her mind to waver toward those who were causing her harm—the hunters, Alampāyana, and the brahmin—he recited the concluding verse beginning with "Api ca. Its meaning has already been explained above.
But when the Great Being had thus fallen into the hands of the snake-charmer, his mother saw a bad dream and, not seeing her son there, was overcome with grief.
Then her eldest son, Sudassana, having heard of this occurrence, said to Subhoga:
"Go to the Himalayas, search for Bhūridatta among the five great rivers and the seven great lakes, and [bring him back]."
He sent [Ehi] with the message: "Go to the world of the gods; if Bhūridatta has been led there by the deities who desire to hear the Dhamma, then bring him back from there.
He himself, however, thinking, "I shall search for him in the human world," departed from the Nāga realm in the guise of an ascetic.
His half-sister named Accimukhī felt an exceeding affection for the Bodhisatta.

He followed him. Having turned himself into a female frog and placed himself within the matted locks, he began his search from the place where the Great Being was observing the Uposatha, and proceeding by stages, he eventually reached Benares and went to the royal gate.
At that time, Alampāyana was in the royal courtyard in the midst of a great crowd, having brought out a casket to display the sport of King Bhūridatta.
Having opened it, he gave the signal, "Come, Great Naga!
The Great Being, having poked out his head and looked about, saw his eldest brother; he emerged from the box and set out toward him.
The great multitude, struck with fear, retreated. He went, paid homage to him, and returning, re-entered the very same box.
Alampāyana, thinking, "This ascetic has been bitten by this [snake]," said, "Do not fear! Do not fear! Sudassana, however, thought, "What can this snake do to me?
There is no snake-charmer equal to me," and having provoked a verbal dispute with him, he said, "You roar while holding this snake; as for me, I desire this frog-skin..."
"I shall destroy her," he thought; so, calling his sister to him, he stretched out his hand.

Hearing his voice, she who had been lying within his matted hair croaked three times like a frog, then emerged, sat upon his shoulder, leaped up, and let fall three drops of poison upon the palm of his hand, whereupon she entered back into his matted hair once more.
Sudassana showed him a drop of poison and said, "If this drop were to fall upon the earth, all medicinal herbs, grasses, and forests would perish.
If it were thrown into the air, there would be no rain for seven years.
If it were cast into water, all living beings born therein would die. Having spoken thus, he caused the king to believe him.
Having caused three pits to be dug, he filled one with various medicinal herbs, the second with cow dung, and the third with divine herbs;
then, having placed a drop of poison in the middle pit, at that very moment it smoked and flames arose.
The fire went and seized the pit of cow dung; from there also flames arose, and having taken the pit filled with divine herbs, [it consumed] the divine herbs.
Having consumed [the fire], he attained parinibbāna. Thereupon, the heat from the pit reached Alampāyana as he stood nearby;
it permeated him and stripped away the skin of his body, so that he became afflicted with white leprosy. Terrified by fear, he cried out three times: "I release the Nāga King!
Hearing this, the Bodhisatta emerged from the jewel casket, adorned with all manner of ornaments.
Having manifested his own form, he stood there with the grace of a deity. Sudassana and Accimukhī likewise remained there.
Then Sudassana informed the king of his status as the king’s nephew.

Upon hearing this, the king embraced them, kissed them on the head, led them to the inner palace, and having bestowed great honor and hospitality upon them, [he treated them] together with Bhūridatta.
While offering him hospitality, he asked, “Dear brother, how did Alampāyana come by such great power?
He related everything in detail and taught his maternal uncle the Dhamma, saying, “Great King, it is fitting for a king to rule his kingdom according to this method.
Then Sudassana said, “Maternal uncle, my mother [gave] Bhūridatta—”

"Seeing nothing, she grows weary; it is not possible for us to indulge in further elaboration here. Having thus taken leave of his maternal uncle, he went back to the Naga-abode together with Bhūridatta and Accimukhī.
Then, while the Great Being was lying there on his sickbed, a great multitude arrived to inquire after his health.
Having gained confidence in the Naga assembly regarding the Vedas, sacrifices, and Brahmins, he refuted the arguments of Kāṇa-Ariṭṭha,
taught the Dhamma through various methods, and established them in the perfection of virtue and the perfection of view.
Having observed the precepts for as long as he lived and performed the Uposatha rites, he filled the city of heaven at the end of his life.
At that time, the parents were members of great royal families. The Brahmin Nesāda was Devadatta;
Somadatta was Ānanda; Accimukhī was Uppalavaṇṇā; Sudassana was Sāriputta; Subhoga was Mahāmoggallāna; Kāṇāriṭṭha was Sunakkhatta;
and Bhūridatta was the Lord of the World.
In this case as well, his remaining perfections (pāramīs) are to be determined according to the method explained below.

Here too, although he dwelt in his own nāga-abode extending for a hundred yojanas, enjoying himself like a picture with sixteen thousand nāga-maidens and established in the sovereignty of the nāga-world which resembled the splendor of the deva-world, he remained free from the intoxication of power. Every half-month...
Attending upon one’s mother and father, honoring those who are senior in the family, and— having immediately severed, in the midst of each respective assembly,
the questions raised by the entire host of Nāgas, the assembly of the Four Great Kings,
and the assembly of the Tāvatiṃsa gods with the sword of his own wisdom as if with a sharp blade through a cluster of lotus stalks— he taught the Dhamma in accordance with their inclinations.
Having abandoned the aforementioned abundance of wealth, he undertook the observance of the Uposatha endowed with its four factors,
regardless of his own body or life; therein, out of fear of deceiving his promise, he went into the hands of a snake-charmer,
and when poison-laced spittle was dropped into his mouth, he was seized by the tail and dragged along the ground.
Even when they inflict various kinds of injuries such as rubbing, crushing, and pounding, and even while he experiences such great suffering,
there is not even the slightest alteration of the mind out of fear of breaking his virtue,
despite his being capable of turning that [offender] into ashes merely by looking at them with anger; nor does he think, "I shall make him obtain wealth."

Such as the Bodhisatta’s compliance with his mind; his freedom from anger even toward the hunter-brāhmaṇa—who was ungrateful, treacherous to friends, and had brought him back with great wealth—despite not being bound by formal precepts;

and his establishing the assembly of nāgas in virtue and right view after refuting the false doctrine propounded by Kaṇāriṭṭha and teaching the Dhamma in many ways. These and others like them [are the deeds of the Bodhisatta].
The power of his virtues is to be made manifest. Therefore this is said: “Thus these wonders... [as before] ...in accordance with the Dhamma.
The commentary on the Bhūridatta-jātaka is finished.
3. Commentary on the Campeyya-nāga-jātaka.
20. Third: Regarding "Campēyyaka," there is a river named Campā between the kingdoms of Aṅga and Magadha;
because a nāga-abode was situated not far downstream from it, it was also called Campā. The nāga-king born there was Campēyyaka.
"At that time too I was righteous" means that even during the time of the nāga-king Campēyyaka, I was a practitioner of the Dhamma.
For at that time, having been reborn in the abode of the Campā nāgas, the Bodhisatta became a nāga king named Campeyya, possessed of great psychic power and majesty.
While exercising sovereignty there and enjoying a wealth of lordship comparable to that of a king of the devas, he thought:
"Since this is no occasion for fulfilling the perfections, what use have I for this animal womb? I shall observe the Uposatha."
"Having lived here and being liberated from this state, I shall fulfill the perfections (pāramīs) in the proper manner.
From that time forth, he performed the Uposatha rites within his own palace itself. Adorned Nāga maidens would come into his presence;
thinking, "An obstacle to my virtue will arise here," he would depart from the palace and sit in the garden. Even there, they would come to him.
He thought: “There will be a defilement of my virtue here; therefore, having departed from this Nāga-abode and gone to the human world, I shall observe the Uposatha.
From that time forth, on Uposatha days, he would depart from the Nāga-abode and, not far from a certain frontier village, stay upon the top of an anthill near the road.
“Let those who need my hide and so forth take the hide and so forth; let those who wish to make a play-snake make a play-snake.
Having thus relinquished his body as an object of generosity, he lay down, folding his limbs, and observed the Uposatha on the fourteenth and fifteenth days.
On the first day of the lunar fortnight, he would go to the abode of the Nāgas. As he was thus observing the Uposatha, a long period of time passed by.
Then the Bodhisatta, having been told by his chief queen named Sumanā, "O Lord,
you go to the human world and observe the Uposatha; however, that place is fraught with danger and fear," stood on the bank of the Maṅgala lotus pond and said,
"If anyone, my dear, should strike me and cause me distress, the water of this pond shall become turbid."
"It will happen thus: if a supaṇṇa seizes it, the water will boil; if a snake-charmer seizes it, the water will become the color of blood.

Having explained these three signs to her, he observed the Uposatha of the fourteenth day, departed from the Nāga realm, went there, and lay down upon the summit of an anthill, [displaying] his bodily splendor.
Adorning the anthill, his body was as white as a silver garland, and his head was like a ball of red wool;
at the time of Bhūridatta, his body was the size of a ploughshare, but at the time of Saṅkhapāla,
it was the size of a ship with a single hold.

At that time, a young Brahmin from Bārāṇasī went to Takkasilā, mastered the Alampāyana charm, and while returning to his own village by that same route, he saw the Great Being. Thinking, "What is the use of my going home empty-handed?
I shall capture this nāga and, by performing spectacles for villages, market towns, and royal capitals, earn wealth before I depart," he reflected thus.
Having taken divine medicinal herbs and recited a divine mantra, he went into his presence.
From the moment he heard the divine mantra, it was as if heated needles were being driven into the Great Being’s ears, or as if his head were being churned by a pestle.
He thought, "Who could this be? and raised his head from within his coils.
Looking about, he saw the snake-charmer and thought: "My venom is of fierce power;
if I were to release a breath from my nostrils in anger, this man's body would be scattered like a handful of chaff, and thus my virtue would be broken.
I will not look at him. So, closing his eyes, he placed his head within the coils of the serpent.
The snake-charmer brahmin, having consumed a medicinal herb and recited a mantra, sprinkled his saliva upon the Great Being’s body.
Through the power of both the herbs and the mantra, every spot touched by the saliva became like the moment of emergence for the sloughed skins of snakes.
Then, seizing him by the tail, he dragged him and laid him down lengthwise;
pressing down with his heel, he weakened him, and grasping his head firmly, he squeezed it. The Great Being opened his mouth.
Then, pouring saliva into his mouth, he broke the teeth by the power of his medicinal mantra. The mouth was filled with blood. The Great Being—
Out of fear of breaking his own virtue, he endured such suffering and did not even so much as open his eyes to look.
The other, thinking, "I shall weaken the Naga king," began from the tip of his tail and, as if crushing his bones,
massaged his entire body and applied what is called a "cloth-wrapping" bandage, then rubbed it with what is called "silk-thread oil."
Seizing him by the tail, he beat him with what is called a "cloth-beating. The Great Being’s entire body became smeared with blood, yet he endured that great pain.
Then, perceiving his weakness, they constructed a cage from creepers, placed him inside it, and [carried him] to a frontier village.
Having led him into the midst of the great multitude, he had him perform for their amusement.

Whether it was regarding colors such as blue and so forth, shapes such as circular or square, or dimensions such as minute or large—whatever the brahmin desired, the Great Being would dance by performing exactly that;
he would even manifest a hundred or a thousand hoods. The great multitude, being filled with faith, gave him much wealth. Thus, in a single day alone...
He received a thousand kahāpaṇas as well as requisites worth a thousand. From the very beginning, the brahmin had thought, "Having received a thousand, I will distribute them.

But having obtained that wealth, he thought, "If I have already received this much wealth even from a mere frontier village, how much more wealth shall I receive when I present myself before the king and the royal ministers?"
Taking both a cart and a pleasure carriage, he placed the requisites in the cart and sat in the pleasure carriage.

Thinking, "I shall entertain the Great Being with a vast retinue through villages, market towns, and royal capitals, and after entertaining him in the presence of King Uggasena in Bārāṇasī, I will release him," he departed.
He would kill frogs and give them to the king of the city. The king of the city [said], "Again and again..."
Thinking, "He will kill me because of me," he did not eat. Then the brahmin gave him sweet rice cakes.
He too did not eat them, thinking, "If I take this food, my death will surely occur right here inside the basket.
After about a month, the brahmin reached Bārāṇasī; while amusing himself in a village near the city gate, he obtained much wealth.
The king also summoned him and said, "Teach us to dance as well. He replied, "Very well, Your Majesty; on the fifteenth day of the coming fortnight, I shall teach you to dance.
The king had a drum beaten, proclaiming, "Tomorrow the Nāga king will dance in the royal courtyard; let the great multitude assemble and watch.
On the following day, having had the royal courtyard decorated, he summoned the brahmin.
Thus, having led the Great Being to the jewel casket and placed the casket upon a variegated rug, he sat down.
The king also descended from the palace and, surrounded by a great multitude, sat upon his royal throne. The brahmin brought forth the Great Being and had him dance;
the Great Being displayed every manner of expression that the brahmin could imagine. The great multitude was unable to maintain their composure.
Thousands of thunderclaps resounded. A rain of jewels fell upon the Bodhisatta. Therefore it was said:
“Even then, [I saw] me practicing the Dhamma,” and so forth.
Therein, “even then” (tadāpi) means even when I was the Naga king Campeyyaka. “Practicing the Dhamma” (dhammacārin) refers to the Dhamma of the ten courses of wholesome action.
He thus conducts himself; he is a practitioner of the Dhamma because he does not practice even the slightest unrighteousness (*adhamma*).

"Having observed the Uposatha" means having observed the Uposatha by way of guarding the noble Uposatha virtue endowed with the eight factors. "He plays at the king's gate" means he causes him to play at the palace gate of King Ugga in Bārāṇasī.
22. "Whatever color he thought of": that brahmin snake-charmer thought, "Let it be whatever color, blue and so forth.
Therefore it is said, "blue or yellow or red. In this context, the word "or" (*vā*) has the sense of indefiniteness;
it is stated in the shortened form for the sake of the meter's ease. By that word "or," the remaining specific colors such as white and so forth are also included.
It encompasses specific distinctions of shape, such as circularity, and specific distinctions of measure, such as minuteness and grossness.
"Following his mind" means following the mind of that snake-charmer. "Appearing like what was thought" shows:
"I appear to the onlooker in whatever manner he has thought."
23. "And it is not only the power of making him see the form I have thought of that is my majesty.
Furthermore, I could turn dry land into water, and I could turn water into dry land; I would even be able to take the great earth and make it water, and take the water and make it earth.
Such is my great majesty. If I were to become angry with that snake-charmer..."
“If I were to become angry, I would turn him to ashes in an instant; at the very moment anger arose, I would reduce him to cinders.

(24) Thus, having demonstrated his capacity to ward off the harm that had arisen for himself at that time, the Blessed One now spoke the words beginning with “If I were master of my mind” in order to show the underlying purpose for which he did not exercise that warding-off power.
The meaning of this is as follows: “This snake-charmer is excessively harassing me; he does not know my spiritual power. Come now, [let me deal with him].”
“I shall show my own power! Thinking thus, he became angry. [He reflected: “If I were a master of my mind even by a mere glance, then this [opponent] would be scattered like a handful of chaff.
In that case, I would fall away from the virtue (sīla) as it was undertaken.

And if that were to happen, for one who has fallen away from virtue and whose virtue is broken—[what would become of] this [merit] of mine toward the Blessed One Dīpaṅkara, the Possessor of Ten Powers?”
If one’s aspiration begins from the soles of the feet, that supreme goal—the state of Buddhahood—will not be accomplished.

(25) “Let this body break apart”: although this body, composed of the four great elements and a mass of boiled rice and sour gruel, is subject to the nature of impermanence, being liable to rubbing, crushing, breaking, and destruction, let it indeed break and perish right here in this very place, like a handful of chaff cast into a great wind.
"Let it be scattered as if it were chaff; yet I shall not break my virtue. This shows that he endured such suffering at that time, having reflected:
"Even if my virtue—which is the cause for the attainment of the supreme goal—is scattered from this body like a handful of chaff, I shall not break it;
being indifferent to both body and life, I shall fulfill only the perfection of virtue (sīlapāramitā)."
Now, when the month had been completed for the Great Being while he was in the hands of the snake-charmer, he remained without food for that entire time.
Sumanā, thinking, "My husband has been gone for too long; what could be happening?", looked toward the lotus pond.
Seeing the water colored red, she realized, "He must have been seized by the snake-charmer. Then, departing from the Nāga realm, she went to the vicinity of the anthill.
Having gone to the place where the Great Being had been seized and the place where he had suffered, she wept and wailed.
Then, going to a border village and inquiring, she heard the news of what had happened. She went to Benares and stood at the king’s gate, weeping in the air.
The Great Being, while dancing, looked up into the air; seeing her, he was ashamed, entered his basket, and lay down.
When the king entered the basket, he looked here and there, wondering, "What could be the reason?
Seeing her standing in the air, he asked, "Who are you? Upon hearing that she was a Naga maiden, he thought, "Without doubt, the Naga king, having seen her, entered the basket out of shame;
and this supernatural power (iddhānubhāva) displayed here belongs to the Naga king alone."
Having reached the conclusion that it was not the snake-charmer’s [power], he asked, "How did this Naga king of such great majesty come into his hands?
and was told, "This Naga king is a practitioner of Dhamma and virtuous;
while observing the Uposatha on the fourteenth and fifteenth days, he offered his own body as a gift at the mouth of a donation and [stood] upon the summit of an anthill near the main road."

He lies down there, having been seized by this [Nāga]; for him there are many thousands of women resembling celestial nymphs, and his prosperity in the Nāga realm is equal to the excellence of the world of the gods.
He possesses great psychic power and majesty, capable of overturning the entire earth;
yet, fearing that "my virtue (sīla) will be broken," he undergoes such a transformation and suffering.
Having heard the words, “...he experiences [the result],” he was immediately moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*).
He gave that brahmin snake-charmer much wealth, great fame, and power, and said, “Come now, sir, release this king of the nāgas,” and had him released.
The Great Being made his nāga-form disappear and stood there in the form of a young brahmin student, like a divine youth. Sumanā too—
Descending from the sky, he stood before him. The Naga king, having made an añjali to the king, entreated him, saying, "Come, Great King, come to see my abode. Therefore the Blessed One said:
"The Campa Naga, being liberated, spoke thus to the king:"
"Homage to you, O King of Kāsi! Homage to you, O Increaser of Kāsi!
I extend my hands in reverent salutation to you; may I behold your dwelling.
Then the king granted him permission to go to the abode of the nāgas. Taking him along with his retinue, the Great Being departed for the nāga realm.
Having led him there, shown him the excellence of his own sovereignty, and had him stay for several days, he caused a drum to be beaten, proclaiming:
"Let the entire royal assembly take as much wealth as they desire, such as gold and bullion.
He also sent wealth to the king by means of many hundreds of carts, saying: "Great King, a king must indeed give gifts and guard his virtue."
"Righteous protection, defense, and security must be established everywhere. Having thus exhorted him with these ten discourses on the duties of a king, he dismissed him.
The king, departing from the Nāga abode with great splendor, returned to Bārāṇasī itself.
From that time forth, it is said, gold and bullion appeared throughout the land of Jambudīpa. The Great Being, having observed the precepts, [went] every half-month...
Having performed the Uposatha ceremony, he, together with his retinue, filled the city of heaven.
At that time, the snake-charmer was Devadatta, Sumanā was the mother of Rāhula, Uggasena was the Elder Sāriputta, and the Nāga king Campeyyaka was the Lord of the World (the Buddha).

Here too, the remaining perfections should be extracted according to their respective contexts. In this case, the marvelous powers of the Bodhisatta are exactly as described by the method stated previously.
The commentary on the conduct of the Campeyya Nāga is finished.
4. Commentary on the Conduct of Cūḷabodhi:
Regarding the fourth [chapter], "Cūḷabodhi" refers to this [existence] as the state of the paribbājaka Mahābodhi. Thus it is called "Cūḷabodhi."
A designation has been applied [to him], but it should be understood that this does not mean the Great Bodhisatta’s status as an elder brother and so forth occurred only in this particular Jātaka.
"Susīlavā" means one who is well-possessed of virtue; the meaning is "one whose virtue is perfected.

Regarding the phrase "bhavaṃ disvāna bhayato," it means having seen existence—such as existence in the realm of sensual desire—as something to be feared. And here, regarding the word "nekkhamma," there is the particle *ca*...
An elision (lopa) is to be understood; by this, the word “having seen” (disvāna) is drawn forward. This is what is meant:

by reflecting upon these eight bases for spiritual urgency—birth, aging, sickness, death, the suffering of the states of misery (apāya), the suffering rooted in the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa) in the past, the suffering rooted in the cycle of existence in the future, and the suffering rooted in the search for nutriment in the present.
Having seen all existence— comprising the divisions of sense-pleasures and the rest— as presenting the fear of *saṃsāra*, [he saw] Nibbāna,

the serenity and insight that serve as its means, and the going-forth (*pabbajjā*) that serves as the means for those; thus, having seen these three kinds of renunciation (*nekkhamma*) through the eye of knowledge established by tradition and other means as being the opposite of that [existence],
[he saw] the state of a householder as crowded with manifold disadvantages due to his undertaking the ascetic going-forth.
"Having gone forth," means having departed.
"The second wife" refers to his former wife, who was his spouse during his time as a householder. "Golden-hued" means having skin resembling gold.
"Indifferent to the round" means having no attachment to *saṃsāra*. "He went forth for the sake of renunciation" means he departed from his home for the purpose of attaining renunciation.
“Nikkhami” means he went forth; “pabbajī” is the meaning. 28.

It is called *ālaya* because beings cling (*ālayanti*) by means of it; it is craving (*taṇhā*). By the absence of that, they are “without clinging” (*nirālayā*). Precisely for that reason, because the bond of craving toward kinsmen has been severed, they are “one whose ties are cut” (*chinnabandhu*).
Having thus shown the absence of the bonds of a householder, [the text now] shows the absence of bonds even for some who have gone forth...
To show the absence even of that which constitutes a bond, it is said: "without regard for family or group. In this context, "family" refers to the family of supporters;
"group" refers to the groups of ascetics—the others being called celibate practitioners (*brahmacārins*).
"We approached" means that both of us approached.
29. *Tattha* means in the vicinity of Bārāṇasī. *Nipakā* means possessed of wisdom (*paññā*).
*Nirākule* means not crowded by people because it is devoid of human traffic; *appasade* means having little noise because it is free even from the sounds of the cries of wild animals and birds.
*Rājuyyāne vasāmubho* means that at that time, we two people were living together in the king’s pleasure garden of Bārāṇasī.

In this regard, the sequential account is as follows: In the past, during this very Bhaddakappa aeon, the Bodhisatta, having descended from the Brahma-world, was reborn as the son of a certain wealthy Brahmin in a village of Kāsī.
At the time of his naming ceremony, they gave him the name “Bodhikumāra. When he reached maturity, he went to Takkaśilā.
Having gone abroad and mastered all the arts, they returned; and although he was unwilling, his parents brought home for him a young maiden of equal caste from a noble family.
She too, having passed away from the Brahma-world, possessed a supreme beauty and resembled a celestial nymph.
Even though both were unwilling, they had them marry one another. Yet, in neither of them did any defilement manifest.
Never before had there even been a mutual glance out of lustful passion, let alone any other form of contact;
thus they were pure in virtue.
Later on, when the Great Being’s parents had passed away, he performed their funeral rites and summoned him.
“Bhadde, take this wealth of eight hundred million and live in happiness,” he said. “But what about you, noble son?
“I have no need for wealth; I shall go forth. “But is going forth not permissible for women as well?
“It is permissible, Bhadde. “In that case, I too have no need for wealth; I also—”
“I shall go forth. Having both renounced all their wealth and given a great gift, they departed, entered the forest, and went forth.
Sustaining themselves by gleaning wild fruits through the practice of alms-gathering, they lived for ten years in the bliss of the religious life.
Then, wandering through the countryside for the sake of seeking salt and sour flavors, they eventually arrived [at Sāvatthī].
Having reached Bārāṇasī, they dwelt in the royal park. Therefore it was said: "We both dwell in the royal park.
Then one day, the king went for a pleasure excursion to the park.

Having gone to the vicinity of those two who were spending their time on the edge of the park in the happiness of the renunciant life, he gazed upon a female wanderer of supreme beauty, possessing the most excellent form.
With his mind bound by defilements, he asked the Bodhisatta, "What is this female wanderer to you?

When the Bodhisatta replied, "She is nothing at all; she has merely gone forth together with me in the same renunciation, though in our time as householders she was my wife," the king thought, "It seems she is indeed nothing to him, yet she is nevertheless..."
"In the time of his household life, she was his attendant; what if I were now to introduce her into the inner palace?

By that very means, I shall learn his conduct toward her. Thus, that blind fool, unable to restrain his own mind which was bound to her, commanded a certain man: "Take this female wanderer to the royal residence!"
Having agreed to her request, he said, "Unrighteousness prevails in the world," and so forth, and departed taking her along as she lamented.
The Bodhisatta, hearing the sound of her lamentation, looked back once; thereafter, he did not look back again.
He thought, "If I were to stop her, she would harbor ill-will toward them [the ascetics] and this would create an obstacle to my virtue."
He sat down, reflecting solely upon the perfection of virtue (*sīlapāramī*). Therefore it is said: “Having gone to see the park, the king saw the brahmin woman,” and so forth.
Therein, the phrase “Whose wife is she? To whom does she belong? means: “To you—yourself—is she who? Is she your wife, or perhaps your sister;
to whom else does she belong as a wife? [The king replied: “She is not my wife. Granted that she was my wife during the time of my household life, from the moment of my going forth...
"From this point on, she is not my wife, nor am I her husband; rather, we are fellow-followers of the Dhamma (sahadhammā) under one teaching (ekasāsanī).
I too am a wanderer (paribbājaka), and she too is a female wanderer (paribbājikā); thus, being of equal status through the teaching of the wanderers, we are fellow-followers of one teaching.
The meaning is that she is a companion in the holy life (sabrahmacārinī)."
32. "Tissa, being infatuated and attached" means having become infatuated and bound by sensual lust (*kāmarāga*).
"Having had him seized by servants" means having had her seized by servants, or having commanded his own royal attendants (*rājapurisa*)—the servants—to seize that female wanderer (*paribbājikā*).
"Oppressing her with force" means oppressing her, even though she was unwilling, by dragging her here and there and so forth.
Although he tried to stop her, she still did not go; nevertheless, by means of force and compulsion, he had her seized by the king’s men and brought into his own inner apartments.
33. Regarding "Odapattakiyā": she is called Odapattikā because she was taken as a wife after touching a water-vessel (*udakapatta*);
this expression should be understood merely as a designation for her status as a former wife, for she had been married to him according to the Brahminical rite.
“Presented by her parents” means she was given away by them; “odapattakiyā” is the locative case used in the sense of characterizing one state by another (bhāvena bhāvalakkhaṇe).
“Born together” means born together by way of birth and renunciation; for this very reason he said, “of the same dispensation” (ekasāsanī).
And here, “ekasāsanī” is a nominative form used in the sense of the locative; the meaning is “in the same dispensation. “Nayantiyā” means “being led. “Anger arose within me”—this...
"In the time of their household life, she was your virtuous wife; in the time of their renunciation, she was your co-practitioner, thus born as a sister to you.
Yet she is being dragged away by force right before your eyes. Thus addressed, Bodhi the brahmin, incited by his pride in manhood, cried out "Sussu!
like a snake that had been lying dormant for a long time and was suddenly prodded by someone from its anthill.
Like a venomous snake raising its hood, anger suddenly arose from my mind.
(34–5) "Simultaneously with the arising of anger" means together with the occurrence of anger; the sense is that it was immediately upon its arising.
"Recalling my virtue and observances" means I brought to mind my own perfection of virtue (*sīlapāramī*). "I suppressed the anger right there" means in that very instance.

While still seated on that very seat, I restrained that anger. "I did not allow it to increase further" means that from the moment that single state of mind arose, I did not permit it to grow upward beyond that.
This is what is meant: as soon as the anger had arisen, [I thought], "O Bodhi-wanderer, have you not fulfilled all the perfections and desired to penetrate the knowledge of omniscience?"
"What is this stumbling of yours over mere moral virtue?
It is like a bull wishing to reach the far shore of the great ocean while sinking in water only as deep as its own hoofprints.
Having thus reproached himself, he suppressed his anger at that very moment through the power of reflection and did not allow it to increase by way of further arising.
For this very reason, he said:

"If, O Brahmin woman," and so forth. Its meaning is as follows: even if that king or anyone else were to strike that female wanderer with a sharp, whetted spear, and were to cut her into pieces, fragment by fragment—even while this was happening—her own virtue, her perfection of virtue (sīlapāramī), [remained unshaken].
"I would not break it. Why? For the sake of enlightenment alone; it is possible to attain supreme perfect enlightenment only by one whose virtue is unbroken in every respect, and not by another. 36.
"That brahmin woman was not to be despised by me"—that is, she was not to be looked down upon on account of her birth, clan, lineage, or excellence of conduct.
"Because of our long-standing acquaintance and because of her perfection in the virtues of renunciation and so forth, she is not unloved by me in every respect;
there is no lack of affection for her on my part. Nor is it that strength does not exist in me:
'strength does not exist in me' is not true, for it certainly does exist. I possess the power of a nāga and am endowed with fortitude; were I to wish, I could rise up suddenly."
This shows that he is capable of seizing those men who are dragging him away, crushing them, and taking him to wherever he desires.
"Omniscience is dear to me": beyond that female wanderer, omniscient knowledge alone is dear to me a hundredfold, a thousandfold, a hundred-thousandfold.
Therefore, "I shall guard my virtue": for that reason, I shall indeed protect my virtue.
Then that king, without making any delay in the park, went even more quickly, summoned that female wanderer, and invited her with great honor.

She spoke of the lack of virtue in worldly glory, the virtue of the renunciant life, and how she had gone forth out of spiritual urgency after abandoning her own Bodhisatta and his vast mass of wealth. The king, by someone...
Failing to win her heart by any means, he thought: "This female wanderer is virtuous and of noble character;
even when she was being dragged away by that male wanderer, he showed no sign of agitation, his mind remaining indifferent toward everything.
Yet it is not fitting that such a disturbance should occur regarding those who possess such qualities."
"What if I were now to take this female wanderer, go to the park, and ask forgiveness both from her and from that male wanderer?

Having thought thus, he commanded his men, "Bring the female wanderer to the park," and having gone there himself first, he approached the Bodhisatta and asked: "O renunciant, what have I done with that female wanderer?"
“Did anger arise in you as you were being led away? The Great Being replied:
“Anger arose in me, yet it was not released; it was not released while I lived.
Like a vast rain of dust, I quickly suppressed it.”
Having heard this, the king thought, "Does he speak only with reference to his anger, or does he mean something else, such as a craft or skill? and asked again:
"What arose for you but was not released? What was not released while you were living?
Like a vast rain of dust, what was it that held it back?"
*Uppajji tattha* means it arose once; it did not arise again.
*Na muccittha* means, however, that it was not released by way of producing bodily and vocal intimation (*vikāra*); the sense is that he did not allow it to go forth externally.
*Rajaṃ va vipulā vuṭṭhī* means just as, for example, dust that has arisen in the last month of summer is instantly [cleansed] by a massive, unseasonal downpour of rain.
"He restrains": thus, while pacifying it, he restrained it; this is the meaning of "he restrained.
Then the Great Man, demonstrating the danger of anger in its various forms, said:
"He who, once born, does not see [the truth], but sees clearly when unborn..."
Thus arose in me, it did not cease: anger, the domain of the foolish.
“He by whose birth enemies who seek suffering rejoice— that arose in me, it did not cease:
anger, the domain of the foolish.”
“When one is born and does not understand their own true welfare—
that anger, the domain of the witless, has arisen for me and has not been released.
Overcome by which [anger], one abandons what is wholesome and even neglects a vast benefit.”
That Bhīmasena is powerful and crushing; O Great King, anger did not release me.
"When wood is being rubbed together, that which is called fire is born;
it burns that very wood from which the flame was born."
“Thus for a dull-witted person, a fool who does not understand,
anger arises from provocation, and he is consumed by that very [anger].
Like a fire in grass and wood, so is the anger of one in whom it increases.”
“His fame diminishes, like the moon in the dark fortnight.
But for him whose anger is stilled— like a smokeless fire—
his fame waxes full, like the moon in the bright fortnight.”
He taught the Dhamma with these verses.
In this context, "he does not see" means he does not see even his own welfare, let alone the welfare of others.
"He sees well" means he sees correctly his own welfare, the welfare of others, and the welfare of both. "The domain of the dull-witted" means it is the sphere of those lacking wisdom.
"Having foolishness as his resort and food"—that is, one for whom foolishness is his fuel; thus he is "one whose resort is dull-wittedness. "Seeking suffering" means desiring suffering.
"His own welfare" means his own benefit or progress. "He would strive against it" means he would drive it away or destroy it.
"Together with Bhīmasena" means he is possessed of a great army of defilements that produces fear. "The crusher" refers to his power.
He was of a habit to cause beings to become intoxicated. "He did not release me" means he did not obtain release from my presence;
the meaning is that he was subdued right there within and rendered harmless. Alternatively, the meaning is that he stood for only a moment in the state of curd, like milk, by means of his mind.
"Manthamānasmin" means while the fire-drills are being rubbed together. "Mathamānasmin" is also a reading.
"Yasmā" means from which [wood]. "Ginī" means fire. "Bālassa avijānato" means of the fool who does not understand.

"Sārambhā jāyate" means that from provocation—characterized by the act of seeking superiority—anger arises like fire from the rubbing of the fire-drills. "Sapi ten'eva" means that very fool, by that same [provocation]...
"By anger one is consumed like wood by fire. "Like a smoke-bannered fire without fuel" means like a fire that has no fuel.
"Of him"—of that person endowed with patience through endurance—"fame, once obtained, fills out further and further, like the moon in the bright fortnight."
Having heard the Great Being’s discourse on the Dhamma, the king apologized both to the Great Man and to the female wanderer who had come from the royal palace.
He said, "May you both dwell right here in this park, enjoying the happiness of the renunciant life;
I shall provide you with righteous protection, defense, and security," and having paid homage, he departed. Both of them remained there.

In the course of time, the female wanderer passed away. The Bodhisatta, having entered the Himalayas and attained the meditative absorptions and higher knowledges, reached the end of his life as one destined for the Brahma-world.
At that time, the female wanderer was Rāhula’s mother; the king was the Elder Ānanda; and the Bodhi-wanderer was the Lord of the World.
In this case as well, the remaining perfections should be extracted according to what is appropriate.
Likewise, there was his renunciation from the home, resembling the Great Renunciation, by abandoning a vast mass of wealth and a great circle of kinsmen;
and likewise, having gone forth and being highly esteemed by the multitude, there was his supreme fewness of wishes among families and groups.
And there was her non-attachment, her absolute loathing for gain and honor, her delight in solitude, and her extraordinary life of austerity;

thus, when that royal woman, having committed an offense, attempted to violate her by force in his presence despite her being unpermitted, she remained free from any mental disturbance or transgression by reflecting upon her perfection of virtue (*sīlapāramī*), even though she was a female wanderer (*paribbājikā*) of such virtuous character and noble qualities. And as for that king who had committed the offense—
Having approached [others], one should establish a mind of welfare and a mind of loving-kindness, and then provide instruction regarding both the present life and future lives;
such qualities and powers of a Great Being (mahāpurisa) are to be illustrated here. Therefore, it is said: "Thus these wonders...
[and so on]... according to the Dhamma that accords with the Dhamma."
The commentary on the *Cūḷabodhicariyā* is finished.
5. Commentary on the *Mahiṃsarājacariyā*: 37.
Regarding the fifth [vow], the construction is: "When I was a forest-dwelling wild buffalo (*mahiṃsa*), a wanderer in the great forest. *Pavaḍḍhakāyo* means...
By virtue of his maturity in age and the stoutness of his limbs, he was one whose body had increased greatly. "Powerful" means possessing great strength and physical vigor.
"Vast" means having a massive body; it is said that at that time the Bodhisatta’s body was the size of a young elephant calf.

"Terrible to behold" means that because of his large physique and his being of the species of a wild buffalo, he inspired fear in those who did not know his character, thus having a fearsome appearance.

38. *Pabbhāre* means on a rock ledge that hangs down. *Dakāsaye* means near a body of water. *Hotettha ṭhānaṃ* means that in this great forest, whatever spot there was served as a place for the forest elephants to stand.
*Tahiṃ tahiṃ* means here and there. 39. *Vicaranto* means wandering about in order to investigate a comfortable place for dwelling.
*Ṭhānaṃ addasa bhaddakan* means, while wandering in this manner, he saw a beautiful and comfortable spot at the foot of a tree in that great forest.
Having seen that place and approached it, he shows that he stands and lies down there after taking his range of movement;
that is, having gone to the foot of that tree during the day, he passes the time standing and lying down.
At that time, it is said, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the region of the Himālaya in the womb of a buffalo; having reached maturity, he was endowed with great strength.
Possessing a massive body the size of a young elephant, he wandered among mountain slopes, ravines, inaccessible peaks, forests, and thickets.
Finding a certain convenient spot at the foot of a great tree, he would take his food there and dwell during the day.
Then, a certain greedy monkey descended from a tree, climbed onto the Great Being’s back, voided excrement and urine upon him, and then seized him by the tusks.
Hanging from his tail and swinging it back and forth, he played. Due to his perfection in patience, loving-kindness, and compassion, the Bodhisatta did not take that misconduct to heart.
The monkey continued to do the same again and again. Thus it is said:
"Then a monkey came there," and so forth.
In that context, "a monkey having come" (*kapi māgantvā*) means a monkey having arrived; the letter *ma* is used for metrical euphony (*padasandhikara*). "Wretched" (*pāpa*) means base.
"Noble-less" (*anariya*) means one who does not proceed in the right way (*aya*) and proceeds in the wrong way (*anaya*); the meaning is one of inferior conduct. "Fickle" (*lahu*) means restless.
"On the trunk" (*khandhe*) means on the part of the trunk. "He urinates" (*muttetī*) means he voids urine. "He defecates" (*ohadetī*) means he emits excrement. "That" (*taṃ*) refers to that.
“Me”—that is, me who had become a buffalo at that time. 41.
“Even for a single day”: it defiles me even for one day, and indeed for all time. Therefore he said, “It defiles me for all time.
And not merely for the duration of the second, third, or fourth day, but rather for all time, [it defiles me] with urine and so forth.
He defiles them. This shows that whenever he wishes to make things such as pearls and the like, he always does so upon me alone.

"Afflicted" means oppressed; by that—namely, by hanging [the pearls] from his horns and so forth, by smearing himself with the impurity of pearls and the like, and by repeatedly sprinkling water mixed with mud and dust many times with the tips of his horns and the tips of his hair in order to carry it away—...
"And by washing, I am squeezed out"—this is the meaning. 42.
"The yakkha" refers to the deity residing in that tree. "He said this to me": standing upon the trunk of the tree, he made this statement, clarifying the matter thus:
"O king of elephants, why do you tolerate this insult from this wicked monkey?"
"Kill this evil carcass with its horns and hooves"—this was the speech he addressed to me.
(43) When the yakkha had spoken thus at that time, at that moment, when the yakkha had said this, I spoke these words to him;
I spoke, I addressed, this which is about to be said, to that yakkha. "With the corpse... [etc.]

By "corpse" (kuṇapa), it is meant that [the body] resembles a corpse because it is utterly loathsome to virtuous people of pure birth due to the oozing of the impurities of the defilements, and because it emits an exceedingly foul odor.

By "evil" (pāpa), it is meant by the evil of killing living beings. By "ignoble" (anariya), it is meant that it is ignoble because it is the nature of ignoble, wicked people such as hunters, fowlers, and the like—base men. Why? For what reason, O deity?
"She reviles me; you have spoken what is improper, inciting me toward evil"—this is what she shows.
Now, revealing the danger (*ādīnava*) in that person of evil nature, he said "If here," and so forth. Its meaning is as follows:
O auspicious deity, if I were to become angry with him, I would become even more base than he. For by that practice of unrighteousness (*adhammacaraṇa*), [he has fallen].
Thus that young monkey became known as "the base one. But if I were to practice an evil nature even more powerful than that, would I not become even more evil than he?

And it is impossible that I, who stand here having understood this world, the world beyond, and what lies beyond them, and who am practicing solely for the welfare of others, would ever practice such an evil nature.
Furthermore: "My virtue might be broken"—if I were to commit such an evil deed, my perfection of virtue (*sīlapāramī*) would be impaired.
"The wise would censure me"—the learned gods and humans would censure me, saying:
"Look, sirs! This Bodhisatta, while wandering in search of enlightenment, has committed such an evil deed."
45. "Even life is despised" (*hīḷitā jīvitā vāpi*): here the word *vā* is used in the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇe*).
Thus, being despised and censured by the wise, even though living with a perfectly pure virtue, death itself—dying—is better, supreme, and more excellent.
Thinking, "What shall I do even for the sake of my own life? I shall not cause harm to others," and knowing this, even for the sake of my own life...
"What will I do? What shall I do with the harming of another being? There is no reason for doing this"—this is the meaning.
Furthermore, thinking "he too will act with such misconduct as I am doing," those fierce beasts of prey toward whom he acts in this way will themselves kill him;
thus, his death by others is more painful to me than [the harm itself].
And he said, "There will be liberation from taking life. Therefore it was said:
"Thinking, 'He thinks only of me,' others will likewise act;
they themselves will slay him, and that shall be my liberation."
In this context, *mamevāyanti* means "they come toward me as toward myself. *Aññepi* means "toward others as well. The rest has already been explained.
47. *Hīnamajjhimaukkaṭṭhe* refers to the inferior, the middling, and the superior, acting as the causal signs (*nimitta*).
*Sahanto avamānitaṃ* means enduring and forbearing the contempt and humiliation directed at one by them, without making any distinction [between oneself and others].

"Thus one gains wisdom": in this way, by not making distinctions among those who are inferior and so forth, but rather establishing patience, loving-kindness, and compassion, and enduring their offenses, one cultivates the perfections such as virtue;
thus, one gains—that is, penetrates—the omniscient knowledge (sabbaññutaññāṇa) that was mentally aspired for and desired.
For such a person, that knowledge is not far off.
Thus the Great Being, making known his own intention, taught the Dhamma to the deity.
After a few days had passed, he went elsewhere. Another fierce buffalo, drawn by the comfort of that dwelling, went to that place and stood there.
The wicked monkey, perceiving him with the thought, "This is he," climbed onto his back and behaved exactly as before in an improper manner. Then [the buffalo] him—
Shaking him off, he threw him to the ground, pierced his heart with his tusk, and trampled him with his feet until he was completely crushed.
At that time, the virtuous king of lions was the Protector of the World (Lokanātha).

In this case as well, the remaining perfections should be inferred according to their respective contexts, following the same method as explained below. Likewise, the power of the Great Being’s virtues should be understood here just as in the accounts of the Elephant King Bhūridatta and the Naga King Campeyya.
The commentary on the Mahiṃsarājacariya is finished.
6. Commentary on the Rurumigarājacariya: 48.
In the sixth [verse], "resembling molten gold" means that just as it has been thoroughly freed from all blackness, so too [the Buddha’s body] was in the fire...
Having cast [the gold] into it, he was like molten gold. "The king of deer named Ruru" refers to the king of deer named Ruru by a name established by birth;
the meaning is that he was a *ruru* by birth and the king of deer. "Composed in supreme virtue" means well-composed in the highest virtue;
the sense here should be understood as one who is both pure in virtue and concentrated in mind, or one whose mind is properly established in pure virtue.
At that time, the Bodhisatta was reborn in the womb of a Ruru deer. The skin of his body was like the color of well-polished, burnished gold;
his hands and feet were as if treated with lacquer; his tail was like that of a yak; his horns had the hue of silver chains;
his eyes were like well-polished jewel-beads; and his face, when turned upward, resembled a red woolen ball set upon a stand.

Thus it was. Having abandoned the company of people and desiring to dwell in seclusion, he cast off his retinue and lived all alone in a delightful grove of flowering *sāla* trees at the bend of the Ganges, a place secluded and devoid of humans. Therefore it is said:
“In a delightful and charming region, secluded and uninhabited by men;”
“I took up residence there, on the delightful bank of the Ganges.

There, in that charming place, with ground surfaces as white as powdered pearls, forest glades carpeted with glossy green grass, rocky plateaus variegated like colorful rugs, and waters as pure as a mass of jewels— *Note:
The phrase "muttātalasadisavālukācuṇṇapaṇḍarehi bhūmibhāgehi" is interpreted as describing the ground surfaces as white as the powder of sand resembling the surface of pearls.*
In delightful forest regions, endowed with reservoirs of water and mostly covered by a species of grass that is red like an *indagopaka* insect,
pleasant to the touch; and which are charming because they are entwined with broad branches adorned with flowers, fruits, and sprouts, resound with the warbling of various flocks of birds,
shine with diverse trees and creepers, and are for the most part graced by groves and thickets of mango and *sāla* trees.
Because it was adorned with forest thickets, it was delightful in the sense of producing delight for people who entered it.
And this has also been said in the *Rurumigarāja Jātaka*:
"In this forest grove, mangoes and sal trees were in full bloom."
"Covered with *indagopaka* insects, it is here that this deer dwells.
"In seclusion" (*vivitte*) means empty due to the absence of human habitation. "Inhabited by non-humans" (*amanussake*) means devoid of humans because of the absence even of people who wander there.
"Delightful" (*manorame*) means that, through the excellence of the aforementioned qualities, it especially delights the minds of those who desire solitude; thus, it is "delightful."
50. Now, regarding the phrase *atha uparigaṅgāya*: here, *atha* is a particle used as a topical marker (*adhikāra*).
By this, it is indicated that while I was dwelling there in such a manner, this other topic arose. *Uparigaṅgāya* means "at the upper reaches of the river Gaṅgā.
*Paripīḷito dhanikehi* means being pressed by creditors—being urged by moneylenders because, having taken a loan, one is unable to repay it.
It is said that a certain merchant of Bārāṇasī, thinking, "This son will grow weary while learning a craft," did not have him learn any craft at all.
He knew nothing beyond singing, instrumental music, dancing, eating, and feasting.
When he reached maturity, his parents married him to a suitable wife, entrusted him with their wealth, and then passed away.
Thus, after their passing, surrounded by women, gamblers, drunkards, and others, he squandered all his wealth through various doors of misfortune.
Having incurred debts here and there, and being unable to repay them, he was pressed by his creditors;
thinking, "What is the use of my life? Because of this very body I have become like another; death is better for me," he reflected thus.
The creditor said, "Come, take your debt-notes; I have ancestral wealth deposited by me on the bank of the Ganges, and I will give that to you.
They went with him. He, as if pointing out the location of a treasure, saying, "The wealth is here, the wealth is there," fled, thinking, "In this way my debt will be cleared."

He fell into the Ganges. Being carried away by its fierce current, he uttered a cry of piteous lamentation. Therefore it was said: “Then, upon the upper Ganges,” and so forth. Therein, “I live or I die” means:
having fallen into this current of the Ganges, I shall either live or die; let there be life for me here or death—either way, there will be no oppression from creditors.
51. “He goes in the middle of the Ganges”: that man, being carried along the Ganges day and night, [due to his love of life...]
Because he was still alive and had not yet reached death, being terrified by the fear of death,
he went through the middle of the Ganges with its great waters,
uttering a piteous cry. Then, at the hour of midnight, the Great Being heard the sound of that man’s piteous lamentation.
Hearing this, he thought, "The sound of a human being is heard; let him not die while I am still alive here; I shall grant him his life.
Having thought thus, he rose from his thicket of grass, went to the riverbank, and said, "O man, do not fear; I shall grant you your life.
Having comforted him and cut through the current, he carried him on his back, brought him to the shore, and set him down.
Having led him to his own dwelling place, relieved his fatigue, and given him various fruits, after two or three days had passed, he said to him:
"O man, I shall lead you to the road leading to the village of Bārāṇasī;
do not tell anyone that 'a golden deer dwells in such-and-such a place. He accepted this, saying, "Very well, Master."
The Great Being, having placed him upon his back, set him down on the road to Bārāṇasī and turned back. Thus it was said:
“Having heard his piteous lamentation,” and so forth.
Therein, “Who are you, O man? means: who are you as a human being, and from where have you come, drifting here?
53. "One’s own doing" means one’s own action. "Terrified by creditors" means agitated by debtors. "Thirsting" means terrified. 54.

"Having felt compassion for him, having sacrificed my life"—having felt compassion, being incited by great pity (*mahākaruṇā*), I abandoned my life for that man. "Having entered, I rescued him"—having entered the river...
Cutting through the stream and going straight ahead, I placed him upon my back and carried him out from there.
*Tassa* is a genitive used in the sense of the accusative. There is also a reading *tatthā*, which means "in that river.
*Andhakāramhi rattiyā* means "during the darkness of the night," that is, during the dark fortnight of the night.

55. "Knowing the time for rest" means: having removed their fatigue and provided them with various fruits, and then, after two or three days had passed, knowing that the time for their exhaustion was gone. "I ask you for one boon":
the meaning is, "I ask you for that one boon; grant me one boon. If it is asked, "What is that boon? he said: "Do not report me to anyone."
"Do not tell anyone—whether a king or a royal minister—that a golden deer dwells in such-and-such a place.
Then, on the very day that man entered Bārāṇasī, the king said:
"Your Majesty, in a dream I saw a golden-colored deer preaching the Dhamma to me; for I am one whose dreams come true, and it must certainly exist."
When the chief queen said, "Therefore, if I am to obtain the Dhamma of the Golden Deer, I shall live;
if not, I have no life," he comforted her, saying, "If it exists in the human world, you will obtain it. Having summoned the brahmins and asked, "Are there such things as golden deer?
and hearing them reply, "Yes, Your Majesty, there are," he [took] a purse containing a thousand [pieces of gold].
Having placed it in a golden casket and mounted it upon the back of an elephant, he caused a drum to be beaten throughout the city, proclaiming:
"To whoever shall point out the golden deer, I will give this [casket] along with the elephant. Then, desiring to give even more than that, he declared:
"I grant him an excellent village, as well as adorned women."
“He who describes this deer to us, the supreme deer among deer.
Having had this verse inscribed on a golden plate, he had it recited throughout the entire city.
Then that merchant’s son, having heard the verse, went to the king’s men and said, “I shall describe such a deer to the king; [let the king] me—”
“Show it to me,” he said. The king’s men led him into the presence of the king and reported the matter.
The king asked, “Is it true, sir? Did you see it? He replied, “It is true, Your Majesty; let him come with me, and I shall show it to you.
The king, making that very man his guide, went to that place with a great retinue.
The man who had betrayed his friend pointed out the location;
men with weapons in their hands surrounded it on all sides and, saying, "Make a loud shout! he himself stood to one side with a few attendants.
That other man also stood nearby. Hearing the sound, the Great Being thought, "This is the noise of a great army; surely from there..."
Realizing, "My men must have been overcome by fear," he rose, surveyed the entire assembly, and thinking,
"Safety shall be mine only where the king stands," he set out toward the king. Seeing him approaching, the king thought,
"He might come charging with the strength of an elephant," so he fastened his armor and, intending to frighten this deer away—
“If he flees, we shall pierce him, weaken him, and capture him,” he said, and turned toward the Bodhisatta. The Great Being said:
“Wait, O Great King; do not pierce me, O bull among charioteers!
Who has told you that this deer stands right here?”
He recited a verse. The king, captivated by his sweet speech, withdrew his arrow and stood there with reverence.
The Great Being also approached the king and exchanged pleasant greetings.
The great multitude also removed all their weapons, came forward, and surrounded the king. Thus it was said:
“Having gone to the city, when questioned, he spoke for the sake of wealth;
having seized the king, he approached my presence.
The meaning of this is: that wicked man, a betrayer of friends, having abandoned his life—thus, from the danger to his life by me—[acted].
"Having been released, he went to the city of Bārāṇasī and informed the king of the wealth he had obtained;
having informed him, he became a guide for the king to seize it, and taking the king with him, he came into my presence.
As if shaking a golden bell, the Great Being asked the king again in a sweet voice: "Who..."
"Now I have told you this: 'The deer stands right here. At that moment, the wicked man stepped back a little and stood within earshot.
The king pointed him out, saying, "He showed you to me. Then the Bodhisatta said:
"Truly, it seems they say here, 'Some men in this world...'"
“A piece of wood that has washed ashore is better than even a single man,” he said, reciting this verse.
Upon hearing it, the king was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency and asked:
“Ruru, what is it that you criticize among deer, what among birds, and what among humans?”
“Indeed, fear seizes me upon hearing that human voice speaking,” he said in this verse.
Then the Great Being, demonstrating, “Great King, I do not blame the deer nor the bird, but rather I blame the human,” spoke:
“That which I rescued while being carried away by the vehicle, amidst the great waters of the swift-flowing stream;”
"Because of that, fear has come upon me; indeed, O King, association with the wicked is suffering.
Thus he spoke. Therein, "niplavitaṃ" means pulled out; "ekacciyoti" refers to a certain treacherous friend, a wicked person, even if he were falling into water...
"Rescued, yet not truly better off. For wood serves as a benefit in many ways, whereas one who betrays a friend leads to ruin;

therefore, wood is indeed superior to him. "Of deer"—he asks whether you are censuring some particular king of deer, such as the ruru-deer, or rather some among the birds or humans. "For fear finds me in various forms."
He experiences great fear; the meaning is that he treats it as if it were his own possession.
"In the current" means in the flow of the Ganges, capable of carrying away whatever falls into it. "In the water of great depth" means in the water that has become deep.
By both [phrases], he shows the abundance of water in the flow of the Ganges. "On account of that," O Great King, whoever...
“The man shown to me by you was one whom I rescued from the Ganges while he was being swept away at midnight, lamenting piteously;
it is because of that rescue that this danger has come upon me. Truly, association with those who are not true men is suffering.

Hearing this, the king became enraged at him and thought, “He does not recognize the virtue of one who has been so very helpful to him, yet he inflicts suffering upon him! Having pierced him, I shall put him to death! Then he fastened his sword. Thus it is said:
“Whatever was to be done has all been reported by me to the king.
Having heard these words, the king prepared his arrow, thinking:
‘I shall have this unrighteous betrayer of friends executed right here.’”

In this context, "to the extent of his doing" refers to all the assistance that had been rendered to him by me. "He plotted" means he resolved upon it. "A betrayer of friends" means one whose nature is to betray those who are his own friends and benefactors.
Then the Great Being, thinking, "May this fool not perish because of me," said:
"Great King, execution—whether of a fool or a wise man—is not praised by the virtuous; on the contrary, it is only censured. Therefore, do not..."
"Kill this one; let this one go as he pleases, and even that which you promised to give him, give it to him without withholding anything," she said. "And I shall do for you whatever you desire;
I give myself to you," he replied. Thus it was said:
“Protecting him, I fashioned him from my own self;
let him remain, O Great King, for I am at your disposal.
In this context, “I fashioned him” means that while protecting that treacherous friend, a person of evil character, [I created him] by means of my own personal form (*attabhāva*).
"I exchanged him" means that by offering myself to the king, I prevented his death at the king's hands by saving the bowl.
"While he stands," and so forth, is a demonstration of the manner of the exchange. 59.
Now, in order to show the purpose for which that self-exchange was made, he spoke the concluding verse. Its meaning is as follows:
"Then, relying on me while that treacherous man desired to deprive the king of his life, I protected my virtue alone by sacrificing myself for the sake of the king; I did not protect my life.
And as for the fact that I was virtuous, regardless of my own life, that was solely for the sake of perfect enlightenment."

Then the king, his heart filled with joy because the Bodhisatta had sacrificed his own life to prevent that man from dying, said, "Go, sir; by favoring the king of beasts, you have been released from death at my hands.
Having spoken thus, he caused the man’s wealth to be given back to him according to their agreement. Having granted the Great Being permission to depart as he pleased, he—
Having led them to the city, and having had both the city and the Bodhisatta adorned, he caused the Dhamma to be taught to the queen.
Beginning with the queen, the Great Being taught the Dhamma in sweet human speech to the king and the royal assembly;
then, after advising the king on the ten duties of a king and instructing the great multitude, he entered the forest surrounded by herds of deer.
He took up residence there. The king, too, abiding by the Great Being’s counsel, granted safety to all beings, performed meritorious deeds such as giving, and became destined for a happy rebirth.
At that time, Devadatta was the merchant’s son, Ānanda was the king, and the Lord of the Deer was the Protector of the World.
In this case as well, the remaining perfections should be extracted according to their respective suitability in the same manner as explained below.
Likewise, here too, through his delight in solitude and his lack of desire for the company of people, he abandoned the herd and dwelt alone;
and at the hour of midnight, having heard the cry of distress from a man who was being swept away by a river and was lamenting piteously, [he rose] from his place of rest...
Having emerged and gone to the riverbank, while a great flood was raging in the Mahāgaṅgā, he sacrificed his own life;

descending into the water, he cut across the current, lifted that man onto his back, brought him to the shore, comforted him, and dispelled his exhaustion by giving him various fruits and other provisions.
Then, having once again placed him on his back, [he carried him] from the forest...
Having led him out onto the great highway, he thought, "I shall discharge my arrow after drawing back my bow.
Yet, instead of approaching the king who stood directly opposite him with fearlessness, he went straight toward him, addressed him first in the human tongue, and offered him a sweet greeting;
and to the king—who was a betrayer of friends and a wicked man intent on killing him—he preached a discourse on the Dhamma.
Furthermore, having sacrificed his own life to bring about liberation from death, he caused that king to give wealth according to his promise;
when the king offered him boons, he granted the gift of fearlessness to all beings;
and, with the king and queen at their head, he taught the Dhamma to the great multitude and established them in meritorious deeds such as giving.
The power of the Great Being’s virtues— such as giving counsel to the deer who had obtained safety, preventing humans from devouring the crops,
and ensuring that the sign of the leaf remained fixed for as long as he lived— should be made manifest.
The commentary on the conduct of the King of Deer, Ruru, is finished.
7. Commentary on the Mātaṅga Conduct 60.
"Jaṭila" means one who possesses matted hair; the meaning is "one whose hair is bound in matted locks.

"Uggatāpana" means one for whom there is fierce asceticism (uggatāpana), which is designated as *tapas*, because of the heating and restraining of the six faculties, with the mind as the sixth; thus he is one of fierce asceticism (*ghoratapa*).

The meaning is "one who possesses the faculty of supreme concentration. Alternatively, he is called *Uggatāpano* because he scorches (*tāpeti*) with the heat of his energy those defilements known as *uggā*—so named either because they vomit out (*uggiraṇato*) various kinds of evils such as those pertaining to the present life and so forth, or because they cast them away outside (*bahi chaḍḍāpanato*), or in the sense of being terrible, fearsome, and terrifying.
"By name Mātaṅga" means that by name he is called Mātaṅga.
This name was given to him because it had come down from his birth in the Mātaṅga clan. "Virtuous" (*sīlavā*) means endowed with virtue, one whose morality is perfectly pure.
"Well-concentrated" (*susamāhita*) means well-composed through access and absorption concentration; the meaning is that he was an attainer of the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*).
For at that time, having been born in the womb of a Caṇḍāla, the Bodhisatta was unsightly in appearance and lived in a Caṇḍāla village outside the city.
He lived there. "Mātaṅgapaṇḍita" was his renowned name. Now, one day when a festival had been proclaimed in that city, most of the citizens were enjoying the festivities.

There was also a certain daughter of a wealthy brahmin, about sixteen or fifteen years of age, beautiful to behold and lovely like a celestial maiden, who thought, "I shall enjoy the festival in accordance with my own means."
Having loaded abundant solid and soft foods and other provisions onto carts, she would mount her all-white mule-chariot and go to the pleasure grove with a great retinue.

She was named Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā; it is said that because she did not wish to see any ill-formed appearance, thinking it to be "inauspicious," the name "Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā" (Auspicious-to-behold) arose for her.
Then the Bodhisatta, having risen early, put on a garment of rags and took up his worn-out bamboo staff;
with a bowl in hand, he entered the city, making gestures with that bamboo staff to keep people at a distance as soon as he saw them.
Then Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā raised a cry of "Clear the way! Clear the way! as she shouted for order.
Being led by her own men, she saw Mātaṅga in the middle of the city gate and asked, "Who is this?
When it was said, "Noble lady, he is the outcaste Mātaṅga," she replied, "For those who go after seeing such a person, whence can there be prosperity? and had the carriage turned back.
The people thought, "We were going to the park where we would have received much food, both hard and soft; instead, we have encountered Mātaṅga."
Thinking, “An obstacle has been created,” they became enraged and cried out, “Seize him, you outcaste! Having struck him with clods of earth until he fell unconscious, they departed.
Before long, he regained consciousness, rose up, and asked the people, “Sirs, is a gate meant for everyone’s common use, or was it made for Brahmins alone?
“It is for the common use of all,” they replied. “If that is so, in a gate meant for the common use of all...”
Having informed the people on the street, "The people have brought this ruin and disaster upon me because they saw me departing to one side," he thought, "Now I shall break her pride.
He went to the door of her residence and lay down, saying, "I will not rise until I have obtained Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā. [Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā...]
When his father heard that a *mātaṅga* had collapsed at the door of the house, he said, “Give him a *kākaṇika*; let him go after anointing his body with oil.
He replied, “I will not rise until I have obtained a sight-omen (*diṭṭhamaṅgalika*). Then the brahmin said:
“Give two *kākaṇikas*, a *māsaka*, a quarter, a *kahāpaṇa*, two, three, and so on, up to a hundred *kahāpaṇas*.”
Even when they said, "Give us a thousand kahāpaṇas," he still would not accept. While they were thus deliberating, the sun set.

Then Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā’s mother, having descended from the palace and had a screen-wall erected, went into his presence and said, "Dear Mātaṅga, forgive Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā’s offense; take two thousand [kahāpaṇas] for now..."
Even when told, "Take a hundred thousand," he did not accept it and remained lying down.

After he had lain thus for six days, on the arrival of the seventh day, people from the neighboring houses and the houses of those who dealt in poison all arose and said, "Either you make Mātanga get up, or give us the girl; do not ruin us!"
They said: "At that time, it seems, this was the local custom in that region:
'If a Caṇḍāla dies lying down right at the door of someone's house, seven families on each side of that house become Caṇḍālas.
Thereupon, Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā’s parents had Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā dressed in a tattered rag-robe suitable for a Caṇḍāla."
