Having given him the necessary provisions, they led him, who was still lamenting, into his presence and said, "Come now, lift up the girl and take her.
She stood by his side and said, "Get up. He replied, "I am extremely exhausted;
take me by the hand and help me up. She did so. Mātaṅga said, "We cannot live within the city..."
“Let us go; come, let us go to the Caṇḍāla village outside the city. Having dismissed her, he went to his own home.
The reciters of the Jātakas say that he climbed onto her back.
But having thus gone home and lived in the house for several days without violating the boundaries of caste distinction, [he regained] his strength.
Having taken her, he thought: "I have caused this daughter of a wealthy brahmin to dwell in my outcaste household;

well now, I shall cause her to reach the pinnacle of gain and the pinnacle of glory. He entered the forest, went forth into homelessness, and within seven days produced the eight meditative attainments and the five supernormal powers. Then, by means of his psychic power, at the gate of the outcaste village—
Having descended and stood at the door of the house, he summoned Diṭṭhamangalika.
As she was lamenting, "Master, why have you gone forth into homelessness, leaving me without a protector?", he said, "Do not worry, Bhaddā;
I shall now bring you even greater glory than your former husband. But you [should know that] Mahābrahmā is my husband, not Mātaṅga; he has gone to the Brahma-world..."
"Go and tell the assemblies: 'On the seventh day from now, on the full moon, he will come, having pierced through the lunar disk,'" and having said this, he departed for the Himālayas.
Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā, too, spoke likewise in various places in the midst of the great crowds in Bārāṇasī. Then—
On the full moon day, when the disk of the moon was situated in the midst of the sky, the Bodhisatta manifested the form of Brahmā;
having pierced through the lunar disk and illuminated the entire city of Bārāṇasī, twelve yojanas in extent, as well as the whole kingdom of Kāsi with a single light,
he descended from the sky, circled over Bārāṇasī three times, and [was honored] by the great multitude with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings.

While being honored, he set out toward the village of the Caṇḍālas. The Brahmabhattas gathered together, went to that Caṇḍāla village, and adorned Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā’s house with pure garments, perfumes, garlands, and other offerings until it resembled a celestial mansion of the gods.
At that time, Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā was in her season. The Great Being went there and [touched] Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā with his thumb.
Having touched her navel, he said: "Bhadde, a fetus has taken root in you; you will give birth to a son.
Both you and your son shall attain the pinnacle of gain and the pinnacle of glory.

The water used for washing your head shall become the consecration water for all the kings of Jambudīpa, while the water used for your bathing shall become the water of immortality (amata). To those who [heard this]...
They will pour [the water] upon your head, and you will be freed from all diseases and liberated from ill fortune;

those who pay homage by placing their heads at the soles of your feet will give a thousand [kahāpaṇas]; those who pay homage while standing in a place where they can hear your discourse will give a hundred;
those who pay homage while standing within the range of your sight will pay homage after giving a single kahāpaṇa each—be heedful!
Having exhorted him with the words, “May it be so,” she departed from her home and entered the lunar disk even as the great multitude looked on.
The Brahmabhattas assembled and, having escorted Diṭṭhamaṅgalika into the city with great honor, caused him to dwell there with great splendor and majesty.
They also had a residence built for him that was like a celestial mansion of the gods.
Having led him there, they presented him with magnificent gains and honor. All matters, such as the obtaining of a son, were exactly as the Bodhisatta had described.
Sixteen thousand brahmins ate regularly together with the son of Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā;
about a thousand attended upon him, and gifts were given to many thousands. Then the Great Being [thought]: "This..."
“Since he has placed his confidence in the wrong place, let me inform him of those worthy of offerings.
While wandering for alms, he went to her house, conversed with him, and departed. Then the youth spoke this verse:
“From where have you come, you ill-clad one, looking like a ragged wretch or a dust-demon?”
“Put this refuse-rag around your neck; who are you, indeed, that you are unworthy of offerings?
Thus it was said. Unable to endure such improper conduct, the deity turned the faces of both him and those sixteen thousand brahmins away.
Seeing this, Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā approached the Great Being and [reported] that matter.
She reported this. The Bodhisatta said, “That misconduct was committed by the yakkhas who could not endure his improper behavior;
however, you should pacify that misconduct by pouring this leftover alms-food into their mouths.
She did accordingly and pacified it. Then Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā said to her son: “Dear child, in this...”

"In this world, those worthy of offerings are like the wise Mātaṅga; they are not like these brahmins, who are arrogant with pride merely on account of their birth or their mere recitation of mantras.

Having said this, he inspired faith in him right there toward those who were at that time endowed with the distinguished qualities of virtue and so forth, as well as those who had attained the meditative absorptions and the Paccekabuddhas.
At that time, in the city of Vettavatī, there was a certain brahmin named Jātimant who, even after going forth into homelessness, maintained great pride on account of his birth.
The Great Being, thinking, "I shall break his pride," went to that place and took up residence near him, upstream. Thus it is said:
“Both I and this brahmin dwell alone on the banks of the Ganges;
I dwell above, while the brahmin dwells below.
Then one day, after the Great Being had chewed a tooth-stick, he said: “May this stick cling to the matted locks of the one who possesses birth!”
Having made a resolution, he threw it into the river. As he was rinsing his mouth, it became caught in his matted locks (*jaṭā*).
Seeing it, he said, "Begone, you outcaste! Thinking, "From where has this ill-omened thing come?
I shall examine it," he went against the current and saw the Great Being. He asked, "What is your caste? "I am a *caṇḍāla*. "By you, in the river..."
“Did you drop a tooth-stick? “Yes, I did. “Begone, outcaste! You caṇḍāla, you ill-omened one!

Do not live here; live by the lower stream! Even though he was living by the lower stream, when a tooth-stick he had dropped came back against the current and got caught in his matted locks, [the other said]:
“Begone, outcaste! If you live here, on the seventh day you will split into seven pieces!”
"Your head shall split apart," he said. Therefore it was said:
"While wandering along a favorable path, I saw a horse above;
having reviled me there, he uttered a curse for the splitting of my head."

Therein, "wandering along the bank" means that while he was wandering along the bank of the Ganges, searching for the source of [the sound] as a discarded tooth-stick had become entangled in his own matted hair;
"he saw my hermitage above" means that he saw my leaf-hut hermitage upstream from his own dwelling place; and "having reviled me there" means having come to my hermitage.
Having heard his birth, he retreated from right then and stood within earshot, saying, "Begone, outcaste, Caṇḍāla! You ill-omened one, do not dwell here!
and so forth, intimidating him with fear. He uttered a curse that would split his head, saying, "If you wish to live, flee from this very spot quickly;
if you do not depart, on the seventh day from now, your head shall split into seven pieces."
"May your head split open!"—thus he uttered a curse against me.

But does his head actually split open because of that curse? It does not. However, he was a deceiver; he spoke thus for the purpose of terrifying him, with the thought: "Thus, driven by the fear of death, he will flee far away.
"If I were to become angry with him"—that is, if I were to feel resentment toward that arrogant, stubborn, and fraudulent ascetic.
"If one does not guard virtue" means if one were not to protect virtue; the sense is:
"if one were not to reflect that this thing called virtue must be protected properly, regardless of one's life. "Having looked at him, I would make him like ashes" means:
had I been dissatisfied with him at that time, he, having understood the movement of my mind, [would have become like ashes] toward me.
The intention was that the well-pleased deities would, in an instant, scatter that handful of ashes like dust.

However, the Teacher, at that time, as if he himself were unable to endure it, taught by acting out—as if he himself were doing so—the harm that should have been accomplished by the deities, saying: "I would turn it into ash."

But the caviller says: "If the Bodhisatta himself, desiring that matted-hair ascetic, had turned him to ash by means of psychic power (*iddhi*), then the meaning of this passage would have been explained straightforwardly. To him it should be said: "You speak of harming others by means of psychic power;

however, what is called psychic power consists of the psychic power of resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna-iddhi*), the psychic power of transformation (*vikubbanā-iddhi*), and the mind-made psychic power (*manomaya-iddhi*)."

There are ten kinds of success (*iddhi*): success through the exercise of knowledge, success through the exercise of concentration, noble success, success born of the ripening of kamma, success belonging to one possessed of merit, success consisting of science, and success in the sense of succeeding through the condition of right application here and there.
Among these, if one asks, "Which kind of success do you speak of? one replies, "That which consists in development. Furthermore—"
“Is there an act of harming others through that which consists of mental development (bhāvanāmaya)? “Yes,” some teachers say, “it occurs once.

For just as when one wishing to strike another throws a water-filled jar, the other is struck and the jar also breaks, even so, through supernormal power consisting of mental development, an act of harming others occurs once; from that point on, however, it perishes.
Then, having said, "By means of supernormal power consisting in development, there is never an act of harming others, whether once or twice," he should be asked:
"Is supernormal power consisting in development wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate;

associated with pleasant feeling, associated with painful feeling, or associated with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling; accompanied by initial application and sustained application (*savitakka-savicāra*),..."

[Are they] with applied thought and sustained thought only, without applied thought and without sustained thought; belonging to the sense sphere, the fine-material sphere, or the immaterial sphere? If he knows [the answer], he will say:

“Supernormal power consisting of development is wholesome or indeterminate, to be experienced as neither-painful-nor-pleasant, without applied thought and without sustained thought, and belongs to the fine-material sphere.
He should then be asked: “To which category among the wholesome and so forth does the volition of taking life belong?”
If he knows, he will say: "The volition of killing living beings is unwholesome, associated with painful feeling, accompanied by applied and sustained thought, and belongs to the sense-sphere.

Being thus, one should convince him by showing the contradiction with the Canon: "In that case, your question does not accord with the triad of the wholesome, nor with the triad of feelings, nor with the triad of applied thought, nor with the classification of planes. But if he says: "Furthermore..."

“Monks, here some ascetic or brahmin, possessing psychic power and having attained mastery over the mind, regards with an evil mind the fetus in another’s womb, thinking: ‘Oh, may that fetus in the womb not emerge safely!
In this way too, monks, there is a destruction of a family. This was not included in the formal recitation (saṅgīti).
One might recite the Kulumpasutta. He too should be convinced: "You do not understand the meaning.

For here, by the phrase 'one possessed of psychic power who has attained mastery over mind,' it is not psychic power consisting in spiritual cultivation that is intended, but rather psychic power of the Atharvavedic (sorcerous) kind.

Since that [sorcerous power] is what is obtained here when one says 'it is obtained,' it is simply impossible for there to be harm to others through psychic power consisting in spiritual cultivation."
If he does not submit to being summoned, he should be sent away after having performed his task. Therefore, the meaning of the verse here should be understood according to the method already stated.
Furthermore, when the Great Being was thus cursed by him, he thought: "If I were to become angry with him, my virtue would remain unprotected;
I shall shatter his pride through a skillful means, and that will be his protection. Thus, on the seventh [day]...
He prevented the sun from rising during the day. People, distressed by the non-rising of the sun, approached the ascetic Jātimanta and asked, "Venerable sir, are you not allowing the sun to rise?
He replied, "This is not my doing; however, there is a Caṇḍāla ascetic living on the bank of the Ganges, and this must be his doing. The people—
Having approached the Great Being, they asked, “Venerable sir, are you not allowing the sun to rise?
“Yes, friends,” he replied. “For what reason? “A forest-dweller who is your spiritual preceptor has cast a curse upon me for no fault of mine;
when he comes and falls at my feet to ask for forgiveness, I shall release the sun. They went and [found] him...
Dragging him along, they brought him and made him lie down at the feet of the Great Being;
having asked for his forgiveness, they said, “Venerable sir, release the sun. “It is not possible to release it; if I were to release it, this man’s head would split into seven pieces.
“Then what shall we do, venerable sir? The Great Being said, “Bring a lump of clay.”
Having had it brought, he said, "Place this upon the head of the ascetic, lower the ascetic into the water, and set him there;
when the sun appears, let the ascetic submerge into the water," and then he released the sun.
As soon as he was touched by the rays of the sun, the lump of clay split into seven pieces. The ascetic submerged into the water. Thus it is said:
“When he, angry and evil-minded, then uttered a curse against me, it fell back upon his own head;
by means of my spiritual power (yoga), I released myself from it.
Regarding this, “when he then uttered a curse against me” refers to that shaveling ascetic of noble birth who, with reference to the splitting of his head—

Then he cursed me; he cast a curse upon me. "It fell right back upon his own head" means that although he intended it for me, it fell instead upon him and remained there by virtue of its falling nature. For it happens thus:
as when one offends against one who is innocent. As it was said by the Blessed One: "He who offends a man who is innocent... [and so forth].
"Like one cast against the wind. "By means of yoga I liberated him" means that by a skillful method I released him from his head-splitting speech, or I liberated that matted-hair ascetic from it;
the meaning is that I acted in such a way that he would not [suffer] by whatever means [he intended].

For when that harsh speech, consisting of an act of reviling the Noble Ones, was uttered by him toward the Great Being— a being whose mental continuum was well-composed through the perfection of virtue and view,
who had fulfilled various meditative attainments and dwellings through the mastery of the cultivation of the perfections, and who was suffused with great compassion—
that [result] arose because of the Great Being’s status as a distinguished field of merit and because of the speaker’s own harshness of intention.
Having become a deed to be experienced in this very life (*diṭṭhadhammavedanīya*), if he had not asked the Great Being for forgiveness, it would have reached the state of ripening on the seventh day;

however, once the Great Being was asked for forgiveness, because it was warded off by the perfection of that effort, it attained the quality of non-ripening due to its becoming a "deed that has already been exhausted" (*ahosikamma*).
For this is the natural law regarding both the evil of slandering the Noble Ones and deeds to be experienced in this very life.
In this context, that which was done by the Bodhisatta on the seventh day—namely, the warding off of the rising sun—is intended here as the "effort" (*yoga*), meaning the skillful means (*upāya*).
For it was because they were tormented by that [heat] that people brought the ascetic into the presence of the Bodhisatta and asked for his forgiveness.
It should be understood that he too, having recognized the virtues of the Great Being, set his mind at peace toward him. As for that which... [of him]...
A lump of clay was placed on his head and split into seven pieces;

this was done to protect the minds of the people, for otherwise, seeing that even these who have gone forth act under the sway of their own minds and do not bring their minds under their own control, they might seize even a Great Being, treating him as equal to those others. This was for his sake...
“...for their long-term harm and suffering.

Now, in order to show for what purpose he had protected his perfectly pure virtue alone at that time without defiling his mind toward that ascetic, he spoke this concluding verse: “I guarded my virtue. Its meaning has already been explained above.
At that time, Maṇḍabya was Udena, and Mātaṅga was the Lord of the World (the Buddha).
Here too, the remaining perfections (pāramīs) should be extracted. Likewise, there was the subduing of pride by Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā according to his intention while he was of low birth;

and having gone forth, with the thought "I shall be a refuge for Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā," he went to the forest and, after going forth, within seven days alone produced jhāna and direct knowledge (abhiññā) according to his intention.
Then, having returned, [the account of] the accomplishment of the means for Diṭṭhamaṅgalikā to attain the pinnacle of gain and the pinnacle of fame;
the subduing of the pride of Prince Maṇḍabya; the subduing of the pride of the ascetic Jātimanta; the removal of a future threat to his life even while he was unaware of it;
the preservation of one's own virtue without becoming angry at him despite his great offense; and the performance of a marvelous and wonderful miracle.
Such are the powers of the Great Being’s virtues that should be made manifest.
The commentary on the Mātaṅga-jātaka is finished.
8. Commentary on the Dhammadevaputta-jātaka.
66. "Aṭṭhama" means having a great retinue. "Mahiddhika" means endowed with great divine power (*deviddhi*).
"Dhammo nāma mahāyakkho" means the son of a deity named Dhamma, who is possessed of great majesty.
"Sabbalokānukampako" means one who, without making distinctions, protects the entire world through great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
At that time, the Mahāsatta was reborn in the world of the gods of the sense-sphere as a divine son named Dhamma.
Adorned with celestial ornaments and mounted upon a divine chariot, surrounded by a host of nymphs, he would descend among humans after their evening meal.

On the full-moon uposatha day, while people were seated at the doors of their respective houses engaged in pleasant conversation, he appeared in the air over the villages, market towns, and royal capitals.

Standing there, he exhorted the people of Jambudīpa to the ten courses of wholesome action, saying: "Abstaining from the ten unwholesome courses of action, such as the destruction of life, fulfill the dharma of the three kinds of good conduct;
be filial toward your mothers and fathers, respectful toward recluses and brahmins, and honor those who are senior in the family;
being intent upon heaven as your goal, you shall enjoy great glory."
He performs a circumambulation. Therefore it was said:
“Exhorting the great multitude to the ten courses of wholesome action, I wander through villages and market towns together with my companions and my retinue.”
In this context, "accompanied" means being with companions who are righteous and proponents of the Dhamma.
At that time, a certain son of the gods named Adhamma was reborn in the world of the sense-sphere deities.
He, by way of such methods as "Kill living beings! Take what is not given! incited beings toward the unwholesome courses of action, [possessing] great...
Surrounded by his retinue, he makes Jambudīpa his left-hand side. Therefore it was said:
“The wicked, miserly yakkha, displaying the ten evils—he wanders here upon this earth together with his friends and his followers.”
In this context, "evil-doer" (*pāpa*) means one endowed with evil qualities. "Miserly" (*kadariya*) means one who is stubborn and stingy. "Yakkha" means a son of the gods (*devaputta*).
"Proclaiming ten evils" refers to the fact that in all the world, what is called the "range of beings" (*gocara*) is produced for the purpose of their enjoyment and utilization.
Therefore, [the view is expressed] that one should satisfy oneself by killing beings and doing whatever it takes, and that one's sense faculties should be gratified, and so forth.
By means of his method, he performed and then proclaimed the ten base deeds, beginning with the taking of life.

"He too here" means that this son of the gods (Devaputta), who is unrighteous (adhamma), was right here in Jambudīpa. "On the earth" means near the ground, within the range of human sight and hearing; such is the meaning.
69. Among those beings there, those who perform good deeds and revere the Dhamma [beheld] the son of the gods, the Dhamma, as he was thus approaching.
Having seen him, they rise from their seats and honor him with perfumes, garlands, and other offerings;
they offer praise as long as he remains within the range of their vision, and stand with palms joined in reverence. Having heard his words, they perform meritorious deeds with diligence and care.
But those beings who are of evil conduct and cruel in their actions, having heard the word of the Dhamma, rejoice excessively [in their own ways].

They commit even more evil deeds. Thus, at that time, they wander about in the world both speaking directly contrary to one another and acting directly contrary to one another. Therefore the Blessed One said:
"The speaker of Dhamma and the speaker of non-Dhamma—both of us are opponents."
As time passed in this manner, one day their chariots came face to face in the sky.
Then their retinues asked, "Whose are you? Whose are you? Having replied, "We are Dhamma's! We are Adhamma's!
they stepped off the path and split into two groups. However, the chariots of Dhamma and Adhamma remained facing each other.

Having struck each other with their goads, they stood [still]. They engaged in a dispute for the sake of yielding the way to one another, saying, "Make your chariot descend and give me the way! Make your chariot descend and give me the way!
And the retinues of both, having brought forward their weapons, became ready for battle. It was with reference to this that it was said:
“Jostling pole against pole, we two have met upon this path.
A terrifying quarrel is underway between the good and the evil;
for the sake of exiting the road, a great battle has been set.”
Therein, "they pull at the yoke" means that while pulling at the yoke, they cause the pole of one [chariot] to strike against the pole of the other.

"We have come together" (*samimha*) means we have met face to face. The repetition of the word "both" (*ubho*) indicates that both of us, wandering in the world as adversaries of one another, once came toward each other on the road from two sides with two assemblies.
It is said for the purpose of showing that "we both have met together along with the chariot" once they had entered [the battle].
*Bhesma* means "fear-inducing. *Kalyāṇapāpakassa ca* means "of both the auspicious and the evil. *Mahāyuddho upaṭṭhito* means a great conflict was present;
for a desire to fight arose among their respective retinues. Therein, indeed, Dhamma spoke to Adhamma.
“Good sir, you are unrighteousness (adhamma), I am righteousness (dhamma); the path is suitable for me. Make my chariot descend and give me the way.
The other replied, “I have a strong vehicle, I am powerful and fearless; therefore, I will not give up the way. Rather, we shall fight.
Whichever of us wins in battle, let his be the way. For this very reason it was said:
“I am one who brings glory, a doer of merit, always praised by recluses and brahmins.
Worthy of the path, honored by gods and humans—I am the Dhamma; give me the way, not the way of non-Dhamma!
Having mounted the firm vehicle of non-Dhamma, I am powerful, though I am not truly powerful.”
“For what reason would you give me the path today, this Dhamma never given before?
“Indeed, the Dhamma appeared first; later, non-Dhamma arose in the world.
It is the eldest, the best, and the eternal. Depart from the path, O younger brother, for the elder.”
“Neither by begging nor by being worthy, nor by your fitness, shall I give you the way.
Let there be a battle between us both today; whoever wins in the battle, his shall be the way.
I have spread throughout all directions—mighty, of immeasurable fame, and peerless.”
Endowed with every excellence, how will you, who are unrighteousness, overcome the Dhamma?
Indeed, iron destroys gold, but gold does not destroy iron;
if unrighteousness were to destroy the Dhamma today, it would be as beautiful to behold as gold is to iron.
“But if you, though possessing the strength for war, are unrighteous, then neither elders nor teachers exist for you.
I shall give you the way through what is pleasant and unpleasant, and I forgive even the harsh words spoken to me.
These indeed were their words and counter-words.
In this context, "one who brings glory" means one who bestows glory upon gods and humans by way of enjoining them to the Dhamma.
The same method applies to the second phrase as well. "Ever-praised" means always praised, constantly extolled. [The opponent asks:
"For what reason do they say, 'May he give today'? [The reply is: "Because I am Adhamma, mounted upon the chariot of the vehicle of Adhamma, fearless and powerful. For what reason? O Dhamma, today—"
"I give you a path never before given to anyone. Regarding the words "it appeared":
at the time of the first aeon (kappa), the dhamma of the ten courses of wholesome action appeared in this world, whereas previously there was non-dhamma. And as for "I am the eldest":
because I arose earlier, I am the eldest, the best, and the ancient one; you, however, are the younger. Therefore he says, "Depart from the paths."
“Nor am I worthy of it”: for I would not give you the road by means of begging, nor by words of flattery, nor by being led by the hand. “Spread abroad” (*anuvisaṭo*):
I am spread out and renowned in all directions—the four cardinal points and the four intermediate directions—by virtue of my own qualities.
“With iron” (*lohenā*): with an iron fist. “He shall strike” (*hañchatī*): he will strike. “The power of battle, unrighteousness” (*yuddhabalo adhammo*).

"But if you are one whose strength lies in battle, O unrighteous one—if for you these elders and venerable ones do not exist as 'elders,' nor as 'venerable ones,' nor as 'wise ones'—then by 'dear and non-dear' is meant: as if by the dear, even by the non-dear;
the meaning is that even while giving with what is non-dear, you give me the way as if with what is dear."

71. Then the Great Being thought: "If I were to take this evil person—who has set out for the harm of the whole world and stands here having adopted such a perverse course—and were to snap my fingers and say, 'You who act improperly, do not stay here!
Depart quickly and perish!', he would, at that very moment, by the power of my Dhamma, [be reduced to] a handful of dust."
It would be like scattering dust; yet this is not fitting for me. Out of compassion for the entire world, I am practicing with the resolve:
"I shall bring the conduct for the welfare of the world to its ultimate peak. This wicked man, moreover, is destined for great suffering in the future;
therefore, he is especially worthy of my compassion. Thus, I shall show him the path. In this way, my virtue remains perfectly pure and unbroken.

“...will happen. Having thought thus, he spoke the verse to the Bodhisatta, “If you are strong in battle,” and as soon as [the chariot] had veered slightly off the road, Adhamma, unable to remain in the chariot, fell headlong to the earth.
When a fissure opened in the earth, he went through it and was reborn in Avīci itself. Therefore it is said: “If indeed...”
"...it might provoke him," and so forth.
In that context, "if I were to be provoked by him" means if I were to become angry with that unrighteousness (*adhamma*).

"If it should destroy my quality of asceticism" means if, by that very act of becoming angry, I were to ruin my own quality of asceticism—that is, my restraint of virtue (*sīlasaṃvara*)—along with my retinue.
“Of that” means of that unrighteousness (adhamma) along with its attendants. “Become like dust” means it has become like dust; I would make it reach the state of dust. 72.
As for “Moreover, I,” here “I” is merely a particle. “For the sake of guarding virtue” means for the purpose of protecting one’s virtue.
“Having extinguished” means, because forbearance, loving-kindness, and compassion have been established beforehand, [having extinguished] the anger that arises toward that unrighteousness.
Having calmed the mind by the very non-arising [of unwholesome states] and by the subsiding of the fever of hatred;
"having stepped down together with the people" means that having stepped down from the path along with my retinue, I gave way to that evil, unrighteous person.
73. "Having stepped down from the path" means that, having brought about the calming of the mind in the manner already described, [I said]: "I give way to you."
Having said this, he descended slightly from the road. "Of the *pāyāsa*-yakṣa" means of the son of a deity who does not follow the Dhamma.
"At that very moment" means that at that very instant the great earth opened up. However, in the *Jātakaṭṭhakathā*, it is stated:
"at the very moment the verse 'And I give you the path' was spoken."
When he had thus fallen upon that ground, the Great Earth— though it is two hundred and forty-four thousand *yojanas* thick and supports all things,
both high and low— split asunder at the spot where he lay, as if saying, "I will not bear this wicked man.
But the Great Being, having fallen there, remained standing right where he was, like one positioned at the front of a chariot, reborn in the Avīci hell.
Together with his retinue, having traveled by way of the very path of his departure through great divine majesty, he entered his own palace. Therefore the Blessed One said:

“Having conquered the strength of battle with the strength of patience, having struck down and eliminated unrighteousness from the earth, Pāyāsi, joyful and exceedingly powerful, mounted his chariot and departed by way of that very path, firm in truth.”
At that time, Devadatta was Adhamma and his retinue was the retinue of Devadatta; the Dhamma was the Lord of the World and his retinue was the retinue of the Buddha.
Here too, the remaining perfections (pāramīs) should be determined as appropriate according to the method explained below.
Likewise, here too, [the Bodhisatta] was endowed with and possessed of sublime celestial objects of sense-desire—celestial in terms of life-span, beauty, fame, happiness, and sovereignty.
Although he was constantly attended by thousands of celestial nymphs and remained in a state of great luxury, he did not fall into even the slightest negligence.
Thinking, "I shall bring the practice for the welfare of the world to its ultimate fulfillment," he taught the Dhamma on every full moon day.
Accompanied by his retinue, he traveled along the public highways and, out of great compassion, [addressed] all beings...
The power of the Great Being’s virtues should be manifested as follows: separating others from what is non-Dhamma and enjoining them to the Dhamma;

and even when encountering one who has come together with non-Dhamma, disregarding the improper conduct committed by that person, not allowing the mind to become disturbed, but instead establishing patience, loving-kindness, and compassion, thereby guarding one’s own virtue so that it remains unbroken and perfectly pure. These and other such qualities of the Great Being are to be illustrated.
The commentary on the conduct of Dhammadevaputta is finished.
9. Commentary on the Conduct of Alīnasattu: 74.
In the ninth [chapter], "in the kingdom of Pañcāla" means in the country of that name; "in the excellent city, Kapilā" means [the city] called "Kapila."

Thus, in that supreme city which had received such a name; having said "in the excellent city" (*nagaravare*), the further statement "in the most preeminent city" (*puruttame*) is for the purpose of showing that at that time, among all cities in Jambudīpa, that city was the foremost city.
"Named Jayaddisa" means he was born when the king had conquered his enemies, or [named after] the female spirit (*yakkhinī*) who was his adversary.
"Jayaddisa" is his name thus acquired because he had conquered [his enemies]. "Sīlaguṇamupāgato" means he had attained both the virtue of conduct and the royal qualities such as excellence in energy;
the meaning is that he was endowed with those.
"Tassa rañño" refers to King Jayaddisa; the ellipsis to be supplied is "I was his son. "Sutadhammo" means...
Because he has heard all that which ought to be heard by a prince, he is "one who has heard the Dhamma" (*sutadhamma*); the meaning is that he is "learned" (*bahussuta*).

Alternatively, "one who has heard the Dhamma" means one whose Dhamma is renowned; the meaning is that he is famous and well-known for his practice of the Dhamma and his upright conduct, with a reputation spread throughout the world.
*Alīnasatta* is his name. He is "virtuous" (*guṇavā*) because of his sublime qualities of a Great Man.

"Endowed with": always having a retinue of followers because of his possession of distinguished qualities such as faith and because of his proper gathering [of people] through the four bases of sympathy; at all times surrounded by a circle of kinsmen.

"My father went hunting and approached Porisada": my father, King Jayaddisa, while wandering on a hunt, went into the middle of the forest and approached Porisada, the man-eater, the son of a *yakkhinī*; he encountered him.
It is said that one day King Jayaddisa, thinking, "I shall go hunting," departed from the city of Kapila with a great retinue suitable for such an occasion.
As soon as he had set out, a brahmin named Nanda, a resident of Takkasilā,
approached him bringing four so-called "four-hundred-verse" stanzas to recite, and explained the reason for his coming to the king.
He reported this. The king, saying, "I shall hear it after returning," had his residence and provisions sent to the man's dwelling and entered the forest.
Having declared, "The side from which the deer escapes belongs to him alone," he wandered about searching for the deer.
Then, at the sound of the great crowd's footsteps, a deer of the *pasada* species emerged from its lair and came toward the king.
He went and fled. The ministers laughed at him. The king pursued him and, when he was three *yojanas* away, struck down that deer whose speed was exhausted.

Having cut the fallen deer in two with his sword, although he had no need for it, he hung it on a carrying-pole to clear himself of the statement, "I could not catch the deer for its meat," as he was returning. Along the way, one man...
Having sat down on the *dabba* grass at the foot of the *nigrodha* tree and rested for a short while, he began to depart.
At that time, the king’s eldest brother—who had been seized by a *yakkhinī* on his very day of birth to devour him—was being followed by her guards;
as she was passing along the exit path, she placed him upon her breast.
Having conceived maternal affection by perceiving her as his mother, grasping her breast with his mouth, and being nurtured by her, he grew up consuming human flesh as his food.
Gradually reaching adulthood, he vanished through the power of a medicinal root given to him by a *yakkhinī* for the purpose of concealing himself;
while living on human flesh, he remained under the care of that *yakkhinī*.
Having destroyed that medicinal root through his own negligence, he was seen by the king’s men as he wandered naked, with a terrifying and deformed appearance, devouring human flesh.
Pursued by them, he fled into the forest and took up residence at the foot of that *nigrodha* tree; there, upon seeing the king, he seized him by the hand, saying, "You are my food!"
Therefore it was said: “He seized my father; you are my food, do not move! and so forth.
Therein, “he seized my father” means that Porisāda, seeing King Jayaddisa—my father—who had come near the tree where he himself was sitting, said, “You have come as my food;
do not move by means of shaking your hands or other such gestures,” for even if one were moving, I...
“I will eat him,” he said, and seized him by the hand.

77. *Tassa* means “of that son of the ogress. *Tasitavedhito*: terrified by mental agitation and trembling with physical convulsion. *Ūrukkhambho*: the stiffness of both thighs, by which he was unable to flee from there.
Regarding the phrase “having taken the deer, release it”: here, *migavaṃ* refers to the deer meat, as it was obtained by means of hunting (*migava*).
He said, “Game,” meaning, “Take this deer-flesh and release me. For that king, upon seeing the son of the ogress, was terrified;
his thighs became paralyzed, and he stood there like a stump. [The ogress] went quickly, seized him by the hand, and said, “You have come as my prey!
Then the king, restoring his mindfulness, said to her, “If—”
“Seeking food, I say: ‘I give this flesh to you; take it, eat it, and release me. Hearing this, Porisāda said, “What is this?
You are conducting business by giving me what belongs to me alone!
Indeed, from the moment this flesh and you both came into my hands, they have belonged to me alone. Therefore, [you should] first eat that...”
"I will eat the flesh afterwards," he said.
Then the king thought, "He does not release me for the sake of the price of the meat;
and when I came out for the hunt, I made a promise to that brahmin, saying, 'When you have returned, I will give you wealth. If this yakkha would grant permission, I must protect the truth."
Having gone home and fulfilled that promise, you should return again for the sake of this *yakkha*'s meal.
Having reflected thus, he informed him of this matter. Upon hearing this, Porisāda said, "If you wish to go while guarding your truth, then go;
having given the wealth that must be given to that brahmin, guard your truth and return quickly."
Having said, "May you come again," he dismissed the king. Thus released by him, the king said, "Do not worry;
I shall return early tomorrow morning," and while observing the landmarks on the road, he approached his own army.
Surrounded by it, he entered the city, summoned the brahmin Nanda, and had him seated upon a magnificent throne.
Having heard those verses, he gave four thousand [pieces of gold], placed him upon a vehicle, and dispatched the brahmin, giving instructions to his men, saying, "Take him to Takkasilā itself.
On the second day, wishing to go into the presence of Porisāda and intending to establish his son in the kingdom, he explained the matter while giving his final instructions. Thus it is said:
“Having taken up the hunt, release it again after you have returned;
having given wealth to the brahmin, my father addressed me:
‘Son, take charge of the kingdom; do not neglect this city.’”
"Porisāda made this promise to me regarding my return.
In that context, "regarding my return" means having made a covenant with Porisāda for his return.
"Having given wealth to the brahmin" means that after hearing those verses, [the king] gave four thousand [pieces of gold] to the brahmin named Nanda who had come from Takkasilā.
Having given the wealth, his father addressed him: "My father, King Jayaddisa, addressed me.
If one asks how he addressed him, it is said: "The kingdom," and so forth. The meaning of this is: "Son, you must take over this hereditary kingdom;
just as I have ruled the kingdom righteously and justly, so too, having raised the royal parasol..."
"Rule the kingdom. While protecting this city and exercising your sovereignty, do not fall into negligence.
At such-and-such a place, at the foot of the banyan tree, I made a pact with the yakkha Porisāda regarding my return to him;
I have come here merely for the purpose of giving wealth to that brahmin. Is this true?"
“Since I am protecting it, I shall go there myself.
Having heard this, the Great Being said, “Great King, do not you go there; I shall go there.
But if you, dear one, must indeed go, then I too will certainly go along with you. “So be it.”
"Since we both shall not exist once [the danger] has subsided, therefore I alone shall go there.
Having thus persuaded the king who was trying to dissuade him in various ways, he paid homage to his parents;

then, having sacrificed himself for the sake of his father, while the father was uttering words of blessing for his safety, he performed an act of truth (*saccakiriya*) regarding his mother, sister, and wife.

While they were doing so, he took up his weapon, departed from the city, and after taking leave of the great multitude who followed him with tearful faces, he set out upon the path to the yakṣa’s dwelling according to the instructions given by his father.
The son of the yakṣiṇī also thought, “Kṣatriyas are full of guile; who knows what will happen? and so he climbed a tree and watched for the king’s arrival.
Sitting there, upon seeing the prince approaching, he thought, "The father must have turned back and the son has come;
I have no fear," and so he descended and sat down showing his back to him. The Great Being arrived and stood before him.
Thus it is said:
“Having paid homage to my parents, and having created [a double] for myself;
laying aside my bow and sword, I approached the man-eater.
(81) “Approached with weapon in hand” means having approached me with a weapon in his hand, with an armament in his grasp. “To me” means to myself.
"Having seen him approached": "Perhaps he will frighten me," thinking this, that *yakkha* might even become afraid. "By that his virtue will be broken":
by that arousal of fear in him, my own virtue (*sīla*) will be destroyed and defiled. "When fear is produced in me":
when fear has been produced in me by him.
82. “Out of fear of breaking my virtue, I did not speak what was to be told to him”:

just as he had approached that man with his weapon laid aside out of fear of violating his virtue, so too, out of fear of breaking my own virtue, I did not speak even the unpleasant thing that was to be told to that man-eater (porisāda).
Rather, with a mind of loving-kindness and speaking for his benefit, I spoke these words which are now about to be related.
The Great Being went and stood before him. Desiring to test him, the son of the yakkhinī asked, "Who are you?
Where have you come from? Do you not know that I am a hunter who eats human flesh? And for what purpose have you come here?
The prince replied, "I am the son of King Jayaddisa; I know you as Porisāda. I have come to protect my father's life."
“I have come here; therefore, release him and eat me,” he said. Again, the son of the female *yakkha*, by way of his facial expression alone, said:
“I know that he is his son, but what you have done in coming like this is truly difficult. The prince replied: “This is not difficult:
the sacrifice of one’s life for the sake of one’s father is indeed a merit performed for the sake of mother and father.”
"Having done so, one rejoices exclusively in heaven. I know that there is no being whatsoever who is not subject to death;
nor do I recall having committed any evil deed myself. Therefore, I have no fear even of death.
This body is surrendered by me to you; light a fire and eat it. Thus he spoke. As it was said:
“Kindle the great fire; I shall leap from the tree.
Knowing that the time has come for me to be cooked, eat me, grandfather!
Hearing this, the son of the female *yakkha* thought, “It is not possible to eat his flesh; I will cause him to flee by some means.”
Having reflected, he said, "In that case, enter the forest, fetch heartwood, and prepare smokeless embers;
there we shall cook and eat your meat. The Great Being did so and informed him.
As he gazed at him, [the man] thought, "This lion among men has no fear even of death; I have never before seen one so utterly fearless."
Lomahaṃsajāta looked at the prince. The prince thought, "Why does he look at me? Is he not doing as was said?
Lomahaṃsajāta, the son of the yakkhinī, said to the Great Being, "May his head split into seven pieces who would eat you!
"If you do not wish to eat me, then why did you cause the fire to be made? "It was for the purpose of testing you."
“Now how will you take me as yours, when even though I was reborn in the womb of an animal, I did not allow myself to be taken by Sakka, the king of the gods? Demonstrating this point, he said:
“For this hare, thinking him to be a brahmin, offered up his own body.”
"For that very reason, this divine son Candima is praised along with his deer; today he is a *yakkha* who grants all desires.
Thus he spoke the verse.
Therein, "he caused the deer to dwell in his own body" means: for the sake of his own body, having eaten this body, he causes [the deer] to dwell here.
Thus, while giving his own body from his own person, he caused Sakka, who was in the form of a brahmin, to dwell there.
"Praised by the hare" means praised with the word "hare" (*sasa*) in this way. "Giver of desires" means the increaser of desires. "Yakkha" means a deity.

In this manner, the Great Being made the hare-mark on the moon—a miracle lasting for an aeon—his witness, and declared that even by Sakka himself it would be impossible to seize him. Upon hearing this, Porisāda was struck with a sense of wonder and amazement.
“Just as the sun, released from the mouth of Rāhu, shines brightly on the fifteenth day,
so do you, O man of great power, shine forth now that you are freed from the man-eater.
Bring joy to your father and mother, and let all your circle of kinsmen rejoice.”
Having spoken this verse, he dismissed the prince, saying, "Go, Great Hero.

The prince, too, having rendered him harmless and bestowed upon him the five precepts, began to investigate, thinking, "Is this a *yakkha* or not? He reflected: "The eyes of *yakkhas* are red and unblinking, their shadow is not perceived, and they are fearless; but this is not so. Therefore..."
"This is neither a *yakkha* nor a human; it must surely be that one of my father’s three brothers was seized by a *yakkhinī*.
Of those, two must have been devoured by her, while the third must have been cared for out of maternal affection.
It must be this one," he concluded with unerring certainty through inference based on grasping the underlying principle, as if by omniscient knowledge. Then, regarding his father—
Having thought, "I will inform him and establish him in the kingdom," he said, "You are not a *yakkha*; you are my father’s eldest brother.

Come, go with me and take over the kingdom that belongs to our family. By this it is meant, "You are my grandfather"; the meaning is, "You are my great-uncle. When the other replied, "I am not a human being," [the king said: "He must be believed by you..."
He led him into the presence of the ascetic endowed with the divine eye. When the ascetic asked, "What are you doing, father and son, wandering in the forest?
and thus spoke regarding his fatherhood, Porisāda believed him and said, "Go, dear one; I have no need for kingship; I shall go forth.
He then went forth into the ascetic life of an *isi* in the presence of that ascetic. Thus it was said:
“Thus, for the sake of those possessed of virtue, I did not spare my own life;
I ordained that man who was always a killer of living beings.

In this context, “for the sake of those possessed of virtue” means for the sake of my parents, who were virtuous. Alternatively, “sīlavataṃ hetu” means for the sake of virtue—that is, on account of my undertaking of the precepts, for the purpose of making him understand. “Tassa” refers to that Porisāda.
Then the Great Being, having paid homage to his own great father who had gone forth into the religious life, went near the city.
Hearing that "the prince has indeed arrived," the king—delighted and joyful—and the citizens, merchants, and countryfolk went out to meet him.
Having paid homage to the king, he reported the entire situation. Upon hearing this, the king immediately caused the drum to be beaten.
Accompanied by a great retinue, he went into his presence and said, "Come, brother, take over the kingdom.
"Enough, Great King," he replied. "In that case, dwell in my pleasure garden," [the king said]. "I will not come," [he replied].
The king, having established a village not far from that hermitage, provided for its alms-food. Thus it became known as the village of Cūḷakammāsadamma.

At that time, his parents were members of a great royal family; the ascetic was Sāriputta; Porisāda was Aṅgulimāla; the younger sister was Uppalavaṇṇā; the chief queen was Rāhulamātā; and Prince Alīnasattu was the Lord of the World.
Here too, as in the previous cases, the remaining perfections (pāramīs) should be extracted as appropriate according to the method already explained.
Likewise, though forbidden by his father, he sacrificed his own life for the sake of protecting his father’s life and went into the presence of Porisāda.
The firm resolve, "I shall go"; his departure while laying aside his weapons in order to avoid causing alarm;
his addressing him with affectionate words so that there might be no violation of his own virtue; the absence of any fear of death despite being scrutinized by him through various methods;
and his state of joy and satisfaction, thinking, "I shall make my body fruitful for the sake of my father."
The knowledge that he was indifferent to his own life for the sake of renouncing even his own kinsmen—something impossible even for Sakka to comprehend;
the absence of any mental fluctuation despite their meeting and separation; the unerring recognition of his human nature and his status as a great father;
and, upon that mere recognition, the desire to establish him in the kingdom inherited by his family through the teaching of the Dhamma.
"Having inspired them with a sense of urgency, he established them in the precepts. Such qualities and powers of the Bodhisatta are to be illustrated here.
The commentary on the *Alīnasattu* Jātaka is concluded.
10. Commentary on the *Saṅkhapāla* Jātaka.
85. Regarding the passage beginning with "In the tenth [birth], Saṅkhapāla," this is the summary of the meaning:

he was possessed of great psychic power (*mahiddhika*) because he was endowed with a great nāga-supernormal power (*nāgiddhi*) equal to the prosperity of the deva-worlds. He was "weapon-toothed" (*dāṭhāvudha*) because he had four fangs as weapons—two below and two above.
He was "of terrible venom" (*ghoravisa*) due to the intensity of his fiery energy (*tejas*). He was "endowed with two tongues" produced by his nāga-birth.

“Double-tongued. He is the “overlord of serpents” (*uragādhibhū*) because he is the sovereign over the *nāgas*—who are called “serpents” (*uraga*) because they move by gliding upon their chests—and who possess great majesty.
At the crossroads, which is a place characterized as a junction where two roads intersect; on the great highway, which is a place where the masses of people travel back and forth;
and for that very reason, crowded with various kinds of people due to being thronged by the multitude.
Now, by way of the four factors that will be explained, [he speaks of] the four factors. "Having resolved," meaning having established them and fixed them in the mind.
When I was the Nāga king named Saṅkhapāla, possessing the form described above, I then made my dwelling—my residence by way of the Uposatha-dwelling—in the place described below.
For the Mahāsatta, having been devoted to the merit of giving, virtue, and so forth,
and wandering from one state to another among the realms of gods and humans in search of enlightenment, was once reborn in a Nāga abode possessing a prosperity equal to that of the gods,
where he became a Nāga king named Saṅkhapāla, possessed of great psychic power and majesty. As time passed, he became remorseful regarding that very prosperity.
Having made offerings, he observed the Uposatha fast while aspiring for rebirth in the human womb.
While he was dwelling in the abode of the Nāgas, his observance of the Uposatha did not succeed and his virtue became defiled.
Consequently, he departed from the Nāga abode and, not far from the river Kaṇhavaṇṇā, surrounded a termite mound situated between a great highway and a footpath, and there observed the Uposatha.

Having made a formal resolve and undertaken the precepts on the fourteenth or fifteenth day of the lunar fortnight, he lies down after offering himself as an object of generosity, thinking, "Let those who need my skin and so forth take them.
On the first day of the waxing moon, he goes to the abode of the Nāgas. Thus it was said:
"Furthermore, when I am Saṅkhapāla," and so forth. The meaning of this has already been explained.
87. Furthermore, the passage beginning with "skin and hide" and ending with "resolving upon four factors" is the demonstration of the resolution upon the four factors (*caturaṅgādhiṭṭhāna*).
For here, skin and hide together constitute a single factor. Thus, as the Great Being dwelt observing the Uposatha, a long period of time passed.
Then one day, while he had thus undertaken the precepts and was lying down, sixteen sons of Bhoja, thinking, "We shall bring meat," [set out].
Wandering through the forest with weapons in hand, they emerged empty-handed;
seeing that [serpent] lying on top of the anthill, they thought, "Today we have not even obtained a young lizard; having killed this king of nagas, we shall eat him.
Then, thinking, "If he were seized by force, he might escape," they [pierced him] with stakes through his coils while he remained exactly as he lay.
"Having pierced him and weakened him, we shall seize him," they said, and taking spears, they approached.

The Bodhisatta’s body was large, measuring the size of a single-droṇa boat; it shone exceedingly, like a garland of *sumana* flowers arranged upon a stand, endowed with eyes like *jiñjuka* fruits and a head like a *jayasumana* flower. He [stood] before them...
Hearing the sound of the footsteps of sixteen men, he drew his head out from within the house, opened his red eyes,
and seeing them approaching with spears in their hands, thought, "Today my heart's desire will reach its fulfillment.
Having thus dedicated himself to the gateway of giving, he said, "Even as these men are hacking my body with spears and making it a mass of holes..."
Thinking, “I shall look [at her],” and having made a firm resolution out of fear that his own virtue might be broken,
he thrust his head right between the coils and lay down.
Then they approached him, seized him by the tail, dragged him down to the ground, and [pierced him] with sharp spikes.
Having pierced him in eight places and thrusting thorny black *vetta* stakes through the openings of his wounds, they took him up in eight baskets and set out upon the main road.
From the moment he was pierced by the stakes, the Great Being did not open his eyes even once to look at them as he was being carried away in the eight baskets. As he was being led away...
Having hung his head down, he struck the ground.

Then, thinking "his head is hanging down," they laid him down on the high road, pierced his nostrils with a fine needle, passed a cord through them, lifted his head, and having fastened it to the tip of a carrying-pole (kāja), they lifted him up again and set out upon the road. Thus it was said:
“O, the sons of Bhoja— cruel, fierce, and pitiless—
saw me there and approached with sticks and clubs in their hands.
Having pierced me through the nose, the tail, and the backbone,”
"Having hoisted me onto a palanquin, the sons of Bhoja carried me away.
In this context, "sons of Bhoja" means hunters' sons. "Harsh" means cruel, those whose bodily and verbal actions are rough.
"Cruel" means dreadful, those with terrible minds. "Merciless" means devoid of compassion. "With sticks and clubs in hand" means having four-cornered sticks in their hands.
"Having pierced through the nose" means having pierced the nostril with a fine needle in order to insert a cord.
"In the tail and along the spine" is connected as follows: having pierced it in various places in the region of the tail and near the vertebrae.
"Having mounted on the yoke" means having pierced it in eight places and bound it to eight circles made of rattan creepers.
In each [of the stakes], one stake was driven in; two by-two *bhojaputta* boys placed it upon their respective shoulders. 90.
"The earth bounded by the ocean" means the great earth extending to the limits of the sea.

"Together with its forests and mountains" means together with the groves and the peaks; thus, it is "with its forests and mountains. "I would burn it up with the breath of my nose"—if I were so to do...
If I so desired, wishing to do so, I could, having become angry, emit a blast from my nostrils that would incinerate this great earth—
bounded by the ocean, together with its forests and mountains— and reduce it to ashes at the mere emission of that breath;
such was my power at that time.
91. Even while being thus pierced by stakes and beaten with spears, I do not feel anger toward Bhojaputta.

This means that even though he was piercing him in eight places with sharp stakes made from hard wood—sharpened for the purpose of weakening him and for the purpose of inserting rattan creepers—and was striking him here and there with sharp spears for the purpose of weakening him...
"Even while being beaten by the hunters of the Bhoja clan, I do not become angry. This is my perfection of virtue (sīlapāramī).

When he, possessed of such great power, made this resolution, his lack of anger toward them out of fear of breaking his virtue was his perfection of virtue, which proceeded solely through disregard for his own life;
the meaning is that, by way of virtue, it became a perfection in the ultimate sense (paramatthapāramī).

While the Bodhisatta was thus being led away by them, a householder named Āḷāra, a resident of the city of Mithilā, who was traveling seated in a comfortable carriage with five hundred wagons, saw those sons of Bhoja carrying off the Great Being;
moved by compassion, he asked the hunters: "Why is this elephant being led away? What will you do with him once you have taken him?"
They said, "Let us cook and eat the meat of this nāga; it is delicious, tender, and abundant.

Then he gave each of those sixteen ox-drivers a handful of gold coins, as well as clothing for all of them and their wives, and ornaments for them too, saying, "Good sirs, this is a nāga king of great power. His own—"
"Because of your virtue of morality, you have not wronged us; however, by tormenting this one, you have produced much demerit.
Release him," he said. They replied, "This is a food we find pleasing, and many snakes have been eaten by us before;
nevertheless, your word must be honored by us. Therefore, we shall release this nāga. Having released him, they [departed] with the Great Being.
Having laid him down on the ground, because of their own hardness, they seized those black *vetta* creepers—
which were covered and entwined with thorns—
at the ends and began to pull. Then, seeing the Naga king growing weary, [the boy], without himself becoming weary, cut the creeper with a sword and [freed] the children.
Without causing him pain, he slowly extracted it according to the method of removing an object from a pierced ear.
At that time, those sons of hunters slowly untied the bond that had been fastened by inserting it into the back of his neck.
Having gone eastward for a moment, the Great Being looked toward Āḷāra with eyes filled with tears. The hunters—
Having gone a short distance, they hid themselves, thinking, "The snake is weak;
we shall take it only when it is dead. Āḷāra, having raised his joined palms to the Great Being, said, "Go on, O Great Naga;
let not those hunters seize you again," and after following the naga for a short while, he turned back.
The Bodhisatta went to the Nāga realm; there, without making any delay, he departed with a great retinue, approached Āḷāra, and after describing the excellence of the Nāga realm, led him there.
Having bestowed upon him great glory together with three hundred maidens, he gratified him with divine sensual pleasures. Āḷāra remained in the Nāga realm for one year.
Having dwelt there and enjoyed divine pleasures, he said to the Naga king, "Friend, I wish to go forth," and after taking the requisites for the life of a renunciant, he departed from there.
Having gone to the region of the Himalayas and gone forth, he lived there for a long time. Later, while wandering on his travels, he reached Benares and met with the King of Benares.
Then, inspired by his excellence in conduct, the king asked with faith, "I imagine you have gone forth from a family of great wealth;

for what reason, pray, did you go forth? Being thus questioned, he related the reason for his own renunciation, explaining the entire sequence of events to the king, beginning with how the Bodhisatta was released from the hands of the hunters.
“I have seen that even human sensual pleasures are impermanent and subject to change;
having perceived the danger in the strands of sensual pleasure, O King, I have gone forth out of faith.
Just as the fruits of a tree fall—whether they be young men or old, when their bodies break up—so do mortals.”
"Having seen this too, O King, I have gone forth; the life of a recluse alone is certainly better.
With these verses he taught the Dhamma.
Having heard it, the king—
“Truly, those who are wise, learned, and contemplate many matters must indeed be served.
Having heard of both Nāga and Tavañcara, I shall perform no small amount of meritorious deeds,” he said.
Then the ascetic said to him:
“Truly, O King, those who are wise, learned, and contemplative on many matters are indeed to be served.
Having heard from me concerning the Naga, perform abundant meritorious deeds.”
Having thus taught the Dhamma and stayed right there for four months of the rainy season, he returned to the Himālayas;
there, until the end of his life, he cultivated the four divine abidings (brahmavihāra) and was reborn in the Brahma-world.
The Bodhisatta also, having observed the Uposatha throughout his life, filled the city of heaven. That king too, having performed meritorious deeds such as giving, departed according to his karma.
At that time, Āḷāra was the Elder Sāriputta, the King of Bārāṇasī was the Elder Ānanda, and Saṅkhapāla the Naga King was the Lord of the World.

His sacrifice of his own body was the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramī*). The fact that his virtue remained unbroken even when afflicted by such terrible poison and pain, despite being possessed of such power, was the perfection of virtue (*sīla-pāramī*). Having renounced wealth equal to the prosperity enjoyed by the gods...
Emerging from the Nāga abode and practicing the duties of a recluse is the perfection of renunciation (*nekkhamma-pāramī*);

resolving, “It is fitting to do this and that for the sake of giving and so forth,” is the perfection of wisdom (*paññā-pāramī*); the removal of sensual thoughts and the energy of endurance are the perfection of energy (*vīriya-pāramī*);

the patience of endurance is the perfection of patience (*khanti-pāramī*); the undertaking of truth is the perfection of truth (*sacca-pāramī*); and the firm resolve upon the undertaking is the perfection of resolve (*adhiṭṭhāna-pāramī*).
The perfection of resolve (*adhiṭṭhāna-pāramī*); the state of loving-kindness and compassion toward all beings, beginning with Bhojaputta, is the perfection of loving-kindness (*mettā-pāramī*);
and equanimity toward feelings and the various manifestations produced by the formations of beings is the perfection of equanimity (*upekkhā-pāramī*). Thus, the ten perfections are obtained.
However, because the perfection of virtue (*sīla-pāramī*) is preeminent, it alone has been included in this teaching. Likewise...

Here, the virtues and power of the Bodhisatta should be elucidated as appropriate, according to the method already stated in the *Bhūridattacariya* beginning with the words, "In the Nāga-abode situated a hundred yojanas [away]," and so forth.
The commentary on the *Saṅkhapālacariya* is finished.
These nine modes of conduct (*cariyā*)— beginning with the "conduct of the elephant-king" (*hatthināga-cariyā*) and others—
which are indicated in this chapter and shown by way of summary in the preceding verse as "the elephant-king Bhūridatta" and so forth,

all possess the power of virtue (*sīla-bala*) because they proceed specifically toward the fulfillment of the perfection of virtue (*sīla-pāramitā*). Of virtue, which has become a supreme perfection (*paramattha-pārami*),...
They are "requisites" (parikkhārā) because they are prepared through the equipment of the personality and by way of cultivating the mental continuum.

They are "partial" (padesikā) and "with limitation" (sappadesā) because, since the perfection of virtue in its ultimate sense has not been fulfilled, there is only a portion of these [virtues] present, not their entirety.
If one asks why, he says: "Having protected his life, he guarded his virtues," because...
Among these practices, such as the conduct of the elephant-king, I protected my precepts by preserving only a portion of my life;

I did not renounce my life entirely. However, for me who was Saṅkhapāla, my life was surrendered at all times to whomever it might belong—specifically to the great-natured Nāga king Saṅkhapāla of fierce and potent splendor.
While remaining mindful even at all times when encountering those hunters—both before and after such meetings—he did not differentiate between individuals;
rather, he dedicated his life single-mindedly solely for the sake of guarding his virtue, relinquishing it through the gateway of generosity.
Therefore, that is the perfection of virtue (sīlapāramī). And since this is so, therefore by him...
By this reason, she demonstrates that she has attained the state of the perfection of ultimate reality (*paramatthapāramibhāva*),
which is my own perfection of virtue (*sīlapāramī*). This concludes the specific section on the Compendium of the Tenfold Conduct within the *Paramatthadīpanī*, the commentary on the *Cariyāpiṭaka*.
The commentary on the meaning of the second chapter, "The Development of the Perfection of Virtue," is finished. 3.
The Chapter on Yudhañjaya.
1. The Exposition of the Deeds of Yudhañjaya 1.

Regarding the first [story] of the third section: “Of immeasurable life” (*amitayaso*) means one whose retinue and wealth are limitless. “Prince Yudhañjaya” refers to the son of King Sabbadatta in the city of Rammanagara, named Yudhañjaya by name.
For this Bārāṇasī was known as the city of Surundhana in the *Udaya-jātaka*, and as Sudassana in the *Cūḷasutasoma-jātaka*.
In the Soṇananda Jātaka it was named Brahmavaḍḍhana; in the Khaṇḍahāla Jātaka it was named Pupphavatī;
but in this Yudhañjaya Jātaka it was named Rammanagara—thus its name changes from time to time.
Therefore it is said: "The prince was the son of the king named Sabbadatta in the city of Rammanagara. Now, of him...
The king had a thousand sons. The Bodhisatta was the eldest son, and the king granted him the rank of viceroy.
In the manner described below, he distributed a great almsgiving day after day.
As time passed in this way, one day the Bodhisatta mounted his excellent chariot at dawn and set out for a pleasure excursion in the park with great splendor and majesty.
Seeing drops of dew clinging to the tops of trees, the tips of grass, the ends of branches, spiderwebs, and so forth, in the shape of nets of pearls, he asked, "Good charioteer, what is this?

Having heard the reply, "These, Your Majesty, are called drops of dew that fall during the winter season," he spent a portion of the day sporting in the park; then, returning at evening time and not seeing them, [he said], "Good..."
“Charioteer, where are those drops of dew? I do not see them now,” he asked.
Having been told, “Your Majesty, when the sun rises, they all break apart and vanish,” he reflected:

“Just as these [drops] arise and then break, so too the life-formations of these beings are like drops of dew on the tips of blades of grass; therefore, I am terrified of sickness, old age, and death.”
“Is it not right to go forth after taking leave of one’s parents as if one were being pressed?
Thinking thus, and regarding the three realms of existence as if they were ablaze while taking a drop of dew as his object of meditation, he returned to his own home.

He went straight to his father, who was seated in the Hall of Justice adorned and prepared for court; having paid homage to his father, he stood to one side and requested the going-forth. Thus it is said:
“Having seen a drop of dew fallen in the heat of the sun, I was moved to spiritual urgency.
Making that very sight my primary motive, I intensified my sense of urgency;
then, having paid homage to my mother and father, I requested permission for the going-forth.”
In that context, "by the sun's heat" means by reason of the sun's heat, with the contact of the sun's rays as the cause.
There is also a reading, "by the sun's heat. "Having seen it fallen" means having seen it destroyed;

that is, having observed with the eye of wisdom that which was previously visible, hanging in the form of a net of pearls and so forth upon the tops of trees and other places, now destroyed through contact with the sun's rays.
Just as these [drops] perish, so too the lives of beings are by nature subject to very rapid destruction;
thus, through the application of attention to impermanence (*aniccatā-manasikāra*), I attained a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*).
Making that very [impermanence] the dominant influence (*adhipati*), I cultivated that spiritual urgency—meaning, making that very impermanence of the dew-drops the dominant influence.
Making the mouth my forerunner and precursor, I likewise brought to mind the short duration and limited time of all conditioned phenomena (*saṅkhāra*).
By repeatedly generating a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) that had arisen once, I caused it to increase. When they requested me to go forth, [I reflected]:
"In life, which does not endure long—like a drop of dew on the tip of a blade of grass—beings are beset by disease, old age, and death."
"Having gone forth as one who is unconquered, that deathless Great Nibbāna where these things do not exist must be sought"—
having thought thus, he approached his parents, paid homage to them, and requested of them, "Grant me permission to go forth.
When the Great Being had thus requested the going forth, a great clamor arose throughout the entire city.
—“It seems the viceroy Yudhañjaya wishes to go forth into the homeless life.
At that time, the inhabitants of the kingdom of Kāsi, having come to see the king, were staying at Ramma.
They all assembled together. Thus, the king along with his retinue, as well as the merchants and the country folk, [gathered before] the mother of the Bodhisatta.
The queen and all the women of the harem tried to dissuade the Great Being, saying, "Dear Prince, do not go forth into the religious life!
Thereupon the king said to him, "If you lack sensual pleasures, I shall provide them for you; take over the kingdom this very day.
To him, the Great Being replied:
“O Lord of Chariots, do not restrain me as I am going forth;
let me not be enslaved by sensual pleasures and fall under the power of old age.
Having thus expressed his own desire for the religious life, and having heard him while his mother and the women of the harem were lamenting piteously—
“Just as dew upon the tip of a blade of grass lasts until the rising of the sun, such is the life of human beings; do not stop me, mother.
Having thus explained the reason for his going forth, even though he was entreated by them in various ways, because his sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) was increasing, [he remained firm].
With a mind free from attachment, he went forth, regardless of his vast circle of kinsmen whom he loved dearly and his great royal sovereignty.
Thus it is said:
“With palms joined in reverence, the people of the towns and the entire kingdom entreated me.”
"Son, rule this prosperous and flourishing great earth this very day!
But he, indifferent, abandoned it— along with its kings, its harem, its townsfolk, and its provinces— as they wailed piteously.
In that context, "with palms joined" means with hands held in the gesture of reverence (*añjali*).
"Together with the townspeople and the country-folk" means that all the king's men, along with the citizens and the inhabitants of the kingdom, entreated me, saying, "O Lord, do not go forth!
But my parents said, "Son, practice [the life of a householder] this very day, for the sake of the growth and the attainment of abundance of villages, market towns, and royal capitals."
"Prosperous through the perfection of the essence of wealth and the production of crops and other goods, and flourishing—govern this great earth!

Raise the royal parasol and exercise sovereignty," they entreated. Thus, together with the king—that is, with the entire royal assembly—and likewise together with the women of the harem, the townspeople, the provincial folk, and the great multitude, [they spoke] in such a way that it was a great [matter], not only for those who saw it, but even more so for those who heard it.
There is compassion; thus, while [others] lament with grief, he shows that at those various times his mind was without regard or attachment, thinking, "At that time, I went forth.
5–6. Now, for the sake of which he abandoned the glory of sovereignty—equal to the splendor of a wheel-turning monarch—as well as his own dear kinsmen and relatives...
He spoke two verses to show that he renounced, without regard, his affectionate wife and retinue, as well as great fame esteemed by the world.
Therein, "entirely" means without exception; [he renounced] the harem and the earth bounded by the ocean with the intention of going forth.

While sacrificing, I thought, "In this way, it will be possible for me to attain perfect enlightenment (sammāsambodhi)"; for the sake of enlightenment alone, I did not think of anything else, nor did I allow even the slightest attachment to arise there—this is the meaning.
Therefore (*tasmā*): because my parents, that great fame, and the kingdom were not to be abandoned by me, but were indeed dear to me;
yet, [the goal of enlightenment was] a hundredfold, a thousandfold, and a hundred-thousandfold more dear than those.
"Omniscient knowledge alone is dearer to me; therefore, I shall renounce the kingdom along with my mother and others at that time.

Having renounced all this and gone forth into homelessness, when the Great Being had departed, his younger brother, Prince Yudhiṭṭhila, paid homage to his father, obtained his permission for the going-forth, and followed after the Bodhisatta.
Both of them, having departed from their respective cities and turned back the great multitude of people, entered the Himālaya mountains.
There, having established a hermitage in a delightful place, they went forth into the ascetic life of an *isi*.

Having attained the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and direct knowledges (*abhiññā*), they sustained themselves on forest roots, fruits, and the like for the rest of their lives, and became destined for the Brahma-world. Therefore, the Blessed One said:
“Both princes have gone forth— Yudhañjaya and Yudhiṭṭhila—
having abandoned their mother and father, and having severed the bond of death. Herein,

“having severed the bond of death” means that both have gone forth after cutting off, by way of suppression, the bond of attachment consisting of lust, hatred, and delusion, which belongs to Māra the Death because he acts as its cooperative cause.
At that time, his parents were great royal families; Prince Yudhiṭṭhila was the Venerable Ānanda, and Yudhañjaya was the Lord of the World (the Buddha).

Prior to his going forth, his practice of great almsgiving and his renunciation of his kingdom and so forth constituted the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*). His restraint of body and speech was the perfection of virtue (*sīla-pāramitā*).

His going forth and the attainment of meditative absorption (*jhāna*) were the perfection of renunciation (*nekkhamma-pāramitā*). Beginning with the mental application (*manasikāra*) on impermanence...

The perfection of wisdom (*paññā-pāramī*) consists of the wisdom that culminates in the attainment of direct knowledge (*abhiññā*), as well as the wisdom that discerns which factors are conducive or non-conducive to generosity and the other perfections.

The perfection of energy (*vīriya-pāramī*) is the energy that accomplishes those aims in every respect. The perfection of patience (*khanti-pāramī*) consists of both intellectual patience (*ñāṇa-khanti*) and patient endurance (*adhivāsana-khanti*).
The perfection of truthfulness (*sacca-pāramī*) is the non-deception of one’s promise. The [perfection of] resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*) is the firm commitment to one’s undertaking in all circumstances.
The perfection of resolve (*adhiṭṭhāna-pāramī*); the perfection of loving-kindness (*mettā-pāramī*) by way of the sublime abiding of loving-kindness through a mind of benevolence toward all beings;

and the perfection of equanimity (*upekkhā-pāramī*) by way of the sublime abiding of equanimity through the observation of the various conditioned states produced by beings—thus ten perfections are obtained.
Specifically, however, it should be understood as the perfection of renunciation (*nekkhamma-pāramī*). Likewise, in the conduct of Akitti...
Just as here, the marvelous qualities of the Great Man should likewise be extracted according to their fitness. Therefore it is said:
"Thus these are marvelous and wonderful for the Great Seer... [and so on] ...in accordance with the Dhamma.
The commentary on the *Yudhañjaya Cariyā* is finished.
2. Commentary on the Practice of Somanassa. 7.
