In the second [verse], "in Indapatta, the preeminent city"—that is, in that excellent city named Indapatta.
"Longed for" means desired for a long time by his parents and others, thinking, "O, would that a son were born to us! "Beloved" means cherished. "Somanassa" means...
“Vissuta” means one whose name is well-known, such as “Somanassa.

“Sīlavā” means endowed with both the virtue of the ten courses of wholesome action and the virtue of proper conduct. “Guṇasampanno” means possessed of qualities such as faith and erudition, or alternatively, complete in them.
“Kalyāṇapaṭibhānavā” means one who possesses excellent eloquence through the accomplishment of whatever is to be done at each respective time.
And he is endowed with excellent eloquence, which is characterized as skill in means (*upāyakosalla*).

"One who honors the elders" (*vuḍḍhāpacāyī*) means one whose nature is to show reverence to those who are elders by birth—namely, mother and father—and to those who are elders in virtue through qualities such as moral discipline (*sīla*).

"Modest" (*hirīmā*) means one who is possessed of a sense of shame (*hiri*) characterized by a loathing for evil. And "skilled in the means of integration" (*saṅgahesu kovidō*) means [skilled] in what is comprised by giving, pleasant speech, purposeful conduct, and impartiality.
He was skilled in gathering beings as appropriate through the four bases of sympathy (*saṅgahavatthu*).
The connection is: "When I was such a one, known as Somanassa, the son of Reṇu, the King of the Kurus. 9.
He was a "counter-actor" (*patikara*) to that king, meaning he was one who constantly acted as a counter-measure against that King of the Kurus by way of being his adversary.
Vallabha: A "deceitful ascetic" (*kuhakatāpasa*) is a certain ascetic who makes his living through hypocrisy (*kohañña*), characterized by the false attribution of non-existent virtues;

he was held in high esteem by that king. An "orchard" (*ārāma*) is a fruit orchard where creepers such as *eḷāluka*, *lābu*, *kumbhaṇḍa*, and *tipusa* are cultivated, as well as vegetables such as *taṇḍuleyyaka*.
A "flower garden" (*mālāvaccha*) is a grove of flowering shrubs such as *jāti* and *atimuttaka*.

By this, he shows a flower garden. And here, the meaning should be understood as follows: having established a grove there, having planted flowering shrubs and the aforementioned fruit-bearing trees, and having set aside the wealth obtained from them, he lives. In this regard, the sequential account is as follows:
at that time, an ascetic named Mahārakkhita, accompanied by a retinue of five hundred ascetics, was in the Himālayas.
Having stayed there, he set out on a journey through the countryside for the purpose of practicing the salt-and-vinegar austerity.
Upon reaching the city of Indapatta, he stayed in the royal park; then, wandering for alms with his retinue, he arrived at the palace gate.

When the king saw the group of seers, he was inspired by their dignified deportment, so he had them seated upon a magnificent, decorated terrace, served them with exquisite food, and said, "Venerable sirs, for this rainy season..."
"Live in my very own park," he said. Having spoken thus, he went to the park with them, had dwellings constructed, provided the requisites for those who have gone forth, and departed.
From that time on, they all ate at the royal residence.
However, the king, being childless, longed for sons, yet no sons were born to him. At the end of the rainy season, Mahārakkhita—
Thinking, "We shall go to the Himavat," they took leave of the king;
having departed with the honors and hospitality bestowed by the king, they left the road at midday and sat down with their retinue beneath a tree providing deep shade.
The ascetics initiated a conversation: "The king is childless; it would indeed be well if..."
"May I obtain a prince. Having heard those words, Mahārakkhita reflected, "Will there indeed be a son for the king, or not?
Discerning that "there will be," he said, "Do not worry;
this very day at dawn, a certain son of the gods will pass away and be reborn in the womb of the king’s chief queen."
Hearing this, a certain false ascetic thought, "Now I shall become an attendant of the royal family.
When the time came for the ascetics to depart, he made a pretense of illness and lay down. When [Mahārakkhita] said, "Come, let us go," he replied, "I am not able.
Mahārakkhita, understanding the reason for his lying down, said, "When you are able, you may come," and taking the company of seers, he departed for the Himālayas himself.
He had gone. The rogue turned back, went with speed, and standing at the king’s gate, had it announced to the king:
“The ascetic who is Mahārakkhita’s attendant has arrived. Summoned by the king with haste, he ascended the palace and sat down on the prepared seat.
After the king had paid him homage and sat to one side, having inquired after the health of the seers, [the king said]: “Venerable sir, very soon—”
"They have returned; for what purpose did they come? he asked.
"Great King," [the sage replied], "a company of seers was sitting comfortably and initiated this conversation: 'It would be well indeed if a son who protects the king's lineage were to be born.
Having heard that conversation, I wondered: 'Will there be a son for the king, or not?'"
Looking with his divine eye, he saw: “A powerful son of the gods, having passed away, will be reborn in the womb of the chief queen Sudhammā.
Seeing this, [the deity] thought, “They might destroy the embryo out of ignorance; I shall first inform them.
Thus he came to speak to you, and I have now spoken to you. “I am going,” he said. The king replied, “Venerable sir, no...”
Thinking, "It is possible to go," he was joyful and delighted; with a clear mind, he led the fraudulent ascetic to the garden, arranged a dwelling place for him, and gave it to him.
From then on, he lived eating at the royal court, and his name became "The One Possessing the Divine Eye.
At that time, the Bodhisatta, having passed away from the Tāvatiṃsa heaven, took rebirth there; and on the day of the naming ceremony of the newborn, [the following occurred]:
They gave him the name Somanassa. He grew up with the care and privileges befitting a prince.

The hypocritical ascetic, for his part, planted various kinds of vegetables, leaf-greens, fruits, and creepers on one side of the park, and gathered wealth by selling them into the hands of vegetable vendors.
Then, when the Bodhisatta was seven years old, the king’s frontier regions rose in revolt.
Thus, saying, "Dear son, do not neglect the ascetic with the divine eye," he entrusted the prince to him and departed to pacify the border region.
Then one day, the prince, thinking, "I shall see the matted-hair ascetic," went to the park;
there he saw the fraudulent matted-hair ascetic wearing a single fragrant saffron robe as an undergarment and another as an upper garment, holding two water-jars in both hands in a vegetable field.
Seeing him sprinkling water, [the monk] realized, "This fraudulent matted-hair ascetic, instead of performing his own duty as a recluse, is engaged in the work of a vegetable seller.
He then shamed him by saying, "What are you doing, you vegetable-selling householder? and departed without even bowing to him.
The fraudulent matted-hair ascetic thought, "He is like this right now; who knows what he might do later? I shall deal with him right now."
Thinking, "It is not right to destroy him," he threw a stone slab aside at the time of the king's arrival,
broke the water jar, scattered the grass in the leaf-hut, smeared his body with oil, entered the hut, covered himself down to his head,
and lay down on the bed as if overcome by great suffering. When the king arrived and circumambulated the city...
Without entering the dwelling she had built, thinking, "I shall see my husband with his divine eye," she went to the door of the leaf-hut.
Seeing that calamity, she wondered, "What is this? She entered within, saw him lying there, and while massaging his feet, she asked:
"By whom, venerable sir, have you been thus afflicted? To whom has the world of Yama been surrendered today?"
“Nemi, tell me that quickly!
Having heard this, Kūṭajaṭila, groaning, rose up and said: “I have seen you, O Great King;
having seen you and because of my trust in you, I have come to this state of ruin, for I have been thus tormented by your son. Having heard this, [the king...]
The king commanded the executioners: “Go, cut off the prince’s head, cut his body into pieces, and scatter them from street to street.

They dragged the prince away—he who had been adorned by his mother and seated upon her lap—saying, “The king has ordered your execution. Terrified by the fear of death, the prince [leapt] from his mother’s lap.
Having risen, he said, "Show me to the king; there are royal duties to be attended to.
Hearing the prince's words, they—unable to bring themselves to kill him—dragged him along with a rope like an ox and led him to the king. Thus it was said:
"Having seen that rogue," and so forth.
In this context, "like a heap of husks without rice" means like a heap of husks devoid of rice grains;

"like a tree" means like a tree that is hollow within. Having seen the ascetic—who was "without core," meaning devoid of the core of virtue (*sīla*) and so forth—just like a plantain tree (*kadali*), I thought:

"This man possesses not even a fraction of the noble qualities such as meditative absorption (*jhāna*). Why? Because of his lack of true asceticism (*sāmañña*), that is, the state of being a recluse, even in terms of mere virtue."
"He has departed; he has fallen away, for he has abandoned the bright quality of moral shame (*hirī*), having cast off that bright quality known as shame.
By the phrase "for the sake of maintaining a livelihood," it shows that they thought: "He wanders in the guise of an ascetic solely for the purpose of his own life. "Border-dwellers" (*parantino*):
those who have borderlands (*paranta*)—that is, frontier regions—as their place of residence are called border-dwellers; they are inhabitants of the frontier regions.
Because of those border-dwelling forest folk, the frontier region became agitated. As my father, the King of Kuru, was departing to suppress and pacify that frontier rebellion, he said:

"Dear Somanassa Kumāra, do not neglect the matted-hair ascetic who is my master—he of lofty austerity, fierce penance, and most perfectly controlled faculties. For he is the granter of all our desires; therefore—"
"Act according to his will, according to his inclination, and in accordance with his mind; follow him and serve him"—this is what he taught me at that time.
This shows how he instructed me. 14. "Having gone there, I attended upon him": not transgressing my father’s word, I went to attend upon that false ascetic.
Seeing him pouring water in a field of vegetables and knowing, "This man is a mere vegetable-seller," I asked: "Is it well?"... [text continues]
"Householder, they are well; householder, is it well with their bodies?

Indeed, it is well, for you are pouring water on the *sāka* field. Or rather, let your bullion or gold be brought back, for you are following the livelihood of a vegetable-seller"—this was the speech I uttered.
15. "By that he was provoked" means: by that accusation of being a householder uttered by me, that deceitful man—who was dependent on pride and attached to pride—became provoked and angry with me.
Being thus enraged, he said: "I shall have you executed today, or I shall banish you from the kingdom."
"In that regard, 'you today' means you this very day, at the time when the king has arrived.
Having suppressed the border region—that is, having pacified the border—he entered the city;
and at that very moment, having gone to the park, he asked the fraudulent ascetic: 'Venerable sir, is it bearable for you? Is hospitality being extended to you?'"
The prince showed them honor. 17. “As for ‘how Nāsiya’”:
he informed the king of that wicked man’s identity in such a way that the prince [Nāsiya] was to be destroyed—that is, executed.
“He gave the order”: while this ascetic possessed of the divine eye is my master, what [need have I]?
"It is not accomplished; therefore, I have no need for a son. Even so, this [other one] is better," he thought, and having reflected thus, he gave the order:

"18. How so? 'Having cut off his head right there'—at the very place where you see that boy, right there, having cut off his head and having divided his body into four pieces—that is, having made it into four portions—[place it] on the road."
"Being led along the road, show it by wandering from street to street! Why? Because that destination is the one despised by the matted-hair ascetics (jaṭila).
That destination, that result, that karmic fruition belongs to those by whom this matted-hair ascetic was despised—thus is the meaning of "despised by the matted-hair ascetics.
Alternatively, the meaning here should be understood as: "Because of being despised by the matted-hair ascetics—that is, on account of such contempt for the matted-hair ascetics—that is his result."
19. *Tattha* means "in that king's command" or "regarding that contempt for the ascetic.
*Kāraṇikā* means executioners; the meaning is "executioners of thieves. *Caṇḍā* means cruel. *Luddā* means very fierce. *Akāruṇā* is a synonym for the same.
There is also a textual reading *akarūnā*, which has the same meaning as "merciless. *Mātu aṅke nisinna-ssā* means "of me sitting on my mother Sudhammā’s lap."
“Of one sitting on the queen’s lap. The term *nisinnassa* (of one sitting) is used in the genitive case with disregard for the subject.

“They drag and lead him away” means that after his mother had adorned him and seated him on her own lap, those executioners, by the king’s command, dragged him toward the place of execution like an ox with a rope and led him away. While the prince was being led away, surrounded by a throng of female slaves...
Together with the women of the harem, Queen Sudhammā, and the citizens also went along with him, saying, "We will not allow them to kill the prince, who is innocent. 20.
"Binding those who bind tightly" refers to those judicial officers who were binding him with tight fetters.
"There are royal duties for me"—this means there are royal tasks that must be performed by me.
Therefore, I spoke these words to them:

"Show me quickly to the king. 21. They showed me to the king; [the words] "of the evil one who associates with the evil" refer to the false ascetic, who was himself of evil character and base conduct.
Because of his association with evildoers, they showed me to the king. Having seen him, they informed him;
and upon seeing my father, the King of the Kurus, I said, "Why, O Lord, did you have me put to death?
To this, he replied, "And why did you address my master, the ascetic with divine vision, as 'householder'? For this and that misconduct..."
When he said, "Do so," [the king] replied, "Your Majesty, what fault is there in my calling a householder 'householder'?
Having thus spoken, he planted various kinds of flowering shrubs for him, and having entrusted them to flower-sellers and leaf-vendors who sold flowers,
leaves, fruits, and other produce daily from his hands, he provided the funds for the purchase of garlands and the purchase of leaves.
Having said, "Consider this," I entered his leaf-hut, had my own men bring out the bag of kahāpaṇa coins obtained from the sale of flowers and other goods, and made the king understand;
I made him recognize that he was a fraudulent ascetic. By that persuasion, [the king thought], "The prince speaks the truth; this is indeed a fraudulent ascetic. And I brought him under my control.
Thus it is said: "And I brought him under my power. Through that persuasion, [he realized], "The prince speaks the truth; this is a fraudulent ascetic."
“Having previously been one of few desires, he has now become possessed of great possessions.
Thus, becoming disillusioned with him, I brought the king under my influence so that he would act according to my will.
Then the Great Being thought, “Since I am living in the presence of such a foolish king, it is better for me to enter the Himalayas and go forth into the homeless life.”
Thinking, "This is fitting," he asked the king: "Great King, I have no need for dwelling here;
grant me leave, for I shall go forth into the religious life. The king said, "Dear son, I commanded your execution without due reflection;
forgive my offense," and having thus asked the Great Being's forgiveness, he said, "Enter upon this kingship this very day. The prince—
“Your Majesty, what is there in human enjoyments? For a long time in the past I have experienced the excellence of divine enjoyments, yet even there I had no attachment.
I shall indeed go forth; I will not dwell in the presence of such a fool whose intellect is led by others.
Having said this, he exhorted him:
“Action performed without reflection, thought out without stability,
has a wicked result, like the failure of medicine.
But action performed with reflection, thought out with stability...”
Just like the excellence of medicine, the result is auspicious.
“A lazy householder who enjoys sensual pleasures is not good; an unrestrained one who has gone forth is not good;
a king who acts without reflection is not good; and a wise man who is prone to anger is not good.”
“A ruler should act with deliberation, not without deliberation, O Lord of the Earth;
for the fame and renown of a king who acts with deliberation increase.
A lord should mete out punishment with deliberation; for if it is done impulsively, O Protector of the World, he suffers remorse.”
Right aspiration brings benefit to a person, and it leads to no regret later on.
For those who perform deeds that are beyond reproach, having analyzed the spheres of action in the world—
deeds praised by the wise, productive of happiness, and approved by the Buddhas— they shall have no cause for regret.
“Doorkeepers with girded swords, clad in saffron robes, came, O Lord of Men, to kill me;
and as I sat upon my mother’s lap, O King, I was suddenly dragged away by them.
For I had fallen into a bitter, narrow, and miserable strait, yet I regained a sweet and dear life, O King.”
"Today, through hardship, I am released from death; indeed, I am intent upon the going-forth"—with these verses he taught the Dhamma.
Therein, "without reflecting" means without having investigated; "without establishing" means without having determined; "disintegration" means failure.
"Result" (*vipāka*) means accomplishment. "Unrestrained" (*asañata*) means uncontrolled and immoral. "Should offer" (*paṇayeyya*) means should present.

"With speed" (*vega*) means with haste or impulsively. And "with right aspiration" (*sammāpaṇidhī*): the meaning is that the aims accomplished by a person through right aspiration—that is, through a mind established with wise reflection—become free from regret later on.
"By discerning" (*vibhajja*) means: "these things are appropriate to do, these things are inappropriate."
Having thus analyzed with wisdom: "Spheres of action" means actions. "Approved by the Buddhas" means they are approved by the wise and are blameless.
"Bitter" means painful, unpleasant, constricting, miserable, and having reached the fear of death.
"Obtained" means having regained my life through the power of my own knowledge. "I am intent on going forth alone" means that my mind is directed solely toward the life of renunciation.
When the Great Being had thus taught the Dhamma, the king addressed the queen, saying, "Queen, please turn your son back.
The queen, however, approved of the prince's going forth.

The Great Being, having paid homage to his mother and father, asked for their forgiveness, saying, "If I have committed any fault, forgive me," and having taken leave of the great multitude, he set out toward the Himalayas.
But when the Great Being had departed, the great multitude beat the fraudulent ascetic and brought him to his death.

The Bodhisatta, too, having turned back the royal officers—the ministers, councilors, and others—who were following him with tearful faces along with the townspeople, was escorted by deities appearing in human form after the people had turned back; he then crossed over seven mountain ranges.
In the Himalayas, he went forth into the ascetic life in a leaf-hut constructed by Vissakamma. Thus it was said:
“There he asked my forgiveness and gave me great sovereignty;
having shattered that darkness, I went forth into homelessness.”

In that context, "having shattered the darkness" means having dispelled the darkness of delusion, which is the adversary to seeing the danger in sensual pleasures. "I approached the going-forth" means I entered the homeless life.

Now, in order to show the purpose for which he then renounced that royal sovereignty, he spoke the final verse beginning with "Nothing is to be seen by me. Its meaning is exactly as previously explained.

When the Great Being had thus gone forth, however, until he reached the age of sixteen, deities alone attended upon him in the guise of female attendants in the royal palace. Having realized the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and direct knowledges (*abhiññā*) there, he was reborn in the Brahma-world.
At that time, Devadatta was the rogue, his mother was Mahāmāyā, the ascetic Mahārakkhita was the Elder Sāriputta, and Somanassakumāra was the Lord of the World.
His ten perfections (*pāramitā*) are to be extracted in the same manner as described in the *Yudhañjayacariya*. Here too, the perfection of renunciation (*nekkhamma-pāramī*) is to be understood.
That very [story] is presented in the teaching as being preeminent. Likewise, [it shows] his capability for royal duties even at the age of seven;
his discernment of that ascetic’s state of being a fraudulent matted-hair ascetic; his lack of fear when the king, incited by him, ordered his execution;
and his going before the king and, through various methods, demonstrating the king's faultiness and his own innocence to the great multitude.

Having revealed this in the midst [of the assembly] and established both the king’s susceptibility to being led by others and his state of childishness, even though he was asked for forgiveness, [the Bodhisatta] felt a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) regarding living in that man's presence and the splendor of sovereignty.
Although entreated in many ways, he cast away the royal glory already in his hands like a globule of spittle; with a mind unattached to anything, he went forth into homelessness.
Having gone forth and delighting in seclusion, he very soon and without difficulty produced the jhānas and direct knowledges (abhiññā).
In this way, such powers of the Great Being’s virtues are to be made manifest.
The commentary on the practice of joy is finished.
3. Commentary on the Practice of the Iron House (Ayogharacariyāvaṇṇanā) 24. Regarding the third [practice], "He grew up in an iron house":

he was raised in a great dwelling made entirely of iron, constructed in the shape of a square hall for the purpose of avoiding harm from non-human beings. He was known by the name Ayoghara precisely because he was born and raised in an iron house.
He became well known by the name “Prince Ayoghara.
For at that time, in a previous existence, the chief queen of the King of Kāsi had been a co-wife and had made this aspiration: “May she devour every child born to you!
Having thus made her wish, she was reborn in the womb of a *yakkhinī*, and having found an opportunity, she [approached] her...
At the time of each birth, she devoured two sons. But on the third occasion, the Bodhisatta took rebirth in her womb.
The king, consulting with his men, thought, "A certain yakkhinī devours every child born to the queen; what indeed should be done?
He concluded, "Non-human beings are afraid of iron houses; it is fitting to build an iron house."
Having spoken thus, he gave orders to the smiths and, beginning with the pillars, completed a great iron house—a square hall—using exclusively all the materials made of iron.
He then had the queen, whose pregnancy was fully matured, reside there.
There she gave birth to a son endowed with the marks of grain and merit. They gave him the name "Ayogharakumāra" (The Iron-House Prince). Having entrusted him to the nurses, [they provided] great...
Having arranged for her protection, the king brought the queen into the inner palace. The yakkhinī, having gone to the water gate while carrying water for Vessavaṇa, met her death there.
The Great Being, having grown up right within the iron house, reached the age of discretion and mastered all the arts right there. The king—
Knowing that his son had reached the age of sixteen, [the king] thought, "I shall give him the kingdom," and commanded his ministers:

"Bring my son here. They replied, "Very well, Your Majesty," and after having the city decorated, they took the auspicious state elephant adorned with all ornaments, went there, dressed the prince in finery, seated him upon the back of the elephant, and circumambulated the city.
Having had it fashioned, they presented it to the king. The Great Being, having paid homage to the king, stood before him.
The king, beholding the splendor of his body and embracing him with intense affection, commanded his ministers: "Anoint my son this very day! The Great Being, having paid homage to his father, said:
"I have no need for the kingdom; I shall go forth into the homeless life. Grant me the going-forth."
“Grant me your permission,” he said. Therefore it was said: “Life has been obtained with difficulty,” and so forth.
Therein, “with difficulty” means: dear son, your two brothers were devoured by a single yakkhinī;
but as for you, life has been obtained through great hardship and exertion caused by the effort made to ward off that danger from non-human beings. [In the state of] oppression...
"Reared" means that from the time of her delivery in the cramped iron house— where she was protected by various kinds of non-human beings—
until she reached the age of sixteen, she was brought up in that confinement. "Son, this very day,
enter upon [the sovereignty] over this entire earth," [said he] as he placed him beneath a white parasol adorned with a golden fringe upon a heap of jewels.
"Except for the three taxes, being consecrated today, my son, take possession this very day of this entire earth—
the great world— along with its kingdoms, its cities, its great villages, its towns, its hamlets, its people, and its kinsmen, extending as far as the ocean's edge."

The meaning is: "Exercise sovereignty. Having paid homage to the khattiya—having paid homage to the khattiya, the King of Kāsi, my father, and having extended my hands in reverential salutation—I spoke these words.
"Whatever beings there are on earth"—whatever beings there are on this great earth; "low, high, and middling."
Those who are inferior and those who are superior—because they exist between these two, they are the middling.

"In their own homes" means all of them are in their own homes. "With their own kinsmen" means that, being greeted by their own kinsmen, they live freely and without longing, increasing according to their respective wealth. 28.
"This is unsurpassed in the world" means that this, moreover, is peerless in this world; it is my own unique possession. What?
"But she was my nourisher in distress" means she was my nurturer in times of confinement.
For it says, "I grew up in an iron house," meaning I grew up in an iron house devoid of the light of the moon and sun; thus, "I grew up" [is said].
"Filled with putrid corpses" means filled with various kinds of putrid-smelling corpses, resembling a hell of excrement. Of the mother...
"Loathsome" means while a danger to life was present, how could one escape and emerge?
"More terrible than that" means more dreadful even than dwelling in the womb, due to the suffering of being confined without release.
"Thrown into an iron house" shows that he was as if cast into an iron house, placed in a prison.
30. Regarding the word *yadi*: here, *yadi* is merely a particle. *Tādisaṃ* means "of such a kind," as was previously stated;

having encountered such extremely dreadful suffering, if I were to take pleasure (*rajjāmi*) or find delight (*ramissāmi*) in kingships, then under such circumstances, I would be the most wretched—the very lowest—among evil, base, and inferior men.
31. "I am weary of this body" means that I am weary of and disgusted with this putrid body, which has not yet been liberated from dwelling in a womb and so forth.
"I have no need for kingship" means that I have no need even for sovereignty. For even though I have escaped from the hands of the yakkhinī, I am neither free from aging nor immortal;
what use have I for kingship? Indeed, kingship is the place where all misfortunes converge.

"From the moment one stands there, it becomes difficult to depart; therefore, without approaching that, I shall seek the extinction where Māra does not crush me—where the great army of King Māra cannot crush, overwhelm, or overpower me standing there.
I shall seek that extinction, the great Nibbāna of the Deathless."
32. "Having thus reflected" means: having wisely reflected in this manner—by contemplating the various kinds of danger in *saṃsāra* as described above, and by seeing the benefits in *nibbāna*.

"While the great multitude was wailing" means: while the great multitude, headed by my mother and father, was crying out and lamenting because they could not endure the suffering of separation from me.

"Like an elephant severing its bonds": just as a mighty elephant easily severs even a weak rope-bond, so too, having severed the bond by cutting the fetter of craving for that person consisting of relatives and the like, I entered the great forest known as the wilderness by way of going forth. The meaning of the concluding verse is already explained.
Thereupon, the Great Being, having made known his intention to go forth, was asked by the king, "Dear son, for what reason do you go forth?
He replied, "Your Majesty, having dwelt in my mother’s womb for ten months as if in a hell of excrement, I emerged from my mother’s womb;
yet, out of fear of a female spirit (*yakkhinī*), I have spent sixteen years in prison, unable even to look outside."
I was as if cast into a hell of extreme suffering; though released from the ogress, I am not free from old age and death.
This Death indeed cannot be conquered by anyone. I am weary of existence;
as long as sickness, old age, and death have not yet come upon me, I shall go forth into homelessness and practice the Dhamma. Enough for me with kingship; grant me leave.
"Your Majesty, let me go forth," he said, and [the King replied]:
"The young man who dwells in the womb for the first time, even as he departs he is already set forth; once gone, he does not return."
Having taught the Dhamma to his father with twenty-four verses beginning with these, he said, "Great King, let your kingdom remain yours alone;
I have no need for it. While I am even speaking with you, sickness, old age, and death would come upon me.
You stay here. Having spoken thus, he broke the iron chain like a rutting elephant, and shattered the golden cage.
Like a lion cub, he abandoned sensual pleasures, paid homage to his mother and father, and went forth.
Then his father thought, "If even this prince desires to go forth, why should I remain? I too have no need for kingship," and so he abandoned the kingdom and went forth along with him.
As he departed, the queen, the ministers, the brahmins, the householders, and others likewise followed.
The inhabitants of the entire city abandoned their enjoyments and went forth. A great assembly gathered, and the crowd became twelve yojanas in extent;
taking them with him, the Great Being entered the Himālaya mountains.
Sakka, king of the gods, having learned of his departure, dispatched Vissakamma [to create] a [shelter] twelve yojanas in length.
He had a hermitage built seven *yojanas* in extent and had all the requisites for those who have gone forth prepared.
Herein, the Great Being’s renunciation, his giving of exhortation, his destination in the Brahma-world, and the correct practice of the assembly—
all this is to be understood according to the method already stated in the *Mahāgovinda-cariyā*.
At that time, his parents were great royal families, the assembly was the assembly of Buddhas, and the wise Ayoghara was the Lord of the World.
His fulfillment of the remaining perfections and the manifestation of his majesty are to be understood in the same manner as described below.
The commentary on the conduct of Ayoghara is concluded.
4. Explanation of the Medical Practice:
Regarding the fourth [verse], "When I was in the most excellent city of the Kāsīs," the meaning is:
when I lived, having been born and raised, in Bārāṇasī, the preeminent city of that kingdom which is conventionally designated by the plural term "Kāsīs."
"Seven brothers and a sister were born into a family of learned brahmins"— the meaning is that Upakañcana and the other six,
together with myself, making seven brothers, and our youngest sister named Kañcanadevī—
all eight of us were then born and produced in a great, most eminent brahmin family devoted to the mastery of mantras.
At that time, the Bodhisatta was born in Bārāṇasī as the son of a wealthy brahmin mahāsāla possessing eighty koṭis of wealth.
They gave him the name Kañcanakumāra. Then, when he was walking about on foot, another son was born to him;
they gave him the name Upakañcanakumāra. From then on, they called the Great Being Mahākañcanakumāra.
They behaved in this manner. In this way, there were seven sons born in succession;
however, the youngest of all was a daughter, for whom they gave the name Kañcanadevī. When the Great Being reached maturity, he went to Takkasila, mastered all the arts, and returned home.
Then his parents, desiring to bind him to the life of a householder, said, "We shall bring you a maiden from a family of equal birth.
He replied, "Mother, father, I have no need for the life of a householder.
To me, the entire world of living beings is like a conflagration, full of peril; it is like a prison, a place of entanglement, a dungheap."
It appeared to him as something loathsome; he said, "My mind does not take delight in sensual pleasures. You have other sons;
let them invite you to the household life. Although he was entreated again and again by his friends, and even though they urged him on his behalf, he did not consent.
Then his friends asked him, "Friend, what is it that you desire, such that you do not wish to enjoy sensual pleasures?"
They questioned him. He declared to them his own inclination toward renunciation (*nekkhamma*). Therefore it was said: "I was the eldest among these," and so forth.
In that context, "I was the eldest among these" means that at that time I was the elder brother of these seven, beginning with Upakañcanaka.
"Hirīsukkam upāgato" means "having attained the white [state]" because of the ripening of the wholesome (*sukka*) and because of the purification of the mental continuum.
He has come to possess *hiri* (moral shame), which is characterized by a profound loathing of evil; the meaning is that he dwells intensely loathing evil.
"Having seen existence as fear, I delight in renunciation":

this means that he sees all forms of existence—such as sense-sphere existence (*kāmabhava*) and so forth—as they approach him like a fierce elephant intent on charging, or like an executioner with a raised sword coming to do him harm.
Having viewed it as being like a lion, like a *yakkha*, like a *rakkhasa*, like a terrible poison, like a venomous snake, and like a burning ember—
seeing it as fearful and terrifying— he went forth, delighting in renunciation for the sake of liberation from it, thinking:
"How indeed might I fulfill the practice of Dhamma and right conduct, and [attain] the meditative absorptions (*jhāna-samāpatti*)?"

"And may [this] arise"—the meaning is: "At that time, I was one who delighted in the dhamma of proficiency in going forth, in the first jhāna, and so forth. 36. *Pahitā* means sent by mother and father. *Ekamānasā* means having a common aspiration;

previously they were of one mind with me and acted agreeably, but because they were sent away by my mother and father, they speak to me in a repulsive and disagreeable manner. From sensual pleasures, me...
"They invite me" means: "With one mind with my great father, they invite me with sensual pleasures. "Support the family lineage" means:
"Establishing a household life, support—that is, establish—your own family lineage"; this is the sense of their inviting me with sensual pleasures. 37.
"The speech that was spoken by them" refers to the speech uttered by those dear companions of mine. Regarding the duties of a householder...

"Bringing happiness" means that for a person remaining in the state of a householder— that is, in the condition of a layman— it brings happiness both pertaining to the present life and the future life, because it conforms to what is right (*ñāya*).
"That was my *kaṭhina* (hardship)" means that those words of my companions and my parents were entirely unpleasant to me because of my absolute delight in renunciation (*nekkhamma*).
That harsh and cruel day was like a glowing hot plowshare, as if burning both my ears. 38.
"They then lifted me up": my companions, while being invited many times by my parents and themselves toward sensual pleasures, were lifting me up, casting me aside, and rejecting them.
They asked: "What is it you have desired?"—meaning, "What indeed is more pure than this that you have desired?
I have asked about that aspiration of yours: 'My friend, what do you desire, since you do not enjoy sensual pleasures?

39. *Atthakāmo* means desiring one's own welfare; the sense is "fearing evil. There is also a reading in the text as *attakāmo*. *Hitesinaṃ* means of those who desire my welfare, my dear friends. Some read *atthakāmahitesinaṃ*, but that is not good.

40. "They announced it to my father and mother": having understood that my desire for the going-forth was irreversible, my companions reported my words—which revealed my wish to go forth—to my father and mother: "Truly, Mother and Father, you should know this:
Prince Mahākañcana will certainly go forth; he cannot be led toward sensual pleasures by any means whatsoever."
They said: "My parents spoke thus. At that time, having heard the words spoken by my companions, my parents said to me: "Let us all go forth together, sir!
If Prince Mahākañcana has found delight in renunciation, whatever he finds delightful is exactly what we find delightful as well; therefore, let us all go forth."
"Bho" is a form of address used for those brahmins. There is also a reading "pabbajāma kho," which means "we shall indeed go forth.
For, having perceived the Great Being's desire for the renunciate life, Upakañcana and the other six brothers, as well as his sister Kañcanadevī, were themselves desirous of going forth;
thus, even though they were being entreated by their parents to remain in the household life, [they refused].
They did not wish for it at all. Therefore, they said, “Sir, let us all go forth together.

Having spoken thus, the parents summoned the Great Being, explained their own intention to him, and said, “Dear son, if you desire to go forth, eighty million pieces of wealth are yours; spend them as you please.”
They said: "Then that Great Being, having distributed [his wealth] among the poor, the needy, and others, made his Great Renunciation and entered the Himālaya mountains.
Along with him, his mother and father, six brothers, a sister, one male slave, one female slave, and one companion abandoned their household life and went forth. Thus it is said:
“Both my mother and father, my sister and seven brothers—having abandoned immeasurable wealth, we entered the great forest.
However, in the *Jātakaṭṭhakathā*, it is stated: “When his parents had passed away, the Great Being performed the duties required for them and went forth on the Great Renunciation.”
Thus, having entered the Himālaya mountains, those disciples headed by the Bodhisatta established a hermitage on a delightful stretch of ground near a lotus pond;
having gone forth, they sustained themselves by subsisting on forest roots and fruits.
Among them, eight men, beginning with Upakañcana, would take turns bringing various fruits and, on a stone slab, divide their own portions as well as those of the others.
Having made a signal with a bell and given notice, they take their own portions and enter their dwelling places. The others also,
having emerged from the leaf-hut upon the signal of the bell, take their respective allotted portions, go to their dwelling places, consume them,
and practice the duties of a recluse.
In a later period, having brought lotus roots, they ate them in the same manner.

There, those practitioners of fierce asceticism, whose faculties were most highly disciplined, dwelt performing the preliminary exercises for the *kasiṇas*. Then, by the power of their virtue, the abode of Sakka trembled.
Sakka, knowing the cause, thought, "I shall test these seers," and by his own supernatural power [approached] the Great Being.
He caused the three portions to disappear over the course of three days.
On the first day, not seeing his portion, the Great Being thought, "My portion must have been forgotten. On the second day, he thought, "It must be because of my fault;
I suspect my portion was not set aside for me due to my dismissal. On the third day, he thought, "Having heard the reason, I shall ask for forgiveness."
At the time of evening, having given the signal by ringing a bell, and when everyone had assembled at that signal, he announced the matter.

Having heard from them over three days that a portion had been set aside for him, he said, "A portion was set aside for me by you, yet I did not receive it; what could be the reason? Upon hearing this, they all became filled with a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*).
In that hermitage, a tree deity also descended from her own abode and sat down near them.
An elephant who had fled from men and entered the forest, a snake-charmer who had escaped from the hands of a snake-handler,
and a monkey who was well-acquainted with those seers, all approached their presence at that time.
They stood to one side. Sakka, thinking, “I shall attend upon this company of seers,” also stood right there with an invisible body.

At that moment, the Bodhisatta’s younger brother, the ascetic Upakañcana, rose, paid homage to the Bodhisatta, showed respect to the others, and said, “Having established mindfulness, I myself shall purify [myself]...”
Having asked, "Do I receive it? and being told, "Yes, you do," he stood in the midst of the company of seers and made this oath:
"May he who took away your lotus roots, O brahmin, obtain here horses, cattle, silver, gold, and a pleasing wife; may he be provided with sons and wives."
He spoke this verse. For, censuring sensual objects as the basis for existence, he said: "For however many dear things there are, just as many sufferings arise upon separation from them.
Upon hearing this, the company of seers covered their ears, saying, "Venerable sir, do not speak; your oath is too heavy. The Bodhisatta also said, "Your oath is too heavy;
you do not grasp it, dear one; sit upon your own seat. The others also—
They made an oath in due order: "May he who took away your lotus roots,
O brahmin, wear garlands and Kāsī sandalwood, have many sons,
and maintain an intense longing for sensual pleasures."
“Let him who took your lotus roots, O Brahmin, be a prosperous farmer, renowned and wealthy, a householder with sons,
possessing all desires, and living at home without seeing any decline.
Let him be a Khattiya, a performer of great deeds, a king of kings, powerful and illustrious.”
“Let him who took your lotus roots, O brahmin, dwell in the majesty of the earth bounded by its four oceans.
Let that brahmin remain one not yet free from passion, engaged for a moment in the paths of the constellations;
let the illustrious lord of the realm honor him, he who took your lotus roots, O brahmin.”
“Let the whole world consider him a reciter, one who knows all the Vedas on every side, and an ascetic;
let the people of the countryside come together and honor him, O Brahmin, for he has taken away your lotus roots.
Let him enjoy a prosperous, excellent village with its four sounds, which has been granted by Vāsava.”
Let him who took your lotus roots, O brahmin, meet his death while still unliberated from passion.
Let him become a village headman among his companions, delighting in dances and songs;
let him suffer some misfortune at the hands of the king—he who took your lotus roots, O brahmin.
“Let that woman who took your lotus roots, O brahmin, be placed at the head of a thousand women by the sole ruler who has conquered the earth;
let her be the most excellent among those with parted hair.
For she may eat the delicious food of all the seers gathered together, without wavering.”
Let him who took away your lotus roots, O brahmin, boast of his gain:
“Let him be a resident monk in the Great Monastery; let him be a supervisor of construction works at Gajaṅgalā;
let him provide light through the window for a whole day—let him who took away your lotus roots, O brahmin, boast of his gain!”
“Thus, let him be bound with six hundred snares and led from the delightful forest to the royal capital.
Let him be struck with sharp whips, O Brahmin—he who has stolen your lotus roots.
Adorned with iron ornaments, with ears pierced by spikes and his back scarred by the staff, let him approach the mouth of a serpent.”
"Let him who stole your lotus roots, O brahmin, wander with his neck bound by a rope!"—they spoke these verses.

Therein, "let him be intense" means let him have great longing for the objects of sensual desire and the defilements of sensual desire. "Skilled in plowing" means one whose work in plowing is accomplished.
"May he have sons; may he be a householder; may he be wealthy with the seven kinds of wealth;

may he obtain all pleasures consisting of forms and so forth. Not seeing his own decline, even in old age, may he not go forth [into homelessness], but dwell only in a household abounding in the five strands of sensual pleasure. May he be a king over kings. Thus, for kings...
"In the interval" means [the time] between [the two kings]. "Not free from lust" means he is still possessed of craving for the position of chaplain.
"Austere" means one whose nature is austerity; let him think of him as being endowed with virtue (*sīlasampanna*).

"Abounding in the four" means it is overflowing with four things: with people because of its crowded population; with grain because of the abundance of crops; with wood because firewood is easily obtained; and with water because it is well-supplied with water. "By Vāsava" means...
"Immovable as if given by Vāsava" means that, having propitiated the king through the power of a boon obtained from Vāsava, she was given by him;
this is the meaning. "One who has not yet abandoned passion" means one who is not free from lust, being submerged in the mire of sensual desire like a pig in mud.
"Headman" (gāmaṇī) means the chief of the village. "Her" refers to that woman. "Sole king" means the pre-eminent king. Regarding the phrase "of a thousand women," because of its figurative sense—
It has been said. The meaning is: "Let her be placed in the foremost position among the sixteen thousand women.
Regarding the word *sīmantinīnaṃ*: it means "of those possessing the parting of the hair," that is, of women. Regarding *sabbasamāgatānaṃ*: having sat in the midst of all who have assembled.
Regarding *avikampamānā*: not shrinking back; the meaning is, "let her enjoy the delicious flavor. Regarding *carātu lābhena vikatthamānā*: on account of gain... [the phrase continues].
"Let him go about assuming a graceful appearance in order to procure gain. "A resident" means one who looks after the monastery.
"To Gajaṅgalā" means to the city of that name; it is said that building materials were easily obtained there.

"Make a window for a day" means let him make only a single opening for light on a single day. It is said that this son of the gods, during the time of Buddha Kassapa, lived in dependence upon the city of Gajaṅgalā.
Having been a resident elder of the Saṅgha at the Mahāvihāra monastery, he experienced great suffering while performing repairs on the dilapidated monastery;
it is with reference to this that [the author] says:
"By hundreds of snares" means by many snares. "In six places" means in six locations: the four feet, the neck, and the waist.
*With all* means with long sticks having two thorns at each end. *With pācana* means with short pācanas, or with hooks.
*Wearing a garland of snakes* means being endowed with a garland of snakes placed around his neck by a snake-charmer.
*With ears and back covered in ash* means having the surface of his ears and back adorned with an ornament of ash. *Staff-bearer* means one who is training in the art of playing with snakes.

Having been struck by a staff, they all—loathing their entire enjoyment of sensual pleasures, their household life, and the suffering each had personally experienced—made oaths in various ways and spoke thus.
Then the Bodhisatta thought, "An oath has been made by all these; it is fitting for me to make one as well," and he made an oath:
“Whether one says that what is not lost is lost, or whether one fears anything at all,
O gods— he shall obtain and enjoy sensual pleasures, while he who fears shall meet death in the midst of his home.
Thus he spoke this verse.
In that context, "bhonto" means "gentlemen. "Saṅkati" means "suspects. "Kañci" means "anyone.
Then Sakka, having understood that "all these are indifferent to sensual pleasures," with a heart moved by spiritual urgency, thought:
"The lotus roots have not been carried off by anyone among these, nor has what was said—'it was not lost by you'—been proven false; rather, it was I who wished to test you."
Showing that they caused [the lotus roots] to disappear, he said:
"While testing, I took the lotus roots from the bank and placed them on dry land;
pure and sinless are the seers who dwell here—these, O practitioner of the holy life, are your lotus roots."
He spoke this concluding verse.
Having heard it, the Bodhisatta said:
"They are not actors, nor are they to be played with; they are not kinsmen, nor are they companions."
"In whom do you find support, O thousand-eyed one? You play with the seers like a king of the gods!"—thus he rebuked Sakka.
Then Sakka said to him:
“You are my teacher and my father, O Brahmā; you are the support for one who has stumbled.
Forgive this one offense, O one of vast wisdom; the wise do not become slaves to anger.
Thus he asked for forgiveness.
The Great Being, having forgiven Sakka, the king of the gods, himself asked forgiveness from the company of seers, saying:
“A single night spent in the sweet fragrance of the seers, when we beheld Vāsava, the lord of beings—
may all these worthy ones be well-disposed, since the brahmin has offered us lotus roots.”
He said:
"In this matter, O King of Devas, we are not your actors, nor are we suitable for your play.
Nor are we your kinsmen, nor companions with whom you should joke. So, in what do you find support? What is it that provides you with stability?"
"Having done what, do you sport with the seers? is the meaning. "This foundation":
may this shadow of your feet today be the foundation for my lapse and offense. "Well-scented":
even a single night spent by the venerable seers in this forest is truly well-scented. Why? Because we have seen Vāsava, the Lord of Beings.
"For if we had lived in the city, we would not have seen this. 'Bhonto' means 'sirs. May all of you be well-disposed and satisfied;
may you forgive Sakka, the king of the gods. For what reason? Because the brahmin has offered these lotus roots, since your teacher obtained the lotus roots.
Having paid homage to the company of seers, Sakka departed for the world of the gods.
He departed. The company of seers, having likewise attained the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and direct knowledges (*abhiññā*), was reborn in the Brahma-world.
At that time, the six brothers beginning with Upakañcana became the Elders Sāriputta, Moggallāna, Mahākassapa, Anuruddha, Puṇṇa, and Ānanda;
the sister became Uppalavaṇṇā; the female slave Khujjuttarā; the male slave Citta the householder; and the tree deity Sātāgira.

The elephant Pālileyya-nāga, the monkey Madhuvāsiṭṭha, Sakka Kāḷudāyī, and the Great Golden Ascetic Lokanātha—here too, his ten perfections (pāramīs) are to be extracted according to the method already stated below. Likewise, the power of his qualities, such as absolute indifference toward sensual pleasures, is to be made manifest.
The commentary on the Bhisacariya is concluded.
5. The Account of the Conduct of Soṇa Paṇḍita 42.
"In the city named Brahmavaḍḍhana" means in the city called Brahmavaḍḍhana. "In a noble family" (kulavare) means in a preeminent clan.

"Most excellent" (seṭṭhe) means most praiseworthy. "Of great substance" (mahāsāle) means of great essence. "I was born" (ajāyahaṃ) means I was born. This is what is intended: [I was born in such a place].
“At that time, when I was born, existed, and resided in the city of Bārāṇasī, which bore the name ‘Brahmavaḍḍhana,’ I was reborn into a wealthy brahmin family of great means,
possessing eighty crores of wealth, preeminent in the excellence of noble birth through a lineage of ever-increasing prosperity,
and supreme in the attainment of mastery in the sciences.”

For at that time, the Great Being, having descended from the Brahma-world, was reborn as the son of a certain wealthy and eminent brahmin possessing eighty crores of wealth in the city of Brahmadatta. On the day his name was given, they named him Soṇakumāra.
When he reached the age of walking on foot, yet another being, having descended from the Brahma-world, [was reborn] for the Bodhisatta...
He took rebirth in his mother’s womb. When he was born, they gave him the name Nandakumāra.

Once they had mastered the Vedas, attained proficiency in all the arts, and reached maturity, their parents—seeing their physical excellence and being filled with joy and delight—said first to Soṇakumāra, "We shall bind you with the bonds of the household life."
“Father, we shall bring a maiden from a suitable family; you should take charge of the household.
The Great Being replied, “Enough of this household life for me. Having looked after you all for as long as I live, I shall go forth into homelessness after your passing.
For at that time, the Great Being regarded even the three realms of existence as a house on fire or a pit of glowing coals.
...appeared as if they were [mere illusions]. However, he was especially inclined toward renunciation and devoted to the life of seclusion.
Not understanding his intention, even though they spoke to him again and again, they could not win over his mind.
Then, addressing Prince Nanda, they said, "Dear son, in that case, you must take charge of the household. To this, he replied, "I cannot [do so] by my brother..."

When he said, "I shall pick up discarded spittle with my head; after you have passed away, I too will go forth together with my brother," [the others] thought, "If even these, so young, renounce sensual pleasures, how much more so should we? Let us all go forth.
Having said, "Father, what need is there for our going forth after you have passed away? Let us all go forth together," they spoke thus.
Having given what was appropriate to be given to their kinsmen, having freed their servants from slavery, having informed the king,

and having distributed all their wealth and performed a great act of giving, the four people departed from the city of Brahmavaḍḍhana and established a hermitage in a delightful forest thicket near a great lake adorned with white lotuses in the Himalayan region.
Having built [the hermitage] and gone forth, they dwelt there. Therefore it was said:
"Even then, having seen the world blinded and shrouded in darkness, The mind recoils from existence, like [an arrow] struck by the force of a goad."
“Having seen various evils, I then thought thus:
‘When shall I, having gone forth from home, enter the forest?
Even then, my kinsmen invited me with the enjoyments of sensual pleasures.”
I declared my intention to them as well: "Do not invite me with them.
"My younger brother, named Nanda, who was wise—he too, training under me, has set his heart on the going forth."
“I was Soṇa and Nanda, both my mother and father;
even then, having abandoned our wealth, we entered the great forest.
In this context, “even then” means when I was the brahmin youth named Soṇa in the city of Brahmavaḍḍhana.
"Having seen the world" means having beheld the entire world of sentient beings with the eye of wisdom (*paññācakkhu*).
"Become blind" means born blind due to the lack of the eye of wisdom, having reached a state of blindness. "Enveloped in darkness" means overcome by the darkness of ignorance (*avijjā*).

"The mind recoils from existence" means that through reflecting upon the grounds for spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) such as birth and so forth, my mind turns away from existence consisting of sensual desire and the rest.
It contracts, it withdraws, and it does not spread out. It is "as if struck by the force of a goad";
here, "goad" (*tutta*) refers to a long-handled iron hook with a pronged head, which is called a *patoda*.

Just as a noble elephant becomes filled with agitation when struck forcefully by that [goad], he shows that his mind at that time became filled with a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) through reflecting on the danger of sensual desires.

Having seen—that is, having perceived—the various evils consisting of the diverse sinful deeds such as killing living beings, as well as the base nature of their causes, which are performed by those dwelling in a household for the sake of domestic life through desire, hatred, and so forth;
he thought thus: "When indeed shall I, like a great elephant, [break] the iron bond of the household?"
“Having cut [my ties], I shall enter the forest by way of departing from the home”—thus did I think at that time when I was Prince Soṇa.

At that time too they invited me; not only during the time of the wise Ayoghara and others, but indeed even then, at that time when I was Prince Soṇa, my parents and other relatives, who were enjoyers of sensual pleasures and inclined toward sensual desires, said: “Come, dear son!”
“Accept this wealth of eighty million and establish the family lineage,” they invited me with such magnificent riches.
When they expressed their desire [to keep me], I also declared my own inclination, saying,
“Do not invite me away from my kinsmen with those sensual enjoyments,” and I spoke of my own deep-seated aspiration for the going-forth.
The intention is: "Practice according to my own inclination.

He too, following my example, reflects in various ways on the dangers of sensual pleasures—according to the method beginning with, "These so-called sensual pleasures provide little gratification, much suffering, and much despair"—and just as I went forth, training in the precepts and other virtues, [he likewise did].
I delighted [in it]. That wise Nanda also, training himself in renunciation just like me, likewise took delight in going forth.
"I and Soṇa and Nanda" means: at that time, I who was named Soṇa and my younger brother Nanda—both of us.
"My mother and father" [said]: "These sons of mine, even while so young, abandon sensual pleasures; how much more so [should others]?"
"By us" refers to our parents, who were filled with a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*).

"Having abandoned wealth" means that, with hearts free from attachment, we four people renounced great riches—abundant with eighty million in assets—as if they were a globule of spittle, and entered the great forest in the region of the Himalayas with a disposition toward renunciation (*nekkhamma*); this is the meaning.
Having entered there, they established a hermitage on that delightful stretch of ground and, having gone forth into the ascetic life, they dwelt there.

Both brothers looked after their mother and father. Among them, the wise Nanda thought, "I shall feed my parents only with the fruits and roots I have gathered myself," and so from the place where he had previously collected his food the day before...
Furthermore, whatever other fruits remained, he would bring them back early in the morning and have his parents eat them.

Having eaten those and rinsed their mouths, they would observe the Uposatha. But the wise Soṇa, having gone a great distance, would return bringing very sweet and well-ripened fruits and offer them to them.
Then they said to him, "Dear son, we have already eaten what was brought by your younger brother."
"We have become observant of the Uposatha; now we have no need for these," they said. Thus, his various fruits did not receive their enjoyment and perished;

on the following day and subsequent days it was the same. In this way, although he went even a great distance and brought them back due to his possession of the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*), they did not eat them.
Then the Great Being thought: "My parents are delicate, and Nanda brings and makes them eat various fruits that are unripe or poorly cooked;
this being so, they will not survive for long. I shall restrain him. Then, addressing him, he said:
"Nanda, from now on, having brought fruits, wait for my arrival."
"Let us eat together from one [portion]," he said. Even when this was said, the other, seeking his own merit, did not do as he was told.
The Great Being, seeing that he had come to serve him, said: "You do not follow the advice of the wise. I am the elder;
my parents are my responsibility, and I alone shall care for them. You—"
"Go elsewhere than this! she said, and snapped her fingers at him.

Being thus dismissed, he was unable to remain there; so, having paid homage to her, he informed his parents of the matter, entered his own leaf-hut, and after gazing upon the *kasiṇa*, that very day [attained] the eight attainments and the five [supernormal powers].
Having developed the supernormal powers, he thought:

"Should I bring sand of jewels from the foot of Sineru and scatter it over the courtyard of my brother's leaf-hut to ask for his forgiveness, or should I bring water from Lake Anotatta to ask for his forgiveness?
Or perhaps my brother will forgive me through the power of the deities—the Four Great Kings and Sakka?"
“I will bring the king of the gods and ask for his forgiveness; however, that would not be fitting.
This Manoja, the King Brahmavaḍḍhana, is the preeminent king over all of Jambudīpa; therefore, beginning with him, I will bring all the kings and ask for their forgiveness.
When this is done, my brother’s virtue will spread throughout all of Jambudīpa, and he will become renowned like the moon and like the sun.”
Thereupon, traveling by means of psychic power (*iddhi*), he descended at the gate of the king’s palace in the city of Brahmavaḍḍhana.

Having announced to the king, "A certain ascetic wishes to see you," and having been granted audience by him, he went into his presence and said, "By my own power, I shall seize the sovereignty over the whole of Jambudīpa and give it to you. [The king asked: "But how?"
“Venerable sir, will you grant us the sovereignty over the whole of Jambudīpa? “Great King, without executing anyone, I shall take it by my own supernatural power and give it to you.
Having taken him along with a great army, he went to the kingdom of Kosala, pitched his camp not far from the city, and said: “Either give us battle, or submit to our rule!”
He dispatched a messenger to the King of Kosala. Enraged by this, the King of Kosala set out fully prepared for battle;

when the conflict began, [the Elder], through the power of his supernormal abilities, acted so that neither of the two armies suffered harm, and he arranged matters through the exchange of messages such that the King of Kosala remained obedient to his will.
By this means, he brought all the kings of Jambudīpa under his control.
Satisfied by this, he said to Nanda Paṇḍita: "Venerable sir, you have done exactly as you promised me;
you have been very helpful to me. What can I do for you? For I [shall provide] for you throughout the whole of Jambudīpa..."
“I wish to give you even half the kingdom; how much more so these elephants, horses, chariots, gems, pearls, coral, silver, gold, female and male slaves, and the retinue of attendants?
Having heard this, Nanda the Wise said, “Great King, I have no need for that kingdom, nor for the elephant-vehicles and such;
however, in a certain hermitage in your realm, my mother and father dwell having gone forth. To them I—”
"While serving him, he was dismissed on account of one offense by my eldest brother, the great seer named Soṇa Paṇḍita.
Therefore, I shall take him and go into his presence to ask for forgiveness; you must be my companion in asking for his pardon.
The king agreed, saying "Very well," and surrounded by an army numbering twenty-four akkhobhaniyas, [set out].
Accompanied by one hundred and one kings and preceded by Nanda the Wise, he reached that hermitage; leaving a space of four finger-breadths [from the ground],
he stood in the air with his carriage, brought water from Anotatta, set out the drinking water, swept the courtyard,
and approached the Great Being who was seated near his parents, absorbed in the delight of meditative absorption.
Nanda the scholar asked his forgiveness. The Great Being, having entrusted Nanda the scholar to his mother, tended to his father for the rest of his life.
Regarding those two kings, it is said: "Ānanda and Pramoda were always laughing and playing."
Having served one's mother, this can be obtained by the wise:
"Joy and delight, and constant laughter and play—
this can be obtained by the wise who have served their father."
“Generosity, kindly speech, beneficial conduct,
and impartiality toward all things as appropriate in each case—
these are the means of integration in the world, like the linchpin of a moving chariot.”
“If these means of integration did not exist, a mother would not receive honor or worship for the sake of her son,
nor would a father receive honor or worship for the sake of his son.
But because these means of integration exist, the wise regard them with right perspective.”
Therefore they attain greatness and become worthy of praise:
"Parents are called 'Brahmās' and 'former teachers';
they are worthy of offerings from their children and are compassionate toward their offspring."
“Therefore, indeed, a wise person should honor and revere them with food and drink, with clothing and bedding,
with ointment and bathing, and by washing their feet.”
“By such service toward one’s mother and father, the wise are praised even in this very world, and after death they rejoice in heaven.
Thus he taught the Dhamma with the grace of a Buddha. Upon hearing it, all those kings together with their entire armies gained confidence. Then—
Having established them in the five precepts and instructed them, saying, "Be diligent in generosity and the other virtues," he dismissed them.
They all ruled the kingdom with righteousness and, at the end of their lives, filled the city of the gods.
The Bodhisatta, having entrusted his mother to the wise Nanda with the words, "From now on, look after your mother," himself [remained] for as long as life lasted...
He looked after his father. At the end of their lives, both of them reached the Brahma-world as their final destination.
At that time, the mother and father were royal families; Nanda the Wise was the Venerable Ānanda; King Manoja was the Venerable Sāriputta;
the one hundred and one kings were the eighty great elders and other distinguished elders; and the twenty-four *akkhobhani* assemblies were the assembly of the Buddha.
Soṇapaṇḍita was a protector of the world.
Although his perfection of renunciation (nekkhammapāramī) was preeminent, nevertheless, the remaining perfections should be deduced according to the method explained above.
Likewise, there was an absolute lack of regard for sensual pleasures, as well as intense reverence and deference toward his mother and father.
One can never have enough of serving one’s mother and father; even while they are being served, [the Bodhisattvas] spend all their time dwelling in meditative attainments (*samāpatti*).
In this way, the power of the Great Being’s virtues should be made manifest.
The commentary on the conduct of the Wise Soṇa is concluded.
The Perfection of Renunciation is concluded.
6. Commentary on the Temiya Deed. 48.
Regarding the sixth [deed]: "When I was the son of the King of Kāsi"—that is, when I was the king's own offspring, his son—then I was known as Mūgapakkha.
The connection is as follows: "By name they call me Temiya," meaning that by the name Temiya, and by the resolve [to remain] like a mute parrot, everyone—including my parents—calls me "Mūgapakkha.
For on the day the Great Being was born, rain fell throughout the entire kingdom of Kāsi;
and because he [filled] the hearts of the king, his ministers, and others with his sublime [virtue]...
Because he was born being drenched with yellow oil (*pīti-sineha*), he was given the name Temiya Kumāra.
Regarding the phrase "of sixteen thousand women": this refers to the sixteen thousand women in the harem of the King of Kāsi.
"A male does not exist" means that a son could not be obtained. Not only was there no son, but he had no daughter either. As the days and nights passed by...
"I alone was reborn as the only son of that childless king; after many years had passed and numerous days and nights had gone by, I alone, while wandering in search of enlightenment,
was then born as his son," so said the Teacher.
In this regard, this is the sequential narrative: In the past, a King of Kāsi reigned in Bārāṇasī.
He had sixteen thousand women, yet not even one among them obtained a son or a daughter.
The citizens became distressed, thinking, "There is not even a single son to protect our king's lineage," and having assembled, they [addressed] the king regarding a son—
"Make a wish," they said. The king commanded his sixteen thousand women, "Make a wish for a son.
Although they performed services such as attending upon the moon and others while making their wishes, they did not obtain one.
His chief queen, however, the daughter of the King of Madda named Candādevī, was endowed with virtue. The king said to her, "You too, make a wish for a son. On the full-moon day, she—
Having observed the Uposatha and reflected upon her own virtue, she performed an act of truth (saccakiriya), saying: "If my virtue is unbroken, by this truth may a son be born to me.
Through the power of her virtue, Sakka’s throne manifested a sign of heat.
Sakka, reflecting and understanding the cause, thought: "I shall devise a means for Queen Candā to obtain a son."
While searching for a son worthy of her, he saw that the Bodhisatta had been reborn in the Tāvatiṃsa heaven,
where he had remained for the full span of his lifespan; seeing that he was now desiring to pass away from there and be reborn in the higher deva-worlds,
he went into his presence and said, "Friend, when you are born in the human world, you will fulfill the perfections and [bring benefit] to the great masses of people."
"Your prosperity will increase; this chief queen of the King of Kāsi, named Candā, yearns for a son. Enter her womb.
Having consented with "So be it," he took rebirth in her womb.
His five hundred companions, sons of gods whose lifespans had expired, passed away from the deva-world and took rebirth in the wombs of the ministers' wives of that same king.
They took [the child]. The queen, having realized that she was pregnant, informed the king. The king provided her with the necessary care for her pregnancy.
When her term was full, she gave birth to a son endowed with the marks of merit and grain-like excellence.
On that very same day, five hundred young sons were born in the houses of the ministers. Having heard both reports, the king thought, "This is the retinue for my son."
Having sent five hundred nurses for these five hundred boys, he also sent ornaments for the princes.
To the Great Being, however, he gave sixty-four nurses who were free from faults such as being too tall, who reached up to his armpits, and whose milk was sweet;
having performed great honors, he also granted a boon to Queen Candādevī. She accepted it and set it aside.
The boy grew up with a great retinue. Then, when he was one month old, they adorned him and brought him into the presence of the king.
The king, gazing upon his beloved son, embraced him, seated him on his lap, and sat there delighting in him.
At that moment, four thieves were brought before him. The king [ordered] a thousand lashings with thorny whips for one of them.
He ordered that one be bound with shackles and cast into prison, that another have a blow from a spear inflicted upon his body, and that the third be impaled on a stake.
Having heard his father’s words, the Great Being was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency and thought: "Alas!
Relying on his sovereignty, my father is committing a grave deed that leads to hell. On the following day, [he saw] him under the white parasol...
They had him lie down upon a decorated couch below.
Having slept for a short while, he woke up; opening his eyes and looking toward the white parasol, he beheld a great display of splendor and wealth.
Then, although he was already moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) by nature, an even greater fear arose within him.
Thus, reflecting, "From where indeed have I come to this royal palace? he perceived through the knowledge of recollecting past births that he had come from the world of the gods.
Looking further back than that, he saw that he had been reborn in the Ussada Hell.
Looking even further back, he saw that he had been the king in that very city. Then he thought, "Having ruled the kingdom for twenty years..."
"I have suffered in the Ussada hell for eighty thousand years, and now I am once again reborn here in this house of thieves.
Indeed, yesterday, when four thieves were brought before me, my father spoke such harsh words that lead to rebirth in hell.
I have no need for this kingdom, which brings about such vast and unknown calamity; how indeed [can I escape] from this..."
Thinking, "May I be released from the house of thieves," he lay down. Then a certain goddess consoled him, saying, "Dear Temiya Kumāra, do not fear;
by resolving upon three qualities, your safety shall be secured.
Hearing this, the Great Being, desiring to be freed from the misfortune known as kingship, for sixteen years maintained those three qualities through the power of an unshakable resolve.
“Resolve upon it. Therefore it was said: “A beloved son, obtained with difficulty,” and so forth.
In this context, “obtained with difficulty” means acquired through hardship, toil, and long-term aspiration.
“Of noble birth” means endowed with a distinguished lineage. “Radiant” means possessing both physical splendor and the splendor of wisdom. “The white parasol”—
Having raised me, my father, the King of Kāsi, nourished me upon his own couch, thinking, "May neither dust nor moisture affect this prince.
From the time of my birth, he had me lie upon a magnificent bed beneath a white parasol and nourished me with a great retinue.
While sleeping on that excellent couch, I woke up and, looking about, saw the pale white parasol.
"By which I went to hell": by means of that white parasol, in my third existence, I went to hell;
he speaks of sovereignty under the heading of the white parasol.
"The moment I saw the parasol": for me, as soon as I saw—that is, upon seeing—that white parasol, together with it...
"By seeing" means at the very moment of seeing. "Terror arose" means a frightening mental dread emerged because the danger was so well known.
"I fell into deliberation" means I entered into such reflection:
"How shall I release him? How indeed might I rid myself of this ill-omened king?"
53. "My former blood-relations" refers to those who were previously my mother in a former existence; the deity dwelling in that parasol was one who desired my welfare and sought my benefit.
Seeing me afflicted with mental suffering, she applied me to three states—meaning she directed me toward the conditions known as being mute, wingless, and deaf.
Seeing me thus distressed by mental anguish, that deity... [applied me to] the states characterized by muteness, lack of wings, and deafness.
He directed [them] toward the three reasons for departing from the suffering of kingship.
54. *Paṇḍiccayantī* means "wisdom" (*paṇḍicca*); or rather, this is the reading *pāṇḍicca*. *Mā vibhāvaya* means "do not reveal. *Bālamato* means "known as a fool.
*Sabbo* means "all," including both those within the household and those outside. *Ocināyatu* means "drive her out; she is an ill-omened one (*kāḷakaṇṇī*)."

"Let him despise you. "In this way your welfare will come to pass": if he is to be despised according to the manner just described, then by your departure from home, there will be benefit for you—the fulfillment of the perfections (pāramī).
55. "This word of his": this word of his, "Resolve upon these three factors. "I am desirous of your welfare, mother."
"O mother deity, you have been desirous of my welfare. "Desirous of benefit" (*hitakāmā*) is merely a synonym for that same thing.
Alternatively, "welfare" (*attha*) here should be understood as happiness (*sukha*), while "benefit" (*hita*) refers to the merit (*puñña*) that serves as its cause.
56. "As one who has reached dry land from the ocean": "I was born in a house of thieves; a great calamity and misfortune befell me"—thus [he spoke] in the ocean of sorrow.
"Sinking down, having heard the words of that deity, I was like one sinking in the ocean who finds firm ground on dry land;

the meaning is that I found the means for departing from my royal family. 'I resolved upon three factors' means that from the time I left the house until I departed, I resolved upon three factors as the causes."
57. Now, in order to show those [conditions] according to their specific forms, he spoke the verse beginning, "He was mute. In that context, *pakkho* means a cripple (a person who moves by crawling).

The rest is easily understood. Thus, while the Great Being—standing by the method given by the deity—displayed himself as being mute and so forth from the time of his birth, his parents, nurses, and others [thought], "The jaw-end of the mute is indeed of such a form..."
"There is no such thing as an ear-canal for the deaf, nor are there such hands and feet for cripples;

there must be some reason for this, so we shall investigate it. Having thought thus, he decided, "First I will investigate with milk," and so they did not give him any milk for the entire day. Even while wasting away, he made no sound for the sake of milk.
Then his mother said, "My son is hungry; give him milk," and she had milk given to him.
Thus, although they tested him for a full year without giving him milk at intervals, they found no opening.
