Then [they thought], "Children indeed love cakes and snacks, they love various fruits, they love toys for playing, and they love food..."
Luring him with various enticing objects to test his affection, they failed to find any lapse in him until he was five years old.
Then, thinking, "Children are afraid of fire, afraid of a rutting elephant, afraid of a snake, and afraid of a man with a raised sword; we shall test him with these," they acted accordingly.
No harm occurred; thus, having made prior arrangements, they caused [the boys] to approach in an extremely terrifying manner.
The Great Being, reflecting on the fear of hell, remained perfectly still, thinking: "Hell must be feared a hundredfold, a thousandfold, and a hundred-thousandfold more than this.
Even after testing him in this way, seeing no opening, they spoke again to the children:
Thinking, “We shall seek him at the festival,” they organized a festival; yet even after surrounding the Great Being with a curtain,
making a sudden, single-sounding clamor from conch shells and drums on all four sides while he was unaware,
and even after suddenly showing light by bringing lamps in jars into the darkness, and even after smearing his entire body with molasses—
Even after having him lie down in a place swarming with flies, or failing to bathe him and so forth, or even while he lies on top of excrement and urine,
or as he lies wallowing there in filth, one may provoke him with derisive laughter and verbal abuse,
or even place a fire-mat beneath his bed and afflict him with the heat and scorching of the flames— thus, by various such means.
Though they examined him further, they saw no flaw within him.
For the Great Being, having focused his mind solely on the fear of hell in every respect, remained motionless, unshakable from his resolve.
Thus, after they had tested him for fifteen years, then at the age of sixteen, [they said], "Whether they be cripples..."

"There is no one who, being mute or deaf, does not feel passion for things that provoke passion, nor does anyone remain without hatred toward things that provoke hatred; therefore, we shall test him by presenting him with dancers.

Having bathed the prince with scented water and adorned him like a son of the gods, they placed him upon a palace resembling a celestial mansion, filled with a single, delightful fragrance from flowers, perfumes, garlands, and the like; then, women possessing supreme beauty...
Women endowed with graceful charms and resembling celestial nymphs were stationed [before him] with the instruction:
"Go and delight the prince with dance and other performances. Having approached, they strove to do so.

Because of his perfection of wisdom, he thought, "Let them not experience the touch of my body," and thus he suppressed his inhalations and exhalations. They [could not endure] the touch of his body...
Not finding [any response], they departed, thinking, "This one has a rigid body; he is not a human, he must be a *yakkha*.

Thus, after sixteen years had passed and having been unable to discern [the truth] through sixteen great investigations and many minor investigations, the parents said, "Dear Temiya Kumāra, we know that you are not deaf and so forth, for..."
“They have such mouths, ears, nostrils, and feet; you are a son obtained by us through our prayers.
Do not destroy us! Save us from the reproach of the kings throughout the whole of Jambudīpa!
Thus they entreated him together and individually on many occasions. Although he was thus entreated by them, he lay down as if he were not hearing them at all.
58. Then the king had the Great Being’s two feet, ears, tongue, and both hands examined by skilled men. [He thought:
“Even though his feet and other limbs are like those of a cripple or the like, nevertheless this cripple seems to be mute and deaf.
While such an ill-omened person as this lives in this house, three obstacles are foreseen.”
"Now it has been stated by the readers of omens that [the marks belong] to his life-span, his parasol, or his chief queen. However,

having heard the ministers announce on the day of his birth, "He was called 'one possessing the marks of grain and merit' for the sake of warding off your own dejection," he became terrified with fear of obstacles and said, "Go, place him in a chariot that is inauspicious..."
Having ordered, "Have him carried out through the western gate and buried in the raw-corpse cemetery," he gave his command.
Upon hearing this, the Great Being was thrilled and elated, thinking, "At long last, my heart's desire will reach its fulfillment!
Therefore it is said: "Then my hands and feet... and so forth.
In this context, *maddiya* means having examined by way of pressing. *Anūnataṃ* means being complete in hands and other limbs.
*Nindisuṃ* means they censured him, saying: "Even though he is thus complete in his limbs, appearing like one who is mute and so forth, he is incapable of ruling;
he is a man of ill omen. There is also a reading *niddisuṃ*, which has the same meaning as *vadiṃsuṃ* (they spoke).

59. "They rejoiced in my casting away": all the inhabitants of the countryside who had come for the purpose of seeing the king, headed by the commander-in-chief and the royal chaplain—all those royal officials—with one mind and a single intention, being commanded by the king to bury [me] in the ground in order to avoid obstacles, did not contract their faces at my casting away, but rather, facing me directly, said, "Excellent! (sādhu).
They gave their approval, saying, "This is indeed well done; it must certainly be performed.

60. "May that purpose of mine be fulfilled": whatever purpose was intended, for the sake of which the practice of difficult deeds was undertaken by way of resolving upon a state such as being mute, may that purpose of mine be fulfilled—for those people, my mother, father, and others.

"Having heard his intention and purpose, I—rejoicing at the fulfillment of my own purpose, yet without further reflection—became as if my heart were filled with agitation by the permission to bury [the child] in the ground";
this connection should be understood through the remainder of the sentence. 61.
Thus, when the King had commanded the burial of the prince in the earth, Queen Candādevī, having heard that news, [approached] the King...
Having approached him, she said, “Your Majesty, you granted me a boon, which I accepted and set aside;
grant it to me now. “Take it, Queen,” he replied. “Grant the kingdom to my son,” she requested. “Your son is ill-fated (*kāḷakaṇṇī*);
it is not possible to give it to him,” he said. “In that case, Your Majesty, if you will not grant it for as long as I live, then grant it for seven years. “Even that—”
"It is not possible," [he replied]. "Then give me six years, five, four, three, two, or one year; seven months, six, five, four, three, two, or one month;
half a month, or seven days. "Very well, take it," he said.
She had her son adorned and, having caused a drum to be beaten throughout the city with the proclamation, "This kingdom belongs to Prince Temiya," she entered the city.
Having adorned her son, placed him upon the back of an elephant, and had a white parasol held over his head, she circumambulated the city and returned.
She laid him down upon a decorated couch of honor and prayed throughout the entire night:
"Dear Temiya, because of you, I have not obtained sleep for sixteen years; my eyes have become inflamed from weeping."
“My heart seems to break with grief; I know your condition as a cripple and so forth, so do not leave me without a protector.
In this manner he entreated him for six days. On the sixth day, the king summoned his charioteer named Sunanda and commanded:
“Tomorrow morning, having taken the prince out in an inauspicious chariot, bury him in the ground in the raw charnel ground and perform the ritual for increasing the earth.”
"Come," he said. Upon hearing this, the queen replied, "Dear father, the King of Kāsi has ordered that you be buried tomorrow in the raw-corpse cemetery;
you will meet your death tomorrow.
When the Great Being heard this, he was delighted and said, "Temiya, the effort you have exerted for sixteen years has reached its ultimate fulfillment."
He was filled with joy; however, his mother’s heart felt as if it were breaking.
Then, at the end of that night, early in the morning, the charioteer took the chariot and, having stationed it at the door, entered the bedchamber.
Saying, "Queen, do not be angry with me, this is the King's command," he pushed aside with his backhand the queen who was lying there embracing her son.
Having lifted up the prince, he descended from the palace. The queen struck her breast and, lamenting with a great cry, remained on the main floor.
Then, the Great Being looked at her and, thinking, "If I do not speak, my mother’s grief will become overwhelming," desired to speak;
yet, though wishing to speak, he thought, "If I speak now, the effort made for sixteen years will be in vain; but if I do not speak..."
"I shall become a support for myself and for my parents," he consented.
The charioteer, thinking, "I will place the Great Being in the chariot and drive it toward the western gate," instead drove it toward the eastern gate.
Having departed from the city, by the power of the deities, the chariot traveled three *yojanas*. The Great Being [became] even more...
His heart was filled with joy. There, the forest thicket appeared to the charioteer like a raw cemetery.
Thinking, "This place is beautiful," he caused the chariot to stop, drew it up to the side of the path, and alighted from the vehicle.
He removed the Great Being’s ornaments and belongings, bundled them together and set them aside, and taking a spade, went to dig a pit not far away.
He began. Therefore it was said: "Having bathed him and having anointed him," and so forth.
Therein, "having bathed" means having bathed him with sixteen jars of scented water. "Having anointed" means having smeared him with fragrant ointment.
"Having bound on the royal turban" means having placed upon his head the royal diadem that has come down through the lineage of the kings of Kāsi.
"Having consecrated him" means having consecrated him according to the royal custom for the coronation of a king in that royal family.
"They had the city circumambulated with a parasol" means they had me circumambulate the city while a white parasol was being held over me.
"Having maintained [the festival] for seven days" refers to the seven days obtained through the occasion of my mother, Queen Candā, receiving her boon.
"Having held my white parasol. "When the orb of the sun had risen" means that on the following day,
as soon as the solar disk had appeared, the charioteer Sunanda took me out of the city with the inauspicious chariot and went to the forest for the purpose of burying me in the ground.
63. *Sajjassaṃ*: I would have been ready; having placed my chariot, which was yoked to the pole, off to one side by moving it away from the path.
*Hatthamuccito*: with hand released; the meaning is that the hand was freed from the chariot-pole.
Alternatively, *hatthamuccito* means "hand-freed," the sense being that it has been released from my hand. *Kāsuṃ*: a pit.
*Nikhātuṃ* means "to bury. 64–5.

Now, in order to show the purpose for which I undertook difficult practices—such as the vow of silence (*mūgavata*) and others—for sixteen years, he spoke these two verses beginning with "the vow undertaken" (*adhiṭṭhitamadhiṭṭhāna*).

Therein, "threatening with various reasons" refers to [the period] from the time of the two-month interval until the completion of the sixteen years, through such acts as the prohibition of suckling and so forth.
Being tormented by various and manifold means, he was harassed through the destruction of his fear.
The rest is easily understood.
Then, while Sunanda was digging the pit, the Great Being thought, "This is my time for effort," and rising up, [placed] his own hands and feet...
Having pushed the chariot, he conceived the thought, "I have the strength to descend from it.
At that very moment, the place where his feet were standing rose up like a leather bag filled with wind and came to rest against the rear of the chariot.
Having descended and walked back and forth a few times, he realized, "I have the strength to go even a hundred yojanas."
Grasping the chariot by its rear end, he lifted it up like a toy carriage for children;
then, observing that "if the charioteer were to oppose me, I have the strength to oppose him," he resolved to adorn himself.
At that very moment, the abode of Sakka manifested a state of heat. Sakka [perceived] the reason for this.
Having understood this, he commanded Vissakamma: “Go and adorn the son of the King of Kāsi.

Saying “Very well,” he adorned him with both celestial and human ornaments until he resembled Sakka himself. Then, proceeding with the majestic grace of a divine king, he went to the spot where the charioteer was digging, and standing on the edge of the pit, he said:
“Why, O charioteer, do you dig up the kāsu tree in such a hurry?
Answer me when asked, my good man: what will you do with the kāsu?”—he said.
Therefore, without looking up, he said:
"The king has borne a son who is mute, wingless, and mindless;
I have been summoned by the king, so bury my son in the forest."
When this was said, the Great Being replied:
“I am not deaf, nor am I mute; I am neither lame nor crippled.
Yet you, O charioteer, would commit an unrighteous act by burying me in the forest.”
“Behold my thighs and my arms, and hear my words:
O charioteer, if you would bury me unrighteously in the forest.
Having said this, he again abandoned the digging of the pit and looked upward; seeing the perfection of his form and not knowing whether he was a man or a god, [he spoke].
“Are you a deity, or a gandhabba, or perhaps Sakka Purindada?
Who are you, or whose son are you? How shall we know you?”—when this was said—
“I am neither a god nor a gandhabba, nor am I Sakka Purindada;
I am the son of the King of Kāsi, whom you are digging up with your spade.
I am the son of that king upon whom you live for your livelihood.”
"O charioteer, you would be acting unrighteously if you were to bury me in the forest.
For one who sits or lies in the shade of a tree should not break its branch;
for the betrayer of a friend is an evil person."
“As the tree, so the king; as the branch, so I;
as the person who has come into the shade, so you are, O charioteer.
If you, O charioteer, had caused me to be buried in the forest, you would have been acting unrighteously.”
Having taught the Dhamma by way of this method, when he was requested to turn back,
[the Buddha] explained in detail the reason for not turning back— his desire for the going-forth (pabbajjāchanda)— and the cause thereof, namely the fear of hell and so forth,
as well as his own conduct in past lives; and when, through that discourse on the Dhamma and that practice, the king also became desirous of going forth, [he spoke this to the king]:
“Having returned the chariot, come back debt-free, charioteer;
for the going forth of one who is free from debt is praised by the seers.
Having said this, he dismissed him.
Thus, taking the chariot and the ornaments, he went into the presence of the king and reported the matter to him.

At that very moment, the king, thinking, "I shall go into the presence of the Great Being," departed from the city together with his fourfold army, the women of the harem, and the citizens and countryfolk.
The Great Being, for his part, having dismissed the charioteer, desired to go forth into homelessness.
He was born. Knowing his mind, Sakka dispatched Vissakamma with these instructions: “The wise Temiya desires to go forth;

construct for him a hermitage and the requisites for the life of one who has gone forth. Having gone there, he constructed a hermitage in a forest grove three leagues in extent, providing it with places for standing at night and sitting by day, walkways, lotus ponds, and fruit trees.
Having prepared all the requisites for a renunciant, he departed for his own place.
The Bodhisatta, seeing him and recognizing that he was a gift from Sakka, entered the leaf-hut, removed his clothes, and assumed the garb of an ascetic.

Sitting upon a bed of wood, he attained the eight meditative absorptions (*samāpatti*) and the five supernormal knowledges (*abhiññā*), and remained in the hermitage in the bliss of the renunciant life.
The King of Kāsi also, having traveled along the path shown by the charioteer, entered the hermitage and,
upon meeting the Great Being and exchanging greetings, invited him to rule the kingdom. The wise Temiya declined that offer and,
with a Dhamma discourse connected to impermanence and its various manifestations, as well as to the dangers of sensual pleasures, [instructed] the king.
He stirred him to spiritual urgency. With a mind thus stirred and weary of the household life, he became desirous of going forth and questioned his ministers and the women of the harem.

They, too, became desirous of going forth. Then the king, having learned that Canda-devī at their head, along with sixteen thousand women of the harem and the ministers and others, were desirous of going forth, caused a drum to be beaten in the city, proclaiming: "Whoever [desires to go forth] with my son..."
“Those who wish to go forth in my presence, let them do so. He had the golden treasuries and other stores opened and distributed.
The citizens, as soon as the shops were cleared and the doors of their houses opened, abandoned their homes and went into the presence of the king.
The king, together with the great multitude, went forth in the presence of the Great Being. [He gave away] the three-league-long park donated by Sakka.
The hermitage was filled to capacity.
Hearing that the King of Kāsi had gone forth, the neighboring kings entered the city intending to seize the kingdom of Bārāṇasī;
however, they beheld a city resembling the city of the gods, filled with the seven treasures, and a royal palace like a celestial mansion.
Thinking, "There must be danger because of this wealth," they departed immediately and set out.
Hearing of their arrival, the Great Being went to the edge of the forest, sat in the air, and taught the Dhamma.
They all, together with their retinues, went forth in his presence. In this way, one after another, there was a great gathering; all [went forth].
Having enjoyed various fruits, they practice the duty of a recluse (*samaṇadhamma*).
When someone thinks thoughts of sensual desire and so forth, the Great Being, knowing his mind, goes there, sits in the air, and teaches the Dhamma.
Having obtained the favorable condition for hearing the Dhamma, that person realizes the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) and the direct knowledges (*abhiññā*). In this way, yet another...
"All others," it is said, "also at the end of their lives became destined for the Brahma-world.

Even the animals, having developed serene confidence in the Great Being and in the company of seers, were reborn in the six celestial realms of sensual pleasure. The Great Being’s holy life continued for a long, extended period.
At that time, the deity residing in the parasol was Uppalavaṇṇā."
The charioteer was the Elder Sāriputta; his parents were members of a great royal family; his retinue was the Buddha’s retinue; and Temiya Paṇḍita was the Lord of the World.
His perfection of resolution (adhiṭṭhāna-pāramī) reached its culmination here, and the remaining perfections should likewise be extracted as appropriate.
Likewise, from the time he was born as Māsa onwards, there arose the fear of hell, dread of evil, loathing for kingship, and the sign of renunciation (nekkhamma-nimitta).
The power of his qualities should be manifested as his maintenance of the state of being mute and so forth, and his immovability even when confronted with opposing conditions;
such are the powers of his virtues that must be made known.
The commentary on the Temiya Cariyā is finished.
The Perfection of Resolution is concluded.
7. Commentary on the Conduct of the Monkey King. 67.
Regarding the seventh [birth], when I was a monkey: at the time when, having been reborn in the womb of a monkey, I had reached maturity...
I was a monkey, possessing the strength and power of a nāga, with a massive body the size of a young horse.
"On the bank of a river, in a cave" means that I made my dwelling in a certain cave on the shore of a particular river.
At that time, it is said, the Bodhisatta lived wandering alone, without leading a herd. And of that river...
In the middle [of the river] was a single island, well-supplied with various kinds of fruit trees such as mangoes and jackfruit.

By virtue of his strength and speed, the Bodhisatta leaped from the near bank of the river and fell upon a flat rock situated between the island and the river. From there, he leaped again and landed on that island. There he remained.
Having eaten various kinds of fruits and nuts, he would return by that same route in the evening and stay at his dwelling place;
on the following day as well, he did exactly the same. He made his residence according to this routine.
At that time, however, a certain crocodile lived in that river together with his wife. His wife [saw] the Bodhisatta...
Seeing him going from one place to another, she conceived a craving for the heart-flesh of that monkey and said to the kumbhīla,
"Noble son, a craving has arisen in me for the heart-flesh of this monkey. He replied, "Very well, my dear, you shall have it," and saying,
"Today we shall catch him as he returns from the island in the evening," he went to the Back Rock.
He lay down. On that day, the Bodhisatta, having grazed for his food, stood upon the rock at evening time and, looking at it, thought:
"This rock now appears higher; what could be the reason?
For the Great Being’s estimation of the water-level and the rock-level was perfectly fixed. Therefore, this thought occurred to him:
“Today the water of this river does not diminish at all, yet this rock appears to have become large;
could it be that a crocodile lies here waiting to seize me?
Thinking, “I shall investigate this first,” he remained right there and, as if speaking with the rock, said: “O sir!”
Having said, "It is a stone," and receiving no reply, he called out "O, it is a stone! up to three times. The stone gave no answer.
Again the Bodhisatta said, "Why, O stone, do you not give me an answer today?
The crocodile thought, "Surely this stone used to give an answer to the lord of monkeys on other days; I suspect it is because of my presence."
"But today, because he has been covered by me, he will not give; well then, I shall give him an answer," he thought, and said, "What of it, King of Monkeys?
"Who are you? "I am a crocodile. "For what purpose are you lying here?
"Longing for your heart. The Bodhisatta thought: "There is no other way for me to go."
“Alas, my departure is obstructed! Thus it was said:
“Oppressed by the crocodile, I cannot find a way to go.
“In whatever place I stood, from which I might leap from this shore to the further shore;”
“There the enemy-slayer, the crocodile of fierce aspect, remained.
Therein, the meaning already stated by the half-verse beginning with “Oppressed by the crocodile” is made clear by the verse beginning with “In which place.
Therein, “in which place” means standing in that spot in the middle of the river known as the Back-Rock (piṭṭhipāsāṇa).
“Oratī” means the near shore, so called because it is designated as a lamp. “Pāram” refers to the opposite bank of the river, which was my place of residence at that time.
“Patāmahaṃ” means: having leaped up, I fall there. “Tatthacchi” means:
on that spot of the back-rock, the enemy—the murderer, the one who would surely kill, the adversary, fierce-looking, terrible in form, and fearsome to behold—sat down.
Then the Great Being thought: “There is no other way for me to go; today I must deceive this crocodile.
For in this way, he will be liberated by me from great evil, and my own life will be saved.
He said to the crocodile: “My good friend, crocodile, I shall leap onto you. The crocodile replied: “O Lord of Monkeys,…”
“Come here without making a fuss,” he said. The Great Being replied, “I shall come;
however, you must open your mouth and seize me when I have arrived before you.
Now, when the mouths of crocodiles are opened, their eyes close. Failing to observe this fact, he opened his mouth. Then [his] eyes—
They closed their eyes. He lay down with his mouth open and his eyes completely closed.

The Great Being, perceiving his condition, leaped from the island, stepped upon the head of the jackal, and springing up from there, stood on the opposite shore, shining like a flash of lightning. Thus it is said:
“Thus he called out to me, ‘Come! and I said to him, ‘I am coming.
Having touched the top of his head, I established myself on the further shore.
In this context, *asaṃsī* means he spoke. *Ahampemīti* means I said to him, “I too am coming.”
However, because that island was adorned with groves of mango, rose-apple, breadfruit, and other fruit trees— delightful and fit for habitation—
and because the Great Being had promised, saying "I am coming," he acted accordingly, thinking, "I shall indeed come," so as to protect his truth. Thus it is said:
“‘No untruth was spoken by him, according to how he acted his word.
And because this preservation of truth was accomplished even at the cost of sacrificing his own life, therefore he said:
‘There is nothing equal to truth for me; this is my perfection of truth (saccapāramī).’”
But the crocodile, seeing that marvel and thinking, "An extraordinary feat has been performed by this lord of monkeys," said:
"O lord of monkeys, a person endowed with four qualities overcomes his enemies;
I suspect that all of them are present within you."
“O Lord of Monkeys, whoever possesses these four qualities—truth, righteousness, fortitude, and generosity—surpasses even what has been seen.
In this context, “yassa” means “of whichever person whatsoever. “Ete” indicates that those [qualities] which are about to be mentioned are being shown directly before one’s eyes.
“Four qualities” means four virtues. “Truth” refers to verbal truth:
having said, “I will come into your presence,” you have indeed come without committing a falsehood; this is your verbal truth. “Dharma” refers to investigative wisdom (*vicāraṇa-paññā*):
this investigative wisdom of yours functions thus, [thinking], “When this is done, such-and-such a result will follow. “Fortitude” (*dhiti*) is unceasing energy (*vīriya*).
It is said: "This too you possess. Generosity (*cāga*) means the relinquishing of oneself;
you have come into my presence having relinquished yourself, yet that I was unable to accept you is my own fault. "Seen" refers to an enemy.
"He overcomes" means that whichever person possesses these four qualities just as you do, he—just like you—[overcomes].
"Today you have surpassed me; likewise, one surpasses and overcomes one's own enemy.

Having thus praised the Bodhisatta, the crocodile went to his own dwelling place. At that time, the crocodile was Devadatta, his wife was the young woman Ciñcā, and the king of the monkeys was the Lord of the World (the Buddha).
Here too, the remaining perfections should be extracted according to the method already explained below. The same applies to the water and the rock.
And by means of determining the proportions, there is the knowledge of the crocodile’s lying position upon the rock through the act of encompassing it—
thinking, "Now the rock appears higher"— the reaching of a certainty regarding that matter by way of the rock's speaking as a pretext,
and his swiftness of action by way of suddenly leaping over the crocodile and landing on the opposite shore.
The power of such qualities as being liberated from great evil, the protection of one's own life,
and the preservation of truthful speech must be made manifest.
The commentary on the Life of the Monkey King is concluded.
8. Commentary on the Practice of the Ascetic Saccaka:
Regarding the eighth [chapter], "The Ascetic named Saccaka" means the ascetic who is to be called by the word *sacca* (truth), that is, the ascetic whose name is Saccaka.
"When I was," means at whatever time I existed. "Protecting the world with truth" means, in Jambudīpa, protecting the world of sentient beings through one's own state of non-deceptiveness.
In various places, I protected the multitude of beings from evil and from manifold misfortunes. And as it is said, "I made the people harmonious," there,
by showing the danger of quarreling to the great masses who had fallen into strife,
contention, and dispute, and by explaining the benefits of harmony, I made them harmonious, free from dispute, and full of mutual joy.
At that time, the Bodhisatta was reborn in Bārāṇasī into a certain prominent brahmin family.

They gave him the name Sacco. When he reached maturity, he went to Takkasilā and, having mastered his craft under a world-renowned teacher, he soon attained perfection in all branches of learning. He then received permission from his teacher to depart.
Having returned to Bārāṇasī and paid homage to his parents, he stayed for a few days in their presence while they expressed their joy,
all for the sake of protecting their hearts. Then his parents, desiring to unite him with a suitable wife,
described their entire wealth and invited him to the life of a householder.
The Great Being, his mind inclined toward renunciation and desiring to bring his own perfection of renunciation (*nekkhamma-pāramī*) to full maturity,
spoke in various ways of the disadvantages of the household life and the benefits of the going-forth (*pabbajjā*).
Then, abandoning his immeasurable mass of wealth, his boundless fame, and his vast circle of kinsmen— while his parents stood weeping with tearful faces— he departed like a great elephant.
Cutting the iron chain of household bondage, he went forth; entering the region of the Himalayas, he took up the ascetic life of an *isi*.
Sustaining himself on forest roots and fruits, before long he attained the eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) and the five higher knowledges (*abhiññā*).
Sporting in the play of meditation, he dwelt in the state of those attainments.

Thus, one day, while surveying the world with his divine eye, he saw that the people throughout the entire Jambudīpa were for the most part steeped in the ten unwholesome courses of action, such as the destruction of life;
they were embroiled in mutual disputes, rooted in sensual desire and caused by sensual desire.
Having seen this, he thought: "It is indeed not fitting that these beings should be so steeped in evil."

"And seeing those who have fallen into dispute, I shall maintain equanimity. For I have set out upon the vehicle of Great Enlightenment with the thought, 'I will lift beings out of the mire of saṃsāra and establish them on the dry land of Nibbāna.
Therefore, not falsifying that promise, what if I were to go to the realm of men and cause those various beings to desist from evil and pacify their disputes?"
Having reflected thus, the Great Being, impelled by great compassion, abandoned the bliss of meditative attainment and traveled here and there by means of his supernormal power.
Teaching the Dhamma according to their inclinations, he showed beings who had fallen into quarreling, strife,
and dispute the danger of conflict both in this present life and in future lives, and [established them] in mutual harmony.
He acted accordingly. Manifesting the danger of evil in its manifold forms, he separated beings from it and established some in the ten wholesome courses of action (*dasakusalakammapatha*).

Having ordained others, he established them as was appropriate in the restraint of virtue (*sīlasaṃvara*), the guarding of the sense faculties, mindfulness and clear comprehension (*satisampajañña*), dwelling in seclusion, and in the meditative absorptions and direct knowledges (*jhānābhiññā*). Therefore it is said:
“Furthermore, when I was the ascetic known as Saccasavhaya, I protected the world by means of truth and made the people live in harmony.
Here too, the remaining perfections of the Great Being should be extracted according to the method explained below; likewise, his qualities and powers should be elucidated.
The commentary on the Conduct of the Truth-Ascetic is finished.
9. Commentary on the Conduct of the Quail: 72.
Regarding the ninth [chapter], beginning with "In Magadha, as a quail," this is the summary of the meaning: in a certain part of the kingdom of Magadha...
When I was still in my nest, having been reborn in a certain forest region in the womb of a quail, I had recently emerged from the eggshell;
being so young that I was merely a lump of flesh, I was a fledgling quail without wings.
At that time, my mother would bring food for me from time to time with her own beak.

"Having brought [food], she nourishes me. 'I live by her touch'—for the sake of being fanned and for the sake of being nurtured, I live, dwell, and maintain my physical existence through the bodily contact of that mother of mine who touches me properly and at the right times while I lie upon her. 'I have no bodily strength'—this is because of my extreme youth."
There is no strength inherent in the body.
74. "Year by year" means in every year. "In the summer season" means during the hot time.
By the fire produced from the mutual friction of the branches of dry trees, a forest conflagration blazes and burns in that region.
Thus it was kindled. It approached us—meaning my mother and father—and because it purifies even an impure place by making it pure, it is called *pāvaka* (purifier);
and because it reduces fuel to ashes on the path it has traversed, it is given the name *kaṇhavattanī* (the black-pathed one).
This fire [consumes] the forest trees and shrubs.
Burning, it approaches from time to time.
(75) Thus, because it approaches, even then it "makes a sound," meaning it produces the sound "dhamadhamā.
For this is a description of the forest fire's resonance. "Mahāsikhī" means that which has great crests (*sikhā*) due to its fuel resembling mountain peaks.
Mahāsikhī. Gradually and step by step, as the fire burned and consumed that forest region, it approached the place where I was standing.
76. *Aggivegabhayā*: terrified by the fear of the fire approaching with great speed; *tasitā*:
trembling because of the physical shuddering arising from mental terror; *mātāpitaro*: mother and father; *attānaṃ parimocayunti*: they sought to liberate themselves from the fire.
By traveling to a place free from danger, they ensured their own safety. For at that time, the Great Being was of immense body, as large as a great boulder.
His parents, unable to capture him by any means and overcome by their own affection for themselves, abandoned their love for their son and fled.
77. "I stretch out my feet and wings"—this means that I extend, move, and exert myself, making both my feet and both my wings ready for movement upon the earth and in the air.
There is also a reading, *paṭīhāmi*, which means "I strive to make [them] suitable for traveling through the sky.
They also read *patīhāmi*; its meaning is: "I strive separately (*pati*) for each, namely for the feet and the wings."
I am striving for the sake of going, yet that striving is for the sake of making an effort [only] because I lack physical strength.

Why? Because I am without recourse there; being thus, deprived of movement due to the lameness of my feet, and having no refuge because of the departure of my parents, I am in that forest afflicted by a forest fire, or in that very nest.
Remaining thus, I then thought in the manner that is now to be stated. And here, the word *aham* (I) in the second instance should be regarded as a mere particle.
Now, in order to show the manner of his own reflection at that time, he said, "Of those whom I...
and so forth. Therein, "whom I might run to" means being afraid, terrified, and trembling because of the fear of death, and for that very reason, with a mind full of trepidation.
"Thirsty from the trembling of my body and pierced by [suffering], those whose wings I would now fly toward—thinking of them as a forest fire afflicts me—I would rush to enter;
yet those parents of mine have departed, leaving and abandoning me all alone.
What should I do today? means: "How indeed must I act today? How should I proceed? is the sense.

Thus the Great Being, standing there bewildered as to what ought to be done, thought again: "In this world there is such a thing as the virtue of moral conduct (sīla), and there is such a thing as the virtue of truth (sacca).

In the past, having fulfilled the perfections (pāramitā) and sat at the foot of the Bodhi tree, those who attained full enlightenment were endowed with virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; they were possessed of truth, compassion, and patience."
There are those called the omniscient Buddhas who have cultivated loving-kindness (mettā) equally toward all beings;

there is also the Dhamma, whose quality is exclusively that of definitive deliverance, which has been penetrated by them; and in me, too, there is one truth. A single phenomenon of an existing intrinsic nature (sabhāva-dhamma) is discerned;
therefore, having brought to mind both the past Buddhas and the qualities they have penetrated, [one should bring to mind] what exists within me.
“Having taken hold of the truth as an inherent quality and performed an act of truth (*saccakiriya*), I shall cause the fire to retreat;
today it is fitting for me to ensure the safety of both myself and all the beings dwelling here.
Having thus reflected, the Great Being, relying on his own spiritual power, acted according to his thought. Thus it is said:
“There exists in the world the quality of virtue, truth, purity, and compassion;
by that truth, I shall perform the supreme act of truth (saccakiriya).
Having invoked the power of the Dhamma and recalled the Conquerors of old,”
“Relying on the power of truth, he performed an act of truth.

(81) Therein, in order to show that verse which the Great Being spoke and by means of which he then performed an act of truth—having reflected upon the qualities of the Buddhas who had attained final Nibbāna in the past and having focused upon the true nature existing within himself—it says: “There exist...”
The passage beginning with “wings” was spoken.
Therein, “there are wings that do not fly” means: I have what are called wings;
they exist and are perceived, yet it is not possible to fly up or travel through the air by means of them—thus they are “non-flyers. “There are feet that do not deceive” means: I also have feet.
But since it was not possible to go by way of the path to avoid being deceived by them, there was no deception.
"My mother and father have gone out" means: even those who would have led me elsewhere have now gone out because of the fear of death.
"Jātaveda"—this is an address to fire. For it is born and knows (vedeti), and it is made known by the rising of its web of smoke; therefore, it is called "Jātaveda."
It is said: "Go back! Return!"—thus he commands Jātaveda.
In this way, the Great Being [thought]: "If I have wings, yet cannot fly through the air even when spreading them;
if I have feet, yet cannot move away even when lifting them; and if my parents [place me] only in the nest..."
"O Jātaveda, the nature of truth is such that even the state of fleeing after having abandoned [something] is itself true;

by this truth, may you retreat from here. While still lying in his nest, he performed this act of truth (*saccakiriya*). Simultaneously with the performance of the act of truth, Jātaveda retreated over an area of sixteen *karīsa*.
As he retreated, he did not go into the forest while burning, but rather into the water.
Like an overturned fire, it was extinguished right there. Therefore it was said:
“When my truth was uttered, the great blazing flame passed over sixteen karīsas, like a fire that has reached water.”

Furthermore, at that time, when the Bodhisattva was in the womb of a quail, this act of truth (*saccakiriyā*)—preceded by a mental advertence to the qualities of a Buddha (*buddhaguṇa*)—was unique and not shared by others.
Thus he said: "There is none equal to me in truth; this is my perfection of truth (*saccapāramī*).
For that very reason, because that spot could not be overcome by fire throughout this entire eon (*kappa*), it became known as the "Eon-lasting Miracle" (*kappaṭṭhiyapāṭihāriya*).
Thus the Great Being, by means of this act of truth, ensured his own safety as well as that of the beings dwelling there; at the end of his life, he departed according to his karma.
At that time, his parents were the parents of the present [Buddha], while King Vaṭṭaka was the Protector of the World (the Buddha).
The remaining perfections should be analyzed accordingly, in the same manner as described below regarding the forest fire.
Likewise, regarding his coming while spreading out in a terrifying form, even though he was alone at that time, one should illustrate his powers— such as how he did not fall into terror,
but by recollecting the qualities of the Dhamma beginning with truth and the qualities of the Buddha, and by relying on his own majesty,
brought about the safety of the beings dwelling there through an act of truth (*saccakiriya*).
The commentary on the *Vaṭṭapotaka* birth-story is finished.
10. Commentary on the *Maccharāja* birth-story: 83.
Regarding the tenth [birth], "When I was Maccharāja in the great lake," it means that in the past, having been reborn in the womb of a fish in the kingdom of Kosala...
At Sāvatthī, in Jeta’s Grove, in the site of a lotus pond surrounded by a thicket of creepers, there was a great lake.
Because I delighted the fish therein by means of the four bases of sympathy, when I am a king, I dwell there surrounded by a multitude of fish.
"In the heat" means during the hot season, the summer time. "Scorched by the sun" means by the heat of the sun. "The water in the lake dries up" means...
The water in that lake dried up and was cut off. For at that time, no rain fell in that kingdom;
the crops withered, and the water in the reservoirs and other places reached exhaustion and depletion. The fish and turtles entered the thick mud.
In that lake as well, the fish entered the thick mud and hid themselves in various places.
84. *Tato tato* means after that, following the exhaustion of the water. *Kulalasenakā* means both hawks (*kulala*) and crows (*senā*).

"They devour them day and night; they sit waiting for fish" means that having sat down here and there upon the mud-banks and entered the thickets of mud, the crows or others, whether by day or by night, [pierce] with their beaks like needle-points the fish lying within the mud.
Having crushed them again and again with their snouts and dragged them out, they devour them while they are still writhing.
Then, seeing that calamity of the fish, the Great Being’s heart was stirred by great compassion, and he thought:
"Apart from me, there is no one else capable of liberating these kinsmen of mine from this suffering; by what means indeed..."
Thinking, "I shall liberate you from this suffering by means of a skillful method," he considered:

"What if I were to perform an act of truth (*saccakiriya*) based on the Truth-Dharma— which was practiced and repeatedly observed by the great seers of old, which exists within me, and which would cause the god to send rain—
and thereby grant the gift of life to my circle of kinsmen, and by that [act], to all those who subsist upon food?"
Having made the resolution, "A great benefit for the world of beings has been accomplished by me," he performed an act of truth (*saccakiriya*) to cause the god to send rain.
Thus it is said: "He thought thus," and so forth.
In that context, "oppressed together with his kinsmen" means he was oppressed along with my kinsmen by that depletion of water.

*Sahā* is merely a particle. The meaning is: "Afflicted by his kinsmen who were suffering from that calamity because of his great compassion; distressed by the suffering of the assembly of his kinsmen.

(86) *Dhammatthaṃ* means a purpose that is itself the Dhamma, or a purpose not departing from the Dhamma. What is that? Truth. *Addasapassayaṃ* means "I saw a refuge for myself and my kinsmen. *Atikkhayaṃ* means a great destruction.
87. "The true Dhamma" (*saddhamma*) means the Dhamma consisting of non-harming toward even a single living being, belonging to the virtuous ones—the Buddhas and others.
"Having recollected" (*anussaritvā*) means having reflected upon that ultimate truth (*paramattha*) by taking it as the reality of an unerring nature.
"That which in the world is stable and eternal" (*dhuvasassata*) refers to that which belongs to even a single one among the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and disciples.
The connection is as follows: "Reflecting at all times on the non-harming of living beings as being constant and eternal by virtue of its true nature, he performed an act of truth (*saccakiriya*).
88. Now, desiring to employ a declaration of truth (*saccavacana*) by taking that quality existing within himself, the Great Being split apart the black-colored mud into two parts;
his great body was the color of a block of heartwood from the *añjana* tree, and [his eyes] were like well-polished red gems.
Opening his eyes and looking up at the sky, he spoke the verse beginning, "As far as I remember myself.
Therein, "as far as I remember myself" means from what point onward I remember—that is, recollect—the self designated as this personal existence (*attabhāva*).
"From when I have attained discretion" means from what point onward I have attained the state of being a person of discernment (*viññutā*) regarding various duties and responsibilities.
I have attained the state of discernment; by way of ascending upwards from this point, my attainment of wisdom consists precisely in the capacity to recollect my own bodily and verbal actions.

Within this interval, although I was born in various places of consumption among beings of similar kind, I have never before eaten even a grain of rice-sized fish, nor do I recall having intentionally harmed or injured any living being whatsoever.
“Even less has life been taken.

(89) “By this declaration of truth”: “If this non-harming of any living being that has been spoken by me is true, real, and unerring, then by this word of truth, may the rain-cloud Pajjunna pour down rain upon the assembly of kinsmen.”

Having said, "May you release me from my suffering," he then addressed Pajjunna, the king of the gods, as if commanding his own personal attendant, reciting the verse beginning with "Abhitthanaya pajjunna.
In this context, "Pajjunna" refers to a cloud; however, this [deity] has received the name by virtue of being a cloud.
He addresses the rain-cloud king, the deity. This is his intention: "A so-called god does not shine even when raining if he does not thunder and does not flash lightning;
therefore, thundering and flashing lightning, cause it to rain.
"Destroy the treasure of the crow" means that crows, having entered the mud, [eat] the fish situated there.
Having crushed them with their beaks and pulled them out, they eat them; therefore, the fish within that internal sludge are called "treasures" (*nidhi*).
By making it rain, you should conceal that treasure of the flock of crows with water and destroy it.
"Expose the crow to grief" means that when this great lake is full of water, the flock of crows will grieve, not finding any fish.
“Fill this mud with that flock of crows and deliver them to sorrow; cause them to rain down for the sake of sorrow.
The meaning is: act in such a way that they reach the state of sorrow characterized by internal burning.
“Deliver all the fish, my kinsmen, from this sorrow of death,” he said. “And deliver me from sorrow,” he said regarding his kinsmen.
They recite [the verse]. And therein, the particle *ca* has the sense of inclusion; thus, "release both me and my kinsmen"—release all from the sorrow of death.
For fish, there is the great sorrow of impending death at the thought, "We shall become food for our enemies due to the absence of water";
however, in the case of the Great Being, the arising of sorrow should be understood as occurring through the medium of compassion, as he felt compassion on account of their misfortune and ruin.
Thus, as if commanding his own personal attendant, the Bodhisatta addressed Pajjunna and caused a great rain to fall throughout the entire kingdom of Kosala.
Indeed, by the power of the Great Being’s virtue, at the very moment he performed the Act of Truth, the sandalwood throne of Sakka manifested a state of heat.
Reflecting on this, wondering "What could this be?", he [perceived the cause].

Having understood the reason, he summoned the divine king Vassavalāhaka and said, "Dear son, the Great Man, the King of Elephants, desires rain because of his grief for the death of his kinsmen; make the entire Kosala kingdom one cloud and cause it to rain.
Having accepted with the words "Very well," he dressed himself in one cloud as an undergarment and another as an upper robe, and while singing the song of the clouds, he—
He sprang forward, facing the eastern world-system. In the eastern quarter, a single cloud-mass the size of a threshing floor arose;

becoming a hundred layers and then a thousand layers, it thundered and flashed forth streaks of lightning, pouring down like water-pots turned upside down, and submerged the entire kingdom of Kosala with a great flood.
The Deva, raining down in an unbroken stream, filled that great lake in a mere moment.
The fish were liberated from the fear of death; the crows and other birds found a place to settle.

Not only the fish, but humans as well—who were producing various crops—and quadrupeds and so forth, all those who depend on rain for their livelihood, were freed from physical and mental suffering. Therefore it was said:
“When the supreme truth has been made, Pajjunna, having roared, shall rain down in an instant,
filling both the dry land and the lowlands. In this context,
“shall rain down in an instant” means that without delay, he rained down at the very moment of the performance of the declaration of truth.

91. "Having exerted supreme energy": when the gods were weeping, instead of falling into indolence by wondering what should be done, I exerted supreme energy by accomplishing the welfare and happiness of the great multitude of beings through the practice of benefiting those I knew.
Supported by the power of the majesty of truth—having relied upon the power of the influence of my own truth—I then caused the great cloud to rain. And since this is so:

"Therefore, 'There is none equal to me in truth; this is my perfection of truth (saccapāramī),' thus did the Dhamma King demonstrate the uniqueness of his own perfection of truth during the time of King Mahāmacchara.

In this way, the Great Being, his heart impelled by great compassion, released the entire populace from the suffering of death by causing a great rain to fall throughout the kingdom; at the end of his life, he departed according to his karma."
At that time, Pajjuna was the Elder Ānanda, the shoals of fish were the assembly of the Buddha, and the king of the fish was the Lord of the World.
The remaining perfections should be deduced from him in the same manner as explained below.
Likewise, having been reborn in the womb of a fish among those of his own kind in a place for eating, starting from even a mere grain of rice-sized fish, he did not give anything to anyone...
Abstaining from eating living beings—let alone eating them—refraining from harming even a single creature; likewise, causing rain for a deity by means of speaking the truth;

and when the water was exhausted, disregarding through his heroism the suffering he himself was experiencing by sinking into the thick mud, instead taking that very suffering upon his own heart for the sake of his kinsmen whom he could not bear to see it.
The power of his virtues, such as his compassion for all beings and his practice accordingly, should be made manifest.
The commentary on the conduct of the Bodhisatta as Maccharāja is finished.
11. Commentary on the Conduct of Kaṇhadīpāyana.

92. In the eleventh [story], the ascetic named Kaṇhadīpāyana is mentioned. For at that time, the Bodhisatta, having approached his own companion, the ascetic Maṇḍabya, who had been impaled on a stake, did not abandon him because of his virtuous character;
instead, he remained by the stake throughout the three watches of the night, and from the body of [Maṇḍabya], as the blood flowed down and fell drop by drop...
Because his body had turned black due to dried drops of blood, he became known as "Kaṇhadīpāyana.
"For more than fifty years" means for over fifty years; the accusative case is used here to express continuous duration.
"I lived dissatisfied" means that while dwelling in remote lodgings and practicing the higher wholesome states, I lived a life of celibacy (brahmacariya) while remaining dissatisfied.
I practiced it. Having gone forth, the Great Being indeed lived delightfully in the holy life for exactly seven days;
after that, he dwelt in a state of dissatisfaction.
But why did the Great Man, throughout hundreds of thousands of existences, possess an inclination toward renunciation and dwell in the holy life?
Having found delight here [in the world], do you not find delight there? Because of the fickle nature of the state of an ordinary person (*puthujjana*).
And why, moreover, did you not return to live at home? First, having seen the fault in sensual pleasures through an inclination toward renunciation (*nekkhamma*), you went forth.
Then, through improper attention (*ayoniso-manasikāra*), dissatisfaction arose within you. Although you were unable to dispel it, [you considered] both the action and its fruit...
Having first placed his faith [in the Buddha], he abandoned great wealth and went forth from the household life; yet now he has returned for that very same purpose.
Out of fear of the destruction of his own shame and modesty (*hiri-ottappa*), he feels loathing for this censure: "This Kaṇhadīpāyana is indeed dull-witted, mute, and fickle.
Moreover, this merit of renunciation is praised by the wise, such as the Buddha and others.
And because they did not carry it out, even with pain and even with dejection, with tearful face and weeping, he lived the holy life and did not abandon it. And this has been said:
"Having gone forth through faith, he returns again; alas, this man is dull-witted, mute, and fickle."
“Disgusted by this way of life, I lead the holy life (brahmacariya) against my will;
yet it is a state praised by the wise and esteemed by the virtuous, and thus I become a doer of merit.
“No one knows this”: this refers to my lack of delight, this mind devoid of joy while dwelling in the holy life.

No one who was a human being knew [this]. Why? Because I did not tell anyone that "discontent (arati) moves and prevails within my mental consciousness," nor did I speak of it to anyone; therefore, no human being knew this.
"My fellow-celibate Maṇḍabya was my friend, a great seer."
Bound by his past karma, he received the punishment of being impaled on a stake.
"Fellow-celibate" (*sabrahmacārī*) means one who shares the same training in the ascetic life of renunciation. "Maṇḍabya" is his name.
"Companion" (*sahāya*) refers to a dear friend due to their firm friendship during both their lay and monastic periods. "Great Seer" (*mahāisi*) means one of great spiritual power.

"Isi": "He received impalement because he was bound by his past karma"—this means that, as the opportunity had been created, he was joined with his own past karma and thus received impalement; he was transfixed upon a stake.
Herein, this is the sequential account: in the past, in the kingdom of Vaṃsa, in Kosambī, there was a king named Kosambika who ruled the realm.
He had it built. At that time, the Bodhisatta was reborn as the son of a wealthy brahmin mahāsāla possessing eighty koṭis of wealth in a certain town; his name was Dīpāyana.
A young brahmin, the son of another equally wealthy brahmin mahāsāla, was his dear friend; his name was Maṇḍabya. Later on, both of them...
After the passing of their parents, seeing the defects in sensual pleasures, they distributed a great almsgiving and abandoned sensual desires.

While their kinsmen, friends, and attendants were weeping and lamenting, they went forth. Having established a hermitage in the Himalayan region and gone forth into homelessness, they lived for more than fifty years, subsisting on forest roots and fruits gathered by gleaning, in order to suppress sensual desire.
They were unable [to attain anything]; they did not even produce a state of meditative absorption (*jhāna*).
While wandering through the countryside for the sake of seeking salt and sour flavors, they arrived at the kingdom of Kāsi.
There, in a certain town, lived a man named Maṇḍavya, who was a householder friend of Dīpāyana. Both of them went into his presence.
They approached him. Seeing them, he was delighted; he had a leaf-hut constructed and attended upon them with the four requisites.
Having stayed there for three or four years, they took leave of him and, wandering on their journey, dwelt in the Atimuttaka cemetery near Bārāṇasī.
There, Dīpāyana remained for as long as he desired, and then [returned] again to that town.
He went to his companion Maṇḍabya, and the ascetic Maṇḍabya remained right there.
Then one day, a certain thief, having committed a robbery within the city and taken valuable goods, was pursued by householders who had awakened and by the city guards.
Escaping through a drain, he fled with great speed.
Having entered the cemetery and discarded his bundle at the door of the ascetic’s leaf-hut, he fled.
When people saw the bundle, they rebuked him, saying, "Hey, you wicked matted-hair ascetic! Having committed theft at night, you wander about by day in the guise of an ascetic!
They beat him, seized him, and presented him to the king. Without even investigating, the king said, "Impale him on a stake!"
Having led him to the cemetery, they impaled him upon a stake of acacia wood. The stake did not penetrate the ascetic’s body.
Then they brought a stake of neem wood, but that too did not penetrate. Then they brought an iron stake, but that also did not penetrate.
The ascetic thought, "What indeed was my past karma? Thereupon, the knowledge of recollecting his former births arose within him. By means of that—

He saw his past karma: it seems that in a previous existence, having been the son of a carpenter, he went to his father’s place of work for planing wood, caught a fly, and pierced it with a thorn like the point of a *koviḷāra* bud.
That evil deed found its opportunity in this present state. Realizing, "It is not possible to escape from this evil," he [addressed] the king’s men...
He said, “If you wish to impale me on a stake, bring a *koviḷāra* stake.
They did so, impaled him on the stake, and having assigned guards, they departed.
Then Kaṇhadīpāyana, thinking, “I have not seen my friend for a long time,” approached Maṇḍabya and [learned] of that occurrence.
Having heard this, he went to that place and, standing to one side, asked, "Friend, are you a wrongdoer?
When the other replied, "I am not," he asked, "Were you able or unable to restrain the malice in your mind?
He answered, "Friend, I have no malice in my mind toward those who seized me, nor toward the king. [The first man said], "That being so, for such a person as you..."
Having said, "The shadow of the virtuous is my comfort," Kaṇhadīpāyana sat down leaning against the stake.

The guards reported this occurrence to the king. The king, thinking, "I acted without due reflection," went there in haste and asked Dīpāyana, "Venerable sir, why are you sitting leaning against the stake? [Dīpāyana replied,] "Great King, regarding this ascetic..."
“I am sitting here guarding it. “But did you do this only after knowing that he was the perpetrator?
He explained that the nature of the crime had not yet been cleared up. Then Dīpāyana said to him: “A king must indeed be one who acts with circumspection.
‘A householder who is lazy and devoted to sensual pleasures is not good; a renunciant who is unrestrained is not good.’”
"A king who acts without reflection is not good; nor is it good for a wise man to be angry.
Having spoken these and other such words, he taught the Dhamma.
The king, having understood that the ascetic Maṇḍabya was innocent, commanded, "Take away the stake! As they were taking away the stake—
They were unable to extract it. Maṇḍabya said: "Great King, due to the fault of karma committed in the past, I have met with such infamy;
it is impossible to extract the stake from my body.
Even if you wish to grant me my life, have this stake sawn through until it is flush with the skin. The king did exactly that. The stake remained inside.
It happened, yet it caused him no pain. It is said that at that time he took a fine splinter of wood and inserted it into the fly’s anus;
it remained inside him. Because of that, he did not die, but died only when his own lifespan was exhausted; therefore, this one also did not die.
The king, having paid homage to the ascetic and asked for forgiveness, [dismissed] both of them.
He had him reside right there in the park and looked after him. From that time on, he became known as Āṇimaṇḍavya;
relying upon the king, he lived right there. But Dīpāyana, having healed his wound, went back to the leaf-hut built by his own lay friend Maṇḍavya. Thus it was said:
“Having attended upon him, I restored him to health;
then, taking leave of him, I returned to my own hermitage.
In this context, “taking leave” means having taken leave of my companion, the ascetic Maṇḍabya. “To my own hermitage” refers to where I belonged.
I went to that leaf-hut hermitage, which was my own property and had been built for me by my lay companion, the brahmin Maṇḍabya. 96.
Seeing me entering that leaf-hut, they informed my companion. Upon hearing this, he was filled with joy.
Taking many perfumes, garlands, molasses, and other offerings, he went with his wife and children to the leaf-hut.
Having paid homage to Dīpāyana, washed his feet, and given him a drink, he sat down listening to news of Āḷina Maṇḍavya.
At that time, his son, Prince Yaññadatta by name, was playing with a ball at the edge of the walking-path. There, in a certain anthill, lived a venomous snake.
He was living there. A ball struck by the prince on the ground rolled away and fell upon the head of a venomous snake inside an anthill.
Unaware of this, the prince thrust his hand into the hole.
Then the enraged snake bit him on the hand. Overcome by the force of the poison, he collapsed right there. Then, for him—

When the parents realized that the boy had been bitten by a snake, they lifted him up, laid him at the feet of the ascetic, and said, "Venerable sir, please cure our little son of his illness with either medicine or a spell. He replied, "I do not know any medicine;
I will not perform the work of a physician, for I am one who has gone forth. [The parents said,] "In that case, venerable sir, in this..."
“Having cultivated loving-kindness toward the boy, perform an act of truth.
The ascetic, saying, “Very well, I shall perform an act of truth,” placed his hand on Yaññadatta’s head and performed the act of truth. Thus it was said:
“The brahmin was my friend,” and so forth.
Therein, "guests came" means they approached as guests (*pāhuṇāgata*). 97.
"Throwing the ball" means throwing a ball—so called because of its round, ball-like shape—and playing the game of balls;
this is the meaning. "He provoked a venomous snake" means that, having been struck by the ground, [he encountered] one dwelling in an anthill hole.
There, having struck the black snake situated there on the head with a ball, he provoked its anger.

(98) "Seeking the path gone by that circle" means searching for the track traversed by that coil. "He touched the head of the venomous snake with his hand" means he touched the head of the viper with his own hand, which had been inserted into the anthill burrow.

(99) "Supported by the power of poison" refers to a snake that arises depending on the force of its own venom. "He bit the boy at that very moment" means that at the very instant he touched him, he bit that brahmin youth.
100. *Sahadaṭṭho* means "together with the bite," that is, at the very moment he was bitten. *Āsivisena* means by a snake of terrible venom.
*Tenā* means by that falling of the child onto the ground while fainting from the force of the venom, I became pained.
*Mama vāhasi taṃ dukkhaṃ* means you have carried away that suffering of both the child and his parents; it has been transferred to my own body.
He carried me away as if out of compassion. 101.
Those, namely the mother and father of that child, I consoled by way of saying, "Do not grieve, do not lament," and so forth.
"Pierced by the dart of sorrow" means afflicted by the sting of grief. "Supreme" means best; for that very reason, it is excellent.
I performed the supreme act of truth (*saccakiriya*).
Now, in order to show that act of truth in its specific form, he spoke the verse beginning with “For seven days only.
Therein, “for seven days only” means for exactly seven days starting from the day of his going forth. “With a serene mind” means through faith in the result of kamma.
"With a serene mind. "Seeking merit" means one who desires merit, one endowed with a longing for the Dhamma. "And thereafter, whatever conduct I practiced" means:
after those seven days, whatever practice of the holy life (*brahmacariya*) I performed.
"Carrying it even against my will" means: even while unwilling to go forth. "By this truth may there be well-being" means: if [I have practiced] for more than fifty years...
"It is true that while living in a state of discontent, I did not inform anyone of this;
by this truth, may it be well with Prince Yaññadatta, and may he regain his life.
When the Great Being had thus performed this Act of Truth, the poison was expelled from Yaññadatta’s body.
He entered the earth. The prince opened his eyes, looked at his mother and father, and having said, "Mother, Father," he emerged.
Thus it was said:
"As soon as my word was spoken, pierced by the force of the poison..."
"Having awakened, he arose; and the young man was free from disease.
The meaning of this is: at the very same moment as my making of truth, prior to that, though pierced and shaken by the force of the poison and standing there unconscious, he did not awaken;
but now, with the poison gone and his consciousness restored, he suddenly arose.
Thus, by the absence of the poison's effect, the young brahmin boy became healthy.
Now, the Teacher, demonstrating the perfection of his own act of truth (*saccakiriyā*), said:
"There is nothing equal to my truth; this is my perfection of truth (*saccapāramī*). The meaning of this is self-evident. [This is] from the *Jātakaṭṭhakathā*.
However, it is stated: "By the Great Being’s act of truth, the poison rose up from the prince's chest and vanished;
by the boy’s father’s act of truth, it rose up from his waist; and by the mother’s act of truth, the poison rose up from the remainder of her body and vanished. For thus it has been said:
“Because I have never taken delight in giving when I see a guest at the time for lodging,
nor have the learned recluses and brahmins ever made it known to me that I am displeased;
even though I give unwillingly, by this truth may there be well-being!
The poison is destroyed; let Yaññadatta live!
“My dear, the venomous snake who bit you has flown away into the sky with its great power.
Today, there is no difference at all between that creature and your father in my eyes, because of my lack of affection for either.”
“By this truth, may there be well-being; may the poison be destroyed and Yaññadatta live!
In that context, “at the time of staying” means at the time of coming to the house for the purpose of residing.
“And they did not know my lack of affection” means that even the learned recluses and brahmins did not know this state of mine—that I neither delight in giving nor am I displeased with it.
"He knew. By this he indicates: "For I look upon you with eyes of affection alone. Regarding the phrase "by this truth":
the meaning is, "If even while giving I do not believe in the karmic result and give without my own desire, and if others do not perceive my lack of desire—by this truth, may there be well-being!
In the other verse, "dear one" (*tāta*) is an address to his son. "Abounding in splendor" (*pahūtatejo*).
“Powerfully venomous. *Patarāti* means *padarā*; or this reading itself is correct. “Having gone upward” (*udiccā*) means having risen up from the hole of an anthill;
this is what is meant: “Dear Yaññadatta, there is no difference in my feeling of aversion toward that poisonous snake and toward your father; indeed, setting aside that aversion,”
"Today no one has been made known by me; if this is true, by this truth may there be well-being.

Thus, when the princes were born healthy, the Bodhisatta established his father in faith in the results of action by saying, "One who gives a gift must give with faith in both the deed and its fruit," and having dispelled his own lack of interest, he attained the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and direct knowledges (*abhiññā*).
Having generated [this resolve], at the end of his life, he was destined for the Brahma-world.
At that time, Maṇḍabya was the Elder Ānanda; his wife was Visākhā; his son was the Elder Rāhula; Āṇimaṇḍabya was the Elder Sāriputta; and Kaṇhadīpāyana was the Lord of the World (the Buddha).

Herein, the perfection of truth (*sacca-pāramī*) has been set forth in this text; the remaining perfections should be extracted according to the method explained below. Likewise, the power of his virtues, such as the relinquishment of his entire great wealth, should be made manifest.
The commentary on the life of Kaṇhadīpāyana is finished.
12. Commentary on the Life of Mahāsutasoma: 105.
Regarding the phrase "In the twelfth [birth], Sutasoma was the lord of the earth," this refers to a kshatriya of that name. For at that time, the Great Being was in the kingdom of Kuru...
He was born from the womb of the chief queen of King Koravya in the city of Indapatta.

Because of his great learning and his beautiful, moon-like, gentle, and excellent complexion, they named him Sutasoma. When he reached maturity and had mastered all the arts, his parents consecrated him in the kingdom.
He was seized by Porisāda, so called because he devours—that is, eats—men, that is, human beings.
Known by the name "Porisāda," he was taken by the King of Bārāṇasī for the purpose of making offerings to the deities.
For at that time, the King of Bārāṇasī, who would not eat without meat, had been made to eat human flesh by his cook when no other meat could be obtained;
thus, bound by craving for flavors, he began killing men and eating their flesh.

The one known by the name “Porisāda,” having been urged by his own general named Kāḷahatthin—who was incited by the city-dwellers, merchants, and country-folk led by the chief ministers and assembly members—was told: “Your Majesty, if you desire the kingdom, desist from eating human flesh.
To this he replied: “Even if I were to renounce the kingdom, I will not desist from eating human flesh.”
Exiled from his kingdom by them, he entered the forest and dwelt at the foot of a banyan tree.
For the sake of healing a wound on his foot caused by the impact of a stump, he made a supplication to a deity, saying,

"I shall perform a sacrificial offering with the blood from the throats of one hundred kṣatriyas throughout the entire land of Jambudvīpa," and for seven days remained without food until the wound was healed.
Having conceived the thought, "By the power of the deity, I have been safe," he set out with the intention, "I shall bring kings for the purpose of making offerings to the deity.
On his way, he encountered a yakṣa who had been his companion in a previous existence;
through the power of a mantra given by that yakṣa, he became endowed with superior speed, agility, and prowess, and within seven days, he brought back one hundred kings.
Having hung his own upper garment from the banyan tree, he prepared to perform the offering ceremony.

Then, the deity dwelling in that tree, being unwilling to accept the offering, thought, "I shall prevent him by some means," and appearing before him in the guise of a renunciant, she followed him for three *yojanas*. Then, once again, she—her own...
Manifesting a divine form, he said: "You are a liar! You promised, 'I will bring the kings of the entire Jambudīpa and perform an offering ceremony. Yet now you have brought only these weak kings.
If you do not bring Sutasoma, the eldest king of Jambudīpa, I have no need for your offering."
Thus, having rejoiced, thinking, "I have seen my own deity," she said, "Master, do not worry; I shall bring Sutasoma back this very day.
With great speed, she went to the Migājina garden, descended into the lotus pond where no guard was stationed, and stood there with her head concealed by a lotus leaf.
While she was still within the garden, at the powerful break of dawn, for three leagues all around—
They took up their guard. At dawn, the Great Being, mounted upon the back of a magnificent, adorned state elephant, departed from the city with a fourfold army.

At that time, a brahmin named Nanda, having learned four hundred stanzas worth a thousand pieces of gold, traveled a road of two hundred yojanas and arrived at that city through the eastern gate to see the king.
Seeing him departing, the brahmin raised his hand, said, "Victory to you, Great King! and thus wished him victory.
The king approached him on the elephant and asked, "From where do you come, brahmin? What do you desire? What shall I give to you?
The brahmin replied, "Having heard that you are 'one who prizes learning,' I have come bringing these four hundred stanzas worth of gold."
“I have come to teach you,” he said. The Great Being, with a joyful heart, replied, “I shall go to the garden, bathe, and return to listen; do not be anxious.
Having spoken thus, he commanded, “Go and provide a dwelling and food and clothing for the brahmin at such-and-such a house,” and then entered the garden, establishing a great guard.
Having prepared himself, he removed his coarse ornaments, had his beard trimmed, and anointed his body.
Having bathed with royal splendor in the lotus pond, he emerged, put on a robe for taking water, and stood there.
Then they brought him perfumes, garlands, and ornaments. Porisāda thought, "When he is fully adorned, the king will become too heavy [to carry]."
"I shall seize him while he is still light," he thought; then, roaring and brandishing his sword, he emerged from the water, proclaiming his name:
"I am Porisāda! Hearing his voice, the elephant-riders and others fled from their elephants and other mounts.
The army, stationed at a distance, fled right where they stood. The other [the Bodhisatta], casting aside his weapons, lay prostrate on his breast.
King Poriyāda lifted the king up, made him sit upon his shoulder, and right there in front of him, leaped over a wall eighteen cubits high;
then, treading upon the frontal globes of excellent, rutting elephants that were flowing with ichor, he made them fall like mountain peaks;
and treading upon the backs of the horse-treasures swift as the wind, he made them fall, and finally, treading upon the poles of chariots—
As he flew along like a bee, as if crushing the blue leaves of the *nigrodha* tree, he traveled the three-league path in a single bound;
seeing no one following him, he proceeded slowly, and perceiving the drops of water falling from Sutasoma’s hair onto his own body as "tears," he thought, "What is this? Is Sutasoma also dying?"
“...grieving, he weeps,” he said.
The Great Being replied, “I do not grieve over death—how could I weep? Rather, it is the practice of the wise to fulfill a promise once made;
that [promise] is not being fulfilled, and for that reason I grieve. This was taught by the Blessed One Kassapa.
“Having taken the four hundred and twenty verses and come from Takṣaśilā, I had the visiting etiquette performed for the brahmin;
then, having made an agreement with him, saying, ‘I will listen after I have bathed and returned; wait until my arrival,’ I went to the park.
And you, without letting me hear those verses, seized me. Thus it was said.
“Having been seized by Porisāda, he recalled his promise to the brahmin.
In this context, “he recalled his promise to the brahmin” means that he remembered the agreement he had made with the brahmin Nanda.
106. “Having bound them and brought them from Karattala”—this refers to those who were brought by his own power after going here and there to places such as parks.
Having made a hole in the palms of one hundred and one kṣatriyas and fastened a rope to them for the purpose of hanging them from a tree.

"Having crushed these" means: having seized these one hundred and one kṣatriyas alive, having turned them upside down with their feet up and heads down, and having wrapped them around the palms by whirling them while striking their heads with his heels, he [hung them] entirely from the tree as a support.
The meaning is: having caused [him] to wither, dry up, and exhaust [him] in every way by cutting off his food.
"For the sake of sacrifice" means for the purpose of accomplishing the ritual offering (*balikamma*). "He led me away" means he brought me [there].
Furthermore, while being thus led away, when Porisāda asked the Great Being, "Are you afraid of death?"...
“I do not fear death; rather, I grieve because the agreement I made with that brahmin has not been fulfilled.
“If you release me, I shall go, listen to that Dhamma, pay him honor and respect, and then return.
“I do not believe this—that once released by you, you will go and return to me again.”

“You will come into my hand,” he said. “Good Porisāda, having been trained in the same teacher’s school as I and being my friend, do you not believe my word when I say, ‘I would not speak a lie even for the sake of my life’?
Although he had spoken these mere words to me—“I grasp both sword and spear, and I even take an oath upon you, good sir;”
"Released by her, having become free from debt, and guarding my truth, I shall return again.

When the Great Being had spoken this verse, Porisāda thought, "This Sutasoma says, 'I am making an oath that must not be made by kṣatriyas. Even if he goes and does not return, he will not escape from my hands. Then he said:
"The covenant that was made with you by the brahmin, while he stood in the sovereignty of his own kingdom..."
"O Brahmin, having fulfilled that promise, return again as one who guards the truth. Thus he dismissed him.
Released from Rāhu’s mouth like the moon, the Great Being—possessed of elephant-like strength and power—quickly reached that city.

He arrived. His army, thinking, "King Sutasoma is wise; having tamed Porisāda, he will return like a noble elephant released from the mouth of a lion," and fearing reproach for having come after giving the king to Porisāda, had encamped outside the city.
