Seeing him approaching from afar, they went out to meet him, paid homage, and said, "We hope you are well, Great King?"
Having offered this hospitable greeting, saying, "I have not been harmed by Porisāda," and when he added, "Porisāda has done what was difficult even for my own parents;

such a fierce and violent man released me out of trust in me," the king adorned him, mounted him upon the neck of an elephant, and surrounded by a retinue, entered the city. Seeing this, all the citizens were filled with joy.
Out of his intense craving for the Dhamma, he did not even visit his parents;

instead, he went to his residence, summoned the brahmin, and after showing him great honor and respect, he himself sat on a low seat out of reverence for the Dhamma and said, "Teacher, I shall listen to the Satārahagāthā brought by you. At the time when the Great Being made this request, the brahmin—
Having rubbed his hands with perfumes and taken out from a bag a beautiful manuscript, he took it in both hands and,
saying, “In that case, Great King, listen,” he recited the verses from the book:
“O Sutasoma, meeting with the virtuous occurs but once.”
She protects him through association, not by frequenting the company of the unwholesome.
“One should dwell only with the virtuous, one should cultivate intimacy with the virtuous;
having understood the true Dhamma of the good, one becomes better, not worse.”
“Indeed, well-adorned royal chariots decay, and likewise the body also undergoes decay;
but the Dhamma of the virtuous does not undergo decay—this is what the good proclaim to the good.
The sky is far away, the earth is far away, and they say the further shore of the ocean is far away.”
"Therefore, they say that the Dhamma of the virtuous and the king of the wicked are indeed far apart.
Having heard this, the Great Being, with a joyful heart, thought: "My coming here has borne fruit. These verses were spoken neither by disciples, nor by seers, nor by poets, nor by gods;
they were spoken by the Omniscient One himself. What indeed could be their value?"
Reflecting thus: "Even if this entire Cakkavāḷa world, up to the Brahma-world, were filled with the seven treasures and given away, it would not truly be a worthy gift;

however, I am able to give him the sovereignty over the Kurū kingdom, three hundred leagues in extent, and the city of Indapatta, seven leagues in size. Yet he lacks the fortune to rule a kingdom. So it was.
"Judging by the marks on his limbs, he appears to be of little power; therefore, even though the kingdom was given to him, it does not remain with him," he thought.
Then he asked, "Teacher, what do you receive when you teach these verses to other kshatriyas?
"A hundred for each one, Great King; that is why they are known as 'the Hundred-Valuable Verses'."
Then the Great Being said to him, "Teacher, you do not know the value of the goods you have taken and are carrying about.
"These verses are worth a thousand; these verses are not worth a hundred.
Quickly take four thousand [pieces of gold], O Brahmin!"
Having caused four thousand [pieces of gold] to be given and having presented a single comfortable carriage, he sent him off with great honor and respect.

Then, after paying homage to his parents, he said: "I have come here after giving my word to the man-eater (porisāda), saying, 'I will return after worshipping the jewel of the True Dharma brought by the brahmin and having rendered him honor and respect. In that regard, whatever..."
"Whatever was to be done and whatever was to be practiced by the brahmin has been accomplished; now we shall go into the presence of Porisāda.
Having said this, they entreated him, saying, "In that case, dear Sutasoma, what is this you are saying? We shall capture the thief with a fourfold army;
do not go into the presence of the thief. There were sixteen thousand female dancers and the rest of the retinue as well.
“Leaving us without a protector, where are you going, O King? they lamented. A great outcry arose as people said, “It seems the king will go to the thief’s side once again.
The Great Being thought, “It is the custom of the virtuous and noble to fulfill their promises; he too has placed his trust in me.”

“I have given them up; therefore, I shall indeed go forth. Having paid homage to his parents and instructed the remaining people, he departed from the city followed by his harem and other folk who were weeping with tearful faces and lamenting in various ways.
To turn back those people, he drew a horizontal line across the path with a staff, saying, “Do not cross this line of mine.”
Having spoken thus, he departed. The great multitude, unable to transgress the command of the majestic Great Being, returned after crying out and weeping with a great sound.
The Bodhisatta went back to his presence by the same path he had come.
Thus it was said: “Porisāda questioned me,” and so forth.
In this regard, when he says, "Why do you wish to sit here? Do you wish to leave my hand in order to go to your own city?
and you say, "I am one who has long been acquainted with Takṣaśilā and other places, and I am a speaker of truth," therefore I shall act according to your intention;
I will do as you desire. "If you would come back to me again"—if you should return once more—then...
"You will come to me with absolute certainty.
(108) Having promised that he would come to me at the time of the question— having given his word, "I shall come early in the morning"— he then surrendered the kingdom to that Porisāda.
Desiring to depart, he handed over his kingdom, which extended three hundred *yojanas*, to his parents, saying, "Please take charge of this kingdom.
Why, then, did he hand over the kingdom? It was because he recollected the Dhamma of the virtuous;

for the fulfillment of a promise is indeed the noble tradition and family lineage of the virtuous Great Bodhisattvas. Therefore, it was out of respect for that Dhamma of the perfection of truth (*sacca-pāramitā*) that he acted.

"Recalling the ancient and primordial practice followed by the Conquerors, the Buddhas and others, and guarding the Truth, I gave my wealth to that brahmin and, sacrificing my own life, approached Porisāda. 110.
‘There is no doubt for me in going there’—regarding that journey to the presence of Porisāda, [he wondered], ‘What will he do to me?’"

"I have no doubt as to whether he will kill me or not. Knowing full well that this fierce and violent man, having prepared a sacrificial offering for the deity with me and one hundred kṣatriyas, would certainly kill us all, I approached him solely to preserve my word of truth, even at the cost of sacrificing my own life. And since this is so,"
"Therefore, there is nothing equal to my truth; this is my perfection of truth, having reached the state of the ultimate goal.
Then, seeing the face of the Great Being, which was as beautiful as a blooming white and red lotus, he thought, "This one has come free from the fear of death;
what indeed is the power behind this? and reflecting, "It must be because of his having heard that Dhamma..."
"This one has thus become so majestic and fearless; I too, having heard it, shall become majestic and fearless," he resolved.
Then Porisāda said to the Great Being: "We wish to hear those hundred precious verses for the sake of which you went to your own city."
Having heard this, the Bodhisatta thought, "This Porisāda is of evil nature; having restrained him slightly and put him to shame, I shall speak. He said:
"For one who is unrighteous, cruel, and always blood-stained, there is no truth;
whence could there be Dhamma? What will you do with what you have heard?"
Having spoken thus, and having developed even greater reverence for hearing the Dhamma, he said again:
“Having heard the Dhamma, people discern what is wholesome and what is evil;
even by hearing a single verse, my mind delights in the Dhamma.”
Thinking, "He has developed great reverence and a desire to hear; well then, I shall speak to him," he said, "In that case, friend, listen well and attend closely.

Then, having respectfully offered praise for the verses according to the very sequence spoken by the brahmin Nanda, he raised a great clamor throughout the six realms of the sense-sphere gods and caused the deities to cry out, "Well done! (sādhukāra).
While they were giving [the food] to the man-eater, the Great Being said:
“O Great King, association with the virtuous occurs but once;
that association protects one, whereas frequent association with the unvirtuous does not.”
“One should associate only with the virtuous, one should cultivate intimacy with the virtuous;
having understood the true Dhamma of the good, one becomes better, not worse.
Indeed, even beautifully adorned royal chariots wear out, and the body itself succumbs to decay.”
The Dhamma of the virtuous does not age; indeed, the virtuous proclaim it to the virtuous.
“The sky is far, the earth is far, and they say the further shore of the ocean is far;
yet they say that which is even farther than those is the Dhamma of the virtuous compared to that of the unvirtuous, O King.”

He preached the Dhamma. Because of his excellent preaching and by the power of his own merit, as soon as he heard the verses, the entire body of the listener was filled with five-colored rapture (*pīti*). With a softened heart toward the Bodhisatta, he said:
"Friend Sutasoma, I see no gold or other wealth worthy of being given; therefore, for each verse, I shall grant you one boon."

He said: Then the Great Being, having rebuked him, saying, "Since you do not even know what is for your own benefit, what boon indeed will you give to another?", was again requested by him, "Please grant a boon.
First of all, he requested the boon: "May I see you healthy for a long time. He [the hunter] thought, "This man now wishes to kill me and eat my flesh..."
“Though he is one who brings me great harm, he desires my very life,” he thought, and with a joyful heart, not realizing that the boon had already been taken by deception, he granted it.
For the Great Being, through his skill in means, requested his own life on the pretext of the king’s desire for him to live long.
Then [the king] granted a second boon, saying, “Grant life to more than a hundred kṣatriyas,” and to them... their own...
He requested the third boon, the restoration of the kingdom, and the fourth boon, the abstaining from eating human flesh.
Having granted him the three boons, the king, unwilling to grant the fourth, said,
"Choose another boon," yet being persistently pressed by the Great Being, he granted that as well.
Then the Bodhisatta, having rendered Porisāda harmless, caused the kings to be released by him;
he had them laid upon the ground, slowly extracted the cords from the children's ears like rolls of thread, and had Porisāda bring a piece of hide.
Having rubbed it with a stone and performed an Act of Truth, he smeared the palms of their hands with it. At that very moment—

Thus it became comfortable. Having stayed right there for two or three days, having ensured they were free from illness, and having established with them a friendship characterized by mutual recognition and intimacy, he led them to that city of Bārāṇasī.
Having installed them in the kingdom, saying, "Be heedful," he sent those kings each to their own city, and [he himself returned] from his own city of Indapatta.
Surrounded by his fourfold army, he returned to his own city;
escorted by the citizens who were joyful and delighted, he entered the inner palace, paid homage to his mother and father, and ascended to the great terrace.
Then the Great Being, having caused six halls of giving to be constructed and distributing great gifts daily while fulfilling the precepts, remained there.

While observing the Uposatha, he cultivated the perfections (pāramitā). Those kings, abiding by the Great Being’s counsel, performed meritorious deeds such as giving and, at the end of their lives, filled the city of heaven.
At that time, Porisāda was the Elder Aṅgulimāla, the minister Kāḷahatthiya was the Elder Sāriputta, and Nanda the Brahmin...
The Elder Ānanda, the tree deity, the Elder Mahākassapa, kings, the Buddha’s retinue, parents, great royal families, and King Sutasoma, the Lord of the World—

by the same method explained below, the remaining perfections should also be extracted for these. Likewise, as in the commentary on the *Alīnasattu-cariyā* (*Cariyāpiṭaka*, 2.74ff.), the power of the Great Being’s virtues should be made manifest.
The commentary on the Mahāsutasoma Cariyā is finished.
The Perfection of Truth (Saccapāramī) is finished.
13. Commentary on the Suvaṇṇasāma Cariyā.

111. Thirteenth: When Sāma was dwelling in the forest. At that time, when there was a young ascetic named Sāma in a great wilderness on the bank of the river called Migasammata in the Himālayas—he was "created by Sakka" because he was born through the attainment of the instruction of Sakka, the Lord of the Devas;
he was produced and generated by Sakka. Herein, this is the sequential account: in the past...
Not far from Bārāṇasī, on the bank of a river, there was a hunters' village.
There, a son was born to the chief hunter, and they gave him the name Dukkula. On the opposite bank of that same river, there was also a hunters' village.
There, a daughter was born to the chief hunter, and they gave her the name Pārikā. Both of them [had previously been] from the Brahma-world...
Pure beings arrived. When they reached maturity, their parents arranged marriages for them even though they were unwilling.
Both of them lived together like Brahmās, without ever descending into the ocean of defilements, and they did not perform any of the work of hunters.
Then their parents said to Dukūla, "Dear son, you do not perform the work of hunters, nor do you desire the life of a householder."
"What will you do? they asked. He replied, "If you grant me permission, I shall go forth.
"Then go forth," they said. Both men entered the Himālaya mountains;
having gone to the place where the river named Migasammata, descending from the Himālaya, joins the Gaṅgā, they left the Gaṅgā and headed toward the Migasammata.
They ascended. Then the palace of Sakka manifested a state of heat. Sakka, understanding the reason for this, had Vissakamma construct a hermitage at that spot.
Having gone there and gone forth, they dwelt in the hermitage given by Sakka, cultivating the loving-kindness of the sense-sphere (kāmāvacara-metta).
Sakka, too, would come to attend upon them.
Then one day, knowing that "their eyesight will fail," he approached them and said, "Venerable sirs, an obstacle to your eyesight is appearing;
it is necessary for you to obtain a son to look after you. I know your purity of heart;
therefore, when Pārikā’s womb is ready, you should touch her navel with your hand, and thus a son will be born to you."
Having said, "He will attend upon you," he departed. The wise Dukūla explained the matter to Pārikā and, when she was in her fertile period, touched her navel.
At that time, the Bodhisatta, having descended from the world of the gods, took rebirth in her womb;
after the lapse of ten months, she gave birth to a son of golden complexion. For that very reason, his name was "Suvaṇṇasāma."

They gave him a name. Later, when he had grown up and reached the age of sixteen, his parents, wishing to protect him, seated him in the hermitage and went themselves into the forest for the sake of roots and fruits.
Then one day, having gathered fruits in the forest and returning, while they were not far from the hermitage, a cloud arose.

Having entered the foot of a tree, while the sweat mixed with water from the bodies of those standing on top of an anthill entered the nostrils of a venomous snake dwelling in that anthill-hole, the snake became enraged and struck them with the breath from its nose.
Having become blind, they both wailed and cried out in lamentation. Then the Great Being thought, "My parents are taking too long."
“What, indeed, is their condition? Thinking thus, he went along the opposite path and made a sound. Recognizing his voice, they responded with a cry;
out of affection for their son, they said, “Dear Sāma, there is an obstacle here, do not come!
Following the sound, they came to him of their own accord. He asked, “For what reason have your eyes been destroyed?”
“Father, we did not know; while it was raining, we were standing at the foot of a tree on top of an anthill, and then we could not see.
As soon as this was said, he realized, “There must be a venomous snake there; it must have been released by that angry creature as a nasal blast.
Then, saying, “Do not worry, I shall look after you,” he led his parents to the hermitage and [prepared] their places for moving about, such as their night-quarters and day-quarters.
He bound them with a rope. From then on, having settled them in the hermitage, he would gather forest roots and various fruits;
at dawn, he would sweep their dwelling place, fetch drinking water, and provide water for washing.

Having given them tooth-sticks and water for rinsing the mouth, he would offer sweet fruits and other produce. Once they had finished rinsing their mouths, he himself would eat; then [he would attend to] his mother and father.
Having paid homage to them, he remained not far from them, thinking, "What indeed are these people commanding?

And because he cultivated loving-kindness (*maitrī*) extensively, sentient beings became non-repulsive to him. Just as the sentient beings were [non-repulsive] to him, so too was that Bodhisatta non-repulsive to sentient beings.
Thus, even as he went day after day into the forest for the sake of fruits, he remained there.
Even when he came, he was surrounded by herds of deer. Even hostile creatures such as lions and tigers were extremely confident in his presence;
moreover, through the power of his loving-kindness (*mettā*), the various animals in his dwelling place attained a state of mutual gentleness of heart.
Thus, through the power of loving-kindness toward all, he was fearless and undaunted, like a Brahmā.
He dwelt free from enmity. Therefore it was said: “In the forest, he extended loving-kindness even toward lions and tigers,” and so forth.
In this context, the *ma*-kāra in the word *mettāyamupanāmayi* serves as a phonetic conjunction (*padasandhikara*).

The intended meaning is that through the cultivation of loving-kindness (*mettābhāvanā*), he pervaded even the lions and tigers of cruel deeds, let alone other beings. Alternatively, *mettā ayati* means that loving-kindness proceeds or functions.
By this [verse], "mettāyo" means the cultivation of loving-kindness (*mettābhāvanā*). I directed that loving-kindness toward beings;
I extended it without limitation. There is also a reading, "sīhabyagghehi. Its meaning is as follows:

not only toward me, but also toward the lions and tigers in the forest—in that great forest where I was dwelling at that time—I maintained loving-kindness toward all beings together with those lions and tigers.
I offered [it]. He shows that even lions and tigers at that time attained a mind of loving-kindness toward beings through my power, let alone other creatures.
112. "With deer, antelopes, and boars" means with both deer and wild boars. "Having surrounded" means having made myself surrounded by these, I dwelt in that forest.
113. Now, in order to show the benefits obtained through his own cultivation of loving-kindness (*mettā-bhāvanā*) and its ultimate perfection, he spoke this concluding verse:

"No one is afraid of me. Its meaning is as follows: no being whatsoever—even one of a timid nature, such as a cat or a wildcat—is afraid of me or terrified by me; nor am I [afraid] of any wild animal, such as a lion or a tiger.
"I do not fear anyone at all—not from a *yakkha*, a non-human being, a hunter, or a blood-thirsty man. Why?

Because, firmly established by the power of loving-kindness (*mettā*) and supported by the majesty of the perfection of loving-kindness (*mettā-pāramitā*) cultivated over a long time, I then delight and take pleasure in that great forest, in that vast wilderness. The rest is easily understood.
Thus, while the Great Being was extending loving-kindness toward all beings and carefully attending to his parents,
one day he brought sweet fruits from the forest, placed them at the hermitage, and after paying homage to his parents,
said, "I shall return having taken water. Surrounded by a herd of deer, he joined two deer together and placed a water-jar upon their backs.
Setting her down and taking her by the hand, he went to a river crossing.
At that time, a king named Pīḷiyakkha was ruling in Bārāṇasī. Out of greed for deer meat, he had his mother take over the kingdom;
then, equipped with the five weapons, he entered the Himālaya mountains. Wandering about killing deer, eating their flesh, and roaming the woods, he reached a river known as Migasammata.
Gradually, Sāma arrived at a ford for taking drinking water. Seeing the tracks of wild animals, he went along;
seeing him proceeding in that manner, [the hunter] thought: "I have never before seen a man wandering in this way for so long.
Is he a deva or a nāga? If I approach and question him, he might suddenly flee."
Thinking, "What if I were to pierce him and weaken him before questioning him? the Great Being bathed, put on his bark garment,
draped his antelope skin over one shoulder, filled a water jar, and while lifting it to place it upon his left shoulder, he thought,
"Now is the time to pierce him," and struck him on the right side with an arrow smeared with poison.
The deer emerged from the left side. Knowing that he had been struck, the herd of deer fled in fear.
But the wise Sāma, although wounded, did not spill the water-jar in any way;
instead, establishing mindfulness, he lowered it gently, covered it with sand, set it down, and determined the direction toward the place where his parents lived.
Having laid his head down and vomited blood from his mouth, he said, "I have no enemy at all,
nor do I have any enmity toward anyone," and spoke this verse:
"Who indeed has pierced me with an arrow, while I was heedless, carrying water?"
“A khattiya, a brahmin, or a vessa—who is this that, having been pierced by me, hides away?
Hearing this, the king thought: “Even though he was struck by me and cast down to the earth, he neither reviles nor insults me;
rather, as if stroking the flesh of my own heart, he addresses me with endearing words. I shall go into his presence.”
Having reflected and approached him, he revealed his own identity and asked the Great Being, "Who are you, and whose son are you?
He replied, "I am named Sāma, the son of the hunter-chief named Dukūla-Paṇḍita; why, then, do you strike me?"
He said: Having first uttered the falsehood, "I mistook him for a deer," and having lamented, "I have pierced this innocent man for no reason," he revealed the truth as it was.
He asked for the dwelling place of the boy's parents, went there, and after revealing himself to them, he was received with hospitality by them. He then said, "Sāma has been pierced by me."
Overcome with grief, they lamented; but he, having comforted them by saying, "Having performed whatever service is to be done for Sāma, I shall attend upon you," brought them into Sāma's presence.
Having gone there and lamented in various ways, they placed their hands upon his chest and said, "Heat still courses through my son’s body; it is not due to the force of the poison—"
Thinking, "He will fall into unconsciousness; let us perform an act of truth for the sake of his recovery from this state of poison," they said:
"Whatever merit has been performed by me and by my father—by all that wholesome deed, may the poison be destroyed in Sāma."
Mātarā said: “Whatever merit has been performed, both by me and by my mother—
by all that wholesome deed, may the poison be destroyed for Sāma.”
“Father,
I have dwelt for a long time on Mount Gandhamādana;
there is no one else more dear to me than Sāma.”
“By this utterance of truth, may Sāma’s poison be destroyed!
As soon as the deity had performed this act of truth (*saccakiriyā*), the Great Being quickly arose.
Like a drop of water on a lotus leaf, the affliction was cast off and vanished. The site of the wound became healthy and returned to its natural state. [Thus it was for] his mother and father.

Their eyes were restored. Thus, the Great Being’s recovery from illness, his parents’ regaining of their sight, the rising of the dawn, and the fact that all four of them remained right there in the hermitage—all occurred at one and the same moment.
Then the Great Being, having exchanged greetings with the king, said: “Practice the Dharma, O Great King,” and so forth.
Having taught the Dhamma and further exhorted him, he gave him the five precepts.
He, having received that exhortation with his head bowed in reverence, paid homage and went to Bārāṇasī; there, performing meritorious deeds such as giving alms, he became destined for heaven.
The Bodhisatta, together with his mother and father, developed the higher knowledges and the meditative attainments, and at the end of his life, he was reborn in the Brahma-world.

At that time, King [Brahmadatta] was the Elder Ānanda, the celestial maiden was Uppalavaṇṇā, Sakka was Anuruddha, his father was the Elder Mahākassapa, his mother was Bhaddakāpilānī, and the wise Sāma was the Lord of the World.
The remaining perfections (pāramīs) should be extracted according to the method explained below.

Likewise, even when pierced by a poison-tipped arrow entering through his right side and passing through to his left, he did not exhibit any bodily reaction, just as [the heat of a flame does not affect] a water jar.
The following qualities and powers should be made manifest: placing [the child] on the ground; the absence of mental agitation even when the executioner is unknown, as if he were known;
addressing him with affectionate words; merely lamenting, "I am declining in merit from serving my parents";
and, once the boy was born healthy, establishing compassion and loving-kindness toward the king and giving a Dhamma teaching and advice. Such are the qualities and powers that must be revealed.
The commentary on the Suvaṇṇasāma Cariyā is finished.
14. Commentary on the Ekarāja Cariyā: 114.
Regarding the phrase "renowned as Ekarāja," he was well-known throughout the surface of Jambudīpa by this name, which is descriptive of his actual nature.
For at that time, the Mahāsatta was reborn as the son of the King of Bārāṇasī.
Having reached maturity and attained mastery in all the arts, he ruled the kingdom upon his father’s passing.

Due to his possession of extraordinary qualities—such as skillful conduct, virtue, right behavior, faith, and wisdom—which were not shared by others, and because of his cultivation of the perfections (pāramīs), he was peerless on the surface of Jambudīpa. Consequently, through his preeminence, he was known by the descriptive name “The Sole King” (Ekarāja).

"Ahosi. "Having resolved upon the supreme virtue" means: having resolved upon and practiced the supreme, most excellent virtue of the ten paths of wholesome action—which consists of the perfectly pure restraint of body and speech as well as the perfectly pure conduct of mind—both by way of formal undertaking and by way of non-transgression.
"I shall rule over a great assembly" [means] over a [gathering] extending three hundred yojanas.
I rule over a great territory in the kingdom of Kāsi; I exercise sovereignty. 115.

Regarding the ten courses of wholesome action (*dasakusalakammapatha*): from abstaining from taking life up to right view—within these ten kinds of wholesome courses of action, I abide having undertaken them in their entirety. Regarding the four bases of sympathy (*saṅgahavatthu*): generosity...

The connection is as follows: when I was renowned as "the Sole King," by means of these four bases of sympathy (*saṅgahavatthu*)—which are the causes for gathering people, namely, kind speech, beneficial conduct, and impartiality—I gathered the great multitude according to their respective needs. 116.
Thus, [it refers to] the fulfillment of the virtue of the ten paths of wholesome action and the gathering of the great multitude through the four bases of sympathy.
"In this manner" refers to the way already described.

"For one who is heedful" means for me, who am heedful regarding that which is to be attended to in this world—in matters pertaining to the present life—and regarding that which is to be attended to in the next world—in matters pertaining to future lives.
"Dabbasena" is the name of the King of Kosala. "Having approached" means...

Having arrayed a fourfold army and set out on an expedition to seize my kingdom, he was "seizing my city by force," that is, taking my city of Bārāṇasī by means of military might. Herein, this is the sequential account:
at that time, the Great Being had stationed four [guards] at the four gates of the city and one in the center.
Having constructed six alms-halls—one at the gate of each residence—he bestowed gifts upon the poor, the destitute, and others;

he observed moral discipline, performed the Uposatha rites, and, endowed with patience, loving-kindness, and compassion, he ruled the kingdom according to the Dhamma, gladdening all beings as if he were delighting a son sitting on his own lap. One of his ministers...
Having corrupted the inner court, he later became publicly known for it. The ministers informed the king.
The king, investigating the matter and having personally ascertained the truth, summoned that minister and said: "Blind fool, you have done what is improper;
you do not deserve to dwell within my realm. Take your own wealth, your children, and your wife, and go elsewhere."
"Go! he said, and banished him from the kingdom.
He went to the Kosala country and, while attending upon the Kosalan king named Dabbasena, gradually became his trusted confidant.
One day, he said to that king: "Your Majesty, the kingdom of Bārāṇasī is like a mass of honey free from flies."
“The king is too mild; you are able to seize that kingdom with ease.
Disbelieving those words due to the great majesty of the King of Bārāṇasī, Dabbasena dispatched men to carry out the plundering of villages and other such acts in the Kāsi country.
Upon hearing that those thieves had been released by the Bodhisattva after he gave them wealth, [Dabbasena thought], “He is exceedingly righteous.”
Knowing that he was the king, and thinking, "I shall seize the kingdom of Bārāṇasī," he set out taking a great army with him.
Then, when the great warriors of the King of Bārāṇasī heard that the King of Kosala was coming,
they said to their own king, "Let us strike and capture him before he even crosses our royal boundary."
The Bodhisatta said, “Dear ones, there is no need for others to trouble themselves on my account; let those who desire the kingdom take it, do not go,” and thus he restrained them.
The King of Kosala entered the middle of the country. The great warriors spoke to the king in the same manner once more.
The king restrained them in the same way as before. Standing outside the city, Dabbasena said, “The kingdom—”
He sent a message to Ekarāja, saying, "Either give me battle or [surrender]. Ekarāja sent back a reply, saying, "I will not give battle;
take the kingdom. Again the great warriors said, "Your Majesty, we do not allow the King of Kosala to enter the city;
let us strike him down and capture him while he is still outside the city. The king, in the same manner as before, [acted].
Having closed the city gates and caused them to be barred, he sat cross-legged upon the great terrace.
Dabbasena, having entered the city with a vast army and seeing not even a single adversary, took possession of the entire kingdom.
He went to the royal palace, ascended the great terrace, had the Bodhisatta—who was innocent—seized, and cast him into a pit.
He had it buried. Therefore it was said:
“Dabbasena, having approached and plundering my city, [plundered] the royal dependents in the market towns, along with the army, the staff, and the entire kingdom.”
"Having brought everything into his hands, he buried me in a pit of kāsū grass.
In that passage, "those who live off the king" refers to ministers, members of the assembly, brahmins, householders, and others who depend upon the king for their livelihood.

"In the town" means among the townspeople (*negama*). "Those standing with the army" (*sabalatthā*) refers to those who stand within the military force because they belong to the army; these are the elephant-riders and so forth.
"With the army and the officials" means together with the army and the officials. "With the district" means together with the province;
having brought under his control the towns dependent on the king and everything else, he said, "He has buried me in a pit.
Having seized my entire kingdom along with the army and the vehicles, he had me buried in a pit up to my neck. Also in the *Jātaka*: [it says...]
“Having formerly enjoyed supreme sensual pleasures as a sole monarch, he is now cast into a difficult hell;
yet he does not abandon his former beauty and strength. Thus is the state of being cast into a pit described.
However, in the *Jātakaṭṭhakathā*, it is stated: “Having had him placed in a sling, they suspended him head-downwards from the top of a rampart.”

The Great Being, having cultivated loving-kindness toward the king of thieves, performed the preliminary exercises for the kasiṇas, and having attained the jhānas and higher knowledges (abhiññā), rose up from his seat and sat cross-legged in the air. Thus it was said:
“Behold my circle of ministers, my kingdom, and my prosperous harem, which have been seized after being taken away—just as one might look upon a beloved son.”
In this context, "the circle of ministers" (*amaccamaṇḍala*) refers to those who, in various royal affairs, act together with the king (*amā*);
or it is the circle, that is, the assembly, of such people. "Prosperous" (*phīta*) means a kingdom flourishing with armies, vehicles, cities, provinces, and so forth;
it is also prosperous with the women's quarters, female and male slaves, attendants, and the requisites for enjoyment such as clothing and ornaments.
When I looked upon my enemy king— who had seized my inner palace and was taking what was not given—
with the same loving-kindness (*mettā*) that I would have shown toward my own dear son, there was no one equal to me in such a state of loving-kindness in the entire world. Therefore,
the intention is that this perfection of loving-kindness of mine has thus reached the state of a supreme perfection (*paramatthapāramī*).
But when the Great Being had thus radiated loving-kindness toward that king of thieves and was seated cross-legged in the air, a burning heat arose in the thief’s body.
He rolled back and forth on the ground, crying out, “I am burning! I am burning!
When asked, “What is this? he replied, “Great King, you had a righteous king who was innocent buried in a pit.”
“Go then with speed and rescue him,” he said. The men went and, seeing the king sitting cross-legged in the air, returned and reported this to Dabbasena.
He went in haste, paid homage, and asked for forgiveness, saying, “Rule your own kingdom yourselves; I shall ward off the thieves from you,” and then [addressed] that wicked minister.
Having caused the royal decree to be issued, he departed. The Bodhisatta, too, having handed over the kingdom to his ministers, went forth into the ascetic life of an *isi*;
and having established the great multitude in virtues such as moral discipline (*sīla*), at the end of his lifespan, he was destined for the Brahma-world.
At that time, Dabbasena was the Elder Ānanda, and Ekarāja was the Protector of the World (the Buddha).

Day after day, by bestowing six hundred thousand [pieces of gold] at the six halls of almsgiving and by renouncing his entire kingdom to his enemy king, he fulfilled the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramī*).

By means of constant observance of the precepts and the Uposatha rites, and through the complete restraint of moral conduct as one who had gone forth, he fulfilled the perfection of virtue (*sīlapāramī*).

Through the state of having gone forth and the attainment of meditative absorption (*jhāna*), he fulfilled the perfection of renunciation (*nekkhammapāramī*). And by means of investigating what is beneficial and harmful for sentient beings...
The perfection of wisdom (*paññā-pāramī*) consists in the maintenance of generosity, virtue, and so forth;

the perfection of energy (*vīriya-pāramī*) consists in the exertion for the accumulation of merit such as generosity and the dispelling of sensual thoughts and the like; the perfection of patience (*khanti-pāramī*) consists in the endurance of offenses, as in the case of King Dabbasena and his wicked minister;

the perfection of truth (*sacca-pāramī*) consists in not deceiving others through acts such as giving in accordance with one's promise; and [the perfection of renunciation] consists in [the relinquishing of] generosity and so forth...
The perfection of determination (*adhiṭṭhāna-pāramī*) is by way of the firm resolve of unwavering commitment;

the perfection of loving-kindness (*mettā-pāramī*) is by way of bringing about exclusive benefit even toward enemies and by way of the generation of the meditative absorption of loving-kindness (*mettā-jhāna*);

and [the perfection of equanimity] is by way of maintaining neutrality toward the assistance rendered by one’s own ministers and others who seek one’s welfare when one has been wronged by a wicked minister such as Dabbasena, as well as toward an enemy king at the time one has attained the happiness of sovereignty.
The perfection of equanimity (upekkhā-pāramī) is to be understood through the state of even-mindedness when cast into hell at the time of being thrown there. For this has been said:
"O Lord of Men, having dispelled happiness with suffering, or suffering with happiness, endure what is difficult to bear;
for the virtuous, because they are fully quenched in both respects, remain the same in both happiness and suffering."
However, because the perfection of loving-kindness (*mettā-pāramī*) is preeminent here, that very text was included in order to illustrate its significance.
Likewise, in this context, the specific qualities of the Great Being—such as his equal compassion toward all beings as if toward his own biological son—should be extracted.
The commentary on the Conduct of the Single King is concluded.
The Perfection of Loving-kindness is concluded.
15. Commentary on the Great Hair-raising Deed (Mahālomahaṃsacariyā). 119.
Regarding the fifteenth [deed], "I made my bed in the charnel ground," this is the sequential account:
For at that time, the Mahāsatta, having been reborn into a family of great and magnificent wealth, grew up and lived as a student under a world-renowned teacher.
Having attained mastery in all arts, he returned to his family home;
and although his relatives requested him to establish a household upon the passing of his parents, he—by way of reflecting on impermanence—refused.

With a sense of spiritual urgency increasing toward all states of existence, having acquired the perception of the foulness of the body and not entering the thicket of defilements overcome by the shackles of household life, he further cultivated his long-accustomed inclination toward renunciation.
Desiring to go forth after abandoning his great mass of wealth, he thought again: "If I am to go forth..."
“I shall become renowned for my accumulation of virtues.
Loathing gain and honor, yet not having gone forth into homelessness, he reflected, “I am capable of remaining unperturbed amidst gain and loss and the like,” and thus,
specifically fulfilling the practice of enduring insults from others and so forth, he [practiced] the perfection of equanimity (*upekkhāpāramitā*).
Thinking, “I shall reach the very pinnacle,” he departed from his home wearing only the garment he had on.

Although his life was one of supreme austerity, appearing weak and feeble, he wandered through villages, market towns, and royal capitals for only a single night’s stay at a time, treated with contempt and disdain by others in a manner that showed no regard for him.
Yet, wherever he encountered great humiliation, there he would remain for a long time.

He lived there. When his lower garment wore out, he used a piece of rag; when that too wore out, not accepting anything given by anyone else, he went about merely to cover his private parts with shame.
As time passed in this manner, he went to a certain market town.
There, some village boys—of a rogue disposition, fond of mischief and quarrels, and some being the sons, grandsons, or slaves of royal favorites—[encountered him].
They were arrogant, haughty, fickle, talkative, and loose-tongued; from time to time they wandered about, full of playfulness.

Seeing poor, elderly men and women passing by, they would scatter ashes over their backs from a bag, hang *ketakī* leaves from their waistbands, and by such means, turning them around and looking at them, they displayed their vulgar playfulness.

They mocked him. Seeing those young ruffians wandering about in that town in such a manner, the Great Man thought, "Ah, now I have found the means for fulfilling the perfection of equanimity (upekkhā-pāramī)," and he remained there.
Upon seeing him, those young ruffians began to act with hostility toward him.
The Great Being, unable to endure it and as if being tormented by them, rose up and went away. They followed after him.

Being pursued by them, thinking, "There is no one here who can turn back," he went to a cemetery, made a pillow of bones, and lay down. The wicked boys also went there and spat upon him and did other such things.
Having caused various kinds of disturbances, they depart. In this way, they do so day after day.
However, those who are wise men see them acting in this manner;
having restrained them and recognizing, "This ascetic is of great power, a great yogi," they offer him sublime honor and respect. But the Great Being remains exactly the same in all circumstances.
He becomes neutral. Therefore it is said: “I make my bed in the charnel ground,” and so forth.
Therein, regarding the phrase “I make my bed in the charnel ground, taking a corpse-bone as a reference”:

in a fresh charnel ground, from among the bones scattered here and there by dogs, jackals, and other animals after a carcass has been discarded, one takes a single bone and makes it a pillow for the head.
"Because of having an equal mind toward both the pure and the impure, I make my bed—that is, I lie down—in that charnel ground.

"Village boys" means village children. "Displaying various forms" means that through indecent play such as spitting, mocking, and leering, and by thrusting sticks into their ear canals and so forth, they cause many kinds of excessive and manifold bodily distortions.
120. "Others" refers to some among those very village boys.
"They presented various offerings" means that, observing him closely—thinking, "While these others are performing such a display of misconduct out of contempt, he shows no sign of agitation;
what will his reaction be toward honor?"—they presented many various kinds of perfumes, garlands, food, and other gifts and tokens of respect.

They bring [it] and offer it. Or else, other wise people, seeing those village children of improper conduct who were causing him such various disturbances, thought, "He is not angry with them even as they act in this way;

on the contrary, he maintains only patience, loving-kindness, and compassion toward them—oh, what a marvelous person! And being delighted, they said, "Indeed, much must have been done by these who have acted improperly toward him..."
Thinking, "He has been devoted to demerit," with minds filled with agitation, they brought and presented many perfumes, garlands, various kinds of food,
and other offerings. "Those who bring me suffering" refers to those village children who bring and present physical pain to my body.

“*Upadahantī*” is also a reading, meaning “producing. And those who give me happiness refers to those wise persons who give me—my own—happiness, bringing me pleasure through various requisites such as garlands, perfumes, and food.
“I am equal toward all” means that because no transformation arises in any situation whatsoever, there is equanimity of mind even toward diverse things.

"I am equal to those people; I become one and the same. He shows that he is equal toward all because "neither compassion nor anger exists in me"—that is, because neither compassion, consisting of a mind of loving-kindness (*mettā*) toward those who help, nor anger, consisting of mental malice (*manopadosa*) toward those who harm, exists in him.
Thus, he demonstrates that he is equal toward everyone.

122. Now, in order to demonstrate that at that time his mind was equanimous toward beings who had helped him and those who had harmed him, that there was no change in him despite the vast accumulation of the equipment of knowledge he had gathered, and that he remained unsullied by the worldly conditions (*lokadharma*), the Blessed One spoke this concluding verse:
"He was like a scale in both pleasure and pain."

In this context, "pleasure and pain" (*sukhadukkha*) refers to both pleasure and pain. "Become like a scale" (*tulābhūta*) means that, like a scale held evenly, one has become equanimous by avoiding depression and elation;

it should be understood that by the mention of pleasure and pain, gain and loss—which serve as their causes—are also included. "In fame" (*yasesu*) means in reputations. "In disrepute" (*ayasesu*) means in blame. "In all cases" (*sabbattha*) means in all these things beginning with pleasure.
Regarding worldly conditions: thus the Blessed One, having praised his own state of equanimity— which is not shared by any other— toward all beings and all worldly conditions at that time,
and thereby clarifying how he had reached the pinnacle of the perfection of equanimity (*upekkhā-pāramī*) within that very existence,
concluded the teaching with the words, "This is my perfection of equanimity."

Here too, for the Mahāsatta, first is the perfection of giving (*dānapāramī*), which consists specifically in the relinquishing of all wealth and the relinquishing of one’s own person through a state of non-attachment,
thinking, "Let whoever takes this body do with it whatever they desire.
Then there is the perfection of virtue (*sīlapāramī*), which is the non-doing of everything that ought not to be done, such as base actions and the like.

For one who has turned away from the gratification of sensual desires and has gone forth from the household life, the cultivation of the perception of foulness regarding the body is the perfection of renunciation;

the skill in grasping the qualities that assist the requisites for full enlightenment and in abandoning their opposites, as well as the contemplation of the true nature of phenomena without error, is the perfection of wisdom;
and the dispelling of thoughts of sensual desire and so forth, as well as the fortitude in enduring suffering, [constitute the perfection of energy].
The perfection of energy (*vīriya-pāramī*); all forms of patience that endure [hardships] constitute the perfection of patience (*khanti-pāramī*);

verbal truth and the truth of non-deception through one’s commitments constitute the perfection of truth (*sacca-pāramī*); the firm resolve and commitment to blameless qualities constitutes the perfection of resolve (*adhiṭṭhāna-pāramī*);

the state of loving-kindness and compassion toward all beings without exception is the perfection of loving-kindness (*mettā-pāramī*); and his perfection of equanimity (*upekkhā-pāramī*) is likewise according to what has already been described.

"Should be known" means that the ten perfections (pāramīs) are found [here]. And because the perfection of equanimity (upekkhā-pāramī) is preeminent in this instance, it alone has been brought forward in the teaching.
Likewise, here the Great Being’s departure from the home—resembling the Great Renunciation—after abandoning a vast mass of wealth and a great circle of kinsmen;
and likewise, having thus departed, his [renunciation of] gain and honor...
For one who feels revulsion and wishes to avoid the esteem of others, there is the supreme dwelling in happiness, supreme fewness of desires, delight in seclusion,

indifference toward one’s own body and life through the intention of equanimity, and the endurance of mistreatment inflicted upon oneself by others— all this occurs even without having taken the outward signs of renunciation,
provided one resolves in the mind alone upon the entirety of the virtues of renunciation.
His mode of life was one of supreme effacement; through the attenuation of the defilements that are the adversaries of the requisites for enlightenment,
he was free from attachment to all worldly phenomena— unaffected by praise or blame from others, like those whose taints are exhausted—
due to a state of universal equanimity that arose from the perfection of equanimity (upekkhā-pāramī), which is the pinnacle of all perfections.
"Attaining the crest" and so forth—such manifestations of the power of his virtues are to be understood.
The commentary on the Great Hair-Sacrifice Conduct is finished.
The Perfection of Equanimity is finished.
The commentary on the third chapter is finished.

Regarding the commentary on the summary verse (*uddānagāthā*) beginning with “Yudhañjaya”: therein, by means of the term *bhisa* (lotus root), the Great Golden Conduct (*mahākañcanacariya*) is [indicated].
He shows this. By the name "Soṇananda," he shows the conduct of the wise Soṇa. Likewise, by the designation "Mūgapakkha," he shows the conduct of the wise Temiya.
By way of the perfection of equanimity (*upekkhā-pāramī*), he shows the conduct of Mahālomahaṃsa.
"Thus it was spoken by the Great Seer"—just as it is being taught to you now, Sāriputta, so too was it [spoken] by this method.
The meaning is: "At that time, when I was a Bodhisatta, I searched for the great requisites of enlightenment, such as the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*) and so forth;

what was 'dwelt,' 'practiced,' 'conducted,' and 'followed' by me—that is, what occurred—has now been brought together here, both what is explicitly stated and what is unstated, concerning my own difficult deeds performed over a long period through the fulfillment of the perfections (*pāramitā*), for the sake of which [I acted]."
That [suffering] has been set forth; and in order to show it concisely, he spoke the verse beginning with "Thus manifold.

Therein, "thus" (evaṃ) means by the method already stated. "Manifold suffering" (bahubbidhaṃ dukkhaṃ) refers to the various kinds of suffering experienced during the time of Akitti Paṇḍita and others, such as subsisting on leaves of the *kāra* tree and so forth, and the suffering resulting from giving those to beggars and the subsequent deprivation of food. Likewise...
In the time of the Kuru kings and others, there were various kinds of prosperity equal to the attainment of Sakka.
Regarding "from existence to existence" (*bhavābhava*), this refers to both minor and major existences.

Or, having experienced increases and decreases from existence to existence, being neither distressed by manifold sufferings nor dragged away by manifold prosperities, he remained solely intent upon fulfilling the perfections (*pāramitā*).
Having sacrificed and practiced the corresponding conduct, I have attained the supreme, unsurpassed, and perfect enlightenment (sammāsambodhi), which is omniscience;
the meaning is that "I have realized it.
Now, for the sake of fulfilling those perfections (pāramīs) for which this difficult course of conduct was practiced for a long time, [I shall describe them] without exception.
In order to demonstrate the state of perfection and the fact that he himself had attained the fruit to be reached by means of that [perfection], it was said:
"Having given the gift that ought to be given, having fulfilled morality without remainder," and so forth.
Therein, "having given the gift that ought to be given" refers to the supreme vehicle of practice for the purpose of awakening to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment at that time.

The meaning is: having completely fulfilled, without exception, the giving that is divided into the perfection of giving (*dānapāramī*), the near-perfection of giving (*upapāramī*), and the ultimate perfection of giving (*paramatthapāramī*)—which consists of external objects of gift such as kingdoms and so forth, and internal objects such as the sacrifice of one's own self, culminating in the five great sacrifices (*mahāpariccāga*)—by the Mahābodhisatta who has set out [on the path].
In this regard, during the time of the Brahmin Akitti and the time of the Brahmin Saṅkha...

In these and other such cases—whether they occurred in the past or have yet to come—in times such as the era of the merchant Visayha and the time of Velāma, there is no limit to the number of existences in which the Great Being fulfilled the perfection of giving.
However, it was during his birth as the Wise Hare that he said:
"Seeing one who had approached for alms, I surrendered my own body."
“There is no one equal to me in giving; this is my perfection of giving.

Thus, for one who practices self-sacrifice in this way, the perfection of giving becomes what is called a perfection in the ultimate sense (*paramattha-pāramī*). As for the others, however, they should be understood as perfections (*pāramī*) or near-perfections (*upapāramī*) according to their respective suitability.
“Having fulfilled morality without remainder”: likewise, bodily restraint, verbal restraint, and both bodily and verbal restraint in their entirety.
By one fulfilling the bodhisatta’s virtue— consisting of restraint, restraint of the sense faculties, moderation in eating, and a perfectly pure livelihood— one must fulfill all virtue,

which is divided into the perfection of virtue (*sīlapārami*), the near-perfection of virtue (*sīla-upapārami*), and the ultimate perfection of virtue (*sīlaparamattha-pārami*). Having fulfilled and properly accomplished all this virtue, even here [in this life], as in the time of the virtuous Nāga King and the time of the Campeyya Nāga King.

In such instances as these—whether referring to those already mentioned or yet to come, such as the time of the Great Monkey and the time of the Six-Tusked Elephant—there is no limit to the number of existences in which the Great Being fulfilled the perfection of virtue (*sīlapāramitā*). However, during his time as Saṅkhapāla, it was said:
"Even while being pierced by stakes, or even while being crushed by spears..."
“I am not angry with the son of a Bhoja;

this is my perfection of virtue (sīlapāramī). Thus, for one who makes such a sacrifice of self, the perfection of virtue becomes what is called the ultimate perfection (paramatthapāramī). As for the others, the perfections (pāramīs) and secondary perfections (upapāramīs) should be understood accordingly.
“Having reached the perfection in renunciation” means having reached the supreme excellence (paramukkaṃsa) in the threefold Great Renunciation.
Having gone there—among those such as Yudhañjaya at the time of Somanassa Kumāra, and others who have already come here or are yet to come, such as Hatthipāla at the time of Maghadeva and so forth;
for those who, having renounced great sovereignty, fulfilled the perfection of renunciation (*nekkhamma-pāramī*) throughout their successive existences, there is no limit to their number.
However, it was during the time of Cūḷasutasoma that he [reached] absolute certainty.
“I cast away the great kingship that had come into my hand like a globule of spittle;
for one who relinquishes it, there is no clinging—this is my perfection of renunciation.

Thus, as he departed after casting away the kingdom with total detachment, his perfection of renunciation became known as a perfection of the ultimate meaning (*paramattha-pāramī*). In the other cases, however, the perfections (*pāramī*) and secondary perfections (*upapāramī*) should be understood according to their respective contexts.

"Having questioned the wise" means: having questioned the wise and sagacious regarding the classification of wholesome and unwholesome states—such as "What is wholesome? What is unwholesome? What is blameworthy?

What is blameless?"—and regarding the classification of karma and its fruit, as well as those things that bring benefit to beings, such as blameless fields of action, fields of craft, and branches of knowledge (*vijjāṭṭhāna*).
By this, he demonstrates the perfection of wisdom (*paññāpāramī*). In that regard, during the time of Vidhura Paṇḍita:

There is no limit to the number of existences in which he fulfilled the perfection of wisdom during such times as those of the sage Mahāgovinda, the sage Kudāla, the sage Araka, the wanderer Bodhi, and the sage Mahosadha. However, it was entirely during the time of the sage Senaka that he said:
“Discerning with wisdom, O Brahmin, I liberated the brahmin from suffering.”
“There is no one equal to me in wisdom; this is my perfection of wisdom.
Thus, for one who showed the snake that had entered inside his own belly, the perfection of wisdom became known as the ultimate perfection (*paramattha-pāramī*).
“Having exerted supreme energy” means the supreme striving (*padhāna*) which is energy, capable of reaching full enlightenment (*sammāsambodhi*).
Having performed and brought forth various perfections of energy (*vīriya-pāramī*).

In this regard, there is no limit to the number of existences in which he fulfilled the perfection of energy during such times as his birth as the noble king Mahāsīla, as the youth Pañcāvudha, and as the great lord of monkeys;
however, it was exclusively during his birth as Mahājanaka that—
“Failing to see the [other] shore in the midst of the water, all the men were destroyed;
there was no alteration in my mind—this is my perfection of energy.
Thus, for one crossing the great ocean, the perfection of energy became known as the perfection in the ultimate sense.

"Having reached the perfection of patience" means: having reached the perfection, the supreme limit, of patience by bringing to fulfillment the excellence of patience—such as patience as endurance (*adhivāsana-khanti*) and so forth; that is to say, having accomplished the perfection of patience.

In this regard, it refers to those existences in which the perfection of patience was fulfilled during his births as the Great Monkey, the King of Elephants, the King of Ruru Deer, the Son of the Devas of Dharma, and so on.
There is no measure [to its extent]. However, at the time when he was a teacher of patience, it was said:
“Even while they were hacking at me with a sharp axe as if I were insentient matter, I felt no anger toward the King of Kāsi; this is my perfection of patience.”
Thus, for one experiencing great suffering as if it were insentient, the perfection of patience (khantipāramī) becomes what is called the ultimate perfection (paramatthapāramī).
"Having made firm the resolve" means having made firm and unshakable the resolve regarding the undertaking of wholesome qualities—
the resolve for the undertaking of each respective perfection and for the undertaking of those practices conducive to them— and thus [fulfilling] each respective vow.
The meaning is: "having resolved with the state of non-retrogression.

In that regard, there is no measurable limit to the number of existences in which he fulfilled the perfection of resolution (adhiṭṭhāna-pāramī) during such times as his birth as Jotipāla, as Sarabhaṅga, as Nemi, and so forth. However, it was certainly during his time as Prince Temiya that he said:
"My mother and father are not to be given away, nor am I myself to be given away."
“Omniscience is dear to me; therefore, I resolved upon the vow.
Thus, for one who has renounced life and resolved upon the vow, that resolution-perfection (*adhiṭṭhāna-pāramī*) becomes what is called the perfection of the ultimate goal (*paramattha-pāramī*).
“Guarding truthful speech”: having guarded truthful speech, even when life was at stake, he avoided ignoble discourse, [treating it] like excrement.
Having avoided [falsehood] as if loathing it, and having guarded his state of being entirely non-deceptive;
therein, there is no limit to the number of existences in which he fulfilled the perfection of truth during such times as his birth as King Kapi, as the ascetic Saccatāpasa, and as King Macchara.
However, it was most preeminently during his time as Mahāsutasoma—
“Protecting my word of truth, even at the cost of my own life, I liberated one hundred kṣatriyas; this is my perfection of truth.
Thus, for one who protects the truth by sacrificing his life, that perfection of truth becomes known as the ultimate perfection (paramattha-pāramī).

"Having reached the perfection of loving-kindness" means having attained the ultimate excellence (paramukkaṃsataṃ) of loving-kindness characterized by the impartial promotion of the welfare of all beings.

In this regard, there is no limit to the number of existences in which he fulfilled the perfection of loving-kindness during such times as his birth as Cūḷadhammapālaka, Mahāsīlavara, and Sāmapaṇḍita. However, it was most pre-eminently during his time as Suvaṇṇasāmaka—
“‘No one terrifies me, nor do I fear anyone at all;
supported by the power of loving-kindness (mettā), I then delight in the forest.
Thus, for him who practiced loving-kindness without regard even for his own life, the perfection of loving-kindness (mettāpāramī) became a perfection in the ultimate sense.”

Regarding "honoring and dishonoring": this means that whether there is honoring through respectful worship and service, or dishonoring through spitting and the like, he remains equal-minded and unperturbed in all worldly conditions (*lokadhamma*).
The meaning is: "I have attained the supreme, unsurpassed state of worthiness.

In this regard, [he remained so] during his time as the Great Lord of Monkeys, during his time as the King of Kāsi, during his time as the Brahmin Khema, and during his time as the Wanderer Aṭṭhisena.

In such instances as these, there is no measure to the number of existences in which he fulfilled the perfection of equanimity (*upekkhā-pāramitā*). But specifically during his time as Mahālomahaṃsa, it was said:
“I make my bed in the charnel ground, with a human skeleton for my pillow;
village girls come and show me their forms, not few in number.”

Thus, even when village boys caused him pleasure and pain by spitting on him and so forth, or by offering garlands, perfumes, and other honors, he never transcended equanimity; for him, this equanimity-parami became known as the ultimate parami. Thus the Blessed One said:
“Having experienced such manifold suffering, And manifold prosperity, In birth after birth, He attained supreme enlightenment.”
Having briefly described the difficult practices he performed himself in order to attain supreme perfect enlightenment during this auspicious aeon (bhaddakappa), he further said:
"Having given the gift that ought to be given, having fulfilled moral conduct without exception,
and having reached perfection in renunciation, he attained supreme enlightenment."
“Having questioned the wise and exerted supreme energy,
having reached the perfection of patience, he attained supreme enlightenment.
Having made firm his resolve and guarded his speech of truth...”
“Having reached the perfection of loving-kindness, he attained supreme enlightenment.
Having become equal toward gain and loss, fame and disrepute,
honor and dishonor— in all things— he attained supreme enlightenment.”
He demonstrates that the ten perfections (pāramitā) have been perfectly fulfilled by himself.

Now, at this point, for the sake of providing skillful insight into the various aspects of the requisites of enlightenment for noble sons who have conceived the aspiration for the practice of the Great Vehicle of Enlightenment, a miscellaneous discourse (pakiṇṇaka-kathā) on all the perfections should be related.
In this regard, the following is the method of questioning: What are these perfections? In what sense are they "perfections"? How many kinds are there? What is their sequence?
What are their characteristics, functions, manifestations, and proximate causes? What is their condition? What is their defilement?
What is their purification? What is their opposite? What is their practice? What is their classification? What is their synthesis? What is the means for their accomplishment?
In what length of time are they accomplished? What is the benefit? And what is their fruit? Here is the answer:

What, then, are these perfections (*pāramī*)? The qualities of giving and so forth, when they are not impaired by craving, conceit, or wrong view, and are embraced by compassion and skillful means, are the perfections.

In what sense are they called "perfections"? Because, through the possession of distinguished qualities such as giving and virtue, Great Beings (*mahāsatta*) are supreme (*parama*) due to their being the highest among beings.
*Bodhisatta*: the state or activity of these [beings] is *pāramī*, namely the practice of giving and so forth. Alternatively, one who "goes beyond" (*paratī*) is *paramo*;
thus a *bodhisatta* is one who fulfills and protects the virtues such as giving. This belongs to the supreme one (*paramassa*), or it is the state or activity of the supreme one;
thus *pāramī* is indeed the practice of giving and so forth. Alternatively, one binds (*mavati*) another being to oneself through the possession of distinguished virtues; [this is a *bodhisatta*].
Or else, it sinks further and is purified from the stains of defilement; or else, it especially reaches (mayati) the supreme (paraṃ), the most excellent (seṭṭhaṃ), Nibbāna;
or else, by means of its distinguished knowledge which has become a standard, it measures (munāti) and delimits the supreme world, just as it does this world;
or else, it measures out (minoti) and places within its own continuum an exceedingly great multitude of qualities such as virtue and the like.
He is called *paramo* because he measures (or weighs) and harms that which is other than his own self—the body of Dhamma—or its opposite, the host of defilements that act as thieves and cause harm.
Or, it should be applied according to the method already stated: "They go to the Supreme One," and so forth.
Alternatively, he rejoices in, purifies himself in, and cleanses beings in *pāra*, which is Nibbāna; or he causes beings to rejoice, be bound, and be joined therein.

It is called *pāramī* because it crosses over (*pāreti*), goes to the further shore (*gacchati*), and causes others to go there (*gameti*); or because it knows that [reality] as it truly is (*munāti*); or because it measures (*minoti*) and places sentient beings therein;
or because it measures—that is, harms—the defilements and enemies of sentient beings therein. Thus, the Great Being (*mahāpurisa*) is the *pāramī*.
Its state or its activity is *pāramitā*, which is simply the practice of giving and the other perfections. In this manner, the meaning of the word *pāramī* should be understood.
How many kinds are there? Briefly, ten kinds. These, moreover, have come down in their specific forms in the Pāḷi itself. As it is said:
“Searching at that time, I saw the first Perfection of Giving, the great path practiced by the Great Sages of old.”
Beginning. And as it is said: “Venerable sir, how many qualities are there that make a Buddha?
Sāriputta, there are ten qualities that make a Buddha. Which ten? Generosity, Sāriputta, is a quality that makes a Buddha;
virtue, renunciation, wisdom, energy, patience, truthfulness, determination, loving-kindness, and equanimity are qualities that make a Buddha.”
“...the Dhamma. These, Sāriputta, are the ten qualities that make a Buddha. This is what the Blessed One said.
Having said this, the Sublime One, the Teacher, further said this:
“Generosity, virtue, renunciation, wisdom, and energy as the fifth;”
“Patience, truth, resolve, loving-kindness, and equanimity—these are the ten.
However, some say they are “sixfold. That statement was made by way of their grouping; that grouping, moreover, will be clarified later. What is their sequence?
Here, “sequence” refers to the order of teaching, and that is based on the order of undertaking [the precepts]. As for the undertaking:
This is based on the cause of analysis; that is, just as they were analyzed and undertaken at the beginning, so too have they been taught.
In this regard, giving is very helpful and easy to perform for the sake of virtue, and thus it was mentioned first. Virtue, when embraced by giving, becomes of great fruit and great benefit;
therefore, virtue was mentioned immediately after giving. Virtue is embraced by renunciation, and renunciation...
Wisdom is embraced by energy; energy is embraced by patience;
patience is embraced by truth; truth is embraced by determination; determination is embraced by loving-kindness;
and loving-kindness, when embraced by equanimity, becomes of great fruit and great benefit. Thus, after loving-kindness, equanimity is mentioned. Furthermore, equanimity is embraced by compassion.
And it should be understood that compassion is embraced by equanimity. But how is it that Bodhisattvas who possess great compassion can be equanimous toward beings?
Some say: "They are equanimous for a time toward those things that require equanimity, but not in all cases and at all times.
Others, however, say: "They are not equanimous toward beings themselves, but they are equanimous toward the misfortunes caused by beings."
Another method: Generosity (*dāna*) is mentioned first because it occurs even among ordinary people, because it is common to all beings, and because it is easy to practice.
Following that, morality (*sīla*) is mentioned because it purifies both the giver and the receiver; because after speaking of benefiting others, it speaks of refraining from harming others;

because after speaking of the phenomena of action (*kiriyadhamma*), it speaks of the phenomena of non-action (*akiriyadhamma*); and because after speaking of the cause for the attainment of wealth, it speaks of the cause for the attainment of existence (*bhava*).

And virtue is stated immediately after giving. Since the attainment of virtue is accomplished through renunciation, after describing good conduct of body and speech, there is the mention of good conduct of mind;

and since meditative absorption (jhāna) is easily achieved by one whose virtue is purified, after describing purity of application through the abandonment of faults in action, there is the mention of purity of disposition through the abandonment of faults in defilement, by means of the abandonment of transgressions.
Renunciation is mentioned immediately after virtue because it is the abandoning of the obsessions of the mind.
Because renunciation is established and purified by wisdom, and because the absence of wisdom is stated to result from the absence of jhāna, it is said:

"Wisdom has concentration as its proximate cause, and concentration has wisdom as its manifestation. This is because, after stating the sign of serenity, the sign of equanimity is subsequently mentioned.
Wisdom is mentioned immediately after renunciation because it is the skillful means for accomplishing the welfare of others through meditation on that welfare;
and because the function of wisdom is fulfilled by the exertion of energy, following the statement of the acceptance of the contemplation of the phenomena of the emptiness of beings,
there is the statement of the wonder of exertion for the benefit of beings, and following the statement of the sign of equanimity, there is the statement of the sign of exertion.

Having spoken of acting with circumspection, and because of the statement regarding exertion, energy is mentioned immediately after wisdom, in accordance with the principle that "the exertion of one who acts with circumspection brings about a distinction in the fruit.

Since endurance is accomplished through energy— "for one possessed of energy, by virtue of having initiated energy, [endures] that which is brought upon by the conditioned phenomena of sentient beings"— ...
“He dwells having overcome suffering. Because endurance is an ornament of energy, it is said: “For one possessed of energy, endurance shines.

Having stated the sign of exertion (*paggaha-nimitta*), the sign of serenity (*samatha-nimitta*) is mentioned; and because it is stated that the fault of restlessness (*uddhacca-dosa*) is abandoned through the acceptance of reflection on the Dhamma (*dhammanijjhānakkhanti*), it is said:
“For through the acceptance of reflection on the Dhamma, the fault of restlessness is abandoned. This is because it is stated that one possessed of energy acts with constancy (*sātaccakaraṇa*).

“For one who abounds in patience is undisturbed and acts with constancy. Because it is stated that for one possessed of diligence there is an absence of craving for a return when undertaking activities for the benefit of others, [the text says]:
“When there is contemplation of phenomena as they truly are, craving does not arise.

Furthermore, because it is stated that even when undertaking the supreme benefit of others, there is endurance of suffering caused by others, patience is mentioned immediately after energy. Through truth, patience is firmly established over a long time; thus, regarding those who cause harm, there is patience toward that harm.
Having spoken thus, because his speech was non-deceptive in performing what was beneficial, and because he did not abandon truthful speech through the unshakability of his words regarding patience,
and because he spoke the truth of reality with knowledge refined by that very patience after having declared the patience that contemplates the dharma of the emptiness of beings,
truth (sacca) is stated immediately after patience.
Because truth is accomplished through resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*), it is said: "For one with unshakable resolution, abstention (*virati*) is perfected.

Because one speaks without contradiction and expresses an unshakable state regarding that [truth], it is said: "One who is true to his word proceeds immovably in accordance with his promise regarding generosity and the other perfections.
Because one speaks of the truth of knowledge (*ñāṇasacca*) and thereby brings the practice of the requisites to completion, it is said: "One who possesses knowledge of things as they truly are..."

For it is said that after truth (*sacca*), resolve (*adhiṭṭhāna*) is mentioned because one resolves upon the requisites for enlightenment and brings them to completion, being unshakable by opposing factors.

Since resolve is established through the undertaking of the resolve to act for the welfare of others via loving-kindness (*mettā*), and because of the statement regarding the bringing about of welfare following the mention of resolve, it is said:
"One who resolves upon the requisites for enlightenment dwells in loving-kindness. This is because of the immovable nature of resolve.

Because loving-kindness (*mettā*) arises from the non-disturbance of one’s undertaking and because it is possible through such an undertaking, loving-kindness is taught immediately after the foundation (*adhiṭṭhāna*).

Having described the bringing about of welfare toward beings through the purification of loving-kindness, and having described equanimity (*upekkhā*) as indifference toward their faults, and having described it as a meditation that flows forth from the meditation on loving-kindness, [equanimity] is taught because it describes a marvelous quality: being equanimous even toward those beings who desire one's welfare.
And since equanimity is said to follow immediately after loving-kindness, their sequence should be understood in this way.
As for their characteristics, functions, manifestations, and proximate causes: here, first of all, without distinction, all the perfections have the characteristic of rendering assistance to others;
their function is to perform service for others, or else their function is to remain unshakable; and they are manifested as the desire for the welfare [of others].
It is manifested as Buddhahood, and its proximate cause is great compassion; alternatively, its proximate cause is compassion and skill in means.
Specifically, however, the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) is the volition of relinquishing oneself and one's requisites when embraced by compassion and skill in means.
Likewise, bodily and verbal good conduct—when embraced by compassion and skill in means—is in fact the volition of abstaining from what should not be done and performing what should be done.

And there is the perfection of virtue (*sīlapāramitā*). The perfection of renunciation (*nekkhammapāramitā*) is the arising of a thought of departure from sensual pleasures and existence, preceded by the vision of their disadvantages and embraced by compassion and skillful means (*upāyakosalla*).
The perfection of wisdom (*paññāpāramitā*) is the realization of the general and specific characteristics of phenomena, embraced by compassion and skillful means.
The perfection of energy (*vīriyapāramitā*) is the undertaking of the welfare of others through body and mind, embraced by compassion and skillful means.

The perfection of patience (*khantipāramitā*) is the arising of a state of consciousness characterized by that mode [of forbearance], consisting primarily of non-hatred, which endures the offenses of sentient beings and conditioned formations while being embraced by compassion and skillful means.
The perfection of truth (*saccapāramitā*) is non-deceitfulness, distinguished by the volition of abstention and so forth, which is embraced by compassion and skillful means.
[The perfection of determination] is the firm resolve of unwavering undertaking, which arises in that same mode [of practice] while being embraced by compassion and skillful means.
The arising of the thought [of enlightenment] is the perfection of resolve (*adhiṭṭhāna-pāramitā*).
The promotion of the welfare and happiness of the world, encompassed by compassion and skillful means, is in substance the perfection of loving-kindness (*mettā-pāramitā*), which is non-malice.

The even engagement toward desirable and undesirable beings and formations, which destroys both attachment and aversion and is encompassed by compassion and skillful means, is the perfection of equanimity (*upekkhā-pāramitā*).
Therefore, the perfection of giving has the characteristic of relinquishing; its function is the destruction of greed for the object to be given;
it is manifested as non-attachment, or alternatively, as the attainment of prosperity in both cyclic existence and the supramundane state; and its proximate cause is the thing to be relinquished.

It has been stated that the perfection of virtue has the characteristic of moral conduct, the characteristic of concentration, and the characteristic of steadfastness; its function is the destruction of immorality.
The perfection of virtue (*sīla-pāramī*) has blamelessness as its characteristic, purity as its manifestation, and moral shame (*hiri*) and moral dread (*ottappa*) as its proximate cause.
