The perfection of renunciation (*nekkhamma-pāramī*) has the characteristic of departing from sensual desire and existence; its function is the discernment of their dangers; it manifests as turning away from them;

and its proximate cause is a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*). The perfection of wisdom (*paññā-pāramī*) has the characteristic of penetrating things according to their true nature; it has the characteristic of unerring penetration.

Or it has the characteristic of penetrating the object like an arrow shot by a skilled archer; its function is to illuminate the object like a lamp; it is manifested as non-delusion like a guide in the forest;
its proximate cause is concentration, or alternatively, the Four Noble Truths.
The Perfection of Energy has the characteristic of exertion; its function is to provide support; it is manifested as non-collapse; its proximate cause is the basis for the arousal of energy.

Or, it has agitation as its proximate cause. The perfection of patience (khantipāramī) has the characteristic of forbearance; its function is to endure the desirable and the undesirable; it is manifested as endurance, or as non-opposition;
and it has the vision of things as they truly are as its proximate cause. The perfection of truth (saccapāramī) has the characteristic of non-deception;
its function is to reveal the true nature of things; it is manifested as goodness; and it has gentleness (soracca) as its proximate cause. Among the requisites for enlightenment...
The perfection of determination (adhiṭṭhāna-pāramī) has the characteristic of resolution; its function is the overcoming of its opposites; it is manifested as unshakability therein;
and its proximate cause is the requisites for enlightenment. The perfection of loving-kindness (mettā-pāramī) has the characteristic of proceeding with a mode of welfare;
its function is the bringing about of welfare, or alternatively, the removal of ill-will; it is manifested as gentleness; and its proximate cause is the perception of beings as being agreeable.

The perfection of equanimity (*upekkhā-pāramī*) has the characteristic of proceeding with a neutral mental attitude; its function is the vision of evenness; it is manifested as the subsiding of aversion and attachment;
and its proximate cause is the reflection on the fact that one is the owner of one's own kamma.

Furthermore, in this context, the fact that generosity and the other perfections are embraced by compassion and skillful means serves as a qualification for their respective characteristics, such as relinquishment.

They should be so described. For it is when acts such as giving, occurring within the mental continuum of a bodhisattva, are embraced by compassion and skillful means that they are called the perfections (pāramīs) of giving and the rest.
What is the condition for them? First, the initial resolution (abhinīhāra) is the condition for the perfections. For this which is—
“Human birth, possession of the male organ, the cause, seeing the Teacher,
Going forth, perfection of virtues, the requisite, and zeal—
Through the convergence of these eight factors, the aspiration succeeds.”
When thus addressed, there arises an aspiration proceeding in such a manner as: "Having crossed over, may I help others cross; being liberated, may I liberate others; being tamed, may I tame others;

being at peace, may I bring others to peace; being comforted, may I comfort others; having attained final Nibbāna, may I lead others to final Nibbāna; being purified, may I purify others; being awakened, may I awaken others.
This is the condition for all the perfections (pāramīs) without distinction. Through its occurrence...
Indeed, for Great Beings (*mahāpuruṣa*), after the perfections (*pāramī*), there arise the stages of discernment, establishment, undertaking, resolution, and fulfillment.
In this context, "humanity" (*manussatta*) means the human state. For it is only by remaining in the human state that the aspiration of one who aspires to Buddhahood succeeds;
it does not succeed for one remaining in the births of *nāgas*, *supaṇṇas*, and so forth. Why is that? Because of the nature of Buddhahood...
Because it is unsuitable.

Regarding "perfection of gender" (*liṅgasampatti*): even for one established in a human existence, the aspiration succeeds only for a male, not for a female, nor for a *paṇḍaka*, a *napuṃsaka*, or a hermaphrodite (*ubhatovyañjanaka*). Why is that? Because of the reasons already stated.
And because of the absence of the fulfillment of the [thirty-two] marks. For this has been said in detail:

"It is impossible, monks, it is out of the question, that a woman should be an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One. Therefore, even for one born as a human being who stands in the female gender, or for those such as eunuchs and the like, their aspiration does not succeed.

"Causes" refers to the perfection of the supporting conditions (*upanissaya-sampatti*). For even in the case of a human male, an aspiration succeeds only through the perfection of causes when one is endowed with supporting conditions, and not otherwise.
"Seeing the Teacher" means being in the presence of the Teacher. For an aspiration succeeds only for one who aspires in the presence of a living Buddha;
however, when the Blessed One has attained final Nibbāna, [it succeeds] either in the presence of a shrine or at the foot of the Bodhi tree.
A wish made before an image, or in the presence of Paccekabuddhas or disciples of the Buddhas, does not succeed.

Why? Because of the absence of strength in the preliminary service (*adhikāra*). However, a wish made in the presence of the Buddhas alone succeeds, because through the loftiness of one's aspiration (*ajjhāsaya*), that preliminary service attains strength.

Regarding "going forth" (*pabbajjā*): even for one who makes a resolution in the presence of the Buddha, the Blessed One, that aspiration succeeds only for one who has gone forth among the ascetics or monks who profess the efficacy of action, and not for one remaining in the garb of a householder. Why?
Because such a state is unsuitable for the attainment of Buddhahood. Indeed, it is only those who have gone forth who, as great bodhisattvas, attain perfect enlightenment.

They attain [these states] while being renunciants, not while being householders; therefore, at the time of making the aspiration, the very sign of renunciation is appropriate, because it serves as the foundation for the perfection of qualities.

"Perfection of qualities" refers to the attainment of qualities such as the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*). For even in the case of one who has gone forth, it is only for one who possesses the eight meditative attainments (*samāpatti*) and the five higher knowledges that [this applies].
The aspiration succeeds, but not for one who is devoid of the attainment of the qualities mentioned above.

Why? Because they lack the capacity to investigate the perfections (*pāramī*). On the contrary, Great Beings (*mahāpurisa*) who have made their resolution and are endowed with the perfection of the decisive support (*upanissaya*) and the perfection of direct knowledge (*abhiññā*) are themselves capable of investigating the perfections.

*Adhikāra* means superior service. For even one endowed with the aforementioned qualities, if he performs superior service at that time by sacrificing even his own life for the Buddhas, only his resolution succeeds, not that of another.

*Chandatā* refers to the wholesome desire to act; for only one who possesses the aforementioned qualities and has a great desire, a great aspiration, and a great will to act for the sake of the qualities that make a Buddha, does [the resolution] succeed, not that of another.
In this regard, here is an illustration of the greatness of his aspiration:

suppose someone, having heard that one who is capable of crossing over and reaching the further shore by the strength of his own arms alone—even if the entire interior of the world-system has become a single body of water—attains Buddhahood;
and not regarding that task as difficult, he conceives an aspiration, thinking, "I shall cross it and go to the further shore. It is not that he does so merely out of pride.

He does not fall into hesitation. Likewise, one who is capable of stepping across and reaching the far side while treading with his feet upon the entire Cakkavāḷa filled with glowing embers from which the flames have subsided and the smoke has vanished… [as before] …does not fall into hesitation there.
Likewise, one who [is capable of crossing] the entire Cakkavāḷa crowded without interval with spears and spikes having very sharp points… [as before] …does not fall into hesitation there.
Treading with his feet, he passes over... [and so on] ...he does not fall into hesitation there.
Likewise, he who is capable of piercing through a whole world-system (*cakkavāḷa*)—dense, covered by thickets of bamboo, and a thicket of forests of thorny creepers—and going to the other side...
[and so on] ...he does not fall into hesitation there. Likewise, he who [for] "four incalculable eons" (*cattāri asaṅkhyeyyāni*)...
Having heard that "after being boiled in hell for a hundred thousand aeons, Buddhahood is to be attained," one does not regard it as difficult;
rather, with the arising of desire, thinking "I shall attain Buddhahood after being boiled there," one does not fall into despondency.
In this manner, the greatness of desire (chanda) is to be understood here.
This aspiration, endowed with these eight factors, should be understood as a state of consciousness that proceeds by the convergence of those eight factors in its essential meaning.
It is characterized by the correct resolution for perfect enlightenment:
"O, may I awaken to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment for the welfare and happiness of all beings."
It has the flavor of aspirations such as "May I bring [them] to completion"; it is manifested by its state of being the cause for the requisites of enlightenment;
its proximate cause (*padatthāna*) is great compassion, or alternatively, the perfection of the necessary conditions (*upanissaya*).

Since it proceeds with reference to the inconceivable plane of Buddhahood and the immeasurable welfare of the world of beings, it is the root of all qualities that produce a Buddha—supremely auspicious, supremely wholesome, and of immeasurable power.
It should be understood as a distinction of merit.

With the arising of this [merit], the Great Being is said to have "embarked upon the practice of the Great Vehicle of Awakening" (*mahābodhiyānapaṭipatti*) because he has attained the state of certainty;
and because his nature is such that he cannot turn back from it, he receives the designation "Bodhisatta," being [destined] for perfect self-awakening in every respect.
His mind becomes fully concentrated, and his capacity for the training that constitutes the equipment for enlightenment becomes firmly established.

For, by the successful fulfillment of the aforementioned resolution—which is the precursor sign to the attainment of omniscient knowledge—Great Beings correctly investigate all the perfections with their self-dependent wisdom, undertake them, and gradually bring them to completion. Thus did the wise Sumedha, having made such a great resolution, [proceed].
He set out in practice. As he said:
“Come now, I shall search here and there for the qualities that make a Buddha—upward, downward, and in the ten directions, as far as the element of phenomena extends.”
"Searching at that time, I saw the first perfection of giving"—this is the detailed account.
Regarding that aspiration, four conditions, four causes, and four powers are to be understood.
In this regard, what are the four conditions? Here, the Great Being sees a Tathāgata with the great majesty of a Buddha.
performing a marvelous and wonderful miracle. Relying on that and making it his object, his mind becomes established upon the Great Enlightenment (Mahābodhi), thinking:

"How truly majestic is this element of Dhamma (dhammadhātu), through the thorough penetration of which the Blessed One possesses such marvelous and wonderful qualities and inconceivable power! He [reflects] upon that very vision of majesty...
Relying upon that condition and making it the basis, one fixes the mind there while resolving toward full enlightenment.
This is the first condition for the Great Resolve.
Furthermore, one does not personally see the aforementioned great majesty of the Tathāgata, but rather hears: "Such is [the Tathāgata]..."
"And such is the Blessed One. Relying on that and making that the condition, he fixes his mind there, resolving upon full enlightenment.
This is the second condition for the Great Resolve.
It may be that he does not see for himself the aforementioned great majesty of the Tathāgata, nor does he hear of it from another.
Furthermore, while the Tathāgata is teaching the Dhamma, one hears a discourse connected with the majesty of the Buddha, beginning with: "Monks, the Tathāgata is endowed with the ten powers.
Relying upon that and making that the condition, one resolves upon full enlightenment and fixes the mind thereon. This is the third condition for the Great Resolve.
He does not indeed see for himself the aforementioned great majesty of the Tathāgata, nor does he hear of it from another, nor does he hear the Dhamma of the Tathāgata;
nevertheless, being of lofty aspiration and resolute in the wholesome, he thinks:
"I shall preserve this lineage of Buddhas, this succession of Buddhas, this tradition of Buddhas, this nature of Buddhas," to whatever extent...
Honoring, revering, esteeming, worshipping, and paying homage to the Dhamma alone,
relying upon it and making it the condition, one fixes the mind there while resolving upon full enlightenment.
This is the fourth condition for the Great Resolve.

In this regard, what are the four causes for the Great Resolve? Here, the Great Being is by nature endowed with the necessary support (*upanissaya*) and has performed meritorious services under previous Buddhas. This is the first cause for the Great Resolve.
Furthermore, the Great Being is by nature inclined toward compassion (*karuṇā*), devoted to compassion, and desirous of removing the suffering of sentient beings.
Furthermore, having sacrificed his own body and life—this is the second cause for the Great Resolve.

Moreover, the Great Being, for the sake of the welfare of beings, remains untiring and undaunted even while striving and exerting himself for an extremely long time in difficult practices throughout the entire cycle of existence, until the fulfillment of his desired goal. This is the third.

This is the cause for the Great Resolve. Furthermore, the Great Man relies upon a spiritual friend who restrains him from what is harmful and establishes him in what is beneficial. This is the fourth cause for the Great Resolve.
In this regard, the Great Man’s perfection of the necessary support is as follows: his aspiration is directed exclusively toward awakening.
He becomes inclined toward full enlightenment and leaning toward full enlightenment, as does his conduct for the welfare of beings.
This is because he has previously made an aspiration for full enlightenment in the presence of former Buddhas, both mentally and verbally, thinking:
"May I too become such a perfectly enlightened Buddha and properly bring about the welfare and happiness of beings. For one who has thus acquired the necessary supporting conditions...
These are the signs of the perfection of the decisive support (*upanissaya*),
endowed with which a Great Man is seen to possess a great distinction and a vast difference from the disciples’ bodhisattvas and the solitary buddhas’ bodhisattvas, both in terms of his faculties,
his practice, and his skill. Here, the Great Man who is endowed with the decisive support possesses clear faculties and clear knowledge.
The others are not like that. He practices for the benefit of others, not for his own benefit.
For he practices for the welfare of the many, for the happiness of the many, out of compassion for the world, and for the good, benefit, and happiness of gods and humans;

the others do not practice in such a way. Furthermore, he brings skill in this regard through spontaneous presence of mind and through proficiency in discerning what is possible and what is impossible.
Likewise, the Great Man is by nature inclined toward giving and delights in generosity; whenever there is something to be given, he gives it and does not shrink from the act of giving.
He is constantly and continuously disposed to sharing, and he gives with joy and reverence, never with an indifferent mind.
Even after giving a great gift, he is not satisfied by that gift, much less so when it is small.
The signs of the Great Being’s perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), whose inclination is toward generosity, are as follows: he speaks in praise of giving while inspiring others;
he delivers discourses on the Dhamma connected with giving; he is delighted upon seeing others giving to others;
and he grants fearlessness to others in situations of danger, and so forth.
Likewise, he feels shame and dread of wrongdoing regarding evil states such as the destruction of life;
he is by nature non-violent toward beings, gentle, easy-going, honest, and free from deceit; he is upright by nature, easy to speak to, and endowed with those qualities that make one easy to address;
he is mild by nature, not stubborn, and not conceited; and he does not take what belongs to others, even so much as a blade of grass.
Having received a debt placed in his own hand, he does not deceive another;
or, when something belonging to him has been lost or forgotten by another, he informs them and restores it so that it does not fall into the hands of others.
He is free from greed and does not give rise to even an evil thought regarding the possessions of others, nor toward the misfortunes of women and the like.
He avoids [evil] from afar; he is a speaker of truth, faithful to truth, a reconciler of those who are divided, and a promoter of harmony among those who are united.

He speaks kindly, is preceded by a smile, and is the first to speak. He speaks of what is beneficial, speaks of the Dhamma, is free from covetousness, has a mind devoid of ill will, and possesses unperverted vision.
Through the knowledge that one's own actions are one's own property, through the knowledge that accords with truth, he is grateful, appreciative, and respectful toward his elders.
One whose livelihood is perfectly pure, who loves the Dhamma, who encourages others in the Dhamma, who restrains beings from what is entirely improper in every way,
who establishes them in their duties, and who personally applies himself to those duties—
or having himself done what should not be done, quickly desists from it thereafter— such are the qualities of a Great Man whose inclination is toward virtue (*sīla*).
These are the signs of the perfection of virtue.
Likewise, he has dull defilements and dull hindrances; his inclination is toward seclusion, and he abounds in non-distraction.
Evil thoughts do not flow into his mind, and when he has attained seclusion, his mind becomes concentrated with ease.
Furthermore, he quickly establishes a mind of loving-kindness even toward the side of his enemies, let alone toward others;
he is mindful, remembering and recollecting what was done long ago and what was spoken long ago; he is wise, endowed with the wisdom that is the strength of the Dhamma;
he is discerning in various matters of duty; and he is energetic in performing deeds for the welfare of living beings.

One should understand that the marks of the Great Being’s perfections, such as the perfection of renunciation, are indicated by such qualities as: being endowed with the power of patience and thus overcoming all things;
having unshakable resolve and firm commitment; and maintaining equanimity toward those phenomena that call for equanimity.
Thus, these marks are to be understood through the Great Being’s inclination toward renunciation and so forth.
Thus, for the Great Being endowed with these marks of the requisites for enlightenment, it has been said:
"The reliance upon a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitta*) is the cause for the Great Resolve. In this regard, the characteristic of a spiritual friend is briefly as follows:
here, a spiritual friend is one who is perfected in faith, perfected in virtue, perfected in learning, perfected in generosity, and perfected in energy.

One who is perfected in mindfulness, perfected in concentration, and perfected in wisdom. Therein, through the perfection of faith, one has conviction in the Tathāgata’s enlightenment and in the fruit of kamma;
by that means, one does not abandon the desire for the welfare of beings, which is the cause of perfect enlightenment.
Through the perfection of virtue, one becomes dear and pleasing to beings, respected and worthy of esteem, an admonisher, a censurer of evil, a speaker who is patient with what is said.
Through the perfection of learning, he is one who delivers profound discourses on the Dhamma that bring welfare and happiness to sentient beings;
through the perfection of generosity, he is one of few desires, contented, secluded, and unattached;

through the perfection of energy, he is one who has aroused energy for the practice of what is beneficial to sentient beings; through the perfection of mindfulness, he is one whose mindfulness is established regarding blameless states; and through the perfection of concentration...

He is undistracted, with a concentrated mind; through the perfection of wisdom, he understands things without error. Seeking out, by means of mindfulness, the courses of wholesome and unwholesome states, and knowing through wisdom the benefit and harm for beings as they truly are, he becomes one-pointed in mind regarding that through concentration.
Then, by means of energy, he restrains beings from what is harmful and enjoins them to what is beneficial. Therefore it was said:
“Dear, venerable, and inspiring; one who speaks and is patient with what is said;

one who delivers profound discourse and does not urge one toward what is improper”—relying upon such a spiritual friend endowed with these qualities, the Great Man [realizes] his own perfection of the supporting condition (*upanissaya-sampatti*).
He purifies it correctly. Having become one whose intention and application are perfectly pure, and being endowed with the four powers,
he soon unites the eight factors and, making the Great Resolve, establishes himself in the state of a Bodhisatta—
one whose nature is not to turn back, who is fixed, and destined for supreme enlightenment.
In this regard, there are these four powers. The internal power is that delight, absolute inclination, and devotion toward Perfect Enlightenment based on oneself through reverence for the Dhamma;

by means of which the Great Being—having himself as his own authority, supported by moral shame (*lajjā*), and being endowed with resolute determination—fulfills the perfections and attains Perfect Enlightenment. The external power is that [devotion] toward Perfect Enlightenment...

The power of decisive support (*upanissaya-bala*) is the inclination toward and the one-pointedness of disposition toward perfect enlightenment (*sammāsambodhi*), by means of which the Great Being— having become a lord of the world, a refuge for those with pride,
and endowed with the great resolve (*abhinīhāra*)— fulfills the perfections (*pāramitā*) and attains supreme perfect enlightenment.
It is that inclination toward and one-pointedness of disposition toward the excellence of the decisive support for perfect enlightenment, by means of which the Great Being...
Having possessed sharp faculties, a clear constitution, reliance upon mindfulness, and being endowed with resolute determination, one fulfills the perfections and attains perfect enlightenment.
As for the power of application (*payogabala*), it is that excellence of application, diligent practice, and constant practice pertaining to perfect enlightenment,
by which the Great Being becomes one of purified application, one who acts without interruption, and one endowed with resolute determination.
Having offered sacrifices and fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs), he attains perfect enlightenment (sammāsambodhi).

Thus, this resolve—endowed with four conditions, four causes, and four powers, accomplished through the convergence of eight factors—is the condition for the perfections by virtue of being their root cause.
And through the occurrence of which, in the Great Being, four...
Wondrous and marvelous qualities become established;
he embraces the entire multitude of beings with a heart of love, as if they were his own legitimate children. Yet his mind is not defiled by the defilements of those children.
His intention and his application are directed toward bringing welfare and happiness to sentient beings. And the qualities that constitute his Buddhahood increase further and further.

They increase and reach maturity. And because the Great Being is endowed with the most sublime outflow of merit, the outflow of the wholesome, the condition for existence, and the sustenance of happiness, he becomes one worthy of offerings from beings, a supreme object of veneration, and an incomparable field of merit.
Thus, the Great Resolve possesses manifold qualities and manifold benefits; it is [the foundation] of the perfections.
It should be understood as a condition (*paccaya*).
And just as with the initial resolution (*abhinīhāra*), so it is with great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and skill in means (*upāyakosalla*).

In this context, "skill in means" refers to the wisdom that serves as the cause for giving and the other perfections becoming the requisites for enlightenment; it is by means of these qualities—great compassion and skill in means—that the Great Beings [attain their goal].

Disregard for one’s own happiness, constant devotion to working for the welfare of others, the absence of despondency even through the most difficult practices of a Great Bodhisattva, and the state of being a cause for sentient beings to obtain benefit and happiness even at the times of seeing, hearing, or recollecting a Buddha with serene confidence—all these come to pass.
For thus, through wisdom, the attainment of Buddhahood is accomplished; and through compassion, the performance of the Buddha-deeds is accomplished.
Through wisdom one crosses over by oneself; through compassion one causes others to cross over. Through wisdom one fully understands the suffering of others;
through compassion one undertakes the remedy for the suffering of others. Through wisdom one becomes disenchanted with suffering; through compassion one accepts suffering.
Likewise, through wisdom one is oriented toward Nibbāna; through compassion one enters the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa). Thus, through compassion, one is oriented toward the round of rebirth (saṃsāra).
He exists; yet through wisdom he does not take delight therein, and through wisdom he is dispassionate toward everything.
Because he is followed by compassion, his activity is not one that fails to assist all beings; through compassion he sympathizes with everyone.

Because he is followed by wisdom, his mind is not dispassionate toward everything; yet through wisdom there is an absence of the notions of "I" and "mine," and through compassion there is an absence of indolence and dejection.
Likewise, through wisdom and compassion, there arise respectively: the state of being one's own protector and the protector of others;

the nature of the steadfast and the heroic; the state of neither tormenting oneself nor tormenting others; the accomplishment of one’s own welfare and the welfare of others; the state of being fearless and unshakable; the state of being a lord of the Dhamma and a lord of the world;

the state of being grateful and a doer of what was done for one in the past; the removal of delusion and craving; the perfection of true knowledge and conduct; and the accomplishment of the powers and intrepidities—this constitutes the fruit of all the perfections.

In particular, wisdom and compassion are conditions for the perfections (*pāramī*) by way of being their means. Furthermore, these two are conditions not only for the perfections but also for the aspiration (*paṇidhāna*).
Likewise, it should be understood that enthusiasm, ingenuity, steadfastness, and conduct for the welfare of others are conditions for the perfections, which lead to the state of Buddhahood.
They are called "Buddha-grounds" because they are the place of arising. In this context, "exertion" refers to the energy of striving for the requisites of enlightenment.
"Ingeniousness" refers to the wisdom consisting in skillful means regarding those requisites of enlightenment. "Steadfastness" refers to resolve, specifically the quality of unshakable resolve.
"Conduct for the welfare of others" refers to the cultivation of loving-kindness and the cultivation of compassion.
Likewise, there are six inclinations, distinguished as renunciation, seclusion, non-greed, non-hatred, non-delusion, and escape.

For Bodhisattvas have the inclination toward renunciation because they perceive the faults in sensual pleasures and in the household life; likewise, they have the inclination toward seclusion because they perceive the faults in social company;
they have the inclination toward non-greed because they perceive the fault in greed; and they have the inclination toward non-hatred because they perceive the fault in hatred.
They have a disposition toward non-delusion and see the fault in delusion; they have a disposition toward renunciation and see the fault in all states of existence.
Therefore, it should be understood that these six dispositions of Bodhisattvas are the conditions for the perfections (pāramīs) such as giving and the rest.
For indeed, the perfections of giving and the others do not arise without seeing the danger in greed and the like, and without the predominance of non-greed and the others.

For it should be understood that the state of having a disposition toward non-greed and so forth (*alobhajjhāsayatādi*) refers to the mind being inclined toward relinquishment and other virtues by virtue of the predominance of non-greed and the like.

Just as these [dispositions] are so, so too the state of having a disposition toward giving (*dānajjhāsayatā*) and the rest serve as conditions for the perfections (*pāramī*) of giving and so forth in Bodhisattvas who practice for enlightenment.
For, through their disposition toward giving, Bodhisattvas come to perceive the fault in its opposite, namely, stinginess.
They fulfill the perfection of generosity correctly. Through their inclination toward virtue, seeing the fault in immorality, they fulfill the perfection of virtue correctly.

Through their inclination toward renunciation, [they fulfill it] regarding sensual pleasures and the household life; through their inclination toward knowledge of things as they truly are, [they fulfill it] regarding ignorance and doubt;
through their inclination toward energy, [they fulfill it] regarding laziness; and through their inclination toward patience, [they fulfill it] regarding impatience.

Through an inclination toward truth (*sacca-jjhāsaya*), they avoid deception; through an inclination toward resolve (*adhiṭṭhāna-jjhāsaya*), they avoid non-resolve; through an inclination toward loving-kindness (*mettā-jjhāsaya*), they avoid ill-will (*byāpāda*);

and through an inclination toward equanimity (*upekkhā-jjhāsaya*), having seen the danger in the worldly conditions (*lokadhamma*), they rightly fulfill the perfections (*pāramī*) such as renunciation.
Because the inclinations toward giving and so forth are the causes for the accomplishment of the perfections of giving and so forth, they are the requisite conditions (*paccaya*).
Likewise, among non-renunciation, renunciation, and so forth, the reflection upon disadvantages and advantages in their respective order is a condition for the perfections of giving and the rest.

In this regard, the method of reflection is as follows: for beings whose minds are attached to possessions such as fields, lands, gold, bullion, cattle, buffaloes, female slaves, male slaves, children, wives, and so on, [one reflects] because these fields and other things—being objects of sensual desire—are highly sought after and are common property shared with kings, thieves, and others.
Objects of possession are said to bring about various and extensive misfortunes because they are the basis for disputes, because they cause enmity, because they are devoid of substance,

because they lead to harming others in both acquiring and protecting them, because they are a cause for destruction, because they bring about many kinds of calamities such as sorrow, and because they serve as the cause for rebirth in the states of misery for those whose minds are obsessed by the stain of stinginess rooted in attachment to them.
Thus, objects of possession are indeed the bringers of manifold and vast harm.
Since generosity alone is their one means of safety, one should practice diligence in giving.
Furthermore, when a beggar comes seeking, he is like one who reveals his own secrets; thus the giver thinks, "He is my confidant," and "He is my instructor, saying:
'Take what belongs to you and depart for the next world, leaving it behind. And when [the house] is set ablaze...
Because it acts as a companion that carries away what belongs to me from this world— which is like a house set ablaze by the fire of death—
and because it serves as the place for depositing what has been carried away so that it is not consumed; and because, through its state as a companion in the wholesome deed known as giving,
it becomes the cause for attaining the stage of Buddhahood, which is the foremost of all perfections and most difficult to reach.
And one should reflect: "He is my supreme spiritual friend. Likewise:
"I have been honored by him with sublime tasks; therefore, that honor must be made not false.
And: "Since life is subject to absolute destruction, I must give even without being asked, much less when asked."
“Since it must be given even after being sought by those with noble aspirations, it has come to me of its own accord through my merit”;
and “Under the pretext of giving to a beggar, this is actually a favor for me alone”; and “Just as I am, this entire world must be favored by me”;
and “In the absence of a beggar, how could my perfection of generosity be fulfilled?”; and “It is solely for the sake of the beggars themselves...”
“May I embrace everything,” and “When will beggars take what belongs to me of their own accord, even without asking me? and “How may I be dear and pleasing to beggars?
and “Or how may they be dear and pleasing to me? and “How may I be joyful and delighted while giving, and even after having given?”
“Born of joy and gladness,” and, “How might there be supplicants for me, and how might my inclination toward giving be sublime?
and, “How might I give to supplicants even without being asked, having understood their hearts?
and, “If wealth exists and there are supplicants, not relinquishing it would be a great deception on my part. And, “How might I [give] my own limbs and life...”
Furthermore, one should establish an inclination toward relinquishment by thinking, "I shall give even to beggars. Moreover,

one should generate a mind characterized by detachment toward material goods, thinking, "This thing called 'wealth' follows after the donor who is indifferent to it, just as a chip of wood follows a thrower who is indifferent to it."
If the person who is making the request is a dear one, one should arouse joy thinking, "A dear person is requesting me.
If, however, it is a neutral person, one should arouse joy thinking, "Since this person is requesting me, they will surely become a friend through this act of relinquishment";
for even while giving, one becomes dear to those who ask. But if it is a hostile person...
When someone asks, one should generate a particularly joyful thought: "An adversary is asking me;

since this person, while asking, will surely become dear and a friend through this act of relinquishment. In this way, even toward neutral or hostile persons, one should give only after establishing compassion preceded by loving-kindness, just as one would toward a beloved person.
But if, due to the long-term cultivation of greed, thoughts of greed regarding objects to be given should arise in him,
he who has made the vow of a Bodhisatta should reflect thus: "When you were making the aspiration for the enlightenment of a True Person,
did you not relinquish this body for the sake of benefiting all beings, and [did you not dedicate] the merit consisting in that relinquishment?"
In that case, your attachment even toward external objects is like a bath for an elephant; therefore, you should not give rise to attachment anywhere.

Just as when a great medicinal tree stands, those who need its roots take the root, and those who need the bark, the rind, the trunk, the branches, the heartwood, the twigs, the leaves, the flowers, or the fruit, they take what they require.
Those seeking fruit take it away, yet that tree has no occurrence of thought such as, "They are taking what belongs to me.

In the same way, while this body—which is for the benefit of the whole world, which is subject to great suffering, ungrateful, and perpetually impure—is being employed for the sake of helping others, not even the slightest wrong thought should be allowed to arise. Who...
Or rather, there is no distinction here between the internal and external great elements, all of which are by nature subject to breaking up, dispersal, and destruction;
this insistence that "this is mine," "I am this," or "this is my self" is merely a manifestation of delusion.
Therefore, one should be without regard for the hands, feet, eyes, and so forth, as well as the flesh and other parts, both internally and externally, just as with external things.
"Having offered it, one must have the intention of relinquishment, thinking: 'Let those who need it take it.

For one who reflects in this way, whose mind is directed toward enlightenment, and who is indifferent toward body and life, the actions of body, speech, and mind become thoroughly purified without difficulty.
Thus, with his actions of body, speech, and mind thoroughly purified, he is one of purified livelihood.

Established in the practice of the right method, one becomes capable of assisting all beings even more extensively through the relinquishment of gifts to be given—endowed with skill in means regarding the lower and higher realms—and through the giving of fearlessness and the giving of the true Dhamma. This, first of all, is the method of reflection regarding the perfection of generosity (*dānapāramitā*).
As for the perfection of virtue (*sīlapāramitā*), it should be reflected upon in this way: "This thing called virtue cannot be purified by water from the Ganges or other such means..."

It is the water for washing away the stain of hatred, which cannot be removed by other means; it is the remedy for the fever of passion and the like, which cannot be dispelled by yellow sandalwood and such things;
it is the extraordinary ornament of the virtuous, unlike the common ornaments of necklaces, crowns, and earrings worn by ordinary people;
and it is a fragrant scent that is universal, blowing in all directions, and appropriate for all seasons.
Because it brings about a state worthy of veneration by wealthy kṣatriyas and other deities, it is the supreme mantra for subjugation;

it is a flight of stairs for ascending to the celestial realms of the Four Great Kings and others; it is the means for attaining the jhānas and direct knowledges (abhiññā); it is the path leading to the great city of Nibbāna;
it is the ground for establishing the enlightenment of disciples, the enlightenment of pacceka-buddhas, and perfect full enlightenment (sammāsambodhi)—whatever [it may be].
Or it is that which is sought and desired; because it serves as the means for the fulfillment of each such wish, it surpasses even the *cintāmaṇi* jewel, the wish-fulfilling tree, and so forth.
And this was said by the Blessed One: “Monks, the mental aspiration of one who is virtuous succeeds because of its purity.
Furthermore, it has been said: “Monks, if a monk should desire: ‘May I be dear to my fellow practitioners of the holy life…’”
"Being pleasing, venerable, and worthy of development"—thus one should fulfill the precepts themselves.

Likewise, one should reflect upon the virtues of virtue by means of such suttas as: "Virtuous conduct, Ānanda, has non-regret as its purpose," and "Householders, there are these five benefits for one who is virtuous through the perfection of virtue.
Likewise, one should reflect upon the faults of being devoid of virtue by means of such suttas as the *Agniskandhopama-sūtra* (The Simile of the Mass of Fire).
The dangers [of immorality]. Virtue should be reflected upon because it is a cause of rapture and gladness;

because it is free from the fear of self-reproach, the censure of others, punishment, and rebirth in the miserable states; because it is praised by the wise; because it is a cause for freedom from remorse; because it is a state of security; and because it surpasses the excellence of wealth, sovereignty, long life, beauty, status, kinsmen, and friends.
For indeed, due to his own perfection of virtue, one who possesses virtue [attains] great...
Joy and gladness arise [in him] thus: "I have indeed done what is wholesome; I have done what is beautiful; I have provided a refuge for those who are afraid.
Likewise, the virtuous person does not reproach himself, nor do wise others reproach him; there is simply no possibility of punishment or fear of an evil destination.
A virtuous person, possessing beautiful qualities, becomes praised by the wise. Likewise, for the virtuous person...
That remorse which arises in one of immoral conduct, thinking, "Alas, I have done evil; I have done a cruel deed;

I have done a foul act," does not exist here. Furthermore, this virtue (sīla) is the supreme state of security because it is established upon heedfulness (appamāda), because it accomplishes great benefit by way of averting the ruin of wealth and other calamities, and because it is a source of auspiciousness (maṅgala); thus, even one of low birth [attains it].
Because one who possesses virtue becomes worthy of honor by kṣatriya great householders and others, the perfection of virtue surpasses the perfection of lineage;
the statement beginning with, "What do you think, Great King? Suppose you had here a slave or a laborer," serves as proof in this regard.

External wealth [is surpassed] because it is shared with thieves and others, because it does not follow one to the next world, because it yields little fruit, and because it is not a basis for qualities such as serenity (samatha).
Virtue excels [all other things]. Because it serves as the basis for the supreme sovereignty of the mind, virtue excels the sovereignty of kshatriyas and others.
For the sovereignty of beings within their respective classes of existence is caused by virtue;
and because it is said that even a single day’s life of one possessed of virtue is superior to a lifespan of a hundred years, and because one who possesses life may yet cast aside the training.
Because it speaks of the inevitability of death, virtue is more distinguished than life itself.
Because it brings even enemies into a state of affection and because it cannot be overcome by old age, disease, or misfortune, virtue surpasses physical beauty.

Because it is the foundation for specific excellences of happiness, virtue surpasses specific positions such as palaces and monasteries, as well as specific stations such as those of kings, crown princes, and generals. Even toward kinsmen who are naturally affectionate and remain close at hand—

And it surpasses one’s circle of friends because it accomplishes absolute welfare and follows one even into the next world; here, the statement beginning with “Neither mother nor father could do that” serves as proof.

Likewise, morality alone is more distinguished than the protection afforded by an army consisting of elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry, or by the employment of mantras, medicinal herbs, and charms, because it is easy to guard, whereas those other means are difficult to protect; for morality is dependent on oneself and not dependent on others.
And because it has a great scope. For this very reason it was said: “Dhamma indeed protects the one who lives by Dhamma,” and so forth.
Thus, for one who reflects upon virtue as being endowed with these manifold qualities, an incomplete accomplishment of virtue reaches completion, and that which is impure attains purity.
However, if through long-standing habituation, states opposed to virtue such as hatred and the like should arise from time to time, [one must apply the appropriate remedy].
That one who professes to be a bodhisatta should reflect thus: "Have you not made a vow for full enlightenment?
And it is not possible for one deficient in virtue to attain even worldly success, let alone the supramundane;
for supreme perfect enlightenment, which is the pinnacle of all successes, has virtue as its foundation, and that virtue must reach the highest excellence."

It must be so; therefore, by guarding virtue properly according to the method stated in the passage beginning with "like a hen guarding her eggs," you, being well-behaved, must become even more excellent.
Furthermore, through your teaching of the Dhamma, you must effect the introduction and maturation of beings in the three vehicles; for one who is deficient in virtue—
Furthermore, one's word must not be disregarded, just as a physician’s treatment is not ignored when it is beneficial;
therefore, thinking, "How may I become trustworthy so that I may perform the work of introducing and maturing sentient beings? one must possess a nature of perfectly pure virtue.

Moreover, through the possession of distinguished qualities such as the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*), one possesses the capacity to benefit sentient beings and the fulfillment of the perfection of wisdom (*paññā-pāramī*) and the rest.
Since qualities such as the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) do not arise without the purity of virtue (*sīla*), one must thoroughly purify virtue.
Likewise, one should reflect on the household life through such passages as, "Household life is crowded and dusty," and so forth;

on sensual pleasures through such passages as, "Sensual pleasures are like a skeleton," and so forth, and "Even a mother disputes with her son," and so forth; and on the world through such passages as, "Just as a man, having taken a loan, engages in his work..."

By means of the passage beginning with “one should apply oneself,” preceded by the vision of the danger in sensual desire and so forth, and by way of reflecting on the benefits of renunciation—such as “the life of renunciation is like the open air”—contrary to what was previously stated, the reviewing of the perfection of renunciation (nekkhamma-pāramī) is to be understood. This is the summary here;
the detailed exposition, however, should be understood by way of the *Dukkhakkhandha Sutta*, the *Āsivisopama Sutta*, and others.
Likewise, one should attend to the qualities of wisdom, reflecting: "Without wisdom, the states such as giving are not purified, nor are they capable of performing their respective functions.
For just as the entire body does not shine without life and is incapable of engaging in its own activities, and just as the sense faculties such as the eye [do not function] without consciousness...

Just as [the other faculties] are unable to perform their respective functions regarding their objects without it, so too the faculties such as faith are incapable of fulfilling their own functions without wisdom;
thus, wisdom is the primary cause for the practice of relinquishment and the rest.
For the Great Bodhisattvas, having opened the eye of wisdom, give even their own limbs and members while remaining free from self-exaltation.
They do not disparage others; like medicinal trees, they are free from discrimination and possess a state of joy throughout the three periods of time.
Indeed, through the application of skillful means by way of wisdom, renunciation directed toward the welfare of others attains the status of the perfection of giving (*dānapāramī*).
For a gift given for one's own sake is merely like an increase in wealth.
Likewise, in the absence of wisdom, because one cannot be separated from defilements such as craving, even the purification of virtue itself is impossible;

how much less, then, can there be the state of being the foundation for the qualities of omniscience? Only one possessed of wisdom, clearly perceiving the danger in household life, in the strands of sensual pleasure, and in saṃsāra, as well as the benefit in renunciation, in meditative attainments, and in Nibbāna, would go forth into homelessness.
Having produced the meditative attainments (*jhāna-samāpatti*), one faces toward Nibbāna and establishes others therein as well.
Furthermore, energy devoid of wisdom does not accomplish the desired goal because it is difficult to undertake; indeed, it is better not to begin at all than to undertake what is difficult.
However, with energy accompanied by wisdom, nothing is difficult to attain, owing to the application of skillful means (*upāya*).
Likewise, it is only the wise person who is naturally disposed to endure injuries inflicted by others, not the one lacking wisdom.

For one devoid of wisdom, injuries brought upon him by others only serve to nourish their very opposite—impatience—whereas for the wise person, those same injuries lead to the strengthening of his perfection of patience and result in its firmness. It is only the wise person who [endures] even the three...
Having understood, as they truly are, the truths that serve as the causes for these [defilements] and their opposites, he does not deceive others.
Likewise, having fortified himself with the power of wisdom, through the perfection of steadfastness, he maintains an unwavering resolve and commitment toward all the perfections.
And being wise, he does not differentiate between those who are dear, neutral, or hostile, but is skillful in promoting welfare everywhere.
Likewise, by way of wisdom, one remains neutral amidst the gathering of worldly conditions such as gain and loss due to being free from agitation.
Thus, since wisdom alone is the cause for the purification of all the perfections (*pāramī*), the qualities of wisdom should be reflected upon.

Furthermore, without wisdom there is no excellence of vision; and apart from the perfection of view, there is no perfection of virtue. For one who is devoid of both the perfection of virtue and the perfection of view, [there is no success].
Since one cannot accomplish even one's own welfare when lacking concentration—let alone the supreme welfare of others—one who is practicing for the sake of others should admonish himself thus:
"Must you not indeed apply yourself with diligence to the growth of wisdom?
For it is by the power of wisdom that the Great Being remains established in the four foundations.
Favoring the world with the four bases of sympathy, he introduces beings to the path of deliverance and brings their faculties to maturity.

Likewise, through the power of wisdom, by frequently investigating the aggregates, sense-bases, and so forth, he thoroughly understands, as they truly are, the processes of worldly involvement and its cessation.

By defining the qualities of wisdom in their many aspects— such as how giving and the other virtues lead to a state distinguished by penetration and how one becomes a fulfiller of the Bodhisattva training— one should cultivate the perfection of wisdom (*paññāpāramī*).
Likewise, even those worldly tasks that appear to be unattainable for one of inferior energy can be accomplished by one who disregards weariness.

However, for one who has initiated energy, there is nothing that cannot be attained. For one of inferior energy is not even able to begin with the thought, "I shall ferry all beings across the great flood of saṃsāra.
One of middling energy, having begun, falls into despondency midway.
But one of superior energy, being indifferent to his own happiness, reaches the perfection of the undertaking; such is the excellence of energy.

It should be reviewed. Furthermore, even for one whose own undertaking is for the sake of pulling oneself out from the mire of *saṃsāra*, it is impossible to expect the fulfillment of one’s aspirations if one’s energy (*vīriya*) becomes slack;
how much more so for one who has made the resolve to pull out the world together with its devas! And regarding the host of defects such as lust (*rāga*) and the rest...
Because they are as difficult to restrain as intoxicated great elephants; because the undertaking of kamma resulting from them is like that of an executioner with sword raised;
because the miserable rebirths caused by them always have their mouths wide open;
because evil friends who incite one to them are always present; and because it is possible for an ignorant worldling to act upon their advice.

One should reflect upon the qualities of energy in such ways as: "It is fitting that I myself should emerge from the suffering of saṃsāra," whereby wrong thoughts are driven far away by the power of energy;
and, "If full enlightenment can be attained through energy that depends on oneself, what is difficult about this? and so forth.

Likewise, this so-called patience is the unimpeded weapon of the virtuous for the accomplishment of good qualities, owing to its dispelling of anger, which is the adversary of all virtues without exception;
it is the ornament of those capable of overcoming others, the perfection of strength for recluses and brahmins, a stream of water for subduing the serpent of anger,
the birthplace of the sound of one’s own fame, and [a deterrent] for wicked persons...
One should reflect: "It is a mantra-remedy that pacifies the poison of speech; it is the supreme nature of the wise for those established in restraint;
it is an ocean by virtue of its profound depth; it is the shoreline for the great ocean of hatred; it is the closing door-leaf for the gates to the states of misery;
it is the staircase for ascending to the worlds of the devas and brahmās; it is the ground for the abiding of all virtues; it is the highest purity of body, speech, and mind."
Furthermore: "These beings burn in this world due to the absence of perfection in patience, and in the next world because of their engagement with things that cause burning";

and "Even though suffering arises caused by the harm done to others, it is my own personal existence (*attabhāva*) that serves as the field for that suffering, and my own karma that serves as its seed"; and "This [patience] is the means for becoming free from debt regarding that suffering."
And: "How can my perfection of patience arise if there is no one who harms me? and: "Even though this person is harmful now, in the past he actually performed a service for me";
and: "Indeed, harm itself is a service by virtue of being the occasion for patience";
and: "All these beings are like my own children; and who would be angry at the offenses committed by a child?"
And [he thinks]: "By whatever possession of the demon of anger this person has offended me, that very possession of the spirit of anger must be subdued by me";
and "Whatever harm caused this suffering to arise for me, I too am the cause of that";
and "All those phenomena by which the harm was done, and the place where it was done—all of them have ceased at that very moment; who now [is there to be harmed]?"
“By whom should anger be directed? and “Since all phenomena are non-self, who can offend whom?”—thus reflecting in this way, he should cultivate the perfection of patience.
However, if through long-standing habituation, anger caused by the thought of another’s harm should seize his mind and persist, [he must apply the appropriate remedy].
He should reflect thus: "This patience is indeed the means of counteracting those who act with hostility toward others";

and, "Furthermore, harm toward me is a condition for faith by way of producing suffering, and it is also a condition for the perception of non-delight in the entire world"; and, "For this is the very nature of the faculties, namely—"
“Association with desirable and undesirable objects. In that regard, as for the thought ‘May I not have association with undesirable objects’—how could that possibly be obtained here?
And: “A being under the sway of anger is crazed and distracted in mind by that anger; what is the use of retaliating against him? And:
“All these beings are protected by the Perfectly Enlightened One like his own biological sons; therefore, there is no [need for retaliation] in that case.”
"I must not give way to anger," "when there is an offender, I must not be angry even toward one who possesses virtues," "if he lacks virtues,
he should especially be treated with compassion," "by anger my own qualities and fame are diminished," "by becoming angry,
undesirable things such as ugliness and painful sleep come upon me, which are dear to my enemies," and "anger..."
And: "This one is indeed a powerful adversary who brings about all that is harmful and destroys all that is beneficial"; and: "When there is patience, there is no adversary whatsoever"; and:
"Whatever suffering an offender might incur in the future on account of his offense, by means of my patience, that shall not happen for me";
and: "By thinking ill and becoming angry, I have become nothing but an adversary."

And: “He becomes one who is followed”; and: “When anger has been overcome by me through patience, that adversary, having become my slave, is truly overcome”; and: “It is not fitting for me to abandon the quality of patience for the sake of anger”; and:
“While anger—a state opposed to and contrary to wholesome qualities—exists, how could my qualities such as virtue reach fulfillment?”
And [he thinks]: "In their absence, how shall I, being of great benefit to sentient beings, attain the supreme success corresponding to my promise?

And: "When there is patience, because there is no external distraction, for one who is concentrated, all conditioned phenomena are contemplated as impermanent and suffering, all phenomena as non-self, and Nibbāna as unconditioned, deathless, sublime, and so forth."
"And the Buddha-dhammas are patient, possessing inconceivable and immeasurable power.
Then, established in that conformable patience, one sees that these are merely phenomena (dhamma), devoid of self or anything belonging to a self;
they arise and pass away according to their respective conditions, coming from nowhere and going nowhere.
It is not established anywhere, nor is there any activity here belonging to anyone;

thus, the patient acceptance of non-insistence upon "I-making" and "mine-making" is what is intended, by which the Bodhisatta becomes fixed for enlightenment and subject to the nature of non-retrogression.
In this way, the reflection on the perfection of patience (khantipāramitā) is to be understood.
Likewise, because virtue and the other [perfections] cannot exist without truth, and because there is no practice that accords with one's promise;
because all evil qualities converge upon the transgression of the dharma of truth; because one who is untruthful and deceitful is not to be trusted;
because such a person brings about the state of having speech that is not to be accepted in the future; and because one endowed with truth serves as the foundation for all virtues.

The perfections of the perfection of truth should be reflected upon by way of its efficacy in bringing about the complete purification and fulfillment of all the requisites for enlightenment through the resolution of truth;
by its performance of the function of all the requisites for enlightenment through non-deception regarding phenomena that possess intrinsic nature;
and by the accomplishment of the bodhisattva’s practice, and so forth.

Likewise, regarding generosity and the other perfections, one should reflect upon their virtues in terms of resolve (*adhiṭṭhāna*), considering that without a firm undertaking of generosity and so forth,

and without an unshakable determination even when encountering their opposites, as well as a courageous and heroic spirit therein, the requisites for enlightenment such as generosity cannot possibly arise.
Thus should the virtues of resolve be contemplated.

Likewise: “Even for one who abides solely for his own benefit, it is impossible to attain the perfections of this world and the next without a mind of benevolence toward beings, let alone for one who desires to establish all beings in the perfection of Nibbāna”; and:
“For one who later desires the supramundane perfection of all beings, a desire for mundane perfection at present is now appropriate.”
And: “Now, being unable to bring about the welfare and happiness of others through mere intention alone, when shall I accomplish this through actual application?
And: “Those whom I have now nurtured by providing for their welfare and happiness will later become my companions in the sharing of the Dhamma.
And: “Without these, the requisites for enlightenment cannot arise for me; therefore...”

Thinking, "Because they are the cause for the accomplishment of the manifestation of all the Buddha-qualities, these [Buddhas] are my supreme field of merit, the unsurpassed basis of the wholesome, and the highest object of reverence," one should especially establish an inclination toward the welfare of all beings;
furthermore, through the foundation of compassion, loving-kindness (*mettā*) should be cultivated toward all beings without limit. By means of that which is free from barriers...
For one who, with a mind intent on bestowing welfare and happiness upon beings, a powerful desire arises to remove their harm and suffering, and that desire becomes firmly rooted.
Furthermore, compassion is the beginning, the footing, the foundation, the root, the mouth, and the foremost of all the qualities that make a Buddha;
in this way, the virtues of loving-kindness should be reflected upon.
Likewise: "In the absence of equanimity, the disturbances caused by sentient beings would produce a distortion of the mind;
and when there is a distortion of the mind, there can be no arising of the requisites such as giving. And:
"When the mind is moistened by the moisture of loving-kindness, there is no purification of the requisites without equanimity. And: "One who lacks equanimity toward the requisites..."
"...one cannot dedicate the accumulation of merit and its ripening for the benefit of sentient beings," and, "in the absence of equanimity,
one cannot relinquish the gift without making a distinction between the recipients of the objects to be given," and, "devoid of equanimity,
one cannot purify one's virtue without disregarding obstacles to the requisites of life and to life itself."

And because he is able [to endure], and likewise because the power of renunciation (*nekkhamma-bala*) is established through equanimity (*upekkhā*) by means of the very endurance of both displeasure and pleasure;

because all the functions of the requisites are accomplished through the act of observing; because the function of striving (*padhāna-kicca*) cannot be performed if over-exerted energy is not observed;

because the attainment of patience and meditative absorption (*jhāna*) occurs only for one who is equanimous; and because the seven formations (*saṅkhāra*) are not contradicted by means of equanimity.
The perfection of equanimity (*upekkhā-pāramī*) should be reflected upon in this manner:

because one achieves an unshakable resolve regarding the qualities one has undertaken through the practice of equanimity toward the worldly conditions (*lokadhamma*), and because the state of abiding in loving-kindness (*mettā-vihāra*) is accomplished effortlessly even when faced with harm from others, the undertaking, the resolution, the fulfillment, and the accomplishment of all the requisites for enlightenment are brought to completion through the power of equanimity.
Thus, in such a way, the perfection of equanimity should be reviewed. In this way...

It should be understood that the contemplation of the disadvantages and advantages, respectively, regarding non-renunciation and renunciation, is the condition for the perfections of giving and the rest.
Likewise, the fifteen factors of conduct together with their requisites, as well as the five direct knowledges, are conditions. Therein, the "factors of conduct" (caraṇadhammā) are:
restraint by virtue, guarding the doors of the sense faculties, moderation in eating, devotion to wakefulness, and the seven...

The true qualities (*saddhamma*) and the four meditative absorptions (*jhāna*). Among these, for the four beginning with virtue (*sīla*), the thirteen ascetic practices (*dhutadhamma*), fewness of wishes (*appicchatā*), and so forth, are the requisites.

Regarding the true qualities: for faith (*saddhā*), the requisites are the recollections of the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, virtue, generosity, and the deities; tranquility (*upasama*); avoidance of coarse persons; association with pleasant persons;
contemplation of the qualities that inspire confidence; and devotion to those same qualities. For moral shame (*hirī*) and moral dread (*ottappa*)...

Reflecting on the danger of unwholesome states, reflecting on the danger of the lower realms, reflecting on the support of wholesome qualities, avoiding persons devoid of moral shame (*hirī*) and dread of blame (*ottappa*), associating with persons endowed with moral shame and dread of blame, being intent upon that [virtue], possessing great learning,

having practiced former applications, inquiring deeply, devotion to the true Dharma, familiarity with blameless fields of knowledge and the like, the ripening of the faculties, and the distancing of the defilements from one who has heard little.

For energy: avoidance [of the unwholesome], associating with those of great learning, and being intent upon that; reflecting on the fear of the states of woe, reflecting on the path of progress, reflecting on the greatness of the Dhamma, dispelling sloth and torpor, avoiding persons who are indolent, associating with persons who have aroused energy, reflecting on the right exertions, and being intent upon that.
For mindfulness: mindfulness and clear comprehension, avoiding persons who are forgetful, associating with persons whose mindfulness is established, and being intent upon that.

Through wisdom: posing questions, purifying the basis [of meditation], performing the duties, balancing the faculties, avoiding persons of deficient wisdom, associating with persons possessed of wisdom, reflecting on the course of profound knowledge, and being intent upon that.

Through the four meditative absorptions (jhānas): the fourfold set beginning with virtue, the preliminary development regarding the thirty-eight objects, and the mastery of [mental functions] such as adverting.

“Requisites. In this context, one should determine, as appropriate, how conduct and the other factors serve as conditions for the requisites of giving and so forth—such as being capable of giving fearlessness to beings through purity of means by way of virtue and the rest, giving material things through purity of intention, and giving the Dhamma through both purities—and so on.
We have not determined them here for fear of excessive prolixity. In the same way, the wheels of success and the rest [should also be understood].
It should be understood as the condition for generosity and the other perfections.
What is defilement? In general, being grasped by craving and the like is the defilement of the perfections;

specifically, however, conceptualization regarding the object to be given and the recipient is the defilement of the perfection of generosity. Conceptualization regarding sentient beings and time is the defilement of the perfection of virtue.
Conceptualizations regarding delight or non-delight in sensual pleasures and existence and their pacification belong to the perfection of renunciation;

conceptualizations of "I" and "mine" belong to the perfection of wisdom; conceptualizations of dullness and agitation belong to the perfection of energy; conceptualizations of self and other belong to the perfection of patience;

conceptualizations of having seen what was not seen and so forth belong to the perfection of truth; and conceptualizations of faults and virtues regarding the requisites for enlightenment and their opposites [belong to the perfection of skillful means].

It should be understood that the defilement of the perfection of resolve consists in conceptualizing what is beneficial and harmful; the defilement of the perfection of loving-kindness consists in conceptualizing what is pleasant and unpleasant; and the defilement of the perfection of equanimity consists in conceptualizing what is desirable and undesirable. What is their purification?
It should be known that the non-affliction by craving and so forth, as well as the absence of the aforementioned conceptualizations, constitutes their purification.

For when they are unimpaired by the defilements—namely, craving, conceit, views, anger, enmity, denigration, spite, envy, avarice, deceit, fraud, obstinacy, impetuosity, pride, and negligence—and are free from conceptualizations regarding the recipient of the gift and so forth, the perfections such as giving become completely pure and radiant.
What is their opposite? In general, all defilements and all unwholesome states are their opposites.
In particular, however, it should be understood that the stinginess and so forth mentioned previously are what are meant.

Furthermore, giving is the opposite of greed, hatred, and delusion, due to its association with the qualities of non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion regarding the object to be given, the recipient, and the fruit of the gift;

virtue is the opposite of greed and so forth, due to the removal of crookedness such as bodily faults; and [renunciation] is the opposite of the three types of hatred, due to the avoidance of sensual pleasure, harming others, and self-mortification.
Renunciation (*nekkhamma*) is wisdom (*paññā*), which is the antidote to greed and the rest because it blinds greed and the like while keeping knowledge unblinded;
energy (*vīriya*) is the antidote to greed and the rest by way of initiating the path that is neither sluggish nor agitated;

patience (*khanti*) is the antidote to greed and the rest because it endures both the desirable and the undesirable, as well as emptiness (*suññatā*), through its occurrence in accordance with reality even when there is benefit or harm from others.

It should be understood that truth is the opposite of greed and the rest; resolve is the opposite of greed and the rest because it remains unshakable regarding the requisites undertaken according to one's commitment after having overcome the worldly conditions (lokadhamma);
loving-kindness is the opposite of greed and the rest due to its seclusion from the hindrances (nīvaraṇa);
and equanimity is the opposite of greed and the rest because it destroys attraction and aversion toward the desirable and undesirable, and because it proceeds with evenness.

What is the practice? First, regarding the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*), the practice consists in manifoldly assisting sentient beings by relinquishing the requisites for happiness, the body, and life;

by dispelling fear; and by teaching the Dhamma. In this context, giving is threefold according to the objects to be given: the gift of material things (*āmisa-dāna*), the gift of fearlessness (*abhaya-dāna*), and the gift of the Dhamma (*dhamma-dāna*). Among these, the object to be given by a Bodhisattva...
It is twofold: internal and external. Therein, the external is tenfold: food, drink, clothing, vehicles, garlands, scents, unguents, beds, dwellings, and lighting.
This is further manifold through the divisions of food and so forth into hard food, soft food, and the like.
Likewise, from the perspective of its object, it is sixfold, ranging from the visible-form object to the mental-object (dhamma) object. And of these, the visible-form objects and so forth—

It is of many kinds through the divisions of blue and so forth. Likewise, it is of many kinds by way of various articles of wealth and requisites, such as gems, gold, silver, pearls, coral, and so on;
fields, lands, and groves; and female and male slaves, cattle, buffalo, and so on.
In that regard, when the Great Man gives an external object, he gives to each person whatever they require; and while giving, [he thinks:]...
Knowing for himself, "He has need of it," he gives even when unasked, let alone when asked.
He gives with a mind free from stinginess, not with a mind bound by avarice; he gives what is sufficient, not what is insufficient, provided there is something to be given.

He does not give out of dependence on a reciprocal favor. For even when there is nothing to be given, if there is something sufficient, he shares it with those worthy of sharing. And he does not give that which would bring harm to others.
He does not give intoxicants such as liquor or spirits, nor anything that is a mere plaything, provided it is unwholesome and leads to negligence.
Nor does he give unsuitable food and drink, or anything in excessive measure, to a sick person who asks for them; rather, he gives only what is suitable and in the proper measure.
Likewise, when requested, he gives to householders what is appropriate for householders, and to those gone forth what is appropriate for those gone forth.
He gives without causing distress to anyone among his parents, blood relatives, kinsmen, friends, companions, children, wives, slaves, or laborers;
he does not promise an excellent gift and then give something coarse; he does not give while relying on gain, honor, or fame;
he does not give while relying on a reciprocal return; and he does not give with an expectation of fruit, other than for the sake of perfect enlightenment.
Nor does he give while feeling disgust for the solicitor or the gift to be given; nor does he give a discarded gift even to solicitors who are unrestrained, abusive, or insulting.
On the contrary, with a clear mind and out of compassion, he gives with due care.
He does not give being a superstitious seeker of omens, but rather gives having faith in the fruit of action alone. Nor [does he give] to the solicitor...
Having exhausted [the recipient] through acts such as waiting upon him, one gives; or one gives without exhausting [him];

nor does one give with the intention of deceiving others or with the intention of causing division; rather, one gives with an entirely undefiled mind. Nor does one give with harsh speech or a frowning face;
instead, one gives being pleasant-spoken, the first to speak, and moderate in speech. And in that which...
When greed becomes excessive— whether due to the excellence and desirability of the object to be given,
long-standing habituation, or a greedy nature— the Bodhisatta, knowing this, quickly dispels it and gives even after seeking out a petitioner;
and as for the gift that is meager while the petitioner stands before him, he does not consider his own [lack], but gives.
By giving after having exhorted the supplicant, he honors him, just as the wise Akitti did.
Furthermore, the Great Man does not give to supplicants his own children, wife, slaves, laborers, or servants when they have been unprepared and are in a state of dejection;
rather, he gives only when they have been properly prepared and are in a state of joy. And when giving, [he gives] even to yakkhas, rakkhasas, pisācas, and so forth.
Or, knowing that certain people among humans have cruel deeds, he does not give to them; likewise, he does not grant even sovereignty to such as these.
He gives, however, to those who act for the welfare, happiness, and benefit of the world, and to those who are righteous and protect the world according to Dhamma.
In this way, first of all, the practice regarding external giving is to be understood.

Internal giving, moreover, should be understood in two ways. How so? Just as some man, for the sake of food and clothing, surrenders himself to another and enters into a state of servitude, becoming subject to their will;

even so, the Great Being, for the sake of supreme enlightenment, with a mind free from worldly attachment and desiring the unsurpassed welfare and happiness of beings, [offers] his own perfection of giving.
Desiring to fulfill [the perfections], he relinquishes himself to others and enters a state of being subject to their will, such that they may do with him as they please.

He bestows his hands, feet, eyes, and other major and minor limbs upon those who require them—unshaken and without shrinking—neither clinging to them nor experiencing any contraction of mind regarding them, just as he would toward external objects; for such is the Great Being.

One renounces external objects in two ways: either by fulfilling the wishes of beggars so that they may enjoy them as they please, or for the sake of gaining mastery over oneself by relinquishing everything entirely;
thinking, "In this way, through the cultivation of non-attachment, I shall attain full enlightenment. It should be understood that the same applies to internal objects.
In that regard, he gives whatever internal object being given leads exclusively to the welfare of the supplicant, and not otherwise.

Furthermore, the Great Man does not give his own person or his limbs and members to Māra or to deities belonging to Māra’s host who intend to cause him harm, even while knowing this, thinking, "May there be no misfortune for them. Just as...
Nor does he give to those possessed by the hosts of Māra, nor even to those who are insane.
However, when requested by others, he gives immediately; for such a request is rare, and giving in such a manner is difficult to accomplish.

The gift of fearlessness (*abhayadāna*), however, should be understood as providing protection for beings when danger is present— whether from kings, thieves, fire, water, hostile persons, or wild beasts such as lions and tigers, or from *nāgas*, *yakṣas*, *rakkhasas*, and *pisācas*.
The gift of the Dhamma (*dhammadāna*), on the other hand, is the teaching of the Dhamma by one with an undefiled mind, an unerring instruction in the means for attaining welfare,

according to the categories of the present life, the future life, and the ultimate goal (*paramattha*), by which those who have not yet entered the Dispensation are made to enter, and those who have already entered are [further established].
[This is] the bringing to maturity. Herein, this is the method: in brief, first, there is talk on giving, talk on virtue, talk on heaven;

the danger, corruption, and defilement of sensual pleasures, and the benefit in renunciation.
