In detail, however, for those whose minds are inclined toward the enlightenment of a disciple (śrāvaka-bodhi), there is going for refuge, restraint in virtue, guarding the doors of the sense faculties, moderation in eating, and devotion to wakefulness.
The seven true states (saddhammā) consist of: the application of serenity (samathānuyoga) by way of performing the function [of meditation] upon the thirty-eight objects;
the application of insight (vipassanānuyoga) by way of appropriate modes of attention toward the inclinations for insight regarding the material body and so forth;

as well as the path of purification, the grasping of rightness, the three types of higher knowledge (tisso vijjā), the six direct knowledges (cha abhiññā), the four analytical insights (catasso paṭisambhidā), and the enlightenment of a disciple (sāvakabodhi). These are [the seven true states].
Establishment and purification [of the mind] in various instances as appropriate by means of proclaiming their virtues; likewise,
for those beings inclined toward *paccekabodhi* (solitary enlightenment) and *sammāsambodhi* (perfect enlightenment),

by means of proclaiming the nature, essence, and characteristics of the perfections such as giving (*dāna*) as appropriate, and by manifesting the great majesty of those Buddhas throughout the three stages.
It is for the purpose of establishing beings in the two vehicles and for their purification. Thus does the Great Man give the gift of Dhamma to beings.
Likewise, when the Great Man gives the gift of material things to beings, he gives a gift of food with the thought:

"By this gift may I bring about for beings the excellence of longevity, beauty, happiness, strength, eloquence, and so forth, as well as the delightful excellence of the supreme fruit. In the same way, he gives gifts for the sake of allaying the thirst of sensual desire and the defilements of beings.
He gives drink; likewise, he gives garments for the sake of producing a golden complexion as well as the ornaments of moral shame and dread (*hirī-ottappa*);

likewise, he gives a vehicle for the sake of producing the various supernormal powers (*iddhividha*) as well as the bliss of *nibbāna*; likewise, he gives perfume for the sake of producing the fragrance of virtue (*sīlagandha*);

likewise, he gives garlands and ointments for the sake of producing the splendor of the Buddha’s qualities; and [he gives a seat] for the sake of producing the seat at the terrace of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
He gives a seat; he gives a bed for the purpose of producing the Tathāgata’s posture; he gives a dwelling for the purpose of producing a refuge;
he gives lighting for the sake of obtaining the five eyes; he gives a gift of forms for the purpose of producing the fathom-wide radiance;
he gives a gift of sounds for the purpose of producing the Brahma-voice; he gives a gift of flavors for the sake of being dear to the entire world.
One gives the gift of tangible objects for the sake of the delicate state of a Buddha; one gives the gift of medicine for the sake of being free from aging and death;

one gives the gift of freedom from slavery to slaves for the purpose of liberating them from the servitude of the defilements; one gives the gift of blameless play and delight as a cause for rejoicing in the True Dhamma;
one gives the gift of children for the purpose of bringing all beings into the state of being one’s own children through noble birth; and [for the sake] of the entirety...
He gives a gift of a wife for the sake of attaining beauty in the world; he gives gifts of gold, gems, pearls, coral, and so forth, for the sake of perfecting the primary marks (*lakkhaṇa*);

he gives gifts of various ornaments for the sake of perfecting the secondary characteristics (*anubyañjana*); he gives gifts of a treasury of wealth for the sake of acquiring the treasury of the True Dhamma; he gives gifts of a kingdom for the sake of becoming a King of Dhamma;
he gives gifts of monasteries, parks, ponds, and groves for the sake of attaining the meditative absorptions (*jhāna*) and other perfections; [he gives gifts] marked with the wheel...
He gave his feet for the purpose of approaching the seat of enlightenment; he gave his hands for the purpose of giving the hand of the True Dhamma to beings so they may cross over the four floods;
he gave his ears, nose, and so forth for the sake of attaining the faculty of faith and the rest; he gave his eyes for the sake of attaining the universal eye (samantacakkhu);
and [he gave them] because they bring benefit and happiness to all beings at all times through seeing, hearing, recollecting, serving, and so on.

He gives the gift of flesh, blood, and so forth, thinking, "May my body be sustained by the entire world," and he gives the gift of his supreme limbs, thinking, "May I become the most excellent in the entire world.
Giving in this way, he does not give for the sake of improper search, nor through the harming of others, nor out of fear, nor out of shame.
He does not give out of anger toward those worthy of offerings; nor does he give coarse goods when fine ones are available;
nor does he give by way of self-exaltation, disparagement of others, calculation for the sake of a fruit, loathing for the beggar, or lack of respect.
Rather, he gives with care, with his own hand, at the proper time, with reverence, and without partiality. This applies to all three times.
He gives with joy, and having given, he has no regret afterwards. He does not act out of pride or contempt toward the recipients;
rather, he treats the recipients with affection, being generous, devoted to giving, and a donor who provides for their needs.
For when giving a gift of food, thinking, "I shall give it together with its accessories," he gives it along with clothing and other items. The same applies to the gift of clothing.

When giving food, one gives it together with other items such as rice and so forth, thinking, "I shall give this along with its accessories. The same principle applies to the giving of vehicles and other gifts.
Likewise, when giving a gift of form (*rūpa-dāna*), one gives it while making other objects of sense (*itara-ārammaṇa*) its accessories; the same holds true for the remaining [types of gifts].
In this context, a "gift of form" refers to any one among the colors—blue, yellow, red, white, and so forth—found in flowers, garments, or precious minerals.
Having obtained a form and having directed the mind toward it, one thinks, "I shall give a gift of form;
this gift of form is mine," and establishes the gift in such a worthy recipient (dakkhiṇeyya), making it have a physical basis. This is what is called a gift of form.
A gift of sound, however, should be understood by way of the sound of drums and so forth. In that case, one does not uproot the sound like a bulbous root.
It is not possible to give by placing [the gift] in the hand like a blue lotus;
rather, one gives what is called a "gift of sound" by giving after having established a physical basis.

Therefore, when one makes or causes to be made an offering to the Three Jewels with any musical instrument such as a kettle-drum or a drum, thinking, "I shall give a gift of sound," or [when one thinks], "This is my gift of sound," regarding the drums and so forth—
He establishes [the teaching] himself and causes others to establish it. Furthermore, when he gives excellent medicines such as oil and molasses to those who preach the Dhamma,
proclaims the hearing of the Dhamma, recites the *sara-bhañña*, delivers a discourse on the Dhamma,
and engages in or causes others to engage in informal conversation and discourses of thanksgiving, then that is called the gift of sound.

Likewise, regarding the gift of fragrance (*gandhadāna*): having obtained any fragrant substance whatsoever—whether it be one of the various pleasing bases of fragrance such as root-fragrances and so forth, or even ground sandalwood or the like—one applies oneself to the quality of fragrance with the thought, "I shall give a gift of fragrance;

this gift of fragrance is mine," and thereby performs or causes to be performed worship of the Buddha-jewel and the others for the purpose of offering fragrance, using materials such as *agaru* and sandalwood.
One relinquishes a fragrant substance. This is the gift of fragrance.

Likewise, having obtained any delightful object of taste among roots, juices, and so forth, and having relished it as a flavor, one gives it to those worthy of offerings, thinking, "I shall give a gift of flavor;
this gift of flavor is mine," or else one gives the very substance of the taste, such as grain, cattle, and so on.
He relinquishes it. This is the gift of flavor.
Likewise, the gift of tangible objects should be understood by way of beds, chairs, and so forth, as well as by way of coverlets, blankets, and so forth.
For when one gives a bed, chair, couch, pillow, or the like, or clothing for wearing or wrapping that is pleasant to the touch and delightful—

Having obtained an irreproachable object of touch and having directed the mind toward it by way of that touch, one gives it to those worthy of offerings, thinking, "I shall give a gift of touch; this gift of touch is mine.
Having obtained such an object of touch as described, one relinquishes it; this is the gift of touch.

As for the gift of the Dhamma (*dhammadāna*), since it is intended here as having the Dhamma as its object (*dhammārammaṇa*), it should be understood by way of the "sustenance of nutritive essence" (*ojāpāna*) and life-force (*jīvita*).

For, having obtained some other delightful object among those such as nutritive essence, one applies the mind by way of the Dhamma as the object and gives a gift of nutritive essence such as ghee or fresh butter, thinking, "I shall give a gift of the Dhamma; this is my gift of the Dhamma. [Likewise,] there is the gift of the eight kinds of drinks, such as mango juice and so forth.
He gives; giving the gift of life means that, having resolved upon it, he gives tickets for meals, fortnightly meals, and so forth;
he provides medical attendants for those overcome by ill health and afflicted with disease;
he causes nets to be torn down, traps to be destroyed, and bird-cages to be demolished; and he effects the release from bondage for beings bound by fetters.
He causes the drum of non-killing to be beaten and performs or causes others to perform such deeds as these for the sake of protecting the lives of sentient beings.
This is called the gift of the Dhamma.
He dedicates all this aforementioned perfection of giving for the welfare and happiness of the entire world, and for his own attainment of perfect enlightenment.
He dedicates it toward unshakable liberation, toward the non-exhaustion of zeal, the non-exhaustion of energy, the non-exhaustion of concentration,
the non-exhaustion of ingenuity, the non-exhaustion of knowledge, and the non-exhaustion of liberation.
And by the Great Being who practices this perfection of giving, the perception of impermanence must be established regarding life.
Likewise, one should attend to the fact that these enjoyments are common to many, and one should constantly and continuously maintain great compassion toward sentient beings.
For in this way, taking what is essential from enjoyments— like removing all one's property and oneself from a burning house—
one leaves nothing behind and makes no distinction anywhere.
He does not do so with expectation; rather, he relinquishes it entirely without regard for anything else. This, first of all, is the method of practice for the perfection of giving (*dānapāramitā*).

As for the method of practice for the perfection of virtue (*sīlapāramitā*): since a Great Being who desires to adorn sentient beings with the ornaments of the virtues of the Omniscient One must, from the very beginning, purify his own virtue, therein [he should proceed] by way of four aspects.
Virtue is purified through the purity of one’s disposition, through formal undertaking, through non-transgression, and by restoring it to its original state should there be a transgression.

For, due to the purity of one’s disposition, some person—acting as their own master and having a nature that loathes evil—establishes the quality of moral shame (*hiridhamma*) within themselves and becomes one of perfectly pure conduct. Likewise, regarding the undertaking from another:
Being mindful, some person, having become a leader of the world, fearing evil and establishing the quality of moral dread (*ottappa*), becomes one whose conduct is perfectly pure.

Thus, in both ways, these individuals are established in virtue (*sīla*) by way of non-transgression. However, it may happen that through a lapse of mindfulness there occurs a breach or similar flaw in virtue.
By means of that very same aforementioned perfection of moral shame (*hiri*) and moral dread, [one restores it] immediately.
He restores it to its original state by means of confession and other such methods.
This virtue (*sīla*) is twofold: that consisting of abstention (*vāritta*) and that consisting of conduct (*cāritta*).
Among these, this is the method of practice regarding the Bodhisattva’s virtue of abstention: one must possess a mind imbued with compassion toward all beings even in a dream.
No resentment should arise. Because he is devoted to the welfare of others, he should not seize the property of others, which is like grasping a venomous snake.
If he is one who has gone forth, he lives far removed even from unchastity, being free from the seven forms of sexual union, let alone from adultery.
But if he is a householder who has not gone forth, he is always [restrained] regarding the wives of others.
He does not give rise even to an evil thought. And when speaking, he speaks only at the proper time, in a measured way, words that are true, beneficial, and pleasant;
he delivers a discourse on the Dhamma. He is everywhere free from covetousness, free from ill will, and possesses unperverted vision;
endowed with the knowledge that one's own actions are one's own property, he is firmly established in faith and affection toward those who have entered the right path and practice rightly.
Thus, having desisted from unwholesome courses of action and unwholesome states— which are the pathways to the suffering of the cycle of the four lower realms—
a Great Being established in the wholesome courses of action that are the pathways to heaven and liberation,

possesses intentions and applications that are utterly pure; consequently, his heart's desires, which bring about the welfare and happiness of sentient beings, are swiftly [fulfilled] according to his aspirations.
They are quickly accomplished, and the perfections (pāramitās) are fulfilled. For such is this person.
In that regard, by abstaining from harming, he gives the gift of fearlessness to all beings; he accomplishes the meditation on loving-kindness (mettā-bhāvanā) with little difficulty;
he attains the eleven benefits of loving-kindness; he is free from illness and free from affliction; he is long-lived and full of happiness; and he reaches distinguished marks (lakkhaṇa).
And it eradicates the latent tendency toward aversion.
Likewise, by abstaining from taking what is not given, one acquires wealth that is not shared with thieves and the like.

One becomes unassailable by others, dear, pleasing, and trustworthy; with a mind unattached to the attainment of riches, one is disposed toward renunciation and eradicates the latent tendency toward greed.
By turning away from unchastity, he becomes free from longing, with a tranquil body and mind; he is dear and pleasing to beings, beyond suspicion;
a fine reputation for him spreads abroad; his mind is unattached to women and his disposition is free from lust;
abounding in renunciation, he attains distinguished marks and eradicates the latent tendency toward greed.
By abstaining from false speech, one becomes an authority for beings, reliable, trustworthy, and one whose words are accepted;

one is dear and pleasing even to the deities; one’s mouth is fragrant; one’s bodily and verbal conduct is guarded; one attains specific marks of excellence, and one eradicates the latent tendencies of the defilements.

By abstaining from malicious speech, one becomes a body that cannot be divided even by the machinations of others, and one’s retinue likewise remains indivisible; one possesses unshakable faith in the true Dhammas, becomes a firm friend, and—like beings known from previous lives—is exclusively beloved and largely free from defilement.

By abstaining from harsh speech, one becomes dear and pleasing to beings, virtuous in character, sweet-spoken, and worthy of esteem; moreover, a voice endowed with the eight qualities is produced for such a person.
By abstaining from idle chatter, one becomes dear and pleasing to beings, respected and esteemed, one whose words are authoritative, and who speaks in moderation.
He is of great influence and great power; he is skilled in answering questions with spontaneous eloquence appropriate to the occasion;
and on the level of a Buddha, he is capable of answering the many questions of beings who speak many languages with a single utterance.
Through freedom from covetousness, he obtains what he desires and gains a taste for magnificent wealth among the wealthy nobles and others.
He is highly esteemed, invincible by adversaries, does not suffer from any deficiency of the faculties, and becomes a peerless individual.

Through non-malice, he is lovely to behold; he is respected by beings because he delights in their welfare, and through his delight in the welfare of beings, he inspires confidence in them with ease. Being of a gentle nature and dwelling in loving-kindness (*mettāvihārī*), he possesses great influence and great power.
Due to the absence of wrong views, he obtains virtuous companions; even when facing execution, he does not commit an evil deed.

He does not perform [superstitious rites], because he perceives that one is the owner of one’s own kamma; he is free from the superstition of seeking luck through omens, and his faith in the True Dhamma is firmly established and rooted.
He has faith in the enlightenment of the Tathāgatas, and like a royal swan in a place of filth, he finds no delight in other systems.
He is skilled in thoroughly understanding the three characteristics, and in the end, he attains unobstructed knowledge.
Until one attains enlightenment, one remains the most excellent among each respective class of beings and achieves the most sublime successes.
Thus, this thing called virtue (sīla) is the foundation for all success,
the source-ground for all the qualities of a Buddha, and the beginning, the foot, the mouth, and the foremost of all the factors that make a Buddha.

Having generated great respect, one should—by means of the power of mindfulness and clear comprehension regarding restraint of body and speech, taming of the sense faculties, purity of livelihood, and the use of requisites—be heedful and regard gain, honor, and fame as enemies with pleasant faces;
then, in the manner described in the passage beginning "As a hen guards her eggs," one should carefully fulfill virtuous conduct (*sīla*). This is...
Such is the method of practice regarding the virtue of restraint (*vāritta-sīla*).
However, the practice regarding the virtue of conduct (*cāritta-sīla*) should be understood as follows:

here, the Bodhisatta from time to time performs salutation, rising from his seat, joining of palms, and respectful service toward spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitta*) who occupy the position of teachers; likewise, [...]* *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly.*
From time to time, he attends upon them and provides physical service to those who are ill.
Having heard well-spoken words, he expresses his approval; he praises the virtues of those possessed of virtue, is patient toward the wrongs of others, and remembers their favors.
He rejoices in the merits of others and dedicates his own merits toward supreme perfect enlightenment at all times.
He dwells in heedfulness regarding wholesome states; having seen a transgression as a transgression, he confesses it truly to his fellow practitioners of the Dhamma;
and he further brings to full perfection right practice.
Likewise, he is skillful and untiring in providing assistance to beings in their appropriate duties conducive to their welfare.
He approaches [others]. And when beings encounter sufferings such as disease that have arisen, he provides the appropriate remedies.
When they have fallen into calamities regarding relatives, wealth, and so forth, he dispels their grief;

established in a nature that is supportive and uplifting, he restrains those who deserve restraint solely through the Dhamma, for the purpose of raising them out of unwholesome states and establishing them in the wholesome. As for those who deserve encouragement...
One who exerts himself solely through the Dhamma; having heard of those most sublime, supremely difficult, and inconceivable deeds of former Great Bodhisattvas—
which brought about the exclusive welfare and happiness of beings and by which their accumulations for enlightenment reached full maturity—
one should be neither agitated nor terrified, thinking, "Those great beings were also human beings."

However, through the gradual fulfillment of the training, they developed their own being and attained such supreme excellence of power that they reached the highest perfection in the requisites for enlightenment; therefore,
I too must practice correctly in the trainings of virtue and so forth, by means of which practice I too shall gradually fulfill the training and, in every respect—
Thinking, "I shall attain that state," he does not relinquish his energy, which is preceded by faith, and thus becomes one who perfectly fulfills the moral precepts.
Likewise, he is one whose virtue is concealed and whose transgressions are laid bare;

he is of few desires, contented, secluded, unattached, enduring suffering, free from anxiety, not restless, not arrogant, not fickle, not garrulous, not loose-tongued, and possessed of peaceful faculties.
With a peaceful mind, free from wrong livelihood such as hypocrisy and the like, perfected in conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults,
he undertakes and trains in the rules of training; with energy aroused and resolute,
regardless of body or life, he does not tolerate, abandons, and dispels even a slight regard for body or life, much less an excessive one.
He abandons and dispels all secondary defilements such as anger and resentment, which serve as causes for immorality.
Not being satisfied with a slight attainment of distinction, he does not fall into despondency, but strives for further and higher attainments of distinction.
In such a way that the prosperity already attained does not become subject to decline or stagnation, the Great Man—
He acts as a guide for the blind, pointing out the path; he provides signs by means of hand gestures for the deaf and explains their meaning;
and likewise for the mute. He gives a chair to those who are cripples, or provides a vehicle, or has one brought for them.
For those lacking faith, he exerts himself so that they may acquire faith; for the lazy, so that they may generate energy; and for those of muddled mindfulness...
He strives for the attainment of mindfulness; he strives for the perfection of concentration in those whose minds are distracted; and he strives for the acquisition of wisdom in those who lack it.
He strives to dispel sensual desire in those obsessed by sensual desire. He strives to dispel doubt in those obsessed by ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt.
He strives to dispel wrong thoughts such as sensual thoughts in those who are afflicted by them.

He exerts himself. Relying on gratitude toward beings who have previously done him a favor, he is the first to speak, speaks kindly, is inclusive, and honors them with a reciprocal service that is either equal or superior.
He performs the duty of a companion in times of misfortune. And having thoroughly understood the natural disposition of various beings, [he acts accordingly].
He dwells with those with whom he ought to dwell in such a manner; and he behaves toward those toward whom he ought to behave in such a way.
Moreover, this is done by causing them to emerge from the unwholesome and establishing them in the wholesome, and not otherwise.
For the protection of the minds of others by Bodhisattvas serves solely for the increase of the wholesome. Thus...
Even with a well-intentioned disposition, one should not harm another, nor revile them,
nor cause them embarrassment, nor arouse remorse in another, nor accuse them when they are not in a position to be censured,
nor place oneself on a higher level than one who has entered upon a lower practice, nor should one be entirely unassociating with others, nor excessively associating.
One should be one who associates at the proper time, not one who associates at the wrong time. Furthermore, one associates with beings suitable for association in accordance with the place and time.
One does not criticize those dear to others in their presence, nor does one praise those who are disliked. One is not one who betrays confidence. One does not refuse a righteous invitation.
He does not yield to persuasion, nor does he accept anything in excess. He encourages those endowed with faith by discourse on the benefits of faith;
he encourages those endowed with virtue, learning, generosity, and wisdom by discourse on the perfection of wisdom.

Furthermore, if the Bodhisatta has attained the power of the higher knowledges (*abhiññā*), he leads beings who have fallen into negligence to the various realms such as hell, according to their deserts, by means of his power of higher knowledge.

By bestowing [these gifts], he inspires a sense of spiritual urgency and establishes those lacking faith and other virtues in faith and the like. He causes them to enter the Teaching and brings to maturity those already endowed with the qualities of faith and so forth.
Thus, it should be understood that this immeasurable flood of merit and flood of skillfulness, which constitutes the conduct of the Great Being, increases further and further.
Furthermore, that detailed exposition of virtue (*sīla*) in its various aspects—which was set forth in the *Visuddhimagga* following the question, "What is virtue? In what sense is it virtue?

and the answer, "The states such as volition (*cetanā*) of one who abstains from killing living beings and so forth, or who fulfills the performance of duties, are virtue"—all of that should be brought here and explained. For only...

In that context, the discourse on virtue was presented from the perspective of the disciple and the bodhisatta; here, however, it must be spoken from the perspective of the *mahābodhisatta*, preceded by compassion and skillful means—this alone is the distinction.

Since this virtue is such that the Great Being does not [practice it] for the sake of liberation from defilement in an unfortunate rebirth, nor even for a fortunate rebirth, nor for the attainment of sovereignty, nor as a universal monarch (*cakkavatti*), nor as a deity...

Sakka, he does not dedicate it for the attainment of the state of Māra, nor for the state of Brahmā; likewise, he does not dedicate it for his own possession of the three knowledges (*tevijjā*), nor for the six direct knowledges (*chaḷabhiññā*), nor for the acquisition of the four analytical insights (*catuppaṭisambhidā*), nor for the enlightenment of a disciple (*sāvakabodhi*), nor for the enlightenment of a solitary buddha (*paccekabodhi*).
Rather, he dedicates it solely for the sake of providing all beings with the supreme ornament of virtue through the state of omniscience (*sabbaññubhāva*).
This is the method of practice for the perfection of virtue (sīlapāramī).

Likewise, because the arising of wholesome consciousness— which is embraced by compassion and skillful means, preceded by the vision of danger, and proceeds by way of renunciation from sense pleasures and states of existence—
is the perfection of renunciation (nekkhammapāramī), therefore, insofar as it is the place of dwelling for all defilements...
Because of the great confinement caused by children, wife, and so forth, and because of the agitation involved in being intent upon various occupations such as farming and trade,
the household life offers no opportunity for the happiness of renunciation and the like; furthermore, sensual pleasures— like a drop of honey clinging to the edge of a sword-blade—
are fleeting, provide meager satisfaction, and are followed by vast calamities, and thus they are to be grasped only by the flash of a lightning bolt.
They are to be found only for a brief moment; they are to be experienced through perverted perception, like the ornaments of a madman;

they serve as a remedy, like a covering of dung; they bring no satisfaction, like drinking thin water with fingers dipped in it; they are harmful, like food eaten by one whose stomach is already full;
they are a cause for the convergence of calamities, like bait on a hook; and like the heat of a fire, they persist throughout the three periods of time.
They are the cause for the arising of suffering; they are like monkey-glue, being a cause of bondage; they are like the concealment of executioners, being a covering for harm;
they are like dwelling in an enemy village, being a place of fear; they are like a nourisher of adversaries, being the bait for the Māra of the defilements and others;

they are like the pleasures of a festival, being suffering through change; they are like a fire in the hollow of a tree, burning from within; and they are like honeycombs on *bīraṇa* grass hanging over an old well.

Having observed the danger [of sensual pleasures] by way of such similes as being like a snake with many disadvantages, like drinking salt water which causes thirst, like liquor and spirits which are frequented by base people, and like a skeleton due to their meager gratification—
and having seen the benefits in renunciation as the opposite of that— with a mind inclined, leaning, and bent toward the bliss of renunciation, seclusion, and tranquility...
One should practice the perfection of renunciation (*nekkhamma-pāramitā*). Since renunciation is rooted in going forth (*pabbajjā*), one must first undertake going forth.

And when undertaking going forth, if no Buddha has appeared in the world, the Great Being should go forth under ascetics or wanderers who profess the efficacy of action (*kammavādī*) and the efficacy of deeds (*kiriyavādī*).
However, when Fully Enlightened Buddhas have appeared, one should go forth only in their dispensation.
Having gone forth and being established in the virtue as previously described, the ascetic qualities (dhutaguṇa) should be undertaken for the sake of purifying that very perfection of virtue.
For great beings who have undertaken the ascetic practices and maintain them correctly become few in wishes, contented, austere, secluded, unattached, energetic, easy to support, and so forth.
With all their conduct purified by the quality of faultless virtue and observances through the washing away of the stains of defilement by the water of the [three] qualities,
they are established in the first three ancient noble lineages; and in order to attain the fourth noble lineage,
known as delighting in meditation, they enter and dwell in jhāna— distinguished as access and absorption— upon any of the forty meditation subjects as appropriate.
In this way, indeed, his perfection of renunciation is rightly fulfilled.

At this point, however, regarding the fortyfold development of concentration— consisting of the thirteen ascetic practices (dhutaṅgas), together with the ten kasiṇas, the ten foulness meditations (asubha),
the ten recollections (anussati), the four divine abidings (brahmavihāra), the four formless attainments (āruppa), one perception (saññā), and one analysis (vavatthāna)— it is said:
The meditation subjects and the methods for their development should be explained in detail.
Since all of this has been set forth in every aspect and in detail in the *Visuddhimagga*, it should therefore be understood according to the method stated therein.
For while that was taught with reference to the disciple-bodhisatta, here it is taught with reference to the Great Bodhisatta, preceded by compassion, skillful means, and wisdom.
"Having done this, it should be said"—this is the specific distinction. Thus, the sequence of practice for the perfection of renunciation (nekkhamma-pāramī) should be understood here.

Likewise, by one desiring to accomplish the perfection of wisdom (paññā-pāramī), since wisdom—like light—cannot coexist with the darkness of delusion (moha), the Bodhisatta must first avoid the causes of delusion. In this regard, these are the causes of delusion:
— lack of interest, lethargy, yawning, laziness, delighting in socializing with crowds, a habit of sleeping, a habit of indecisiveness,
a lack of curiosity regarding knowledge, false conceit, failure to inquire, improper care of the body, an unconcentrated mind,
associating with persons of poor wisdom, not honoring those possessed of wisdom, self-deprecation, and wrong conceptualization.
Perversion, attachment to the body, excessive physical rigidity, a lack of sense of urgency, and the five hindrances—these are the causes of delusion.
In brief, they are those qualities which, when practiced, prevent unarisen wisdom from arising or cause arisen wisdom to decline.
Thus, avoiding these causes of confusion, one should apply oneself to great learning and to the meditative absorptions and other such practices.
In this regard, the following is the classification of the scope of great learning (*bāhusacca*): the five aggregates (*pañcakkhandhā*), the twelve bases (*dvādasāyatanāni*),
the eighteen elements (*aṭṭhārasa dhātuyo*), the four truths (*cattāri saccāni*), the twenty-two faculties (*dvāvīsatindriyāni*), the twelvefold dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppādo*),

as well as the foundations of mindfulness (*satipaṭṭhānādayo*) and the various classifications of wholesome and other phenomena (*kusalādidhammappakārabhedā*), those branches of knowledge (*vijjāṭṭhānāni*) which are blameless in the world, and those [skills] of beings...

The specific details of the grammatical analysis are suitable for the accomplishment of welfare and happiness; thus, having thoroughly penetrated the entire domain of the Sutta in this manner— by means of wisdom preceded by skill in means,
and through mindfulness, energy, and the acts of grasping, hearing, retaining, familiarizing oneself with, and questioning—
one should develop the wisdom consisting in what has been heard (*sutamaya-paññā*) by establishing others therein as well.
Likewise, the wisdom that constitutes immediate presence of mind regarding what must be done for beings, and which consists in skillfulness regarding means for their welfare and advancement,
should be exercised in various instances as appropriate, based on the desire for their benefit. Similarly, there is the wisdom consisting of reflection,
which involves contemplating the specific characteristics of phenomena such as the aggregates by way of investigating their modes.

They must be brought about. Furthermore, by one who is producing mundane full understanding through the discernment of the specific and general characteristics of the aggregates and so forth, the wisdom of preliminary-stage development must be accomplished.
For in this way, this mere name-and-form arises and ceases according to its respective conditions; herein there is no agent or instigator, in the sense of being non-existent after having been.

Understanding without distinction that internal and external phenomena are impermanent, suffering in the sense of being oppressed by arising and passing away, and non-self in the sense of being devoid of mastery,
and thereby abandoning attachment to them while leading others to abandon it as well—
driven solely by compassion— he continues in this way until the qualities of a Buddha come within the palm of his hand.

Establishing beings in the three vehicles through their introduction and maturation, and attaining mastery over the mundane jhānas, liberations, concentrations, attainments, and direct knowledges (abhiññā), he reaches the pinnacle of wisdom.

In this regard, there are these [knowledges]: the knowledge of the various supernormal powers, the knowledge of the divine ear-element, the knowledge of the penetration of others' minds, and the knowledge of recollecting past lives.

The divine eye-knowledge, the knowledge of the passing away and rebirth of beings according to their karma, and the knowledge of future existences—these, together with their respective adjuncts, are the five mundane supernormal powers (abhiññā) comprised under the wisdom of development (bhāvanā-paññā).

Furthermore, there is the wisdom consisting in the cultivation of knowledge through study and inquiry regarding those phenomena that serve as the foundation for the various categories such as the aggregates, bases, elements, faculties, truths, and dependent origination; and [the wisdom] based upon the purification of virtue and the purification of mind.

Having established oneself in these two purifications, one should develop the wisdom of cultivation—which is divided into the mundane and the supramundane—by accomplishing these five purifications that constitute its body:

purification of view, purification by overcoming doubt, purification by knowledge and vision of what is and is not the path, purification by knowledge and vision of the way, and purification by knowledge and vision. This is the method for accomplishing them.

Because [this] has been explained in detail in all its aspects in the *Visuddhimagga* according to the classification of objects, starting with: "In that regard, by a beginner yogi who desires to perform the supernormal transformations such as 'having been one, he becomes many,'" and so forth, as well as:
"'The aggregates' means the aggregate of form, the aggregate of feeling, the aggregate of perception, the aggregate of mental formations, and the aggregate of consciousness," and so forth.
It has been stated; therefore, it should be understood according to the method explained therein.

For while there wisdom was presented from the perspective of the disciple-bodhisatta, here it must be described from the perspective of the great bodhisatta, preceded by compassion, skillful means, and ingenuity.
Without reaching the purification of knowledge and vision, insight occurs specifically within the purification by knowledge and vision of the way.
"It should be set aside"—this alone is the distinction. In this way, the sequence of practice for the perfection of wisdom (paññā-pāramī) should be understood here.

Likewise, because a Great Being who has made the aspiration for perfect enlightenment must at all times be ever-exerted and prepared for the sake of fulfilling the perfections, with his equipment bound on, he should from time to time reflect: "Who indeed today..."
One should exert effort for the welfare of beings by reflecting day after day: "Have I accumulated a store of merit or a store of knowledge? Or have I performed any benefit for others?
One should relinquish whatever material possessions one holds as one's own, regarding both body and life, with a mind free from attachment, for the sake of assisting all sentient beings. Whatever...
Whatever action one performs, whether by body or by speech, all of it should be done with a mind inclined toward full enlightenment alone, and it should be dedicated to enlightenment.
One must have a mind that has turned away from both sublime and inferior sensual pleasures.
In all duties that ought to be performed, one should practice only after establishing skillful means (*upāyakosalla*).
In each instance for the welfare of beings, one should exert energy, enduring all things—whether desirable or undesirable—and remaining free from deceit.
All beings whatsoever should be pervaded with boundless loving-kindness and compassion.
Whatever suffering arises for any beings, all of that should be expected to happen to oneself. And the merit of all beings should be rejoiced in. [And likewise] of the Buddhas...

One’s greatness and majesty must be constantly reflected upon. Whatever action one performs, whether by body or speech, all of it should be preceded by a mind inclined toward enlightenment (*bodhininnacitta*).
For by this means, for the Great Being, the Bodhisatta who is steadfast, firm in exertion, and devotedly engaged in giving and the other perfections, [merit] becomes immeasurable.
The equipment of merit and the equipment of knowledge increase day by day.

Furthermore, for the sake of the enjoyment and protection of sentient beings, one should seek out and provide remedies for the sufferings of hunger, thirst, cold, heat, wind, sun, and so forth, even at the cost of sacrificing one’s own body and life. And whatever [merit arises] from that remedy for the aforementioned suffering—

He obtains happiness for himself; likewise, because he is thoroughly calmed through the absence of physical and mental distress in delightful monasteries, parks, palaces, ponds, and other such forest retreats, he obtains happiness for himself.

Furthermore, he hears that the Buddhas, the Buddhas who followed them, the Paccekabuddhas, and the Great Bodhisattvas—standing firm in the practice of renunciation—have attained a dwelling in happiness pertaining to this very life.
Thinking, "They are experiencing such bliss of meditative attainment (jhāna-samāpatti)," he directs all that [bliss] toward all beings without exception.
This, first of all, is the method for one established on the plane of non-concentration.
However, one established on the plane of concentration [directs it] toward others by means of the rapture (pīti) produced through the attainment of specific distinctions as experienced by himself.
Resolving upon tranquility, happiness, concentration, and knowledge of things as they truly are, he directs and dedicates [these qualities] toward all beings. Likewise,

seeing the multitude of beings submerged in the great suffering of saṃsāra and in the suffering of defilements and volitional formations which are its cause, he likewise [directs them] toward the sufferings produced therein by cutting, splitting, cleaving, crushing, and the heat of fire, and so forth.
In the hells, beings experience intense, harsh, and bitter sensations continuously for a long time;
among animals, they undergo great suffering through mutual anger, torment, harassment, injury, and subjection to others;

and among those such as the *nijjhāmataṇhika* (those who burn with thirst), whose bodies are covered in flames, who are scorched and withered by hunger, thirst, wind, and heat, and who cry out with upraised arms while feeding on vomit, spittle, and the like.
To those experiencing great suffering as hungry ghosts (*petas*); to those undergoing immense ruin and calamity rooted in their quest for existence;
to those who, through being subjected to punishments such as the severing of hands and so forth, become ugly, unsightly, and destitute; to those afflicted by hunger, thirst, and other ailments;
and to those who, because they are overcome by the powerful, carry the burdens of others, and are dependent on others—namely, hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals (*tiracchānagata*).
And [he saw] humans who, being overwhelmed by the fever of passion and other defilements due to their minds being distracted by the enjoyment of the poisons of sense-objects,

experience suffering no different from the suffering of the woeful states; and likewise [he saw] the gods of the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*), whose fever is unappeased, who live in dependence on others,
and who are like a mass of fire where dry wood is piled up and ablaze with flames fanned by the force of the wind— [all these he saw] with great...
Seeing that even the gods of the fine-material and immaterial realms— like birds that have plunged into the distant sky through exertion, or like arrows shot from a powerful hand into the distance—
are, despite their long duration, subject to falling due to impermanence and have not transcended birth, aging, and death,
one should arouse a great sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*) and [apply] loving-kindness (*mettā*).

And one should pervade all beings with compassion without exception. Thus, by constantly accumulating the requisites for enlightenment through body, speech, and mind, one should exert effort—acting with diligence, acting with persistence, and maintaining an undaunted disposition—so that the perfections reach their fulfillment;
in this way, the perfection of energy (vīriya-pāramitā) is to be brought to completion.

Moreover, the energy (*vīriya*) that is capable of aspiring to and gladdening oneself toward the state of Buddhahood— which is a treasury consisting of a mass of qualities that are inconceivable, immeasurable, vast, lofty, stainless, incomparable, and free from defilement— is indeed of inconceivable power,
such that ordinary people are not even able to hear of it, let alone practice it. For instance, there are three ways in which the arising of the mind of resolution occurs:
The four stages of Buddhahood, the four bases of sympathy, the single flavor of compassion, the condition for distinction through the realization of the Buddha-qualities—
namely, reflective acceptance (nijjhānakhanti)— unstainedness regarding all phenomena, the perception of all beings as one's own beloved children, tirelessness amidst the sufferings of saṃsāra,
the relinquishing of all things worthy of giving, and the absence of pride because of that, as well as the foundation of the higher training in virtue and so forth.
And therein: steadfastness; joy and gladness in performing wholesome deeds; a mind inclined toward seclusion; devotion to meditation; insatiability for the blameless Dhamma;
teaching the Dhamma as it has been heard to others with the intention of their welfare;
establishing beings in the true method (ñāya); firmness in undertaking; the state of being wise and brave; and the absence of agitation in the face of the censure or harm done by others.
The resolution of truth, mastery over meditative attainments, the acquisition of power in the higher knowledges, the realization of the three characteristics,
the accumulation of the requisites for the supramundane path through application to the practice of the foundations of mindfulness and so forth, and the entry into the nine supramundane stages—
all such practices for the equipment of enlightenment are accomplished solely by the power of energy; thus, from the initial aspiration...
Until the attainment of great enlightenment, one must diligently and continuously cultivate energy in such a way that it brings about ever-increasing distinction.
And when this aforementioned energy is successfully accomplished, all the requisites for enlightenment— such as patience, the resolve of truth, and so forth,
as well as generosity, virtue, and the rest— become perfected, since they exist in dependence upon it.
The practice regarding patience and the other [perfections] should also be understood by this same method.
Thus, the practice through giving (*dāna*) consists in providing manifold assistance to beings by relinquishing the requisites for their happiness;

through virtue (*sīla*), the causes for protecting their lives, property, and wives, as well as non-divisiveness, agreeable and beneficial speech, non-harming, and so forth; and through renunciation (*nekkhamma*),...
Their manifold conduct for the welfare of others consists of receiving material gifts and giving the gift of the Dhamma; their skill in means for accomplishing the welfare of others through wisdom;
their enthusiasm, undertaking, and steadfastness therein through energy; their endurance of others' offenses through patience;

their non-deception of them, their commitment to performing beneficial acts, and their freedom from falsehood through truthfulness; and through determination, even when encountering obstacles to performing those beneficial acts—

Non-wavering, reflecting upon their welfare and happiness through loving-kindness (*mettā*), and remaining free from mental disturbance or change toward them regardless of benefit or harm through equanimity (*upekkhā*)—
thus, the immeasurable accumulation of the requisites of merit and knowledge, unique to the Great Bodhisattva who has compassion for all beings and not shared with ordinary worldlings (*puthujjana*),
should be understood as the practice (*paṭipatti*) herein. And as for that which...
The condition has been stated, as well as its careful fulfillment.
What is the classification? There are thirty perfections (pāramīs): ten perfections, ten secondary perfections (upapāramīs), and ten ultimate perfections (paramatthapāramīs).
In this regard, for a Bodhisatta who has made the resolution and whose application is directed toward accomplishing the welfare of others, [there arise] qualities mixed with dark states...

Some say that the bright qualities (*sukkadhammā*) are the *pāramīs* themselves; the bright qualities not mixed with those [dark ones] are the *upapāramīs*; and the neither-dark-nor-bright is the *paramatthapāramī*.

Alternatively, they are called *pāramīs* when being fulfilled during the periods of their attainment; *upapāramīs* when full on the stage of a bodhisattva; and *paramatthapāramīs* when complete in every aspect on the stage of a Buddha.
Or else, it is because of the performance of the welfare of others on the stage of a bodhisattva...

The *pāramīs* are so called because they bring about one's own welfare; the *upapāramīs* because they bring about the welfare of both oneself and others through the attainment of the powers (*bala*) and intrepidities (*vesārajja*) on the stage of Buddhahood;
and the *paramattha-pāramīs* because they fulfill the welfare of both in its ultimate sense.

Thus, according to others, their classification is according to their beginning, middle, and end—that is, their aspiration, undertaking, and completion. [This applies] to those whose nature is compassion that pacifies the faults of others.

Others say that the classification [of the perfections] is according to the different ways of accumulating merit for those who have attained the happiness of existence, the happiness of liberation, and the supreme happiness.

From the arising of the Bodhisatta, there are the *pāramī*, *upapāramī*, and *paramatthapāramī* belonging to those who rely on shame (*lajjā*), mindfulness (*sati*), and self-respect (*māna*); who have the supramundane states as their masters; who revere virtue, concentration, and wisdom;
and who are the crossers, those already crossed, and those who cause others to cross—namely, the *anubuddha*, the *paccekabuddha*, and the *sammāsambuddha*.

Some say that the classification is as previously stated. Others hold that the *pāramīs* are the requisites active from the mental aspiration (*cittapaṇidhi*) up to the verbal aspiration (*vacīpaṇidhi*);
the *upapāramīs* are those active from the verbal aspiration up to the bodily aspiration (*kāyapaṇidhi*);
and from the bodily aspiration onwards are the *paramatthapāramīs*. Still others, however, maintain that the requisites active by way of rejoicing in the merit of others...

Some say: "The *pāramīs* are those that proceed by way of causing others to act; the *upapāramīs* are those that proceed by way of acting oneself; and the *paramatthapāramīs* are those that proceed by way of acting oneself [to the ultimate degree].

Likewise, some hold that the equipment of merit and knowledge which brings about one's own happiness in existence is the *pāramī*; that which brings about one's own happiness of Nibbāna is the *upapāramī*;
and that which brings about both kinds of happiness for others is the *paramatthapāramī*. [Furthermore,] the relinquishing of children, wife, wealth, and other requisites...

Furthermore, the perfection of giving (*dānapāramī*) consists of the sacrifice of limbs; the secondary perfection of giving (*dānaupapāramī*), the sacrifice of one’s own life; and the ultimate perfection of giving (*dānaparamatthapāramī*).
Likewise, there are three perfections of virtue (*sīlapāramī*) by way of not transgressing for the sake of the three types [of objects] beginning with wife and children;
and there are three perfections of renunciation (*nekkhammapāramī*) by way of departing after cutting off attachment to those same three types of objects.
The three perfections of wisdom (*paññā-pāramī*) consist in the eradication of craving for requisites, limbs, and life, by means of discerning what is beneficial and harmful for sentient beings.
The three perfections of energy (*vīriya-pāramī*) consist in the exertion toward the aforementioned types of relinquishment and so forth.
The three perfections of patience (*khanti-pāramī*) consist in the endurance of those things that create obstacles to requisites, limbs, and life. [For the sake of] requisites, limbs, and life...
The three perfections of truth (*sacca-pāramitā*) consist in the non-abandonment of truth;
the three perfections of resolve (*adhiṭṭhāna-pāramitā*) consist in the unshakable firmness of one's resolve even when one’s requisites and so forth are destroyed;

the three perfections of loving-kindness (*mettā-pāramitā*) consist in not relinquishing loving-kindness toward sentient beings who harm one’s requisites and so forth; [and] regarding the triad of bases as previously described...

The classification of these perfections should be understood through such passages as: "The three perfections of equanimity (upekkhā-pāramī) are so called by way of attaining neutrality toward beings and formations, whether they cause benefit or harm. What is their synthesis?
Herein, although these are thirtyfold when classified, they are tenfold by way of being the perfection of giving (dāna-pāramī) and the rest.
Thus, they are sixfold by way of generosity (*dāna*), virtue (*sīla*), patience (*khanti*), energy (*vīriya*), meditation (*jhāna*), and wisdom (*paññā*).

Among these, the perfection of renunciation (*nekkhamma-pāramī*) is included within the perfection of virtue, insofar as it consists in the state of going forth (*pabbajjā*); however, in its aspect of seclusion from the hindrances (*nīvaraṇa-viveka*), it is included in the perfection of meditation, and in its aspect of wholesome states (*kusala-dhamma*), it is included in all six.
The perfection of truth (*sacca-pāramī*) is merely a portion of the perfection of virtue, belonging to the side of truth as verbal abstinence (*vacī-virati*).

Furthermore, on the side of the truth of knowledge (*ñāṇasacca*), they are subsumed under the perfection of wisdom (*paññāpāramī*); the perfection of loving-kindness (*mettāpāramī*) is subsumed under the perfection of meditation (*jhānapāramī*) alone;

the perfection of equanimity (*upekkhāpāramī*) is subsumed under both the perfections of meditation and wisdom; and the perfection of resolution (*adhiṭṭhānapāramī*) is subsumed under all of them as well.
Moreover, regarding these six qualities—generosity and the rest—which are mutually interconnected, there are fifteen pairs and so forth that accomplish fifteen pairs and so forth.

They are as follows: by the pair of giving and virtue, there is the accomplishment of the pair of performing what is beneficial for others and refraining from what is harmful; by the pair of giving and patience, there is the accomplishment of the pair of non-greed and non-hatred;

by the pair of giving and energy, there is the accomplishment of the pair of generosity and learning; by the pair of giving and jhāna, there is the accomplishment of the pair of abandoning sensual desire and abandoning hatred.
By the pair of giving and wisdom, there is the accomplishment of the pair of the burden of the Noble Vehicle and the burden of the Great Vehicle; and by the pair of virtue and patience...

The accomplishment of the two purities—of application and of intention—is achieved through the pair of virtue and energy; the accomplishment of the two types of development is achieved through the pair of virtue and jhāna;

the accomplishment of the twofold abandonment of unvirtuousness and its obsession is achieved through the pair of virtue and wisdom; the accomplishment of the two kinds of giving is achieved through the pair of virtue and wisdom; the accomplishment of the two powers of forbearance and ardor is achieved through the pair of patience and energy;
the accomplishment of the twofold abandonment of opposition and compliance is achieved through the pair of patience and jhāna; and [the same is achieved] through the pair of patience and wisdom.
The accomplishment of the pair of patience and penetration regarding emptiness; the accomplishment of the pair of exertion and non-distraction by means of the pair of energy and jhāna;

the accomplishment of the pair of refuge by means of the pair of energy and wisdom; the accomplishment of the pair of vehicles by means of the pair of jhāna and wisdom; the accomplishment of the triad of abandoning greed, hatred, and delusion by means of the triad of giving, virtue, and patience;

the accomplishment of the triad of taking hold of wealth, life, and the essence of the body by means of the triad of giving, virtue, and energy; and the accomplishment of the triad of bases for meritorious action by means of the triad of giving, virtue, and jhāna.
The accomplishment of the triads consists in the giving of material things, the giving of fearlessness, and the giving of the Dhamma, by means of the triads of generosity, virtue, and wisdom.
In this way, the other triads and the tetradic groups and so forth should also be combined as far as possible with the triads and tetradic groups respectively.
Furthermore, the inclusion of these sixfold perfections (pāramīs) within the four foundations (adhiṭṭhānas) should be understood.
Indeed, from the grouping together of the collection of all the perfections (pāramīs), there are four foundations (adhiṭṭhānas), namely:
the foundation of truth (sacca), the foundation of generosity (cāga), the foundation of peace (upasama), and the foundation of wisdom (paññā).

In this context, it is called a "foundation" (adhiṭṭhāna) because one stands firm by means of it, or because one stands firm in it, or simply because it is a foundation; and since it is both truth and a foundation, it is the "foundation of truth."
Or, it is the resolution upon truth (*sacca*), or that which has truth as its resolution; thus it is "resolution upon truth" (*saccādhiṭṭhāna*). The same applies to the remaining [resolutions].

Therein, first of all, in a general sense, for the Great Being who has directed his aspiration toward supramundane qualities and who has compassion for all beings, there is the resolution upon truth by virtue of embracing all the perfections (*pāramī*) in accordance with his vow, and by virtue of abandoning their opposites.

It is the foundation of relinquishment (*cāgādhiṭṭhāna*). It is the foundation of tranquility (*upasamādhiṭṭhāna*) because of its peace through all the qualities of the perfections (*pāramitā*). It is the foundation of wisdom (*paññādhiṭṭhāna*) because of skill in the means for the welfare of others by means of those very same qualities.

In particular, it is the foundation of truthfulness (*saccādhiṭṭhāna*) because of not deceiving supplicants when promising "I shall give," because of giving without deceiving the promise, because of rejoicing without deceiving the act of giving, because of the abandonment of the opposites such as stinginess, and because of the non-destruction of the gift, the recipient, the act of giving, and the object to be given.

Generosity is the foundation for the four bases of confidence through the pacification of greed, hatred, delusion, and fear; by giving appropriately, at the right time, and according to the proper method;

and because it is preceded by wisdom among wholesome states. Likewise, the undertaking of restraint is the foundation for the four bases of confidence through non-transgression, the relinquishing of immorality, the pacification of misconduct, and because it is preceded by wisdom.

Virtue (*sīla*). Patience (*khanti*) has its proximate cause in the four foundations: because of enduring according to one's promise, because of relinquishing conceptualizations regarding the offenses of others, because of the subsiding of the obsession of anger, and because it is headed by wisdom.

Generosity (*cāga*) has its proximate cause in the four foundations: because of performing the welfare of others in accordance with one's promise, because of clear relinquishment, because of the subsiding of the unwholesome, and because it is headed by wisdom.

Energy: Jhāna has the four foundations as its proximate cause because it contemplates the welfare of the world in accordance with one’s promise, because of the abandoning of the hindrances, because of the calming of the mind, and because of having wisdom as its culmination.

Wisdom: Wisdom has the four foundations as its proximate cause because it possesses skill in means for the welfare of others according to one’s promise, because of the abandoning of unskillful action, because of the calming of the fever born of delusion, and because of the attainment of omniscience.

Therein, the foundation of truth (*saccādhiṭṭhāna*) consists in conformity with what is to be known and with one's promise; the foundation of relinquishment (*cāgādhiṭṭhāna*) consists in the abandoning of sensual objects as things and sensual objects as defilements;
the foundation of peace (*upasamādhiṭṭhāna*) consists in the subsiding of hatred and suffering; and the foundation of wisdom (*paññādhiṭṭhāna*) consists in full understanding and penetration.

The foundation of truth is embraced by the three kinds of truth and opposes the three kinds of corruption. The foundation of relinquishment is embraced by the three kinds of relinquishment and opposes the three kinds of corruption.
The foundation of tranquility, which is opposed to the three types of corruption, is embraced by the threefold tranquility.
The foundation of wisdom, which is opposed to the three types of corruption, is embraced by the threefold knowledge.

The foundations of relinquishment, tranquility, and wisdom are embraced by the foundation of truth because they do not deceive and because they conform to one’s promise; and the foundations of truth, tranquility, and wisdom are embraced by the foundation of relinquishment.

Because they result from the relinquishing of all opposites; because the foundations of truth, relinquishment, and peace are embraced by the foundation of wisdom due to the subsiding of the fever of the defilements, the subsiding of sensual desires, and the subsiding of the fever of sensual desires;
and because the foundations of truth, relinquishment, and peace are embraced by the foundation of wisdom due to being preceded by knowledge and following after knowledge—thus, all [of them]...
The perfections are manifested by truth, embellished by generosity, nourished by tranquility, and purified by wisdom. Indeed, truth is their cause of birth;
generosity is their cause of acquisition; tranquility is their cause of growth; and wisdom is their cause of purification.
Likewise, at the beginning, there is the foundation of truth because of the declaration of truth; in the middle, there is the foundation of generosity for one who has made the aspiration.
The foundation of self-sacrifice is for the sake of the welfare of others. At the end, there is the foundation of tranquility, because it is the ultimate consummation of all forms of peace.

Throughout the beginning, middle, and end, there is the foundation of wisdom, because when that [wisdom] exists, [the other foundations] arise, and when it is absent, they do not; and because they exist exactly as promised.

In this regard, Great Beings constantly possess the foundations of truth and relinquishment, which bring about their own welfare and the welfare of others, and which produce a state of being both venerable and beloved.
Having become householders, they assist others by means of the gift of material goods (*āmisa-dāna*).

Likewise, having become renunciants, they assist others by means of the gift of the Dhamma (*dhamma-dāna*), through the bases of serenity and wisdom which bring about one's own welfare and the welfare of others, and which produce a state of being revered and beloved.
In that regard, the fulfillment of the four bases occurs for a Bodhisatta in his final existence. For one whose four bases are fulfilled—

For some say it was during his final birth. For there, during the descent into the womb, the stay therein, and the emergence, through the attainment of the foundation of wisdom, he was mindful and clearly comprehending;

and through the fulfillment of the foundation of truth, having been born, he walked seven steps facing north, surveyed all directions, and with speech following the truth, said: "I am the foremost in the world, I am the eldest."
“I am the best in the world, I am supreme in the world”—thus he uttered the lion’s roar three times.

Through the realization of the foundation of tranquility, for one who perceives old age, sickness, death, and renunciation, and who is skilled in the four sections of the Dhamma, there is tranquility that overcomes the intoxication with youth, health, and life.
Through the realization of the foundation of generosity, [he abandoned] a great circle of kinsmen...
And it is the relinquishment, without regard, of the sovereignty of a wheel-turning monarch already in his hands.
Regarding the second station, some say that the four foundations are fulfilled at the moment of full enlightenment (*abhisambodhi*).

For there, through the realization of the foundation of truth (*saccādhiṭṭhāna*) in accordance with his promise, there is the direct realization (*abhisamaya*) of the four noble truths; from that, indeed, comes the foundation of truth.
It is fulfilled. Through the realization of the foundation of generosity, there is the relinquishing of all defilements and secondary defilements; thus, the foundation of generosity is fulfilled.
Through the realization of the foundation of peace, there is the attainment of supreme peace; thus, the foundation of peace is fulfilled.
Through the realization of the foundation of wisdom, there is the acquisition of unobstructed knowledge; thus, the foundation of wisdom is fulfilled.
"Complete": this is not established, because even at the moment of full enlightenment (abhisambodhi), it exists only in the ultimate sense (paramattha).
Others say that in the third stage, the Turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, the foundation of the Four Truths (catur-adhiṭṭhāna) is complete.
For there, through the teaching of the Noble Truths in twelve aspects by one who has mastered the foundation of the Truths (sacca-adhiṭṭhāna), the foundation of the Truths [is fulfilled].
It is fulfilled. For one who has accomplished the foundation of generosity, the foundation of generosity is fulfilled by performing the great sacrifice of the true Dhamma.
For one who has accomplished the foundation of tranquility, the foundation of tranquility is fulfilled by being tranquil oneself and bringing tranquility to others.
For one who has accomplished the foundation of wisdom, the foundation of wisdom is fulfilled by thoroughly understanding the inclinations and other traits of those to be trained.
"Complete": this too is unestablished, because the Buddha’s duty (*buddhakicca*) has not yet been brought to its conclusion.
Others say that in the fourth stage, at the time of final Nibbāna (*parinibbāna*), the four foundations are complete.

For there, due to having attained final Nibbāna through the perfection of the ultimate truth (*paramatthasacca*), the foundation of Truth (*saccādhiṭṭhāna*) is complete; and through the relinquishing of all acquisitions (*upadhi*), the foundation of Generosity (*cāgādhiṭṭhāna*) is complete.
The foundation of tranquility is fulfilled through the subsiding of all conditioned phenomena. The foundation of wisdom is fulfilled through the final consummation of the application of wisdom.

In this regard, for the Great Being, the fulfillment of the foundation of truth is especially manifest in his birth within the field of loving-kindness (*mettā*), having emerged from the foundation of truth; and [it is likewise] especially [manifest] within the field of compassion (*karuṇā*).

It should be understood that at the time of the full enlightenment (abhisambodhi), the fulfillment of the foundation of wisdom (paññādhiṭṭhāna) attained through the foundation of wisdom is made manifest;

specifically, at the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma in the field of sympathetic joy (muditā), the fulfillment of the foundation of generosity (cāgādhiṭṭhāna) attained through the foundation of generosity is made manifest;
and specifically, at the final Nibbāna in the field of equanimity (upekkhā), the fulfillment of the foundation of peace (upasamādhiṭṭhāna) attained through the foundation of peace is made manifest.
In this regard, the virtue of one who has accomplished the foundation of truth is to be known through living together with them;

the purity of one who has accomplished the foundation of generosity is to be known through their dealings; the fortitude of one who has accomplished the foundation of peace is to be known in times of adversity;
and the wisdom of one who has accomplished the foundation of wisdom is to be known through discussion. Thus are the purifications of virtue, livelihood, mind, and view.
They should be understood as follows: through the accomplishment of the foundation of truth, one does not go to the wrong course of hatred because of non-deceptiveness;

through the accomplishment of the foundation of generosity, one does not go to the wrong course of greed because of non-attachment; through the accomplishment of the foundation of peace, one does not go to the wrong course of fear because of innocence;
and through the accomplishment of the foundation of wisdom, one does not go to the wrong course of delusion.
Through the realization of things as they truly are:
by the first [foundation of mindfulness], one endures without hatred; by the second, one partakes without greed; by the third, one avoids without fear;
and by the fourth, one dispels without delusion. Through the first, there is the attainment of the bliss of renunciation; through the others...
It should be understood that there are the attainments of the bliss of seclusion, the bliss of tranquility, and the bliss of enlightenment.

Likewise, by means of these four foundations, there are respectively the attainment of the joy and bliss born of seclusion, the joy and bliss born of concentration, the bodily bliss born of the absence of joy, and the bliss of equanimity born of the purity of mindfulness.

Thus, the inclusion of the entire collection of all perfections (pāramīs) should be understood as being comprised within these four foundations, which are accompanied by manifold virtues. And just as the inclusion of all perfections is achieved through these four foundations, [so too...]
The same should be understood for compassion (*karuṇā*) and wisdom (*paññā*). For the entire equipment for enlightenment (*bodhisambhāra*) is comprised within compassion and wisdom.
Indeed, qualities such as giving (*dāna*), when embraced by compassion and wisdom, become the equipment for great enlightenment, culminating in the accomplishment of Buddhahood.
In this way, their inclusion should be understood.
What is the method for its accomplishment? It is the complete gathering of the entire equipment of merit and so forth, dedicated toward perfect enlightenment, by way of practicing without deficiency;

therein, it consists of practicing with care through the application of reverence and great respect, practicing with constancy through uninterrupted application, and the application over a long period of time by not reaching completion prematurely. As for the measure of that duration:
This will be explained later. Thus, the practice of the four factors is the means for accomplishing these perfections (pāramīs).
Likewise, a Great Being practicing for enlightenment must offer himself to the Buddhas even before his attainment of perfect self-awakening, thinking:
"I offer this personal existence (attabhāva) to the Buddhas. And he must likewise offer each object of possession even prior to its acquisition.
It should be relinquished through the gateway of generosity: "Whatever kind of requisites for life arise for me, I shall give them all when there is a petitioner;
however, I shall use only what remains after they have been given.
For when he has thus formed a mental volition for complete renunciation, whatever object of possession arises [for him]...

Whether it be inanimate or animate, therein there are these four obstructions to giving: lack of prior practice in giving, the meagerness of the object to be given, the excellence and desirability [of the object], and anxiety regarding its depletion.
When these are present, and when the objects to be given exist for the Mahābodhisatta and supplicants have appeared before him, his mind [turns toward] giving.
It does not leap forward, it does not incline toward it. Therefore, one should reach this conclusion: "Surely I have no prior familiarity with giving;
that is why my desire to give does not settle in my mind now. Thinking, "In this way my mind will henceforth delight in giving;
come now, I shall give from this point on," [he reflects: "Is it not the case that I should have secured the objects of possession beforehand?"

He gives gifts to supplicants with a mind relinquished, being one who has abandoned stinginess, whose hands are pure, who delights in renunciation, who is devoted to begging, and who rejoices in giving and sharing.
In this way, the Great Being’s first bond of giving is struck down, shattered, and utterly cut off.
Likewise, when the object to be given is limited or deficient, the Great Being reflects thus:
“Indeed, because of my lack of generosity and moral habit in the past, I have now become so destitute of the necessary requisites;

therefore, even by afflicting myself with whatever gift I have obtained—whether it be meager or inferior—I must now give that gift alone, so that in the future I may bring the perfection of giving to its ultimate consummation. Thus, he gives that gift with whatever is available, being one who has abandoned all attachment.
With hands purified, delighting in relinquishment, devoted to begging, and rejoicing in giving and sharing— thus the Great Being’s second bond of giving was struck down,
shattered, and utterly cut off. Likewise,
when a thought of unwillingness to give arose in the Great Being due to the excellence and desirability of the object to be given, he reflected thus:
He reflects: "O worthy man, have you not indeed aspired to the most sublime and most excellent perfect enlightenment?
Therefore, for that purpose, it is fitting for you to give gifts that are both sublime and agreeable.
Thus, he gives what is sublime and agreeable—liberal-handed, pure-handed, delighting in relinquishment, devoted to supplicants, and rejoicing in giving and sharing. In this way...
The Great Being’s third bond to generosity was destroyed, abolished, and utterly cut off.
Thus, while giving a gift, when the Great Being saw that the objects to be given were being exhausted, he reflected:
"This indeed is the inherent nature of wealth, namely its liability to exhaustion and its liability to decay. Moreover, previously..."
“Because such giving was not performed, this depletion of wealth is seen;
well then, with whatever gift I have obtained—whether small or great—I shall give only in charity, so that in the future I may reach the pinnacle of the perfection of giving.
Thus, he gives with whatever he has obtained, being one who is generous, pure-handed, and delighting in relinquishment.
He is devoted to begging and delights in giving and sharing. In this way, the Great Being’s fourth bond of generosity is struck down, destroyed, and utterly severed.
Thus, the method for dispelling whatever obstacles there may be to the perfection of generosity is to reflect upon them as appropriate and remove them.
And just as it is with the perfection of generosity, so too should it be understood for the perfections of virtue and the rest.
Moreover, that self-surrender to the Buddhas by the Mahāsatta is precisely the means for the perfect accomplishment of all the perfections (*pāramīs*).
For the Great Being, having surrendered himself to the Buddhas, remained there striving and exerting himself toward the fulfillment of the requisites for enlightenment in various circumstances,
even amidst unbearable hardships that cut short his life and his means of bodily comfort.

Even when faced with misfortunes that are difficult to overcome, brought about by the conditioned nature of beings—misfortunes that are severe, life-threatening, and calamitous—he does not waver or tremble on account of them, thinking, "This body has been surrendered by me to the Buddhas; let whatever may happen here, happen.
He does not undergo even the slightest change, but remains instead like one whose resolve is utterly immovable in the undertaking of what is wholesome.
In this way, the surrendering of oneself is also a means for accomplishing these perfections.

Furthermore, in brief, the means for accomplishing them is the drying up of attachment to oneself and the increasing of attachment toward others for one who has made the great aspiration for the attainment of perfect enlightenment.
For it is said: "For one who has made the great vow for the attainment of perfect enlightenment..."
Through the thorough understanding of all phenomena as they truly are,
the Great Being becomes unstained by them, and his attachment to himself comes to exhaustion and total end; however, through the cultivation of great compassion,
as he regards all beings as if they were his own dear children, his affection of loving-kindness and compassion for them increases, and from that, in accordance with each respective state—

The Great Being, having distanced himself from stinginess and other factors opposed to the requisites for enlightenment through the disappearance of greed, hatred, and delusion within his own and others' continuums,
brings people to entry into the three higher vehicles by means of the four bases of sympathy—
generosity, pleasant speech, purposeful conduct, and impartiality— which are accompanied by the four foundations and consist in the ultimate gathering of the people.
And they bring about maturation.
For the great compassion and great wisdom of the Great Beings are adorned by generosity; generosity is adorned by pleasant speech;
pleasant speech by beneficial conduct; and beneficial conduct is adorned and embraced by impartiality. [They bring this] to all those beings...
