For those who practice the requisites of enlightenment while making no distinction from themselves, success is achieved through equanimity (*samānattatā*) and the state of having equal pleasure and pain in all circumstances.

Furthermore, even for those who have become Buddhas, the complete training (*abhivinaya*) of people is accomplished by means of the same four bases of sympathy (*saṅgahavatthu*), which have increased through the fulfillment of the four foundations (*adhiṭṭhāna*), thereby effecting their ultimate gathering.
For indeed, giving (*dāna*) belongs to the Perfectly Enlightened Ones.
Loving speech is fulfilled and increased by the foundation of generosity; beneficial conduct by the foundation of truth;
and impartiality by the foundation of peace. For the Tathāgatas’ impartiality toward all disciples and paccekabuddhas is complete in parinibbāna;
for therein they are without distinction, becoming one. Therefore it was said: "There is no difference in liberation..."
“...diversity. And there are these verses:
“The truthful, generous, peaceful, wise, and compassionate one—having gathered all the necessary provisions, what purpose would he not accomplish?”
“The Teacher is possessed of great compassion, seeking the welfare of others and yet impartial;
he is indifferent toward everything—oh, how wonderful is the Conqueror!
Detached from all phenomena, he is equanimous toward all beings.”
Always intent on the welfare of beings— oh, how wonderful is the Conqueror! “Ever devoted to the benefit and happiness of all beings,
and untiring in his efforts— oh, how wonderful is the Conqueror!”
In what length of time is it accomplished? At the minimum limit, it is four incalculables (asaṅkhyeyya) and one hundred thousand great aeons (mahākappa);
at the intermediate limit, eight incalculables and one hundred thousand great aeons;
and at the maximum limit, sixteen incalculables and one hundred thousand great aeons. And these divisions are, respectively:
They are to be understood by way of those predominant in wisdom, those predominant in faith, and those predominant in energy.

For it is stated in the Commentary that for those predominant in wisdom, faith is dull while wisdom is sharp; for those predominant in faith, wisdom is middling; and for those predominant in energy, wisdom is dull.
Furthermore, it is through the power of wisdom that perfect enlightenment (sammāsambodhi) is to be attained.
Others, however, say: "This division of time for Bodhisattvas is due to the sharp, middling, or dull nature of their energy (vīriya).

But generally speaking, through the sharp, middling, or dull nature of those qualities conducive to the maturation of liberation, the requisites for enlightenment reach fulfillment according to the aforementioned divisions of time; thus, these are the three divisions of time.

They also say they are "joined. Thus, at the moment of the initial resolve (*abhinīhāra*), Bodhisattvas are of three kinds, distinguished as those who understand by a brief hint (*ugghaṭitaññū*), those who understand by exposition (*vipañcitaññū*), and those who must be guided (*neyya*).

Among them, one who understands by a brief hint, while hearing a four-line verse in the presence of a Perfectly Enlightened One, attains Arhatship together with the six direct knowledges (*abhiññā*) and the analytical insights (*paṭisambhidā*) even before the third line of the verse has been completed.

There is the supporting condition of capability; if one were intent upon the enlightenment of a disciple (sāvakabodhi), [the first person] would possess the supporting condition of capability to attain arahantship by means of the six direct knowledges (abhiññā) while hearing a four-line verse from the presence of the Blessed One, even before the fourth line of that verse was finished, provided they were intent upon the enlightenment of a disciple. There is the supporting condition of capability; if one were intent upon the enlightenment of a disciple, [the second person] would possess the supporting condition of capability to attain arahantship by means of the six direct knowledges while hearing a four-line verse from the presence of the Blessed One, even before the fourth line of that verse was finished, provided they were intent upon the enlightenment of a disciple.

But another, having heard a four-line stanza in the presence of the Blessed One, possesses the necessary potential (upanissaya) to attain Arahantship with the six higher knowledges (abhiññā) once that stanza is finished.
All three of them, having made their resolution (abhinīhāra) without distinction as to time, received a prophecy (byākaraṇa) in the presence of the Buddhas;
and by gradually fulfilling the perfections (pāramī), they reach Perfect Enlightenment (sammāsambodhi) in due order at the times specified above.
Yet, throughout those various periods when they were not yet fulfilled, those Great Beings— though giving great gifts day after day like the gift of Vessantara,
though accumulating all the qualities of the perfections such as virtue and the rest, though relinquishing the five great renunciations,
and though bringing to their ultimate peak the conduct for the sake of relatives, the conduct for the sake of the world, and the conduct for the sake of Buddhahood—
And it is impossible that there will be perfectly enlightened Buddhas in the interval. Why?
Because of the incompleteness of their knowledge and because the qualities that constitute a Buddha have not yet reached their final consummation.
For just as a crop is produced within a specific time, so too is perfect enlightenment brought to completion within the aforementioned time-limit; and immediately thereafter, with all effort...

It should be understood that even with effort, it is not possible to attain [the goal] without the fulfillment of the perfections (pāramī) being accomplished according to the specific time-periods already mentioned.
What is the benefit? For those Bodhisattvas who have made their resolution:
"Thus, men endowed with all factors are destined for enlightenment..."
Throughout the long course of saṃsāra, even for hundreds of millions of eons,
they do not arise in the Avīci hell, nor likewise in the Lokantara hells; their craving is parched away,
they suffer neither hunger nor thirst, and they do not become Kālakañjika spirits.
“Small creatures do not fall into an evil rebirth;
when born among humans, they are not blind from birth.
They have no deficiency of hearing, nor do they become mute.”
They do not undergo rebirth as females, nor as those with dual sexual characteristics or as eunuchs.
These men are not included among those subject to the lower realms;
they are destined for enlightenment, freed from the deeds of immediate retribution, and pure in their conduct in every respect.
“They do not practice wrong view, seeing the efficacy of kamma;
even while dwelling in the heavens, they are never reborn in the realm of non-perception.
Among the gods of the Pure Abodes, no cause for such rebirth exists.”
“True persons, inclined toward renunciation and detached from existence after existence, practice deeds for the welfare of the world and fulfill all the perfections.
Thus were the benefits described. And as for those [passages] such as: “Mindful and clearly comprehending, Ānanda, the Bodhisatta, having passed away from the Tusita realm...”
The sixteen modes of wonderful and marvelous phenomena, beginning with "he descends into the mother's womb," and the thirty-two modes of portents,
beginning with "coldness is dispelled and heat is stilled" and "Sāriputta, when the Bodhisatta is being born,
this ten-thousandfold world system trembles, shakes, and quakes."
Furthermore, whatever other benefits— such as the fulfillment of the aspirations of Bodhisattvas, mastery over karma and so forth—
are shown in various places in the Jātakas, Buddhavaṃsas, and other texts, all of these are also their benefits. Likewise,
it should be understood that they include the pairs of qualities such as non-greed and non-hatred, according to the classifications already indicated.
Moreover, because from the moment of his initial resolve the Bodhisatta has been like a father to all beings through his desire for their welfare;
and because, by virtue of his distinguished qualities, he is worthy of offerings, venerable, adorable, and the supreme field of merit;
and because his mental continuum is permeated with loving-kindness and compassion, he is generally dear to human beings, dear to non-human beings, and protected by the deities.
He becomes invincible to wild beasts and the like; and in whichever order of beings he is reborn, by virtue of his connection with distinguished merit,
he surpasses other beings in that very realm through superior beauty, superior fame, superior happiness, superior strength, and superior sovereignty.
He is free from illness and free from affliction; his faith is perfectly pure and clear, as are his energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom.
He has dull defilements, dull distress, and dull fever.
Precisely because his defilements are dull, he is easy to speak to, receptive to instruction, patient, gentle, amiable, and skilled in hospitality.
He is free from anger and free from malice; he is without hypocrisy and without spite;
he is not envious and not miserly; he is not fraudulent and not deceitful; he is not stubborn and not conceited; he is not agitated and is diligent;
he endures the provocations of others and does not provoke others; and whatever village or field he dwells in, there he [removes] the calamities of beings such as fear.
For the most part, [evil states] that have not yet arisen do not arise, and those already arisen are stilled.

Furthermore, even when he is reborn in the states of misery (*apāya*), he is not oppressed by suffering as excessively as ordinary people are; rather, he experiences an even greater degree of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*).
Therefore, these qualities—such as being equal to a father and being worthy of offerings—which are found in various births according to the Great Man’s capacity, [are to be understood in this way].
The specific qualities (*guṇavisesa*) should be understood as the benefits (*ānisamsa*).

Likewise, the perfection of lifespan, the perfection of physical form, the perfection of lineage, the perfection of sovereignty, the quality of having authoritative speech, and great majesty—these too should be understood as the benefits of the perfections (*pāramī*) of a Great Being (*mahāpurisa*). Among these, "perfection of lifespan" refers to that [lifespan]...
In that rebirth, there is long life and longevity; by means of that, one brings to completion the wholesome undertakings already begun and accumulates much merit.
"Perfection of form" means being handsome, beautiful to behold, and pleasing;
by means of that, one inspires confidence in beings who judge by physical appearance and becomes worthy of esteem. "Perfection of family" [is as follows:]...

"High birth" means being reborn in noble families; because of that, one becomes approachable and worthy of attendance even by those intoxicated with the pride of birth and so forth, and thereby one brings them to the performance of service.
"Perfection of sovereignty" means great wealth, great influence, and a large retinue;
by means of these, one is able to win over those who should be won over through the four bases of sympathy (*saṅgahavatthu*), and to restrain those who should be restrained.
And he is capable of restraining by means of the Dhamma.
"Having speech that is authoritative" means being trustworthy and reliable; through this, he becomes an authority for beings, and his command is not to be transgressed.
"Possessing great majesty" means the greatness of one's power; through this, one is not overcome by others.
Furthermore, it should be understood that when one personally overcomes others entirely through righteousness,
equity, and qualities as they truly are, these perfections of a Great Being— beginning with the perfection of longevity— are the benefits of the *pāramīs*.
They should be known as the causes for the increase of one's own immeasurable accumulation of merit, and as the means for introducing and maturing sentient beings within the Three Vehicles.
What is their fruit? Briefly stated, the state of being a Perfectly Enlightened One (*sammāsambuddha*) is their fruit.

In detail, however, it is the glory of the Dhamma-body (*dhammakāya*), which is adorned by an infinite and immeasurable collection of qualities, beginning with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man (*mahāpurisalakkhaṇa*), the eighty minor characteristics (*anubyañjana*), the fathom-wide radiance (*vyāmappabhā*), and other such multitudes of radiant virtues;

as well as the perfection of the physical body (*rūpakāya*), the ten powers (*bala*), the four grounds of self-confidence (*vesārajja*), the six kinds of uncommon knowledge (*asādhāraṇañāṇa*), the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha (*aveṇikabuddhadhamma*), and so forth—qualities that cannot be fully described even in many eons. As for all the Buddha-qualities...
Even the Perfectly Enlightened One would not be able to bring these to an end with words; this is their fruit.

And so it has been said: “Were a Buddha to speak the praise of a Buddha, Without speaking of anything else for an eon, That eon might be exhausted in its long duration, But the praise of the Tathāgata would not be exhausted.”
In this way, the miscellaneous discourse regarding the perfections (pāramīs) should be understood here.

As for the two concluding verses stated later in the text— beginning with "Having seen laziness as a danger" and so forth— which show all the perfections together after the passage beginning with "The gift that ought to be given,
having given"— those [verses] concern those who, through the exertion of energy and the cultivation of loving-kindness (mettā),...

Through dwelling in heedfulness (*appamāda*), the qualities that constitute a Buddha, as previously described, attained clarity, and his own liberation—designated as Perfect Enlightenment (*sammāsambodhi*)—was brought to maturity.
For the sake of giving instruction to those to be trained (*veneyya*) so that their own liberation might likewise reach maturity, he dwelt [in this manner].
Therein, by seeing indolence as a danger and the exertion of energy (*vīriyārambha*) as security, he demonstrated the perception of the disadvantage in its opposite by way of this [verse].
He shows the benefit in the exertion of energy. By saying, "Be those who have aroused energy," he enjoins one to the exertion of energy. And because it has been said:
"To refrain from all evil, to cultivate the wholesome, and to purify one's own mind—this is the teaching of the Buddhas."

In brief. In detail, however, all forms of excellence proclaimed throughout the entire word of the Buddha depend entirely upon right effort; therefore, having directed [the practitioner] toward the arousal of energy, the Blessed One said, "This is the instruction of the Buddhas.
Herein, this is the summarized meaning: that which is called indolence, because it is the root of all defilements and the bringer of all misfortune, should be viewed as a terror;
and the arousal of energy, being its opposite, should be seen as the means for achieving a state free from calamity through the four applications of mindfulness.
Having seen [the world] as secure, the undertaking of energy by way of accomplishing the training in higher virtue and so forth is the application of right effort (*sammappadhānānuyoga*).
In that regard, the proper exhortation, "Be energetic," is the instruction, the teaching, and the admonition of the Blessed Buddhas.
The meaning of the remaining verses should also be understood in this same manner.
This, however, is the distinction: *vivāda* means contradictory speech; the meaning is "quarreling by way of the subject matter of dispute.
*Avivāda* is the opposite of quarreling, namely, friendly verbal action or the cultivation of loving-kindness (*mettā*).

Alternatively, *avivāda* refers to the sixfold quality of conciliation (*sāraṇīyadhamma*), which serves as the cause for the absence of quarreling. *Samaggā* means not being divided, both in body and in mind.
"And together" means unbroken, uninterrupted, and inseparable. "Amiable" means possessing gentle virtue; the meaning is that they have hearts that are soft toward one another.

"This is the instruction of the Buddhas": here, it should be connected as follows—by not engaging in any dispute whatsoever and by being directed toward living in harmony through the fulfillment of the six qualities conducive to concord, this is the exhortation of the Buddhas. For those living in harmony...

"Having attained commonality in virtue and view, and being without dispute, they will easily fulfill the three trainings"—thus the Teacher showed that his own teaching consists in enjoining communal living.
"Negligence" (*pamāda*) means neglecting; it is the forgetting of wholesome states (*kusaladhamma*) and the mind’s relinquishing itself to unwholesome states.

For this has been said: "In this context, what is negligence? It is the relinquishing of the mind, the continued relinquishing of the mind, toward misconduct of body, misconduct of speech, or misconduct of mind;

or toward the five strands of sensual pleasure; or it is the lack of earnestness in the cultivation of wholesome states, the lack of constancy in their practice, the lack of steadfastness in their practice, a state of sluggish conduct, and the laying aside of the desire for them."
“Neglecting one’s duty, lack of practice, lack of cultivation, lack of frequent exercise...
whatever is such negligence, the act of being negligent, the state of being negligent—this is called negligence.
As for “heedfulness” (*appamāda*): it is the absence of negligence. It should be understood as the opposite of negligence; for in terms of its meaning, heedfulness is...
“Non-separation from mindfulness” is its name; and this name “non-separation from mindfulness” applies specifically to mindfulness that is constantly established.
Others, however, say: “Appamāda (heedfulness) consists of the four immaterial aggregates occurring in such a manner, with mindfulness and clear comprehension as their predominant factors.
For there is no such thing as a separate meditation called the development of heedfulness (*appamādabhāvanā*). Whatever meritorious deed there may be...
All wholesome activity should be understood as nothing other than the development of diligence (*appamādabhāvanā*).
Specifically, however, with reference to taking refuge as a support for turning away from the round of existence (*vivaṭṭūpanissaya*) and the restraint of body and speech,

all development of virtue (*sīlabhāvanā*), all development of concentration (*samādhibhāvanā*), all development of wisdom (*paññābhāvanā*), all development of the wholesome, and the development of the blameless are included.
The cultivation of heedfulness (*appamādabhāvanā*). For this term "heedfulness" (*appamāda*) illuminates a great significance;

it stands having encompassed a great significance. A preacher of the Dhamma who, having brought forward even the entire word of the Buddha consisting of the Three Pitakas, explains the meaning of the term "heedfulness," cannot be said to have "leaped across with a shallow ford. Why? Because of the term "heedfulness" (*appamādapada*).

Because of his greatness. For thus, at the time of his final nibbāna while reclining between the twin sāla trees in Kusinārā, the Fully Enlightened One—summarizing the Dhamma he had spoken over forty-five years since his full awakening into a single phrase—gave this exhortation to the bhikkhus: "Strive with diligence."
And so it was said: "Just as, monks, whatever footprints of living beings that move about there may be, they all fit within the footprint of the elephant;

the elephant's footprint is declared to be the foremost among them by reason of its size—even so, monks, whatever wholesome states there are, they all have heedfulness as their root and converge upon heedfulness."
"Among them, heedfulness is declared to be the foremost. In this context, showing that the cultivation of heedfulness has reached its culmination, the Teacher said:
"Cultivate the Eightfold Path. Its meaning is as follows:
that which comprises the three aggregates beginning with virtue, preceded by right view, and consisting precisely of right view and the other [factors]...
The Noble Eightfold Path consists of eight factors; cultivate it, cause it to arise within your own continuum.
Do not rest merely at the path of seeing, but increase it by means of producing the three higher paths.
In this way, your cultivation of diligence will reach its culmination. This is the instruction of the Buddha regarding wholesome states.
"Non-forgetfulness"—and having made that one's primary endeavor, this cultivation of the Noble Path is the instruction and advice of the Blessed Buddhas.
Thus, the Blessed One brought the teaching of the *Cariyāpiṭaka* to its conclusion with the very pinnacle of Arahantship.

In the phrase "Iti bhagavā arahattanikūṭenaiva," *iti* means "in this manner," by way of the passage beginning "In a hundred thousand aeons. *Sudam* is merely a particle. *Bhagavā* [is so called] because of his possession of fortune (*bhāgyavantatā*) and other such qualities.
For these reasons, O Blessed One. "His own former conduct" refers to his practice and performance of difficult deeds during his previous births as the wise Akitti and others.
"Manifesting" means showing it correctly, just as one might show an *āmalaka* fruit upon the palm of the hand.
It is called the "Buddhāpadāniya" because it is set forth and taught with reference to the ancient karma and the former difficult deeds of the Buddhas.
"Of such a name. "A discourse on the Dhamma" (*dhammapariyāya*) means a teaching of the Dhamma or a cause that is itself the Dhamma.

"Was spoken" (*abhāsittha*) means he said it. Furthermore, whatever has not been stated here should be understood as not being stated because it follows the method explained below and because its meaning is obvious.
This concludes the concluding remarks.
And to this extent:
The Teacher of purified conduct, who has reached the further shore of the practice of wisdom,
skilled in all modes of conduct, the unsurpassed teacher of the world.
The Protector, who has transcended all forms of stinginess,
taught the *Cariyāpiṭaka*, which reveals the power of his own former deeds and those wondrous qualities that surpass all wonders.
The Elders who compiled the Dhamma likewise recited it.
Relying upon the method of the ancient commentaries, I have undertaken this exposition of the meaning in order to clarify its significance.
That which, having extracted the ultimate meanings therein as appropriate,
explains them, is by name called the *Paramatthadīpanī*.
It has reached completion through its unconfused analysis.
From the recitation sections of more than twenty-eight texts—
whatever merit has been gained by me while compiling this—
by the power of that merit, [may there be success for] the teaching of the Lord of the World.
Having plunged into the practice of virtue and the other perfections that lead to purity,
may all embodied beings partake of the essence of liberation.
May the teaching of the Perfectly Enlightened One endure for a long time in the world.
May all living beings always be full of reverence toward him.
May the Lord of the World, the deity, also rain down in due season;
and may he, devoted to the True Dhamma, govern the world through the Dhamma alone.
Thus ends the Commentary on the Cariyāpiṭaka composed by Ācariya Dhammapāla,
resident of the Badaratittha Monastery.
